Most people think first of the Disney mermaid, so when you talk about the biblical figure or city, say so. A natural reply to 'Who is Ariel in Isaiah?' is 'It's a name for Jerusalem, the city where David camped.'

distinctions.note: Another biblical name with a similar sound; Ariel is a leader in Ezra and a name for Jerusalem, while Arioch is a king or royal officer.
A fictional mermaid; in Bible discussion, make clear that you mean the biblical person or city.

collocations: Ariel as a name for Jerusalem

examples.everyday: At Bible study, someone asked who Ariel was, and I said it's a name for Jerusalem in Isaiah.
examples.professional: In the commentary, Ariel is one of the leading men Ezra sent to recruit ministers for the temple, so the note explains his role in the return.
examples.analytical: Isaiah's use of the name Ariel for Jerusalem turns the city's own title into a sign of mourning, so the oracle reverses the expected meaning of a place God loves.

nuance.analogy: Like a nickname for a famous city that carries more meaning than its ordinary name.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'ariʾel', traditionally read as lion of God or hearth of God; the exact meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying the name as 'ah-ree-EL' in American speech, when the usual American form is AIR-ee-uhl
Confusing Ariel with Arioch, a different biblical name
Assuming the Bible name refers to the Disney character when you are talking about Scripture
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew 'ariʾel' is used in Scripture as a personal name in Ezra 8:16 and as a poetic name for Jerusalem in Isaiah 29:1–2. In Ezra 8:16, Ezra sends for Ariel among the leading men to bring ministers for the temple from Casiphia. In Isaiah 29, the prophet calls Jerusalem Ariel, a city where David once camped, and announces distress and mourning for it.

senses.definition: Actually, in fact.

core.definition: Used to add or correct information, often in surprise or contrast: actually, in fact, in truth.

pronunciation.tip: The words as, a and of are reduced to weak sounds, so the phrase sounds like 'az uh MAT-er uv FAKT' in fast speech. The t in matter is a flap, sounding like a soft d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound mildly confrontational when used to correct someone, so soften it with a friendly tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say as a matter of fact to add a fact that is surprising, relevant or contrary to what someone assumed. It is common in both casual talk and business meetings. A natural reply is 'Really?' or 'Oh, nice.' Using it to correct someone can sound sharp, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Actually is the most general and flexible; as a matter of fact often signals that you are giving a surprising or corrective detail.
In fact is more neutral and common in writing; as a matter of fact sounds more conversational and emphatic.

collocations: as a matter of fact, I
as a matter of fact, yes
as a matter of fact, not really
as a matter of fact, we were just
as a matter of fact, it was

examples.everyday: Do you still play tennis? As a matter of fact, I joined a club last month.
examples.professional: We were worried about the deadline, but as a matter of fact the model finished two days early.
examples.analytical: As a matter of fact, the study's sample came from one city, which weakens its claim to generalize nationally.

nuance.analogy: It is like a fact-checker stepping into the conversation to say, here is what actually happened.
nuance.etymology: An idiom built on matter of fact, from Latin factum, 'something done'.
common_mistakes: Dropping the article, as in 'as matter of fact' instead of 'as a matter of fact'.
Using it too often in one conversation, which can sound like a verbal habit.

senses.definition: As it is; in its present unchangeable state or condition, especially as a contractual condition and obligation of sale or agreement compliance.
senses.example: I bought the car as is, so the seller was within his legal rights to refuse to repair it when it broke down after two days.

core.definition: In the condition it is in now, with no repairs, changes or guarantees offered by the seller.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, IS, which rhymes with 'fizz'. Many learners say 'as' with a strong vowel, but it is weak and quick here.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in product descriptions, but it signals risk to the buyer, so it can sound negative to a shopper.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see 'as is' most often on listings, used-car lots, yard sales and online marketplaces: 'Sold as is.' It means the buyer accepts any defects and cannot expect repairs or refunds. On receipts and contracts it appears in fuller legal forms such as 'as is, where is'.

distinctions.note: 'Without warranty' is the legal or formal wording in contracts; 'as is' is the everyday phrase on signs and listings.
'As it stands' describes plans, proposals or situations; 'as is' describes physical goods being sold or accepted.
'Used' describes an item that has been owned before; 'as is' adds that the seller offers no repair or guarantee.

examples.everyday: The sofa has a stain on one arm, but I'll take it as is if you knock twenty dollars off.
examples.professional: The laptops are sold as is, so Procurement has to approve the purchase before we accept the return.
examples.analytical: A sale as is transfers the risk of defects to the buyer, and courts usually enforce that allocation when it is stated clearly.

nuance.analogy: Like buying a house with its cracks and quirks: you accept it exactly as it stands.
common_mistakes: Assuming 'as is' protects the seller from every claim; in many states some implied warranties still apply unless the sale states otherwise.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'AS iz', instead of the main stress on the second syllable.

senses.definition: To or on one side so as to be out of the way.
senses.example: Move aside, please, so that these people can come through.

senses.definition: Not in perfect symmetry; distorted laterally, especially of the human body.
senses.example: Years of carrying one heavy bag had left her spine slightly aside, so her coat hung unevenly.

senses.definition: An incidental remark to a person next to one made discreetly but not in private, audible only to that person.
senses.example: During the meeting, she leaned over and made an aside to me about the CEO's tie.

senses.definition: A brief comment by a character addressing the audience, unheard by other characters.
senses.example: In the play, Iago delivers an aside to the audience, revealing his scheme against Othello.

senses.definition: A minor related mention, an afterthought.
senses.example: The report spent three pages on the budget, with a brief aside about parking.

core.definition: To or on one side, out of the way; or set apart from the main subject, as in joking aside.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the first vowel is a weak uh sound. Do not say AH-side or uh-SIGHT; the final d is a clear d sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is used in ordinary speech and writing without any emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use aside in set phrases such as joking aside, put aside, set aside, and aside from. As a noun, an aside is a quick comment made to one person or to the audience, and in meetings people often say as an aside before a side point. Aside from means except or besides, as in Aside from the cost, the plan is good.

distinctions.note: Beside means next to, so say sit beside me, not aside me; aside means to one side or apart from the main topic.
Apart stresses separation or distance, while aside suggests deliberately putting something to one side for now.
Besides adds something to the list, while aside from can mean except, depending on the sentence.

examples.everyday: Could you move your bag aside so I can sit down?
examples.professional: Let's set the budget question aside and finish the launch timeline before we discuss costs.
examples.analytical: The author sets aside the question of intent and asks instead what the text does to its readers.

nuance.analogy: Like clearing a plate off the table to make room for the next course.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English on side, meaning on the side.
common_mistakes: Saying aside me when you mean beside me, which means next to.
Writing aside of or adding of after aside from, which is incorrect.

aside.etymology: From Middle English *aside*, *asyde*, *a-side*, *oside*, from Middle English *on side*, from Old English *on sīdan*, equivalent to *a* + *side*.

senses.definition: One who commits assault.

core.definition: A person who commits an assault, meaning who attacks someone physically or violently.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on SAWL, with the l silent, and the final syllable is a reduced 'er' sound. Americans say it quickly, so the last syllable almost disappears.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It names a violent offender and is usually used in legal or news contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use assaulter in everyday conversation, because they prefer assailant or attacker. You will see it in police and legal writing, though assailant is still more common. Use it carefully; in a report, assailant is the standard term.

distinctions.note: Assailant is the more common word and is standard in police and news reports, while assaulter is rarer and sounds more mechanical.
Attacker is the everyday word, while assaulter is tied to the legal idea of committing an assault.

examples.everyday: The police said the assaulter had left the scene before the officers arrived.
examples.professional: Our incident report must name the assaulter only after the investigation confirms the identity.
examples.analytical: The law distinguishes between the assaulter's intent and the victim's experience of harm, which can produce different verdicts.

nuance.analogy: An assaulter is like the person who throws the first punch: the one who started the violence.
nuance.etymology: From assault, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using it casually for any rude person, which sounds too extreme.
Choosing assaulter when assailant is the more natural word in American news.
Pronouncing the l in the stressed syllable.

senses.definition: Boldly self-assured; confident without being aggressive.
Pungent.
senses.example: an assertive taste or odor

senses.definition: An assertion.
senses.example: The debate turned on a single assertive that no one could verify.

core.definition: Confident and direct in stating your views or claiming your rights, without being rude or aggressive.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the vowel is r-colored like the vowel in 'bird'. The final -ive is short, like 'iv', not 'eve'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most workplace and personal contexts, praised as a skill. It can shift to negative if the speaker seems pushy or domineering, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use assertive in workplace advice, such as 'be more assertive in meetings' or 'learn to be assertive with your manager'. It is a common term in self-help books and HR training. A natural reply to praise is 'Thanks, I've been working on it'.

distinctions.note: Assertive means stating your position firmly while respecting others; aggressive means attacking or overriding them.
Confident describes an inner feeling of self-trust; assertive describes how you act when you state your needs or opinions.
Forceful stresses power and impact; assertive stresses clarity and self-possession, and it is usually the gentler word.

examples.everyday: You should be more assertive when the waiter brings the wrong order.
examples.professional: She was assertive in the sprint review and pushed back on the unrealistic deadline.
examples.analytical: Assertive speech differs from coercive speech in that it acknowledges the listener's standing to disagree.

nuance.analogy: Like a firm, steady handshake: clear and confident, but not crushing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin assertus, past participle of asserere, to claim or affirm.
common_mistakes: Using assertive and aggressive as synonyms, which can sound like an insult.
Saying 'make an assertive' when the noun you want is 'assertion' (make an assertion).

senses.definition: To determine, estimate or judge the value of; to evaluate; to estimate.
senses.example: He assessed the situation.

senses.definition: To impose or charge, especially as punishment for an infraction.
senses.example: The referee assessed a penalty for delaying the game.

senses.definition: To calculate and demand (the tax money due) from a person or entity.
senses.example: Once you've submitted a tax return, the Tax Department will assess the amount of tax you still owe.

core.definition: To evaluate or judge the quality, level, or value of something or someone, often before deciding what to do.

pronunciation.tip: There is one stressed syllable, with a short e vowel. The final s is unvoiced, like the s in 'bus', not a z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and professional. It suggests careful, fair judgment rather than a quick opinion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use assess often in education, healthcare, HR, and government, such as 'assess the damage' or 'assess student learning'. In casual speech people say 'figure out', 'look at', or 'size up' instead. A natural reply to 'What's the damage?' is 'Let me assess it first'.

distinctions.note: Evaluate often means judging against set criteria; assess can focus more on estimating the current state of something.
Estimate produces an approximate number; assess includes a judgment about quality, risk, or need.
Judge is more personal and can be final; assess sounds more systematic and professional.

examples.everyday: Let me assess the damage to my car before I call the insurance company.
examples.professional: We need to assess the risk of this migration before the Q3 release.
examples.analytical: A fair account of moral character must assess action in its context rather than by a single rule.

nuance.analogy: Like a doctor checking a patient before deciding on treatment.
nuance.etymology: From Old French assesser, from Latin assessare, to fix a tax, from assidere, to sit beside.
common_mistakes: Confusing assess (judge) with access (reach or entry).
Writing 'assess to' or 'assess about' instead of using a direct object: 'assess the situation'.

assess.etymology: From Middle English *assessen*, from Old French *assesser*, from Medieval Latin *assessare*, originally the frequentative of Latin *assessus*, past participle of *assideo*, from *ad* (“to, towards, at”) + *sedeō* (“sit; settle down”).

senses.definition: An assumption.
senses.example: Her assuming that the data was clean led to a flawed model.

senses.definition: Haughty; arrogant.
senses.example: His assuming manner made the new employees feel unwelcome from the first day.

core.definition: Taking something as true for now, as in 'assuming it stops raining, we'll go'.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SOO, and the -ing ending has a short i sound. Keep the ending light and unstressed, and do not stretch the middle vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a conjunction; negative when used as an adjective meaning arrogant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'assuming that' or simply 'assuming' to set up a condition, often in meetings and planning: 'Assuming we get approval, we start next week.' The adjective meaning arrogant is less common and sounds stiff; in everyday speech 'pushy' or 'presumptuous' is more natural.

distinctions.note: If states a condition neutrally, while assuming signals that you are taking a premise as a working basis, often when planning.
Supposing is more informal and often starts a hypothetical question, as in 'Supposing he says no?'.
Presumptuous describes someone who oversteps, while the adjective assuming is close in meaning but much less common.

examples.everyday: Assuming the weather holds, let's grill on Saturday.
examples.professional: Assuming the API responds within two seconds, the timeout setting should be fine.
examples.analytical: Assuming that moral law binds all rational agents equally, we still need to explain why it requires obedience.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge sketched on a map: you plan the rest of the route on it before you see the actual span.
nuance.etymology: Present participle of assume, from Latin assumere 'to take up'.
common_mistakes: Starting a sentence with 'Assuming' and then leaving out the clause, as in 'Assuming, we'll go'; add a complete clause after it.
Using the adjective 'assuming' to mean arrogant in everyday speech; 'presumptuous' or 'cocky' is more natural.

senses.definition: To astonish, bewilder or dazzle.
senses.example: The sheer speed of the new model's training run astounds everyone on our team.

core.definition: To surprise someone so much that they are speechless or find it hard to believe.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, which contains the 'ow' diphthong. The final 'd' is clearly pronounced, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes strong surprise, and it can be used positively for impressive achievements.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'astound' most often in the passive, as in 'I was astounded by the results.' It is a bit more emphatic than 'surprise' and slightly more formal than 'blow someone away' in casual speech. In conversation, you might say 'You'll be astounded' to hype something impressive.

distinctions.note: Astonish and astound are close in meaning, but astound often suggests a more sudden or overwhelming shock.
Amaze emphasizes wonder and admiration, while astound emphasizes shock and disbelief.

examples.everyday: Wait until you see how she sings, it will astound you.
examples.professional: The results from the pilot test will astound the leadership team when we present them on Friday.
examples.analytical: The sheer scale of the ancient archive is enough to astound any reader who tries to survey it in a single lifetime.

nuance.analogy: Like a magic trick that makes the whole room stop talking at once.
nuance.etymology: Blend of astony and astonish, from Middle English astonen, 'to stun or astonish'.
common_mistakes: Using 'astound' as an adjective, as in 'an astound result'; use 'astounding' for that.
Spelling it 'astond' by dropping the middle letter.

astound.etymology: From Middle English *astouned*, *astoned*, *astuned*, past participle of *astounen*, *astonen*, *astunen* (“to astonish”).

senses.definition: Pertaining or relating to astronomy.
senses.example: Her astronomic calculations predicted the eclipse to within a single second.

senses.definition: Of very large or immense proportions; colossal.

core.definition: Very large or immense, especially of a cost or number; a less common form of 'astronomical'.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on the third syllable, 'nom,' and reduce the 'o' to a short 'ah' sound. Many learners stress the first syllable or drop the 'tr' cluster into 'as-uh-nomic'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative when describing prices or costs; it suggests something far beyond what is reasonable.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'astronomical' is much more common than 'astronomic' for both the science sense and the figurative sense of 'huge.' Americans say 'astronomical prices' or 'astronomical costs' in everyday speech; 'astronomic' sounds dated or formal. You may see it in older writing or in a deliberately elegant style.

distinctions.note: Astronomical is the standard, common form in both senses; astronomic is a less usual variant that most Americans would find stiff.
Astronomic relates to the science of stars and planets; astrological relates to the belief that stars influence human lives.

examples.everyday: Tickets for the game were astronomic, so we watched it at a bar instead.
examples.professional: The vendor's quote for the GPU cluster was astronomic compared with our cloud budget.
examples.analytical: Early astronomic theories treated the heavens as governed by laws different from those on earth.

nuance.analogy: An astronomic number is like a distance you cannot measure with a ruler: it is so large that ordinary units no longer feel useful.
nuance.etymology: From astronomy, from Greek astron, 'star,' and nomos, 'law.'
common_mistakes: Using 'astronomic' in everyday American speech where 'astronomical' is the normal word.
Confusing it with 'astrological,' which relates to horoscopes rather than the science of stars.

senses.definition: Free of anxiety; not stressed or tense.
senses.example: Once the interview started, she relaxed and felt at ease talking about her research.

senses.definition: In a relaxed position with the feet apart rather than at attention.
senses.example: The sergeant told the recruits to stand at ease, feet apart and hands behind their backs.

senses.definition: Allowed to refrain from being in rigid formation.
senses.example: After the inspection, the captain let the platoon stand at ease until lunch.

senses.definition: A command to be at ease.
senses.example: At ease, privates!

core.definition: Free from worry or tension; feeling relaxed and comfortable in a situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EASE, the second word. In fast speech at links to the next word and sounds like uh-TEEZ, with a quick, lightly softened t.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes comfort and is often used to reassure someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say at ease to describe someone who feels relaxed in a social or formal setting, for example, I felt at ease with her right away. In a military setting it is a command to relax from attention. People also say make yourself comfortable, which is more common in homes.

distinctions.note: Relaxed describes a general calm manner; at ease often describes feeling comfortable in a particular situation, especially a social or formal one.
Uneasy is the opposite: nervous or uncomfortable about something.

examples.everyday: Relax, my cousin's really nice, you'll feel at ease with him in five minutes.
examples.professional: Ask the new hire a few easy questions in the first meeting to help her feel at ease.
examples.analytical: Philosophers distinguish a mind at ease with uncertainty from one that merely suppresses its anxiety.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-fitting sweater: nothing pulls or pinches, so you forget you're wearing it.
nuance.etymology: Ease comes from Old French aise, meaning comfort or leisure.
common_mistakes: Saying at easy or in ease instead of at ease.
Using at ease as a verb phrase without a verb, as in I at ease now; say I feel at ease now.

conversation.text: Her friendly smile put me at ease right away.
I never feel completely at ease around my boss.
The nurse did a great job putting the kids at ease.

senses.definition: Randomly, haphazardly.

core.definition: Without a plan, pattern or deliberate choice; by chance, randomly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'RAN', and make the final syllable a reduced 'dum' with a schwa, not 'dome'. The r is clearly pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound careless when used for decisions that should be deliberate, but it is fine for sampling or drawing lots.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'at random' when choosing something without a clear method, such as drawing names from a hat or sampling customers. It is neutral in everyday speech, but it can sound careless when applied to important choices, as in 'You can't just pick projects at random.' A natural reply is 'Got it, so there's no set method.'

distinctions.note: At random is a fixed prepositional phrase often placed after the verb, as in 'chosen at random', while randomly is an adverb that is common in technical writing.
Haphazardly suggests disorder or carelessness, while at random focuses on the lack of a pattern and is often used neutrally or statistically.

examples.everyday: We drew names out of a hat, so the winner was picked at random.
examples.professional: We sampled 500 customers at random from the database to test the survey.
examples.analytical: A sample drawn at random from the population lets us generalize the findings with a known degree of uncertainty.

nuance.analogy: Like shaking a jar of mixed candies and grabbing one without looking.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'randon', meaning speed or rush; the sense of no pattern developed later.
common_mistakes: Saying 'by random' or 'in random' instead of 'at random'.
Pronouncing the last syllable as 'dim' or 'dome' instead of a reduced 'dum'.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to attention.

core.definition: Relating to attention, especially the mental process of selecting and focusing on certain information.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TEN, and the -al ending is a reduced 'ul', not 'all'. Say it as the noun attention with a quick, weak -al added at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: This word is used mainly in psychology, neuroscience, and AI research, in phrases like attentional control and attentional bias. Everyday speakers say focus or attention instead. Using it in casual conversation sounds like jargon, and a natural reply to a technical use is a simple question such as 'What do you mean by that?'

distinctions.note: Attentional describes the mechanism or process of attention; attentive describes a person who listens closely or is considerate.
Attentional refers to the mind's process of focusing; attention-grabbing describes something that draws notice from others.

examples.everyday: After three hours of meetings, my attentional focus is shot, so I'm going home to rest.
examples.professional: The model uses an attentional mechanism that reweights the input tokens so the decoder focuses on the most relevant parts.
examples.analytical: Because attentional capacity is limited, perception is always a selection among competing demands on the mind.

nuance.analogy: Like a flashlight beam that lights only part of a dark room at once; attentional control decides where the beam goes.
nuance.etymology: Derived from attention with the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Using attentional for a person who listens well; say attentive for people.
Pronouncing the -al as 'all', as in 'uh-TEN-shun-all', instead of 'uh-TEN-shuh-nul'.
Pronouncing -tion as 'tee-on' rather than 'shun'.

senses.definition: The act of attributing something.
senses.example: The article's attribution of the quote to the senator turned out to be a simple mistake.

senses.definition: An explicit or formal acknowledgment of ownership or authorship.
senses.example: The attribution of the quote is widely regarded as dubious.

senses.definition: A legal doctrine by which liability is extended to a defendant who did not actually commit the tortious or criminal act.
senses.example: The judge relied on attribution to hold the company liable for its contractor's negligence.

core.definition: The act of identifying who created, caused, or is responsible for something, or the credit given for it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BYOO, the third syllable, and the -tion ending is 'shun'. Keep the middle syllable reduced and quick, and don't stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In business, analytics, and law it describes assigning credit or cause, which can carry legal or reputational weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use attribution in marketing, analytics, journalism, publishing, and law. In a marketing meeting someone might ask which channel gets attribution for a sale, meaning which one receives credit. In everyday talk people say 'credit' or 'source' instead.

distinctions.note: Credit is the general word for recognition; attribution is the more formal act of identifying the specific source, author, or cause.
Causation means one thing actually produces another; attribution is the act of assigning a cause or source, which may or may not be correct.

examples.everyday: Hey, you should give her attribution if you share that quote.
examples.professional: Our attribution model gives the paid search team too much credit for signups.
examples.analytical: Causal attribution in complex systems is difficult because many factors interact and no single variable dominates.

nuance.analogy: Attribution is like naming the author of a song: it tells you who made it, even if many people helped.
nuance.etymology: From Latin attributio, from attribuere, to assign to.
common_mistakes: Confusing attribution with attributes; attribution means assigning credit or cause, while attributes are qualities.
Using attribution only for giving credit; in analytics and law it can mean identifying a cause or responsibility.
patterns: [U, C] attribution of sth to sb/sth

senses.definition: Of or relating to autumn.
Past the middle of life; in the third stage.
senses.example: At fifty-five, he felt autumnal, past the middle of life but not yet finished.

senses.definition: Relating to colors associated with autumn.

core.definition: Relating to or typical of autumn, the season between summer and winter, such as cooler weather and falling leaves.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TUM, the second syllable. Many Americans drop the 't' in 'autumn,' so the middle sounds like 'um' with a light 'n.' Do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It sounds poetic and reflective, often associated with decline, maturity, or nostalgia.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say 'fall' for the season in everyday speech, so 'autumnal' sounds literary or formal. You might hear it in writing about colors, gardens, or weather, as in 'autumnal colors.' Calling someone 'autumnal' is rare, though it can describe the mature stage of life in literature.

distinctions.note: Fall is the everyday American word for the season. Autumnal is the more formal or literary adjective for things related to that season.
Vernal means relating to spring. Autumnal and vernal are opposite seasonal adjectives, and vernal is also more literary.

examples.everyday: Man, that autumnal chill just rolled in, so I finally have to dig out my jacket.
examples.professional: Our October campaign will use an autumnal palette of rust, gold, and deep green for the holiday packaging.
examples.analytical: Dante's autumnal imagery of falling leaves and fading light can signal the poet's own reckoning with middle age.

nuance.analogy: Autumnal is like a warm amber glow over the trees: it suggests change, harvest, and the start of something quieter.
nuance.etymology: From Latin autumnus 'autumn,' with the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable with a long oo sound, as in AW-toom-nul, instead of the short AW and the reduced middle.
Using 'autumnal' in casual speech where 'fall' is the natural American word.

senses.definition: A confused noise made by a number of voices.

core.definition: A confused noise made by many voices talking or shouting at once.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable is a syllabic l, so do not say 'bab-ell' with a full vowel; the l itself carries the syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, describing noisy confusion; often used with a slightly dramatic or literary tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use babel mostly in writing or formal speech, for example a 'babel of voices' at an airport or a 'babel of opinions' online. In everyday speech they more often say 'a racket,' 'a mess' or 'everyone talking at once.' When capitalized, Babel refers to the Tower of Babel in Genesis.

distinctions.note: Cacophony stresses harsh, unpleasant sounds, while babel stresses many voices or languages mixed together.
Babble is the sound of talk, often incoherent, while babel is the state of noisy confusion created by many voices.

examples.everyday: The gate at the airport was a babel of languages, so I had to shout just to hear my wife.
examples.professional: The meeting became a babel of overlapping questions until the moderator asked everyone to speak one at a time.
examples.analytical: The story of the Tower of Babel in Genesis presents the diversity of languages as a result of divine judgment, so the word babel carries the sense of confusion itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a dozen radios tuned to different stations and turned up at once.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Babel, meaning Babylon, linked with the Tower of Babel in Genesis.
common_mistakes: Confusing babel with babble; babble is the sound of talk, while babel is a noisy confusion of many voices.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'ba-BEL'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word Babel names Babylon. In Genesis 11:9 the name is connected with the Hebrew verb balal, meaning to confuse or mix, so the city's name is explained by the Lord confusing the language of all the earth. Genesis 11:1-9 tells how humans building a city and tower are scattered and divided by different languages.

senses.definition: The state or period of infancy.

core.definition: The earliest period of a person's life, when they are an infant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -hood is a short, unstressed-sounding 'hud,' so do not stress it or say it as 'hood' with a long oo.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to nostalgic, often used when recalling a person's early years.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use babyhood mostly in writing or formal speech, such as 'since babyhood' or 'in her babyhood.' In everyday speech, people more often say 'since she was a baby.' It is rarely used as a complaint, and it usually refers to the first year or two of life.

distinctions.note: Infancy is more formal or technical and often refers to the period from birth to about one year, while babyhood is more personal and can cover a longer time.
Childhood covers the whole period before adulthood, while babyhood is only the earliest stage.

examples.everyday: She has loved the ocean since babyhood, so she's always the first one in the water.
examples.professional: Our pediatric team tracks babyhood milestones during the first year, such as feeding patterns and early speech.
examples.analytical: Erikson places the earliest months of babyhood at the center of the basic trust versus mistrust crisis, which he regarded as foundational for later development.

nuance.analogy: Like the first chapter of a book, which sets the tone for everything that follows.
nuance.etymology: From baby with the suffix -hood, meaning a state or period.
common_mistakes: Confusing babyhood, the stage of life, with baby, the child himself or herself.
Using babyhood to describe a longer stage, when childhood is the correct word for the years after infancy.

senses.definition: To put into a bag or bags.
senses.example: Shall I bag up your groceries for you, sir?

senses.definition: To laugh heartily; crack up.
senses.example: I couldn’t get a sentence out straight; I was baggin' up.

senses.definition: Of the police: to arrest or pick up (someone).
senses.example: Police bagged up two teenagers near the stadium after the fight.

core.definition: To put things into bags, especially groceries or trash, so they can be carried or thrown away.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on UP, the particle, which is stronger than 'bag'. In fast speech the g links into the vowel of 'up', so it sounds like 'ba-GUP'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical, everyday task.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bag up' most often for trash, leaves, or groceries in home and yard work. It is informal and natural in everyday speech. The phrasal verb is separable, so you can say 'bag them up' or 'bag up the leaves'.

distinctions.note: Pack up suggests putting belongings into boxes or suitcases; bag up specifically means putting things into bags.
Bag alone is the basic verb; bag up adds emphasis on completing the task or sealing everything.

examples.everyday: Can you bag up the leftover salad and put it in the fridge before we leave?
examples.professional: Please bag up the old cables and label them before the lab move on Friday.
examples.analytical: The auditor bagged up each piece of evidence in a labeled envelope, a procedure that preserved the chain of custody.

nuance.analogy: Like packing a lunch into a paper sack and sealing it up before you head out the door.
nuance.etymology: Combines the verb bag, from Old Norse baggi, with the particle up.
common_mistakes: Saying 'bagging up them' instead of 'bagging them up'.
Placing the stress on 'bag' instead of 'up', which sounds unnatural.

conversation.text: The cashier bagged up our groceries really quickly.
Can you bag up the cold stuff together?
I'll bag up your order while you finish paying.

senses.definition: It is someone's turn to do something; often making a decision.
senses.example: Well there's not much more I can do, so the ball is in your court now.

core.definition: It is now your turn to make the next decision or take the next action.

pronunciation.tip: 'Your' usually reduces to 'yer' or 'yur', and 'is in' links so it sounds like 'iz-in'. 'Court' has the American 'or' vowel with a clear r, so it does not sound like 'coat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a friendly way to hand responsibility back, but it can sound slightly pushy if used when someone has been waiting a long time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in work, sales, and personal life when they have made an offer or sent something and are waiting for a response. A natural reply is 'Got it, I'll get back to you by Friday' or 'Okay, I'll take a look and let you know.' Use it casually, since it can sound too chatty in a formal letter.

distinctions.note: It's up to you is a plain statement of choice, while the ball is in your court focuses on the fact that the other person must act next.
Pass the buck means avoiding responsibility, which is often negative, while the ball is in your court is usually neutral or positive.

collocations: put the ball in their court
the ball is in the other side's court
I'll leave the ball in your court
now the ball's in your court

examples.everyday: I sent the menu options to my sister, so now the ball's in her court.
examples.professional: We delivered the revised API spec on Monday, so the ball is in the vendor's court until they confirm the timeline.
examples.analytical: Once an offer is made in good faith, the ball is in the other party's court, which shifts the moral burden of responding honestly.

nuance.analogy: It is like a tennis rally: once you hit the ball over the net, the other player has to return it.
nuance.etymology: Likely from tennis, where the ball is in a player's court when it is that player's turn to return it.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the ball is on your court', with the wrong preposition.
Using it for a situation where no decision is needed, which makes it sound confused.

ball-is-in-your-court.etymology: From tennis, as when the ball is in someone's court it is their turn to play.

conversation.text: I've made my offer. The ball is in your court now.
We sent them the proposal on Monday, so the ball is in their court.
"Should I text him?" "No, you texted last. The ball is in his court."

senses.definition: A singer, particularly a professional singer who performs ballads.
To sing a ballad.
senses.example: At the festival, he balladeered old songs of the railroad for the crowd.

core.definition: A singer who performs ballads, often a folk or popular singer accompanying himself or herself on guitar or piano.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, with a weaker secondary stress on the final syllable. The ending is a clear r-colored 'eer', as in 'deer', not 'dare'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a storyteller-singer and can sound slightly old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use balladeer in music writing, reviews and literary descriptions of folk singers or singer-songwriters. In everyday conversation, people more often say folk singer or singer-songwriter. Calling someone a balladeer implies that their songs tell stories, often in traditional or emotional language.

distinctions.note: A singer-songwriter writes and performs their own songs, while a balladeer may perform traditional or other people's ballads.
A troubadour was a medieval poet-singer, so the word is more historical or literary than balladeer.
A crooner is a smooth popular singer of romantic songs, usually with a microphone and orchestra, not necessarily a storytelling singer.

examples.everyday: My uncle hired a local balladeer to play at every family picnic, and everyone knew the words by the second chorus.
examples.professional: The festival booked a balladeer to open the showcase, but the set list changed at the last minute.
examples.analytical: Early Dylan casts the modern songwriter as a balladeer of social injustice, whose narratives carry moral weight.

nuance.analogy: A balladeer is like a town crier who tells the news in song, turning local stories into music people remember.
nuance.etymology: From ballad plus the suffix -eer, meaning a person who does or deals with something.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable, as in BAL-uh-DEER, instead of the first.
Using balladeer for any singer; the word specifically suggests a singer of narrative or emotional songs.

senses.definition: One who is guilty of barratry, vexing others with frequent and often groundless lawsuits; a brangler and pettifogger.
senses.example: The neighbor who filed twelve groundless lawsuits in a year was a notorious barrator.

senses.definition: One who abuses their office by dealing fraudulently.
A judge who accepts bribes.
senses.example: The corrupt judge was called a barrator after prosecutors proved he took bribes for favorable rulings.

senses.definition: A ship's master who commits gross fraud or barratry.
senses.example: The court found the ship's captain to be a barrator who had defrauded the cargo owners.

core.definition: A person who repeatedly files groundless lawsuits to harass others, or who corruptly abuses an official position.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BAIR. The middle syllable is weak, and the final -er is a reduced, unstressed vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word describes someone who abuses the legal system or their office.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use barrator mainly in legal and maritime writing, and in discussions of frivolous litigation. It is rarely used in everyday speech. In ordinary conversation people more often say a person is 'litigious' or 'sues everyone.'

distinctions.note: A litigant is any party to a lawsuit, while a barrator is a person who files lawsuits in bad faith to harass others.
A plaintiff is the person who brings a suit, which is neutral, while a barrator is someone whose lawsuits are considered abusive.

examples.professional: Our legal team flagged the plaintiff as a barrator after reviewing a decade of frivolous filings.
examples.analytical: Legal historians distinguish the barrator, who harasses through litigation, from the honest advocate who litigates in good faith.

nuance.analogy: A barrator is like a bully who uses the courthouse instead of the playground, harassing people with paperwork rather than fists.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French barator, from barat, meaning fraud or deceit; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing barrator with barrister, the British term for a trial lawyer.
Using barrator as a neutral word for any plaintiff; it always implies bad faith.

barrator.etymology: From Middle English *baratour*, from Old French *barateor* (“deceiver”), from Old French *barater*, *bareter* (“to deceive, cheat, barter”).

senses.definition: Having a liking or affection (for). [ with of]
senses.example: I am fond of this song!

senses.definition: Affectionate.
senses.example: a fond farewell

senses.definition: Indulgent, doting.
senses.example: I have fond grandparents who spoil me.

senses.definition: Outlandish; foolish; silly.
senses.example: Your fond dreams of flying to Jupiter have been quashed by the facts of reality.

senses.definition: The background design in lace-making.
Brown residue in pans from cooking meats and vegetables.
senses.example: He used the fond to make a classic French pan sauce.

senses.definition: A group of records having shared provenance.

core.definition: To like someone or something and feel affection for them, often in a warm and lasting way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'fond', which rhymes with 'pond'. 'Of' is reduced to 'uhv' or 'uv' in speech and is not pronounced 'off'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests warm affection that lasts, and it is gentler than 'love'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'be fond of' for people, pets, places, foods and hobbies, often in a gentle or older tone. For everyday liking, they more often say 'like' or 'really like', and 'love' is stronger. A natural reply to 'Are you fond of Thai food?' is 'Yes, I really am.'

distinctions.note: 'Like' is the most common everyday word, while 'be fond of' feels warmer and more lasting.
'Love' is stronger and more emotional, while 'be fond of' is milder affection.
'Keen on' means eager interest in something, while 'fond of' means affection.

examples.everyday: I'm really fond of your dog, he always meets me at the door.
examples.professional: The team is fond of the new dashboard, so we should keep the layout mostly the same.
examples.analytical: A person may be fond of a place without any claim that it is good, so affection and judgment are different things.

nuance.analogy: Being fond of someone is like a warm porch light: it is steady and welcoming, though not a fire.
nuance.etymology: 'Fond' comes from Middle English fonne, meaning fool, so the word once meant foolish before taking on its current sense.
common_mistakes: Using 'fond with' or 'fond to' instead of the correct 'fond of'.
Using 'fond' alone in speech, as in 'I'm fond coffee', instead of the full phrase 'fond of coffee'.

be-fond-of.etymology: From Middle English *fond*, *fonned*, past participle of *fonnen* (“to be foolish, be simple, dote”), equivalent to *fon* + *-ed*.

senses.definition: Able to be beaten or bettered.
Able to be beaten or thrashed.
senses.example: The old champion was no longer beatable by anyone in the regional league.

core.definition: Able to be defeated, surpassed, or bettered by someone or something; not impossible to overcome.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the ending to a schwa plus 'bul.' Do not say BEE-tay-bul, which turns the word into a different sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests a challenge that can be overcome, though calling an opponent beatable can sound dismissive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use beatable for opponents, teams, records, and games: 'Their defense looks beatable.' In business and tech, it can mean a goal or benchmark is achievable. The negative form unbeatable is more common in everyday speech for something very strong or impressive.

distinctions.note: Unbeatable is the opposite: it means no one can defeat it, while beatable means it can be defeated.
Defeatable is less common and more formal, while beatable is the everyday American word.

examples.everyday: Mike is a decent player, but he's beatable if you keep your serves low.
examples.professional: The current benchmark is beatable with a simpler model, so let's run the baseline before adding complexity.
examples.analytical: A theory may be beatable in the sense that a stronger argument can refute it, but being beatable is not the same as being false.

nuance.analogy: A beatable opponent is like a locked door with a loose hinge: strong at first sight, but you can get through it with the right push.
nuance.etymology: Formed from beat (Old English bēatan 'to strike') with the suffix -able, meaning able to be.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as -tay-bul, which is not standard American pronunciation.
Using beatable for the sense of cheap or affordable, which is not its meaning.

beatable.etymology: From *beat* + *able*, in the sense of "able to be bettered" as a.

senses.definition: Below or underneath.
senses.example: The lake was calm on top, but dark currents ran beneath.

senses.definition: Below.
In a position that is lower in rank, dignity, etc.
senses.example: Their despicable behavior is beneath contempt.

senses.definition: Covered up or concealed by something.

core.definition: Lower than something, or under and covered by it; also used for a position below someone in rank.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NEETH, and the th is voiceless as in 'thin', not voiced as in 'the'. The first syllable is a reduced bih.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in physical senses. In phrases like 'beneath me' or 'beneath contempt' it sounds snobbish or dismissive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use under or below in everyday speech, and beneath sounds formal, poetic or emphatic, as in beneath the surface. The phrase 'beneath me' is a snobbish way to say something is unworthy of your time. Beneath can be used as an adverb in writing, as in the sky above and the earth beneath.

distinctions.note: Under is everyday and general for physical position, while beneath is more formal and can suggest a hidden or lower status.
Below means lower in position or level, and does not imply being covered by something.
Underneath is casual and suggests something is directly under or close below, often out of sight.

examples.everyday: The keys were beneath the pile of mail on the kitchen counter.
examples.professional: The critical bug sat beneath three layers of abstraction, which is why the logs never flagged it.
examples.analytical: Beneath the moral language of the essay lies a deeper claim about power that the author never states directly.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone at the bottom of a pond, visible only when the water is clear.
nuance.etymology: From Old English beneoþan, from be- and neoþan, meaning below.
common_mistakes: Using beneath in casual speech where under is more natural.
Writing 'beneath to' or 'beneath of'; beneath takes a direct object, as in beneath the table.

beneath.etymology: From Middle English *benethe*, from Old English *bineoþan* (“beneath, under, below”), equivalent to *be* + *neath*.

senses.definition: A litter to transport the corpse of a dead person.
senses.example: Mourners followed the bier through the village as the church bell tolled slowly.

senses.definition: A platform or stand where a body or coffin is placed.
A count of forty threads in the warp or chain of woollen cloth.
senses.example: The weaver counted each bier of warp threads before tying the loom for the wool.

core.definition: A stand or frame on which a coffin or dead body is placed, or carried, for a funeral.

pronunciation.tip: In most American speech it sounds exactly like 'beer', with a short vowel and a light r. Do not add a long ee or a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Solemn and somber. It evokes funerals, processions and death.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use bier in ordinary speech. It appears mainly in literature, history, church contexts and descriptions of old funeral customs, often in phrases such as 'carried on a bier.' Modern American funerals usually use a casket set on a stand called a catafalque or a cart, so bier is a historical or poetic word.

distinctions.note: A casket is the box that holds the body; a bier is the stand or frame that carries or supports it.
Coffin is an older, often six-sided container; modern Americans usually say casket.
Beer is a homophone with a different spelling and meaning, so take care in writing.

examples.everyday: Did you see that movie scene where they carry the dead queen through the hall on a bier?
examples.professional: The funeral director said the family wants the casket placed on a bier at the front of the sanctuary.
examples.analytical: In Luke's narrative the bier becomes the place where death's procession is halted by a word of Jesus.

nuance.analogy: A bier is like a stretcher for the dead: a platform that carries the body in a solemn procession.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bǣr, related to beran 'to carry'.
common_mistakes: Spelling it beer in writing, or confusing it with the drink.
Using bier to mean the coffin itself; the bier is the stand or frame that holds it.
nuance.biblical_note: In Luke 7:14 the Greek word soros, meaning a bier or coffin, describes the litter carrying the dead son of the widow of Nain; Jesus touches it, the bearers stop, and he raises the young man. In 2 Samuel 3:31 King David follows the bier of Abner, whom Joab killed, and mourns publicly at his funeral. Both passages show the bier as a sign of public mourning and of death's hold over the living.

bier.etymology: From Middle English *beer*, *beere*, *bere*, from Old English *bēr*, West Saxon *bǣr* (“stretcher, bier”), from **bāru*, from Proto-Germanic **bērō*, from Proto-Indo-European **bʰer-* (“to carry, bear”).

senses.definition: Of great size, large.
senses.example: Elephants are big animals, and they eat a lot.

senses.definition: Fat.
senses.example: Gosh, she is big!

senses.definition: Large with young; pregnant; swelling; ready to give birth or produce.
senses.example: She was big with child.

senses.definition: Well-endowed; with a desired body part notably large.
senses.example: I'm the shortest man on the team but in the gym shower everyone can see that I'm also the biggest.

senses.definition: Specifically, big-breasted.
senses.example: Critics claimed the studio marketed the starlet as big, emphasizing her figure in every poster.

senses.definition: Having a large penis.
senses.example: I'm the shortest man on the team but in the gym shower everyone can see that I'm also the biggest.

senses.definition: Having large muscles, especially visible ones such as the chest and arm muscles.
senses.example: I've been lifting weights for a full year now, but I'm finally getting big.

senses.definition: Adult; (of a child) older.
senses.example: Kids should get help from big people if they want to use the kitchen.

senses.definition: Old, mature. Used to imply that someone is too old for something, or acting immaturely.
senses.example: You're too big to still be sucking your thumb, so stop it.

senses.definition: Mature, conscientious, principled; generous. [with of ‘someone’]
senses.example: That's very big of you; thank you!

senses.definition: Important or significant.
senses.example: What's so big about that? I do it all the time.

senses.definition: Popular.
senses.example: That style is very big right now in Europe, especially among teenagers.

senses.definition: Populous.
senses.example: Our town is getting big, and the schools are now overcrowded.

senses.definition: Used as an intensifier, especially of negative-valence nouns.
senses.example: You are a big liar!

senses.definition: Operating on a large scale, especially if therefore having undue or sinister influence.
senses.example: big money

senses.definition: Enthusiastic (about) [with on ‘someone/something’].
senses.example: I'm not big on the idea, but if you want to go ahead with it, I won't stop you.

senses.definition: In a loud manner.
In a boasting manner.
senses.example: He's always talking big, but he never delivers.

senses.definition: In a large amount or to a large extent.
senses.example: He won big betting on the croquet championship.

senses.definition: On a large scale, expansively.
senses.example: You've got to think big to succeed at Amalgamated Plumbing.

senses.definition: Hard; with great force.
senses.example: He hit him big and the guy just crumpled.

senses.definition: Someone or something that is large in stature.
senses.example: The big ones at the bottom of the pile are the heaviest, so lift them carefully.

senses.definition: An important or powerful person; a celebrity; a big name.
senses.example: Half the room was full of bigs from the publishing world, and I felt out of place.

senses.definition: The big leagues, big time.
senses.example: After ten years in minor league baseball, he finally made it to the big.

senses.definition: An initiated member of a sorority or fraternity who acts as a mentor to a new member (the little).
senses.example: My big in the sorority helped me pick classes and learn the traditions.

senses.definition: The participant in age roleplay who acts out the older role.
One or more kinds of barley, especially six-rowed barley.
senses.example: Farmers on Orkney still grow big, a hardy barley used for bannock and whisky.

senses.definition: To inhabit; occupy.
senses.example: Grandpa said his people had big this valley for generations before the mines came.

senses.definition: To locate oneself.
senses.example: He big himself at the corner table, where he could watch the door.

senses.definition: To build; erect; fashion.
senses.example: Don't big it up.

senses.definition: To dwell; have a dwelling.
senses.example: We big in a cabin up the hill, far from the nearest neighbors.

core.definition: Large in size, amount or importance; the opposite of small.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short and lax, like in 'bit', not a long 'ee' as in 'beeg'. The g is a clear hard sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive for achievements and negative for problems, and it can sound childish in formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Big is one of the most common words in American speech, used for physical size, scale and importance, as in 'a big deal' or 'big news.' For people's body size, big can sound rude, so Americans prefer 'large,' 'tall' or 'heavy.' In formal writing use 'large,' 'significant' or 'substantial' instead.

distinctions.note: Large is more neutral and formal, and is standard for sizes and quantities; big is more casual and conversational.
Great often means excellent or intense, as in a great idea; big usually refers to size, scale or importance.
Huge is stronger than big, suggesting something enormous.

examples.everyday: That's a big pizza, so we'll probably have leftovers for lunch tomorrow.
examples.professional: This is a big change, so let's review the timeline with the team before Friday.
examples.analytical: A big question here is whether the theory explains the data or merely fits it after the fact.

nuance.analogy: Like a large suitcase: it gives a quick sense of scale without an exact measurement.
common_mistakes: Using big to describe someone's body weight in polite speech, where 'large' or 'heavy' is safer.
Saying a big number of people in formal writing; a large number of people is more appropriate.

big.etymology: *big*, *bigge* (“powerful, strong”), possibly from a dialect of Old Norse.

senses.definition: An n-gram consisting of two items from a sequence; a 2-gram.
senses.example: bigram model

core.definition: In natural language processing and statistics, a sequence of two adjacent items, such as two words or two characters, in a text.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce bi- as bye, not big, to avoid confusion with bigwig. The second syllable is gram, with a short a as in cat, and the r is pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and linguists use bigram in technical discussions of text analysis, language models, and word frequency. In casual speech it would seem odd unless the topic is computing or linguistics. Often people say 'two-word sequence' when explaining it to nontechnical listeners.

distinctions.note: A unigram is a single item, while a bigram is a pair of adjacent items, so bigrams capture more context.
A trigram uses three adjacent items, which gives more context but is sparser, so it can be harder to estimate reliably.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in linguistics told me that a bigram is just a pair of words that often appear together.
examples.professional: We added bigram features to the classifier, and the accuracy went up about four points on the validation set.
examples.analytical: The bigram model assumes that the probability of each word depends only on the word immediately before it, which is a strong simplification of language.

nuance.analogy: A bigram is like a pair of dance partners who always step together, so you learn their pattern by watching two steps at a time.
nuance.etymology: From bi- meaning two, from Latin bis, combined with gram from Greek gramma, meaning letter or written mark, coined in the context of n-grams.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing bi- as big, which causes confusion with bigwig.
Using bigram for any two-word phrase in everyday speech, when the term is mainly technical.

senses.definition: Any fuel that is obtained from a renewable biological resource, especially from biomass.
senses.example: The airline tested a jet blend containing biofuel made from used cooking oil.

core.definition: Fuel made from recent plant, algae, or animal material instead of from fossil fuels like oil or coal.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable, BY, not on the oh as the dictionary version suggests. The last syllable is reduced to a quick uhl sound, and many Americans say it nearly as fyool.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests a cleaner, renewable alternative to gasoline or diesel, though people may debate its environmental value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use biofuel in news about cars, trucking, farming, and climate policy, such as ethanol blended into gasoline or biodiesel at a gas station. People often say it in the plural, biofuels, when discussing policy. It is not usually used for things that are only renewable energy, like solar power.

distinctions.note: Biomass is the organic material itself, such as wood chips or corn stalks. Biofuel is the fuel made from that material.
Fossil fuels come from ancient buried organic matter and are not renewable on a human timescale. Biofuels come from recently living material that can be replanted.

examples.everyday: Some gas stations near us sell a blend with biofuel in it, which is supposed to be a little cleaner for the car.
examples.professional: Our fleet team is testing a biofuel blend in three delivery trucks to see how it affects engine maintenance costs.
examples.analytical: Whether a biofuel truly reduces emissions depends on the full lifecycle, including the land and fertilizer used to grow its feedstock.

nuance.analogy: A biofuel is like a battery recharged by the sun each year through plants, while fossil fuel is a savings account that was filled millions of years ago and can't be refilled.
nuance.etymology: From bio- (Greek bios, life) and fuel (Old French fouaille, firewood).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (bye-oh-FYOOL) instead of the first syllable.
Using biofuel for all renewable energy; solar and wind are not biofuels.

senses.definition: Any of various trees of the genus Betula, native to countries in the Northern Hemisphere.
senses.example: Paper birch trees line the trail along the lake, their white bark peeling in thin sheets.

senses.definition: A hard wood taken from the birch tree, typically used to make furniture.
senses.example: The dining table was built from birch, so its grain is pale and fine.

senses.definition: A stick, rod or bundle of twigs made from birch wood, used for punishment.
senses.example: The headmaster kept a birch in his desk drawer, though he rarely used it on students.

senses.definition: A birch-bark canoe.
senses.example: We rented a birch on the lake and paddled out past the reeds at dawn.

senses.definition: To punish with a stick, bundle of twigs, or rod made of birch wood.
senses.example: The strict teacher birched the boys who had been caught smoking behind the gym.

senses.definition: To punish as though one were using a stick, bundle of twigs, or rod made of birch wood.
senses.example: The critics birched the director's latest film in a review that left no scene unscathed.

core.definition: A tree with thin, peeling bark and light-colored wood, common in cold northern regions.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the rhotic 'ur' vowel of 'bird' followed by 'ch'. Don't add an 'ih' vowel or say 'bitch' with a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and pleasant when describing the tree; the punishment sense is historical and sounds harsh today.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use birch mainly for the tree, especially in the Northeast and Canada, in landscaping, woodworking and nature talk, as in 'paper birch' or 'birch bark canoe'. The punishment sense, to be birched, is historical and appears mostly in old literature or British school stories. Using it today would sound archaic or alarming.

distinctions.note: Maple trees have lobed leaves and are tapped for syrup; birches have thin, papery, peeling bark and smaller leaves.
Aspen is a poplar with flat leaves that tremble in the wind; birch is known for bark that peels in thin strips.
A cane usually means a walking stick or a rattan or bamboo rod; birch names the tree or its wood.

examples.everyday: Those tall white trees by the lake are birches, aren't they?
examples.professional: The landscaping plan calls for three paper birches near the entrance, because they tolerate our cold winters.
examples.analytical: In Robert Frost's poem 'Birches', the trees stand for the speaker's longing for escape into a quieter, more natural world.

nuance.analogy: Like a sheet of paper that peels off in layers, the birch shows its age in thin, papery strips of bark.
nuance.etymology: From Old English birce, of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'burch' with a short i vowel; the vowel should match the 'ur' of 'bird'.
Using birch in the punishment sense without context; today it sounds archaic or shocking.

birch.etymology: From Middle English *birche*, *birk*, from Old English *birċe*, *bierċe*, from **birkijā*, from Proto-Germanic **birkijǭ*, from Proto-Indo-European **bʰerHǵos*.

senses.definition: A name chosen for a child at birth, as opposed to a different name used subsequently.
senses.example: Her birth name was Elizabeth, but everyone called her Lizzie.

core.definition: The name given to a child at birth, as distinct from a name adopted or used later, such as a married, stage or pen name.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NAME, with BIRTH slightly weaker. The th is voiceless, so place your tongue between your teeth, and the stressed vowel is an r-colored 'ur' sound, not 'bert'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a factual term with no emotional charge, and it often appears on forms and in documents.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'birth name' mostly in biography, legal and official contexts, or when a person has changed their name. In casual talk people say 'her real name' or 'the name she was born with.' Asking someone directly for their birth name can sound personal, so use it only when the context is clear, such as a genealogy form.

distinctions.note: The legal name is what appears on official documents now, which may differ from the birth name after a court-approved change.
A stage name is adopted by performers for their career, while the birth name is the one given to them as a child.

collocations: go by a different name than her birth name

examples.everyday: Did you know her birth name is Maria? Everybody just calls her Mari.
examples.professional: Please use the employee's birth name on the payroll form and note any preferred name separately.
examples.analytical: The author's birth name appears in archival records, but she published under a pseudonym for most of her career.

nuance.analogy: Like the first label on a jar: it may be replaced later, but it was there from the start.
nuance.etymology: Birth from Old Norse byrðr; name from Old English nama.
common_mistakes: Saying 'original name' in a formal or records context; 'birth name' is the standard American term on forms and in biographies.
Pronouncing the th in birth as a /t/ or /d/; it is voiceless, as in 'thin'.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being black in color.
senses.example: The blackness of outer space comes from the lack of anything to reflect light rather than the absence of light.

senses.definition: Any space that such color pervades.
senses.example: Out of the blackness came some flickers of light.

senses.definition: Darkness, gloominess; depression.
senses.example: A deep blackness settled over him after the layoffs, and he stopped answering calls.

senses.definition: The quality of being evil or dismal.
The state of being of African descent.
The experiences and culture of Black people.
senses.example: Her course on Black history explored blackness as both an identity and a cultural tradition.

core.definition: The quality of being black in color, or a dark area or space where no light shows through.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-ness' is a reduced, quiet 'nuhs' sound, and the 'a' is the short vowel of 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in plain color talk, but it can be negative or loaded when used about race, darkness, or despair, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'blackness' mostly for color or darkness, as in 'the blackness of the night sky.' When it refers to race or Black identity, many people prefer 'Black' or 'Blackness' as a cultural term, and it can carry pride or social meaning. Avoid using it casually about people's skin without thinking of how it may land.

distinctions.note: 'Darkness' is the general absence of light, while 'blackness' focuses on the color or the deep black quality of a space.
A 'blackout' is a sudden loss of power or light, while 'blackness' describes a steady dark state.

examples.everyday: When the power went out, the blackness outside was so complete I couldn't see my hand.
examples.professional: The monitor's blackness during the test confirmed that the display had gone to sleep.
examples.analytical: The poet uses blackness as an image of despair, linking the color with the absence of hope.

nuance.analogy: Blackness is like a room with the curtains fully closed at midnight, where even the shapes of furniture disappear.
nuance.etymology: From Old English blæc, meaning black or dark, with the suffix -ness forming a noun of state.
common_mistakes: Using 'blackness' as a casual word for darkness at night; 'darkness' is more natural in everyday talk.
Stressing the second syllable or adding an extra syllable at the end.
nuance.biblical_note: In Song of Songs 1:5 the speaker says 'I am very dark, but comely,' using dark skin and sun exposure as a neutral description, not a judgment. The Hebrew word shachor means dark or black, and it appears in passages about darkness and mourning.

senses.definition: To persuade someone by using flattery; to cajole.
To praise someone dishonestly; to flatter or butter up.
senses.example: The salesman tried to blandish me into buying the extended warranty.

core.definition: To coax or persuade someone with flattering words or gentle charm.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, BLAN. The second syllable is a short, reduced vowel, and the ending is a 'sh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests persuasion by flattery, which may be sincere or manipulative depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blandish mostly in literature, formal writing or old-fashioned speech. In everyday talk, people say 'sweet-talk' or 'butter up' for the same idea. It is best used to describe someone who is being flattered into doing something.

distinctions.note: Cajole means to persuade with pleasant words or light coaxing; blandish stresses the flattery itself.
Flatter means to praise someone, sincerely or not; blandish means to use praise specifically to persuade someone.

examples.everyday: My sister tried to blandish me into driving her to the airport by saying I was the best driver she knew.
examples.professional: The consultant tried to blandish the committee with praise, but nobody changed their vote on the budget.
examples.analytical: Plato's critics suspect that rhetoric can blandish the mind away from truth, even when its words sound gracious.

nuance.analogy: Like a sales clerk who keeps complimenting your shoes until you buy the jacket.
nuance.etymology: From Latin blandiri, 'to flatter', from blandus, 'smooth, soft'.
common_mistakes: Confusing blandish with bland; blandish is a verb about flattering someone into action.
Saying the stress on the second syllable, as in 'blan-DISH'.

blandish.etymology: From Middle English *blaundishen* (“to flatter; to fawn; to be enticing or persuasive; to be favourable; of the sea: to become calm”), from Anglo-Norman *blaundishen*, from blandiss, the extended stem of Middle French *blandir* + Middle English *-ishen*.

senses.definition: Thirsty for blood: inexorably violent or eager for bloodshed; murderous.
Of a book, film, etc.: depicting much violence; gory, violent.
senses.example: The bloodthirsty horror film was rated R for its graphic killings and gore.

senses.definition: Of a mosquito, tenaciously seeking to draw blood.
senses.example: Mosquitoes were bloodthirsty all evening, so we retreated indoors with repellent.

core.definition: Eager for violence or killing; murderous, or describing a violent work full of gore.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Use a voiceless 'th' as in 'think', then the American r sound in 'thur', and end with a clear 'ee'. Do not rush the middle syllable into 'thirsty' with a short i.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes cruel, dangerous or very violent people, films or games.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in everyday talk about movies, video games and people, as in 'a bloodthirsty villain' or 'a bloodthirsty crowd'. It is strong and a little dramatic, so reserve it for real violence. In US summers, people also joke that mosquitoes are bloodthirsty.

distinctions.note: 'Violent' describes behavior; 'bloodthirsty' describes an eager desire to hurt or kill, a stronger inner craving.
'Murderous' implies actual or intended killing; 'bloodthirsty' can describe enjoyment of violence without a killing.

examples.everyday: My brother loves bloodthirsty horror films, but I can't stand them.
examples.professional: The new game got bad reviews for being too bloodthirsty for its rating.
examples.analytical: Shakespeare's Macbeth shows how ambition can turn a soldier into a bloodthirsty tyrant.

nuance.analogy: Like a shark circling for blood, a bloodthirsty person is driven by an appetite for harm.
nuance.etymology: From 'blood' plus 'thirsty' (eager, craving), a compound describing a craving for blood.
common_mistakes: Using a /t/ for the middle sound of 'thirsty'; the 'th' is voiceless /θ/.
Using it for ordinary anger or strong opinions, which makes you sound dramatic.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Psalms, 'bloodthirsty men' (Hebrew anshei damim, 'men of blood') describes violent enemies of the righteous. Psalm 5:6 says the Lord abhors such men, and Psalm 26:9 asks God not to sweep the psalmist's life away with them.

senses.definition: Overexposed.
senses.example: The sunset photo came out washed-out because the sky was blown out completely.

core.definition: Badly defeated by a large margin in sports, or damaged and burst by too much force, such as a tire, speaker or knee.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'out' in this adjective phrase, while 'blown' gets a weaker stress. Say the long oh in 'blown' clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a loss or failure, usually with some embarrassment for the people involved.
nuance.usage_note: In American sports talk, 'we got blown out' means the team lost very badly. People also use it for a burst tire or speaker and, in photography, for an overexposed image. In formal writing, Americans might say 'defeated soundly' or 'routed' instead.

distinctions.note: Routed is a more formal word for a crushing defeat, while blown out is casual sports slang.
Blow up means to explode or to become very angry, so it is not the same as losing badly or being damaged.
Beaten simply means defeated, while blown out adds the idea of a very large margin.

examples.everyday: Our team got blown out 35 to 10 last night, so the coach was not happy.
examples.professional: The budget got blown out after the vendor added a rush fee, so we need to revise the forecast.
examples.analytical: A photograph whose highlights are blown out has lost the detail that makes the image readable, which is why photographers meter carefully.

nuance.analogy: Like a flashlight aimed straight into a camera, too much light wipes out the detail.
nuance.etymology: From blow, in the sense of bursting or puffing, plus out.
common_mistakes: Confusing the adjective 'blown out' with the verb 'blow out' used for blowing out a candle.
Using it in formal writing where 'defeated soundly' would be clearer.

senses.definition: A noisy blowing, as of a blast of wind.
senses.example: The blustering of the gale against the barn doors kept the horses restless.

senses.definition: Swaggering; braggartry; noisy pretension.
senses.example: His blustering about his football days grew tiresome by the second hour.

senses.definition: Engaged in or involving the process of blustering, speaking or protesting loudly.
senses.example: The blustering protester shouted at the council until security escorted him out.

senses.definition: Pompous or arrogant in one's speech or bearing.
senses.example: The blustering manager lectured the entire team about discipline while ignoring his own mistakes.

senses.definition: Very windy; (of wind) blowing very strongly, blustery.
senses.example: We canceled the picnic because the blustering weather made it impossible to set up tables.

core.definition: Loud and aggressive in speech or manner, often bragging or threatening without real strength behind it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable; the middle -ter- is weak, so the word sounds like 'BLUS-ter-ing', not 'blus-TEER-ing'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests loud posturing that hides weakness or uncertainty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blustering for loud, empty posturing, as in 'a blustering manager who yells but never decides.' For weather, Americans prefer blustery. Blustering is not a compliment, and it can describe a person in a meeting, a debate or a sports argument.

distinctions.note: Blustery is mainly for weather with strong gusts; blustering is mainly for people who talk or act loudly.
Bombastic is more formal and describes inflated, pompous language; blustering stresses loud, aggressive posturing.
Bragging means boasting about achievements; blustering is noisier and more aggressive, often masking weakness.

examples.everyday: My uncle was blustering about the Eagles again, but nobody believed a word of it.
examples.professional: The blustering VP threatened to cut the budget without looking at the numbers.
examples.analytical: Political theory has long warned that blustering rhetoric can hide a weak position.

nuance.analogy: Like a leaf blower with no leaves to move, it makes a great deal of noise without doing any work.
nuance.etymology: Present participle of bluster (verb), of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using blustering for wind; Americans say blustery for weather.
Stressing the second syllable and saying 'blus-TER-ing'.

senses.definition: To investigate something, or solve a problem using brainstorming.
To participate in a brainstorming session.
