nuance.usage_note: Americans use defector mainly in news about politics, espionage, sports transfers or business rivalries. Calling someone a defector can sound judgmental, so use a neutral phrase like switched sides if you want to avoid strong feeling. Typical responses in news contexts are questions about asylum or loyalty.

distinctions.note: A deserter abandons military duty without permission, while a defector switches allegiance to the other side, often publicly.
A refugee flees danger, often without changing loyalties, while a defector deliberately joins the opposing side.

examples.everyday: Half our old band went over to the new group, so now they're basically defectors.
examples.professional: Our top engineer is a defector from the competitor, so legal is reviewing the non-compete clause.
examples.analytical: The defector's testimony was valuable precisely because it came from someone who had once been inside the system.

nuance.analogy: A defector is like a player who transfers mid-season to the rival team and changes the balance of the league.
nuance.etymology: From defect, from Latin defectus, failure, with the agent suffix -or.
common_mistakes: Using defector as a verb; the verb is defect, as in defect to the other side.
Using defect with for instead of to, as in defect to the West.

senses.definition: An act or instance of deflating.
senses.example: The loss caused utter deflation and disappointment among the fans.

senses.definition: A decrease in the general price level, that is, in the nominal cost of goods and services as well as wages.
An economic contraction.
senses.example: Rising unemployment and falling demand pushed the economy into deflation last year.

senses.definition: The removal of soil and other loose material from the ground (or another surface) by wind, leaving it exposed to erosion.
senses.example: Deflation of the dry plains exposed the bedrock and left shallow hollows behind.

core.definition: A sustained fall in the general price level, meaning goods, services and wages all become cheaper over time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FLAY. The final '-tion' is pronounced 'shun,' not 'shee-un.' Keep the first vowel reduced to a short 'ih.'

nuance.connotation: Negative in most economic contexts, because falling prices often signal weak demand, job losses and recession.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'deflation' mainly in economics and news about the economy, especially to contrast with 'inflation.' In casual talk, people say 'prices are falling' or 'things got cheaper.' Deflation is less common in everyday speech than inflation, so you will hear it most on business news and in policy debates.

distinctions.note: Disinflation means inflation is slowing but prices are still rising; deflation means prices are actually falling.
A recession is a broad decline in economic activity; deflation is specifically a fall in prices, which can happen with or without a recession.

examples.everyday: My uncle says the price of gas dropping isn't deflation, it's just a temporary dip.
examples.professional: The forecast flags a real risk of deflation if consumer demand stays weak through the quarter.
examples.analytical: Deflation can be self-reinforcing, since consumers delay purchases and firms cut wages, deepening the contraction.

nuance.analogy: Deflation is like a balloon losing air: the prices in the economy slowly shrink, and everything feels smaller and tighter.
nuance.etymology: From 'deflate,' from Latin 'de-' (down, away) plus 'inflare,' to blow into, by analogy with 'inflation.'
common_mistakes: Using 'deflation' for any price drop, when it means a broad, sustained fall in the general price level.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'dih-FLAY-shun' versus 'dee-fluh-SHUN.'

senses.definition: No longer in use or active, nor expected to be again.
No longer in business or service, nor expected to be again; out of business.
Specifically, of a process: having terminated but not having been reaped (by its parent or an inheritor), and thus still occupying a process slot. See also zombie, zombie process.
senses.example: The shell showed a defunct process that never disappeared because the parent never called wait.

senses.definition: Of a language, no longer spoken.
senses.example: Latin is now defunct as a spoken language, though it survives in scholarship and liturgy.

senses.definition: (rare) Deceased, dead.
senses.example: The old preacher spoke of his defunct father as though he were still in the next room.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To render (something) defunct.
senses.example: The new regulation will defunct the old licensing board by the end of the year.

senses.definition: The deceased person (referred to).
senses.example: At the funeral, the family spoke warmly about the defunct and his years of service.

core.definition: No longer existing, operating, or in use, and not expected to return. Often used for businesses, organizations, or old technology.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, FUNGKT, with a short U as in luck. The final NGKT cluster is quick, and learners often add an extra vowel after the NG.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests something has ended, sometimes in a dismissive way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use defunct for companies, websites, products, laws, and sometimes old equipment. It is more formal than out of business or no longer exists, so in casual talk people often say that place is gone or that company went under. A common phrase is 'That store is defunct now.'

distinctions.note: Extinct usually describes a species or a kind of thing that no longer exists, while defunct describes an organization, program, or system that has stopped operating.
Obsolete means no longer useful or replaced by something better, while defunct means no longer functioning or existing at all.

examples.everyday: That little bakery down the street is defunct now, so we have to go somewhere else.
examples.professional: The old API is defunct, so all requests must move to the new endpoint by Friday.
examples.analytical: The argument assumes that the classical model is defunct, though it still shapes current debates.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone line that has been disconnected and will never ring again.
nuance.etymology: From Latin defunctus, past participle of defungi, to finish or discharge, from de- (off) and fungi (to perform).
common_mistakes: Using defunct for people in casual speech. It is rarely used for living people and can sound harsh.
Mispronouncing the vowel as a long U. The vowel should be short, as in luck.

defunct.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *dēfunctus*, past participle of *dēfungor* (“to finish, discharge”).

senses.definition: The act of demonstrating; showing or explaining something.
A prisoner's act of beating up another prisoner. (clarification of this definition is needed)
senses.example: The guards broke up a brutal demonstration in the prison yard before anyone was seriously hurt.

senses.definition: An event at which something will be demonstrated.
senses.example: I have to give a demonstration to the class tomorrow, and I'm ill-prepared.

senses.definition: Expression of one's feelings by outward signs.
senses.example: Her quiet tears were a demonstration of how much she missed her father.

senses.definition: A public display of group opinion, such as a protest march.
senses.example: Thousands joined the peaceful demonstration outside city hall to demand cleaner water.

senses.definition: A show of military force.
senses.example: The admiral ordered a naval demonstration off the coast to warn the rival nation.

senses.definition: A proof.
senses.example: The professor's elegant demonstration of the theorem took only ten minutes on the board.

core.definition: The act of showing or explaining how something works or is done, or a public gathering to protest or support a cause.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on STRAY, not on DEM, and the middle syllable is a reduced 'uh'. Learners often say 'dee-mon-stray-shun' or add a 't' sound to the ending; the '-tion' ending is pronounced 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. A protest demonstration can be seen as positive or negative depending on the speaker's politics, so the context and wording signal the attitude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'demonstration' for a product showing, a cooking or science display, or a public protest. In casual speech a product showing is often called a 'demo', and a protest is usually called a 'protest' or 'march' when the group is large. You can say 'hold a demonstration' or 'stage a demonstration' for protests and 'give a demonstration' for showing how something works.

distinctions.note: 'Demo' is an informal, shortened form used mostly in tech and sales for a quick product showing; 'demonstration' is the standard word and works in formal writing.
A presentation is a talk, often with slides, that informs or persuades; a demonstration focuses on showing that something works or how it is done.
A protest is any organized objection; a demonstration is a public gathering that can protest or support a cause, and it may be peaceful and celebratory.

examples.everyday: Stop by the store on Saturday; they're doing a cooking demonstration with free samples.
examples.professional: Can we schedule a live demonstration of the new dashboard for the operations team on Thursday?
examples.analytical: Euclid's proof is a demonstration in the strict sense: each step follows necessarily from the axioms and earlier results.

nuance.analogy: A demonstration is like a cooking show in real life: you don't just hear the recipe, you watch it work.
nuance.etymology: From Latin demonstratio, from demonstrare 'to point out, show clearly', from de- 'thoroughly' and monstrare 'to show'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'make a demonstration' for a protest; the usual verbs are 'hold' or 'stage' a demonstration.
Confusing 'demonstration' with 'demonstrative' or 'demonstrate' and mixing their stress patterns.
Putting the main stress on the first syllable, as in 'DEM-on-stray-shun', instead of 'dem-un-STRAY-shun'.

demonstration.etymology: From Middle English *demonstracioun*, from Old French *demonstration*, from Latin *dēmōnstrātiō*, from *dēmōnstrō* (“show or explain”), from *dē-* (“of or concerning”) + *mōnstrō* (“show”).

senses.definition: A model in which all parameters are used for every input.

core.definition: In AI, a neural network in which every parameter is used to process every input, unlike a sparse or mixture-of-experts model.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'MAH' in 'model', and 'dense' is less stressed than 'model'. In American speech, the 'o' in 'model' is a short 'ah' sound, and the final syllable is a reduced 'dul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Machine learning engineers in the United States use this phrase in papers, documentation, and team discussions. It is most often contrasted with sparse or mixture-of-experts models. Outside of AI, people would say 'standard model' or 'full model' instead.

distinctions.note: A dense model uses all parameters for every input; a sparse model activates only some of them.
A mixture-of-experts model routes inputs to selected sub-networks; a dense model applies all of its parameters to each input.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the dense model is slower but more accurate, so we might switch back.
examples.professional: For this release, we'll benchmark the dense model against the sparse version to see whether the latency difference matters for users.
examples.analytical: Comparing a dense model with a sparse architecture reveals a trade-off between expressive capacity and computational efficiency at inference time.

nuance.analogy: A dense model is like a full orchestra where every instrument plays on every piece, while a sparse model is a smaller group where only some players are active.
nuance.etymology: 'Dense' comes from Latin densus; 'model' comes from Italian modello, from Latin modulus.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'dense' more than 'model', which reverses the normal American phrase stress.
Using 'dense model' to mean a model that is simply accurate or thorough, instead of one where all parameters are active.

conversation.text: A dense model uses every parameter for every input.
We compared a dense model with a mixture of experts at the same compute per token.

senses.definition: Any agent acting to eliminate, reduce, mask, or control odor.
senses.example: Baking soda works as a cheap deodorant for stinky gym shoes.

senses.definition: An odor-controlling substance applied to the underarm to counteract odor from perspiration.
senses.example: I switched to an aluminum-free deodorant after my skin became irritated.

senses.definition: Acting or including an agent to eliminate, reduce, mask, or control odor.
senses.example: Her deodorant soap kept the locker room smelling fresh all week.

core.definition: A product applied to the underarms or body to reduce or mask body odor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OH, the second syllable. The first syllable is dee, not dih, and the final -ant is a reduced unt sound, not ahnt.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is a normal, polite product word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deodorant for a stick, roll-on, or spray applied to the underarms, and they buy it at any drugstore. It is everyday language, not formal. Many people use antiperspirant instead, which reduces sweat, so check the label if sweating is your concern.

distinctions.note: Deodorant masks or neutralizes odor, while antiperspirant reduces sweat, often using aluminum salts.
Air freshener scents a room or space, while deodorant is applied to the body.
Perfume is a fragrance meant to smell pleasant, while deodorant is meant to prevent body odor.

examples.everyday: I forgot my deodorant before the gym, so I'm grabbing a stick at the drugstore.
examples.professional: The product team wants the new deodorant line on shelves before the summer campaign.
examples.analytical: Marketing claims about deodorant often blur the difference between masking odor and reducing sweat.

nuance.analogy: Deodorant is like a closed door on a smelly room: it hides the smell, but the source keeps working.
nuance.etymology: From deodorize, formed from Latin de- and odor, meaning smell.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as DEE-oh-DOR-ant; the main stress is on OH.
Buying antiperspirant when you only want odor control, or the reverse, because the labels look similar.

deodorant.etymology: From Latin *de-* + *odorans*, present participle of *odorare* (“to smell”), from *odor* (“a smell”); see odor.

senses.definition: To speak ill of; to depreciate; to malign; to revile.
senses.example: Rather than debate the proposal, the critics chose to deprave the mayor's character in print.

senses.definition: To make bad or worse; to vitiate; to corrupt.
senses.example: Constant exposure to violence can deprave a young person's sense of right and wrong.

core.definition: To corrupt someone morally, making them bad, immoral, or wicked; to debase or pervert a person or a society.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, PRAYV, which rhymes with 'brave.' Do not reduce the first syllable to a full 'de' sound; keep it a weak, short vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes serious moral corruption and is strong language, so it is used for grave accusations rather than minor faults.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deprave mainly in formal writing, literature, legal or moral discussions, and sermons about sin or social decline. In everyday speech they say corrupt, ruin, or warp instead. The adjective depraved is much more common, as in depraved behavior. The older sense of speaking ill of someone is rare and mostly found in old texts, so avoid it.

distinctions.note: Corrupt is common and can refer to bribery or dishonesty, while deprave suggests a deeper moral decay, often sexual or ethical in nature.
Deprecate means to express disapproval or belittle something, but deprave means to corrupt someone morally, so the two are easily confused in sound and spelling.

examples.everyday: My grandmother used to say that bad television could deprave a child's taste, which made us laugh.
examples.professional: The editorial board decided the content did not deprave readers, so it kept the story in the magazine.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that certain media depraves public morals, but the question is whether the evidence shows a causal link rather than mere concern.

nuance.analogy: To deprave someone is like rust eating into good steel: the damage starts slowly and spreads until the core is weakened.
nuance.etymology: From Latin depravare, 'to distort or pervert,' from de- and pravus, 'crooked, perverse.'
common_mistakes: Confusing deprave with deprecate, which means to belittle or express disapproval rather than corrupt morally.
Using deprave in casual conversation where corrupt or ruin would sound more natural.

deprave.etymology: From Middle English *depraven*, from Old French *depraver*, from Latin *dēprāvō* (“pervert, distort, corrupt”), from *de-* + *pravus* (“crooked, distorted, perverse, wicked”).

senses.definition: An algorithm for traversing a tree or graph where one starts at the root and explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking.

core.definition: An algorithm that explores a tree or graph by going as deep as possible along one branch before backtracking.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SEARCH, with lighter stress on depth and first. Pronounce the voiceless th at the end of depth, and keep the r in first and search, since American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise technical term
nuance.usage_note: In American computer science and data science courses, depth-first search is usually abbreviated DFS in writing and speech. Engineers say we'll run a DFS on the graph when describing traversal. The term is standard in interviews and textbooks. Speakers often contrast it with breadth-first search.

distinctions.note: Breadth-first search explores all nodes at one level before moving deeper, usually with a queue, while depth-first search goes deep along one path first, usually with a stack or recursion.
Iterative deepening repeats depth-limited depth-first searches with growing limits, combining low memory use with the completeness of breadth-first search.

examples.everyday: I learned depth-first search in a class, but I forgot most of it.
examples.professional: Let's use a depth-first search here, since the graph is sparse and we need to keep memory low.
examples.analytical: Depth-first search trades the level-by-level order of breadth-first search for lower memory use, since it stores only the current path.

nuance.analogy: Like exploring a maze by following one corridor to its dead end before returning to try the next, depth-first search goes deep first.
nuance.etymology: A compound of English depth, first, and search, used as a technical term in computer science.
common_mistakes: Dropping the final th sound in depth, so it sounds like dep.
Stressing depth or first as the main word instead of search.

conversation.text: Depth-first search follows one branch as deep as possible before backtracking.
Depth-first search needs little memory, but it can get lost down a very deep or infinite branch.

senses.definition: To not select; to rule out of selection.
To remove from an existing selection.
senses.example: Make sure you deselect any files you wish to keep before proceeding with the deletion.

core.definition: To remove an item or person from a current selection, or to reject someone as a candidate; to unselect.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -LEKT, with secondary stress on dee-. The prefix de- is pronounced 'dee' (/diː/), not 'dis', and the middle syllable is a reduced uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word in computing and politics, with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deselect constantly with software, such as unchecking boxes or removing items from a list, and in politics when a party drops a candidate. In everyday speech people often say uncheck or unselect, though deselect is common in apps and on websites. For ordinary choosing, people say pick or choose.

distinctions.note: Unselect and deselect mean nearly the same thing, but deselect is more common in software and political reporting.
Remove deletes an item from a list entirely, while deselect only stops it from being chosen and it may remain in the list.

examples.everyday: Can you deselect the remember me box before you log in on this shared computer?
examples.professional: Please deselect the Legacy Systems option on the sprint board so those tickets don't roll into next week.
examples.analytical: Deselecting a candidate in a party primary is a political act whose legitimacy rests on the rules the party has agreed to.

nuance.analogy: Like unchecking a box on a form: the option is still there, just no longer chosen.
nuance.etymology: From de- (reverse) and select, from Latin seligere (to choose out), from se- (apart) and legere (to gather, choose).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the prefix as 'dis' (/dɪs/) instead of 'dee' (/diː/).
Using deselect for choosing something different; it means removing an item from a selection.

senses.definition: A formal, documented general reusable solution to a design problem in a particular field of expertise.

core.definition: A documented, reusable solution to a common software design problem, described in general terms that can be adapted to many specific programs.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PAT in pattern, and the final syllable is a reduced 'ern', not 'pat-tern' with a clear t sound. The t in pattern is a flap, so it sounds close to a soft d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and professional; it signals familiarity with software engineering.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers say design pattern all the time, often naming specific ones such as Observer or Factory. The term comes from the influential book by the Gang of Four. In meetings, people might say we could use a factory pattern here.

distinctions.note: An algorithm is a precise step-by-step procedure for a task, while a design pattern is a general structure for organizing code.
A framework is a concrete library or set of tools, while a design pattern is an abstract idea you can implement in any framework.

examples.everyday: My brother is a developer, and he keeps talking about a design pattern called singleton that he uses for his apps.
examples.professional: Could we use a strategy design pattern here so we can swap out the payment provider without changing the checkout code?
examples.analytical: The authors argue that a design pattern captures a recurring structural solution, making its tradeoffs explicit rather than hidden in code.

nuance.analogy: A design pattern is like a recipe template: it gives the steps for a common dish, but you still choose the ingredients for your own kitchen.
nuance.etymology: Pattern comes from Middle English patron, 'model'; the software sense was popularized in the 1990s by the Gang of Four book.
common_mistakes: Using design pattern to mean a visual or fabric pattern, which is a different sense.
Pronouncing pattern with a clear t sound when Americans flap the t to something like a d.

senses.definition: To set the boundaries or limits of.
senses.example: The judge determined the boundaries of the disputed land using an old survey.

senses.definition: To ascertain definitely; to figure out, find out, or conclude by analyzing, calculating, or investigating.
senses.example: After weeks of analysis, the team determined that the sensor failed due to moisture.

senses.definition: To fix the form or character of; to shape; to prescribe imperatively; to regulate; to settle.
senses.example: The bylaws determined how the committee would elect its officers each year.

senses.definition: To fix the course of; to impel and direct; with a remoter object preceded by to.
senses.example: The news of his father's illness determined him to depart immediately.

senses.definition: To bring to a conclusion, as a question or controversy; to settle authoritative or judicial sentence; to decide.
senses.example: The court has determined the cause.

senses.definition: To resolve on; to have a fixed intention of; also, to cause to come to a conclusion or decision; to lead.
senses.example: I determined to go home at once.

senses.definition: To define or limit by adding a differentia.
senses.example: In the taxonomy, the genus is determined by a differentia that separates it from its relatives.

senses.definition: To bring to an end; to finish.
senses.example: The storm determined our camping trip after only one night.

senses.definition: Decided; resolute, possessing much determination.
senses.example: I'm determined to get a good grade on my exam.

core.definition: Firmly resolved to do something and not easily stopped or discouraged by difficulty.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TUR, and make the final -ed a silent d sound, so it rhymes with mind. Do not pronounce the e as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises persistence and commitment, though it can sound stubborn if used about someone who ignores advice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say she is determined to or he is determined to succeed, and it is common in sports, school, and personal goals. It can also describe someone who will not listen, as in she is determined to do it her way. As a verb, determined usually appears in passive forms such as the cause was determined by investigators.

distinctions.note: Stubborn often has a negative tone of refusing to change; determined is usually positive and focused on a goal.
Persistent stresses continuing over time; determined stresses firm resolve from the start.

examples.everyday: She is determined to finish the marathon even though her knee still hurts.
examples.professional: The team is determined to ship the new dashboard before the holiday freeze.
examples.analytical: A determined agent acts from settled commitments rather than from momentary desires.

nuance.analogy: A determined person is like a river that keeps cutting through rock until it finds its path.
nuance.etymology: From Latin determinare, to limit or define, through Old French determiner.
common_mistakes: Confusing determined with determinate, which is a technical or formal word.
Using determined to mean certain or sure of a fact; use sure or certain for that.

conversation.text: She's determined to finish the marathon this year.
He was determined to fix the sink himself.
I'm determined to learn to cook before I'm thirty.

senses.definition: Initialism of depth-first search.
Initialism of daily fantasy sports.
senses.example: After losing his lineup, Marcus spent every Sunday checking his DFS contests on his phone.

core.definition: Depth-first search, a graph and tree algorithm that explores as far down one branch as possible before backtracking.

pronunciation.tip: Say the three letters separately, D-F-S, with the main stress on the final S. Do not say it as one word like deef-ess.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term in computing.
nuance.usage_note: In computer science courses, coding interviews and software teams, Americans say the letters and usually spell out depth-first search first. In US sports talk, DFS usually means daily fantasy sports, a meaning you will hear in ads and conversations about betting on player performance. Context almost always makes the meaning clear.

distinctions.note: BFS, breadth-first search, explores all nodes at one level before going deeper, while DFS goes deep along one path first.
DFA means deterministic finite automaton in theory of computation, a different concept from search algorithms.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I'm stuck on DFS for my homework, and I can't get the recursion right.
examples.professional: Let's use DFS here, since the dependency graph is deep and sparse, so the traversal stays efficient.
examples.analytical: DFS visits each vertex and edge once, so its running time is linear in the size of the graph.

nuance.analogy: Like exploring a maze by following one corridor to its dead end before returning to try the next.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of depth-first search; the letters stand for the English phrase.
common_mistakes: Saying the letters as one word, such as deef, instead of spelling them out.
Confusing DFS with DFA or with BFS, which are different concepts.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to diagnosis.
Serving to indicate or specify a particular item or thing within a group of similar things.
senses.example: The diagnostic label identified only the second sample in the batch as contaminated.

senses.definition: Intended to assess a student's preexisting knowledge on the material being taught.
senses.example: A diagnostic assessment

senses.definition: Characteristic of a particular disease.
senses.example: The rash was diagnostic of measles, so the nurse ordered an immediate isolation test.

senses.definition: Characteristic of a particular taxon or clade.
senses.example: Its enlarged jaw bone was diagnostic of the genus, distinguishing it from related fossil species.

senses.definition: Any technique used in medical diagnosis.
senses.example: The doctor ordered a diagnostic that would rule out infection before prescribing antibiotics.

senses.definition: Any tool or technique used to find the root of a problem.
senses.example: Our engineers ran a diagnostic on the server to find why the database kept crashing overnight.

senses.definition: That by which anything is known; a symptom.
senses.example: Her constant fatigue turned out to be a diagnostic sign of anemia, not simply stress.

core.definition: Relating to diagnosis; a test, tool or sign that identifies a problem, its cause or its condition.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on NAH, the third syllable. The 'g' is quick and runs into the 'n', so do not add a vowel between them.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a tool or process and carries no judgment about people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use diagnostic mainly for tests, tools and criteria, as in 'a diagnostic test' or 'diagnostic criteria', and in IT and auto repair they say 'run diagnostics' for a system check. In everyday talk, people more often say 'diagnosis' for the result or 'test' for the procedure. Using it as a noun for a result sounds unnatural.

distinctions.note: Diagnostic identifies what is happening now, while prognostic predicts how a condition will develop.
Symptomatic describes signs of a problem, while diagnostic means the sign or test actually helps establish its cause.
Diagnostic focuses on identifying a specific problem, while analytic refers more broadly to breaking something into parts for study.

examples.everyday: My check-engine light came on, so the mechanic ran a diagnostic test and found a loose sensor.
examples.professional: I'll run diagnostics on the data pipeline before we push the model to production.
examples.analytical: A diagnostic framework must distinguish genuine failure modes from the noise of ordinary variation.

nuance.analogy: A diagnostic test is like a smoke detector: it doesn't put out the fire, but it tells you where to look.
nuance.etymology: From Greek diagnōstikos, from diagignōskein 'to distinguish, discern', from dia- 'through' + gignōskein 'to know'.
common_mistakes: Using diagnostic as the noun for the result; say 'diagnosis' or 'the test results'.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'dy-ag-NOS-tic'; the stress is on NAH.

diagnostic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *διαγνωστικός*, adjective from *διαγιγνώσκω* (“to distinguish, diagnose”).

senses.definition: Relating to diet.
Relating to the preparation of food for those on a restricted diet.

core.definition: Relating to diet and nutrition, or to preparing food for people on a restricted diet, especially for medical reasons.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TET, the second-to-last syllable. Do not stress the first syllable, and keep the final -ic short, like tik.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a clinical or professional term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dietetic mainly in professional and medical settings, such as dietetic technician programs, dietetic practice or dietetic care. Most people say dietary or nutritional in everyday speech. Products labeled dietetic in the US usually refer to special foods for people with diabetes, so the word can sound dated outside health contexts.

distinctions.note: Dietary is common and broad; dietetic is more technical and linked to the professional field of dietetics.
Dietetic is an adjective for things related to diet, while dietitian is the person who works in that field.

examples.everyday: My sister is studying to become a dietetic technician, so she is always asking me what I eat.
examples.professional: The hospital's dietetic department will review the meal plans for patients with kidney disease this week.
examples.analytical: Historians of medicine trace the growth of dietetic science from folk remedies to the modern clinical standards of nutrition.

nuance.etymology: From Greek diaitetikos, relating to a way of life or regimen, via Latin dieteticus.
common_mistakes: Using dietetic and dietary as perfect synonyms in everyday speech
Stressing the first syllable as DYE-uh-tet-ik

senses.definition: A polyhedron having two faces.

core.definition: A degenerate polyhedron with exactly two faces, usually two identical polygons joined along their shared edges.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -HEE-, the second syllable. The ending is pronounced 'ahn', not 'un', as in a standard American cot-caught vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term from geometry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dihedron in mathematics courses and geometry texts, usually as a limiting or degenerate case in discussions of polyhedra. It is rare in everyday speech and would seldom come up outside math or geometry. When you need to describe two flat faces meeting in space, dihedral angle is the more common term.

distinctions.note: A polyhedron is a solid with many flat faces; a dihedron is a special degenerate case with only two faces.
A dihedron is a shape; a dihedral angle is the angle between two planes, measured as a number of degrees.

examples.professional: Our geometry library has to handle degenerate cases like the dihedron, which breaks the usual face-counting code.
examples.analytical: A dihedron is not a polyhedron in the strict sense, since its two faces cannot enclose a volume, yet it serves as a boundary case in the classification.

nuance.analogy: A dihedron is like a sandwich with only two slices of bread and no filling: it has faces, but it cannot hold a volume the way a full solid does.
nuance.etymology: From Greek di-, meaning two, and hedra, meaning seat or base, on the model of polyhedron.
common_mistakes: Saying dihedron for any two-faced object in ordinary life; the word is limited to geometry.
Pronouncing the ending as 'dih-drun' with a weak vowel instead of 'ahn'.

senses.definition: Very small.
Of or pertaining to, or creating a word form expressing smallness, youth, unimportance, or endearment.
A word form expressing smallness, youth, unimportance, or endearment.
senses.example: Booklet, the diminutive of book, means ‘small book’.

senses.definition: The smallest, thinnest version of a traditional heraldic ordinary ("geometric shape on a shield"), often used to represent multiple instances of a charge or to modify a main, central, and larger charge; not itself modifiable.

core.definition: Very small in size. In linguistics, it also describes a word form that expresses smallness, youth, or affection.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MIN, the second syllable. The first and last syllables are reduced, so the word sounds like 'duh-MIN-yuh-tiv,' with the final -ive as a short 'iv.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly affectionate. It describes size without judgment, though it can sound a bit literary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use diminutive for small people, animals, or objects in writing and formal speech: 'a diminutive woman' is a polite, slightly elevated description. In everyday speech people more often say 'tiny' or 'petite.' In grammar, the diminutive suffix (such as -let or -ie) is a term that teachers and linguists use.

distinctions.note: Small is the everyday word; diminutive is more formal and can sound slightly literary or affectionate.
Tiny is informal and emphatic; diminutive is more polite and sometimes suggests charm.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was a diminutive woman, but she could still outwork everyone in the family.
examples.professional: The diminutive size of the chip allows us to fit more processing cores on each board.
examples.analytical: In Hebrew poetry, the diminutive is rare, and its appearance often signals an intentional tone of affection or contempt.

nuance.analogy: Like a miniature version of a famous painting, a diminutive thing is a small copy of something larger.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin diminutivus, from Latin diminuere, 'to diminish.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as dih-mih-NYOO-tiv or dy-MIN-yuh-tiv.
Using diminutive as a noun for a small person; it is an adjective in everyday use.

diminutive.etymology: Middle English *diminutif*, Old French *diminutif*, Latin *dīminutīvus*, from *dīminūtus*, of *dīminuō*.

senses.definition: Expressing or conveying disapproval.
senses.example: The word "lazy", when used to describe a person's unwillingness to work, is a disapproving word.

core.definition: Showing that you think someone's behavior or choices are wrong or unacceptable.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PROO, the middle of the word's root. The ending is a short 'ing' sound, not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a look, tone or silence that communicates criticism without words.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disapproving most often for facial expressions, tones and silences, as in 'a disapproving look'. It is used in everyday life, at work and in writing. Do not confuse it with disapproved, which describes something that was rejected by an authority.

distinctions.note: Judgmental describes a general habit of harsh, quick criticism of people; disapproving describes a specific reaction in a given moment.
Critical can be neutral and analytical, as in critical thinking; disapproving always carries emotional displeasure.

examples.everyday: She gave me a disapproving look when I ordered dessert before dinner.
examples.professional: The manager's disapproving tone in the meeting made everyone hesitant to share new ideas.
examples.analytical: Calvin's disapproving tone toward religious images reflects his conviction that such images distort true worship.

nuance.analogy: Like a closed door with a frown on it: the message is clear even though nothing is said.
nuance.etymology: From disapprove plus the -ing adjective ending.
common_mistakes: Using disapproving to with a wrong preposition; the usual form is disapproving of.
Confusing the adjective disapproving with the past participle disapproved, which describes something that was rejected.

senses.definition: To convert (a person) into a disciple.
senses.example: The evangelist hoped to disciple every new convert who came forward that night.

senses.definition: To train, educate, teach.
senses.example: She spent years discipling apprentices in the craft of letterpress printing.

senses.definition: To routinely counsel (one's peer or junior) one-on-one in their discipleship of Christ, as a fellow affirmed disciple.
senses.example: Each Sunday she meets a sister from church to disciple her over coffee.

senses.definition: A person who learns from another, especially one who then teaches others.
An active follower or adherent of someone, or some philosophy etc.
senses.example: He was a devoted disciple of the economist who taught him to question markets.

core.definition: A person who learns from and follows a teacher, leader or set of beliefs, especially someone who later teaches others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, SY, which has a long 'i' sound. The final syllable is weak and reduced to 'puhl', not 'peel'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests loyalty, learning and devotion to a teacher or cause.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'disciple' most often in religious contexts, such as Christian disciples, but also for loyal followers of a teacher or philosophy, such as 'a disciple of Socrates'. It sounds slightly formal in everyday talk. In casual speech, people usually say 'follower' or 'fan'.

distinctions.note: 'Follower' is general and can be casual, while 'disciple' implies deep learning and commitment to a teacher's ideas.
'Student' refers to someone in an academic setting, while 'disciple' suggests loyalty to a leader or a belief system.

examples.everyday: My friend says she's a disciple of that yoga teacher, and she goes to every class.
examples.professional: He was a disciple of the old database architect, and he still uses her design principles.
examples.analytical: The Gospel describes Jesus calling his disciples to follow him and to learn from his teaching.

nuance.analogy: Like an apprentice who watches a master craftsman closely and gradually learns the craft.
nuance.etymology: From Old English discipul, from Latin discipulus, student, from discere, to learn.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'disciple' with 'discipline', which means training or control.
Stressing the first syllable; it is dih-SY-puhl.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is mathetes, meaning learner or pupil, one who follows a teacher and learns from him. In the Gospels, the twelve apostles are called disciples. Matthew 28:19 in the RSV tells the disciples to make disciples of all nations. Luke 14:26 uses the word to describe the cost of following Jesus. John 13:35 says that love among disciples will show that they belong to Jesus.

disciple.etymology: From Middle English *disciple*, *discipul*, from Old English *discipul* (“disciple, scholar”), from Latin *discipulus* (“pupil, learner”).

senses.definition: To free or deprive of illusion; to disenchant.
The act or process of disenchanting or freeing from a false belief or illusion.
senses.example: Her blunt lecture was a disillusion for students who believed in the myth of pure objectivity.

senses.definition: The state of being freed from a constructed or imposed illusion; the recognition of an underlying truth previously obscured by a false or controlled narrative.

core.definition: To free someone from a false belief or comforting illusion, often by showing them the harsh truth.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the -LU- syllable, and the final -sion is pronounced like the zh in 'measure', not 'shun'. Many learners stress the first syllable or say 'dis-ih-loo-SHUN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes a painful but useful loss of false belief, and the tone depends on whether the speaker sees the loss as good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in serious conversation, news, and writing about politics, relationships, religion, or work, such as 'The scandal disillusioned many voters.' It is more formal than 'let down' or 'burst my bubble' in casual talk. Usually it appears in the passive: 'I was disillusioned.'

distinctions.note: Disappoint means you feel let down by an outcome; disillusion means you lose a belief about how things really are.
Disenchant is close in meaning but more literary; disillusion is the more common everyday choice in American English.

examples.everyday: After working at that company for a year, I got really disillusioned with how they treat people.
examples.professional: Our team was disillusioned when the vendor's demo did not match what they actually delivered.
examples.analytical: Her essay argues that disillusion is a necessary step toward a more honest understanding of institutions.

nuance.analogy: Like a magician revealing how a trick works, disillusion removes the spell but leaves you seeing things clearly.
nuance.etymology: From French désillusionner, from des- (undo) and illusion (illusion).
common_mistakes: Saying 'disillusioned of' or 'disillusioned by' where Americans usually say 'disillusioned with'.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'DIS-ih-loo-zhun'.

disillusion.etymology: From *dis-* + *illusion*: literally, the removal or undoing of illusion.

senses.definition: In a manner that is not frank or open; deceptively.
senses.example: She answered the reporter's questions disingenuously, hiding the fact that the merger was already decided.

senses.definition: In an unnoble manner; in a manner unbecoming of true honor or dignity; unworthily.
senses.example: He treated his former mentor disingenuously, taking credit for her work after she had trusted him.

senses.definition: In a manner that adopts a pose of naïveté, possibly to make a point or to deceive.
senses.example: When asked about the spreadsheet errors, he replied disingenuously, as if he had never seen the numbers.

core.definition: In a way that pretends innocence or ignorance in order to hide your real intentions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -JEN-, and the ending -ly is short and unstressed. Keep the -ous sound reduced so it does not become a separate loud syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies deception or insincerity, so it is a strong judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disingenuously in news analysis, reviews, and debate to criticize someone's framing, such as 'She disingenuously asked whether we had any data.' It is rarely used in casual speech. A natural alternative is 'not exactly honestly' or 'with a straight face.'

distinctions.note: Deceptively means in a way that makes something look different from what it is; disingenuously focuses on pretending innocence or naivete.
Insincerely means without real feeling; disingenuously means acting innocent to hide a purpose.

examples.everyday: He disingenuously asked if I'd seen the game, when he was the one who had recorded it.
examples.professional: The report disingenuously presented the average without mentioning the outliers.
examples.analytical: The critic disingenuously treats a contested interpretation as if it were the plain meaning of the text.

nuance.analogy: Acting disingenuously is like a poker player who shows a weak hand with a confident smile to hide a strong one.
nuance.etymology: From disingenuous (not frank, pretending naivete) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'disingenuously' to mean 'innocently,' which is the opposite meaning.
Stressing the first syllable of the word.

senses.definition: The act of disseminating, or the state of being disseminated; diffusion for propagation and permanence; a scattering or spreading abroad, as of ideas, beliefs, etc.
senses.example: The university's dissemination of research findings through open journals reached thousands of readers.

core.definition: The act of spreading information, ideas, or beliefs widely so that many people receive and learn them.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the NAY syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on SEM. Learners often stress SEM, and the ending -tion is pronounced shun, not tee-on.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes the act of spreading something, and it can be positive (sharing knowledge) or negative (spreading rumors or propaganda), depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dissemination in news, academic writing, business, and government contexts, such as 'the dissemination of research findings' or 'the rapid dissemination of information online.' In casual talk they usually say 'spread' or 'share' instead. It sounds polished and stiff in a casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Distribution means delivering physical goods or items to people, while dissemination refers to spreading information, ideas, or knowledge.
Publication is the formal printing or release of a finished work, whereas dissemination is the wider spreading of its content, which can happen by any means.

examples.everyday: My aunt is the one who makes sure the family news gets dissemination through every group text.
examples.professional: Our team plan is to improve the dissemination of the model results to stakeholders through a weekly dashboard.
examples.analytical: Luther's printing press made the dissemination of vernacular Scripture possible on an unprecedented scale.

nuance.analogy: Like dandelion seeds carried by the wind, dissemination scatters something so it takes root in many places.
nuance.etymology: From Latin disseminare, 'to scatter seed', from dis- 'apart' and semen 'seed'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the SEM syllable instead of NAY, which makes the word sound unnatural to Americans.
Using dissemination for physical objects; say 'distribution' for goods and 'dissemination' for ideas and information.

dissemination.etymology: From Latin *dissēminātiō*, from *dissemino* [from *dis-* (“in all directions”) + *sēmināre* (“to plant or propagate”) (itself from *sēmen* (“seed”))] *-tiō*.

senses.definition: To recognize someone or something as different from others based on its characteristics.
senses.example: Our spam filter can distinguish legitimate newsletters from phishing emails by their headers.

senses.definition: To see someone or something clearly or distinctly.
senses.example: Through the fog, we could barely distinguish the outline of the lighthouse.

senses.definition: To make noticeably different or better from others through accomplishments.
senses.example: The soldier distinguished himself in combat and received a medal.

senses.definition: To confer an honor upon.
senses.example: The soldier was distinguished with a medal for his bravery.

core.definition: To recognize that one thing is different from another, or to tell two things apart by their features.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'STING'. The 'gu' is pronounced as a hard 'g' followed by 'w', and the final 'ish' is short. Do not stress the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes the act of recognizing or separating things, and can also praise someone who stands out.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'distinguish between' when separating two things, as in 'distinguish between facts and opinions'. It is common in everyday speech, meetings and writing. The phrase 'distinguish yourself' is a positive phrase used for students, employees or athletes who achieve something notable.

distinctions.note: 'Differentiate' is more technical and often used in science or math. 'Distinguish' is more general and common in everyday speech.
'Tell apart' is a casual phrasal verb meaning the same thing. 'Distinguish' sounds more formal and is often used in writing.

examples.everyday: It's hard to distinguish my twins from each other unless you know their voices.
examples.professional: Can you help me distinguish the errors caused by the data from those caused by the model?
examples.analytical: Scripture calls us to distinguish between what is holy and what is common, and this distinction shapes how we live.

nuance.analogy: Like sorting mail into different slots so every letter ends up in the right place.
nuance.etymology: From Latin distinguere, 'to separate, mark off, distinguish'.
common_mistakes: Using 'distinguish' without 'between' when comparing two things, as in 'distinguish the two' is acceptable but 'distinguish between' is more natural.
Confusing 'distinguish' with 'extinguish', which means to put out a fire.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Old Testament, the Hebrew verb badal (bdl) means 'to separate, divide, set apart', and it is used for separating holy from common and clean from unclean. In the New Testament, the Greek diakrinō means 'to distinguish, discern, judge'. Leviticus 10:10 (RSV) says the priests must distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean. Ezekiel 44:23 (RSV) instructs the priests to teach the people to discern between the holy and the common. First Corinthians 12:10 (RSV) lists the discernment of spirits among the gifts of the Spirit.

distinguish.etymology: From Middle English *distingwen*, from Old French *distinguer*, from Latin *distinguo* (“to separate, divide, distinguish, set off, adorn, literally mark off”), from *di-*, *dis-* (“apart”) + *stinguo*, related to.

senses.definition: (Should we delete this sense?) A function, implemented in many programming languages, that returns the result of a division of two integers.
senses.example: Our code calls div on the two integers before indexing the array.

senses.definition: A section of a web page, or the div element that represents it in HTML code.
Divergence; a kind of differential operator.
senses.example: The physicist applied div to the vector field to measure flux leaving a small volume.

senses.definition: A division.
senses.example: The company's marketing div was merged with sales after the restructuring.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of divide.
senses.example: Her worksheet said to div both sides by three before solving for x.

core.definition: In web development, the HTML div element, a generic container that groups other content on a page for layout or styling.

pronunciation.tip: Say it like 'div' rhymes with 'give,' with a short i, not like 'dive.' In programming talk Americans say it as one word, not as separate letters.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain technical term with no emotional content.
nuance.usage_note: Among American software engineers, 'div' is said as a single word, as in 'wrap it in a div.' The division function sense used in some programming languages is a different technical use, so check context. Outside of tech, Americans would say 'section' or 'box' instead.

distinctions.note: A span is an inline element that wraps text within a line; a div is a block-level element that usually starts a new line.
A section is a semantic HTML element for a thematic part of a page; a div is a generic container with no built-in meaning.
Container is a general design term that may refer to a div or another element; div is the specific HTML tag.

examples.everyday: My cousin says the sidebar is inside a div that does not line up on phones.
examples.professional: Wrap the login form in a div with the class container so the layout stays centered on mobile screens.
examples.analytical: Overuse of nested divs obscures document structure, which is why semantic elements such as article and nav were introduced.

nuance.analogy: Like an unlabeled box that holds other boxes, useful for arranging things but saying nothing about what is inside.
nuance.etymology: Short for division, from Latin divisio, in the sense of a section of a document.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'dive' and saying 'dyve,' which is a different word
Using 'div' for every container; a section or article element is clearer when the content has meaning

senses.definition: Straying off from a course or way.
Incoherent or wandering speech and thought.

core.definition: A wandering away from the main subject or course, or rambling, disconnected speech or thought.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the -GAY- syllable, with the ending -shun pronounced as a reduced syllable. Keep the first vowel short, as in dip.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; it describes a flaw in focus or coherence rather than a neutral change of subject.
nuance.usage_note: Americans seldom use this noun in casual talk. It appears in literary criticism, psychology writing, or formal reviews of speeches and texts. In everyday speech, people say 'rambling' or 'going off on a tangent' instead.

distinctions.note: Digression is the common word for a short aside in speech or writing; divagation is more formal and can describe a sustained wandering.
A tangent is a casual, brief departure from the topic; divagation is a more literary term for wandering in general.

examples.professional: The report should avoid divagation and stick to the three findings the committee asked about.
examples.analytical: The critic reads the novel's middle section as a deliberate divagation that mirrors the narrator's unstable memory.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that leaves its main channel and spreads into side streams, losing its direction.
nuance.etymology: From Latin divagatio, a wandering about, from divagari.
common_mistakes: Confusing divagation with divergence, which refers to moving apart from a common path or value.
Using it in casual conversation where digression or tangent is more natural.

divagation.etymology: Nominalization of *divagate* (from the Latin verb *divagare*) + *-ion* (from the Latin suffix *-io*).

senses.definition: Someone who dives, especially as a sport.
senses.example: The diver executed a flawless backward somersault off the ten-meter platform.

senses.definition: Someone who works underwater; a frogman.
senses.example: The diver inspected the damaged pier pilings beneath the murky harbor water.

senses.definition: Loon (Gavia spp.)
senses.example: A common diver drifted on the lake, calling mournfully as the sun set.

senses.definition: A New Zealand sand diver (Tewara cranwellae)
senses.example: The biologist found a diver buried in the sand near the New Zealand coast.

senses.definition: A long-finned sand diver (Limnichthys polyactis)
senses.example: Snorkelers spotted a long-finned diver hovering over the sandy seabed near the reef.

senses.definition: A competitor in certain sports who is known to regularly imitate being fouled, with the purpose of getting his/her opponent penalized.
senses.example: The soccer diver flopped theatrically in the box, hoping the referee would award a penalty.

senses.definition: (dated) A passenger carrying vehicle using an underground route; specially, a diver tram, one using the former Kingsway tramway subway (1906-1952).
senses.example: In 1948, Grandpa rode the diver beneath Kingsway, hurrying toward work through the tramway tunnel.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A person who goes underwater, either for sport, such as competitive diving or scuba diving, or for work, such as inspection or salvage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DYE. The final -er is a weak, r-colored American vowel, not a full 'ah' or 'air,' and the middle v is voiced, as in 'dive.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a person's activity and carries no judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'diver' for scuba divers, competitive divers who jump from boards, and commercial or military divers. Informal 'frogman' sounds dated or humorous. In American birding the bird is called a loon, while 'diver' for loons is mainly a British and European usage.

distinctions.note: A swimmer may stay on the surface; a diver goes underwater on purpose and often uses equipment.
Scuba diver is a specific kind of diver who breathes from a tank; diver is the broader term.
A snorkeler stays near the surface with a mask and tube; a diver goes deeper.

examples.everyday: My brother is a certified diver and spends most weekends off the coast.
examples.professional: The pipeline inspection requires a licensed diver to check the intake valve underwater.
examples.analytical: Divers depend on pressure equalization to avoid injury, which makes depth a matter of physiology as much as skill.

nuance.analogy: Like a swimmer who goes under the surface and keeps going down, carrying his own air.
nuance.etymology: From dive, plus the English suffix -er, meaning one who does the action.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'dye-ver,' with the final syllable as a full vowel
Calling a loon a diver in American birding, where the usual name is loon

senses.definition: The act, or the result, of diversifying.
senses.example: Diversification of our daily meal plan kept the kids from getting bored with the same dinners.

senses.definition: A corporate strategy in which a company acquires or establishes a business other than that of its current product.
senses.example: The grocery chain's diversification into pharmacy and banking shocked analysts who expected it to stick to groceries.

senses.definition: An investment strategy involving investing in a range of assets with differing features in order to reduce specific risk.
senses.example: Our retirement portfolio uses diversification across stocks, bonds, and real estate to cushion against any single company's collapse.

core.definition: The act of making something more varied, or spreading investments or business activity across many areas to reduce risk.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -KAY-, and the secondary stress falls on the first syllable. Keep the reduced middle syllables short and avoid pronouncing every vowel fully.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it usually describes a prudent strategy to reduce risk or to broaden options.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use diversification in business, finance, and economics, and it appears in news about companies and investments. In casual speech they say 'spreading out' or 'not putting all your eggs in one basket.' It can also describe the variety of a group, such as a diversification of a workforce.

distinctions.note: Diversity is the state of being varied; diversification is the process or strategy of making something more varied.
Variety is a general word for differences; diversification implies a deliberate, planned change.

examples.everyday: My dad keeps some money in stocks and some in bonds, so that's his way of diversification.
examples.professional: Our leadership wants product diversification so we are not dependent on one client.
examples.analytical: Financial theory treats diversification as the main method for reducing unsystematic risk without sacrificing expected return.

nuance.analogy: Like a gardener who plants many kinds of crops so one bad season does not ruin the harvest.
nuance.etymology: From diversify, from Medieval Latin diversificare, to make diverse, from Latin diversus (different).
common_mistakes: Using diversification to mean diversity of people; diversity is the usual word for that.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the main stress is on -KAY-.

diversification.etymology: From Medieval Latin *diversificatiō*, from *diversificātus*, past participle of *diversificō* (“diversify”), from Latin *diversus* (“turned in different ways”) + *faciō* (“make, do”).

senses.definition: To turn aside from a course.
senses.example: The workers diverted the stream away from the road.

senses.definition: To distract.
senses.example: Don't let him divert your attention; keep your eye on the ball.

senses.definition: To entertain or amuse (by diverting the attention)
senses.example: The clown's silly songs diverted the children while their parents finished the paperwork.

core.definition: To change the direction or course of something, or to send it somewhere else.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, -VURT-, with a strong American r. Do not pronounce the t as a clear 't' between vowels if you are in a fast phrase; it can become a soft flap, though here it is at the end and is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a change of route or attention, and can also imply that something was taken away from its intended purpose.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use divert for traffic, flights, money, and attention: 'The road was closed, so we were diverted.' In casual speech they often say 'reroute' for roads and flights. To divert someone's attention means to distract them, so use it when you want to sound precise.

distinctions.note: Redirect is a neutral, everyday word for changing direction on purpose; divert often implies moving something away from its planned route or purpose.
Distract focuses on someone's attention being pulled away; divert can mean changing the route or use of money or resources as well.

examples.everyday: The highway was closed for construction, so the GPS diverted us through town.
examples.professional: We need to divert some of the server load to the backup region while the upgrade finishes.
examples.analytical: Augustine argues that the soul can divert its love from God toward created things, and that this misdirection is the root of sin.

nuance.analogy: Like a river engineer building a channel to carry water away from its usual bed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin divertere, 'to turn aside', from di- 'apart' plus vertere 'to turn'.
common_mistakes: Using divert with 'of' as in 'divert from' when you mean 'divert to'; say 'divert traffic to a side road'.
Confusing divert with deviate; deviate means to depart from a norm or standard, while divert means to change a path or direction.

divert.etymology: From Middle English *diverten*, Old French *divertir* (“to turn or go different ways, part, separate, divert”), from Latin *di-* (“apart”) + *vertere* (“to turn”); see verse.

senses.definition: A cash payment of money by a company to its shareholders, usually made periodically (e.g. quarterly or annually).
A number or expression that is to be divided by another.
senses.example: In "42 ÷ 3" the dividend is the 42.

senses.definition: Beneficial results from a metaphorical investment (of time, effort, etc.)
senses.example: His 10,000 hours of practice and recitals eventually paid dividends when he become first-chair violinist.

senses.definition: To pay out a dividend.

core.definition: A payment a company makes to its shareholders from its profits, usually every quarter or year.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowels are reduced, so say "DIV-ih-dend" with a short, quick second syllable, not "di-VI-dend."

nuance.connotation: Positive; a dividend is a sign of profit and financial health, though a company may choose to reinvest instead.
nuance.usage_note: Americans talk about dividends in everyday money matters, such as retirement accounts and stock investing, and in business news. You often hear "pay a dividend" or "dividend yield." In a metaphorical sense, "dividends" for effort or kindness is a friendly, slightly informal idea. The word is in ordinary use, not formal only.

distinctions.note: Interest is what you earn from lending money or from a savings account; a dividend is a share of a company's profit paid to its owners.
A bonus is a one-time extra payment from an employer to an employee; a dividend is paid to shareholders, who own part of the company.

examples.everyday: The stock paid a small dividend last quarter, so I reinvested it in the same fund.
examples.professional: Our board approved a quarterly dividend of forty cents per share, effective next month.
examples.analytical: Her essay argues that the dividends of patient study appear only after years of unglamorous practice.

nuance.analogy: A dividend is like a share of the harvest from a field you co-own: the field produces, and each owner receives a portion.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dividendum, "something to be divided," from dividere (to divide).
common_mistakes: Confusing dividend with divisor or quotient in math; in arithmetic the dividend is the number being divided.
Pronouncing it with a long i in the second syllable ("dih-VY-dend").
Saying "dividends" for a single payment without considering that Americans often use the plural for regular payments.

dividend.etymology: From Middle French *dividende*, from Latin *dīvidendum* (“thing to be divided”), future passive participle of *dīvidō* (“to divide”), *divide* + *-end*.

senses.definition: Only used in lie doggo and play doggo.
A dog.
senses.example: Look at that fluffy doggo wagging its tail at the park.

core.definition: In the phrases 'lie doggo' or 'play doggo', staying hidden and quiet so as not to be noticed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final vowel is a long 'oh' sound. Keep the first vowel the same as in 'cot' or 'caught'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly humorous; it describes lying low or keeping quiet.
nuance.usage_note: Doggo is mainly British slang and is rarely used in American speech. Americans say 'lie low', 'keep a low profile' or 'stay under the radar' for the same meaning. You might hear 'lie doggo' in a British novel, but in the United States it sounds unusual.

distinctions.note: 'Lie low' is the common American equivalent and is more natural in U.S. speech.
'Keep a low profile' describes avoiding attention in general; 'lie doggo' suggests staying still and hidden.

examples.everyday: When the neighbors knocked, we lay doggo until they gave up and left.
examples.professional: When the budget cuts came, the team played doggo and waited for management to decide.
examples.analytical: Rather than confront the flaw in the report, the committee chose to lie doggo through the review.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat that stays still under the couch when the vacuum is running.
nuance.etymology: From dog (noun), with an informal -o suffix; British slang.
common_mistakes: Using it as an American everyday word instead of 'lie low'.
Using 'doggo' to mean a dog, which is an informal and mainly British usage.

doggo.etymology: The noun is from *dog* + *-o*, perhaps after the adverb.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or situated in the central business district.
senses.example: John walked every day to his downtown job.

senses.definition: In or towards the central business district.
senses.example: You need to go downtown four blocks.

senses.definition: Outside the three-point line, or generally far from the basket.
senses.example: That shot came from way downtown!

senses.definition: The main business part of a city or town, usually located at or near its center.
senses.example: The downtown has several new coffee shops near the river.

senses.definition: The human genitalia.
Heroin.
senses.example: He had been buying downtown for years before his family staged an intervention.

core.definition: The central business district of a city or town, where most offices, shops, and public buildings are.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, DOWN, and make the second syllable a clear, equal-stress town with a flapped t sounding like a soft d. Keep the vowel in both syllables full and American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a place, and it is used in everyday talk about going into the city.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use downtown very often in ordinary speech: 'I'm going downtown' or 'Where's downtown?' It is used as a noun, adverb, and adjective. In British English, the usual phrase is city centre, so Americans would not usually say that.

distinctions.note: City center is a neutral, sometimes more general term; downtown in America usually names the commercial core of a city.
Uptown usually refers to a more affluent or residential district in some cities, while downtown is the main business area.

examples.everyday: Let's meet downtown after work and grab dinner near the theater.
examples.professional: Our new office is downtown, so the commute is easier for most of the team.
examples.analytical: The downtown district reflects a city's history, where commerce, government, and public life once converged.

nuance.analogy: Downtown is like the heart of a city: blood flows through it, and most of the city's activity is pumped through that center.
nuance.etymology: From down plus town, referring to the lower or central part of a town.
common_mistakes: Using the British 'city centre' in American speech.
Writing 'down town' as two words.

conversation.text: I work downtown, so I take the train every day.
Parking downtown costs a fortune on weekdays.
We went downtown for dinner and a show.

senses.definition: A technique for regularizing a neural network by discarding a random subset of its units.
senses.example: Adding dropout to the hidden layers helped the model generalize better to new data.

senses.definition: Someone who has left an educational institution without completing the course.
senses.example: The politicians of the world are mere political university dropouts.

senses.definition: Someone who has opted out of conventional society.
senses.example: The dropout had left the city and lived in a van, off the grid.

senses.definition: One who suddenly leaves anything, or the act of doing so.
senses.example: Half the students who started the bootcamp became dropouts before the first month ended.

senses.definition: The slot in the frame that accepts the axles of the wheels.
senses.example: Check that the dropout in the frame holds the rear axle firmly before tightening.

senses.definition: A damaged portion of a tape or disk, causing a brief omission of audio, video, or data.
senses.example: The backup tape had a dropout near the end, so the last chapter of the file was lost.

senses.definition: Momentary loss of an electronic signal.
senses.example: A brief dropout in the cable signal cut the call twice before the line went dead.

core.definition: A person who has left school or a program before finishing it.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable, DROP, which is the noun pattern. The verb drop out instead stresses OUT, so the two forms shift stress.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral; it is often associated with lacking credentials, but the word itself is descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dropout for someone who left high school or college without finishing, as in high school dropout or college dropout. The label can carry stigma, though some people use it proudly in success stories. In data science and AI, dropout is also a technical term for a regularization method that randomly disables units during training, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A graduate has completed a program; a dropout has left before finishing.
Dropout rate is the percentage of people who leave; dropout is the person or, in AI, the technique.

examples.everyday: He's a college dropout, but he got hired at a tech company anyway.
examples.professional: Our program has a lower dropout rate since we added weekly check-ins with mentors.
examples.analytical: The label dropout describes absence from a credential, not absence of learning, and many critics of credentialing have made this argument.

nuance.analogy: It is like a runner who leaves the race before the finish line.
nuance.etymology: From the phrasal verb drop out, with the noun formed by compounding its two parts.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words when used as a noun; the noun is one word, dropout.
Assuming dropout always means failure; in machine learning it is a training method.

conversation.text: Dropout randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training, which reduces overfitting.
Dropout is turned off at inference time, so remember to put the model in eval mode.
In everyday English, a dropout is someone who left school before finishing.

senses.definition: In a dull manner; without liveliness; without luster.
senses.example: The old lamp glowed dully in the corner, its brass tarnished and its glass fogged with dust.

senses.definition: (rare) Dim, indistinct.
senses.example: In the dully lit basement, I could barely make out the outlines of the old boxes.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: In a flat, listless, or unexciting way; without energy, brightness, or interest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -y is an 'ee' sound, not 'eye'. The vowel in 'dull' is the short 'uh' of 'cut'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests lack of energy, interest, or spirit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dully mostly in descriptive writing, such as fiction or reviews, to show how someone looked, spoke, or moved. In speech, people more often say 'flatly', 'blankly', or 'without any energy'. The adjective sense, meaning dim or indistinct, is rare, and you will mostly see it in old texts or poems.
word_family: dulling (noun or adjective, from the verb dull)

distinctions.note: 'Dimly' describes weak light or vision, as in 'dimly lit'; 'dully' describes feeling, sound, or manner, as in 'dully throbbing'.
'Flatly' describes a tone with no emotion; 'dully' suggests a lack of interest or energy.
'Blankly' describes a face or stare with no expression; 'dully' can describe a manner, a sound, or a pain as well.

examples.everyday: He nodded dully when I asked if he wanted more coffee, like he hadn't slept at all.
examples.professional: She answered dully during the review, as if she had already given up on the project.
examples.analytical: The poem's refrain repeats dully, mirroring the speaker's exhaustion and the monotony of his days.

nuance.analogy: Like a light behind frosted glass: present, but without shine.
nuance.etymology: From dull, from Old English dol, plus the suffix -ly, forming an adverb.
common_mistakes: Confusing dully with dimly; 'dimly lit' is the usual phrase for weak light.
Saying 'dully' for 'boringly' in a presentation review; 'boringly' is more natural there.

related: dulling (noun or adjective, from the verb dull)

senses.definition: The ability to last a long time by virtue of the power to resist stress or force.
senses.example: Engineers tested the durability of the bridge's steel cables against years of salt air.

core.definition: The ability of a product, material or system to last a long time without breaking or wearing out.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on BIL, the third syllable. Reduce the first two syllables to 'door-uh'. In American speech, the r is clear, and the final syllable is 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a valued quality in products, materials and software.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'durability' when comparing products, such as phones, boots or cookware, and in technical contexts like software reliability or engineering. In a product review, people might say 'the durability is impressive'. It is a neutral to formal word, so in casual speech people often say 'how long it lasts' instead.

distinctions.note: Reliability means consistent performance over time, while durability means physically or structurally lasting a long time under stress.
Strength is the ability to resist force at a moment, while durability is about lasting through repeated use or time.

examples.everyday: I bought these hiking boots because the durability is supposed to be great, even on rough trails.
examples.professional: The team ran load tests to check the durability of the new server hardware before we deployed it to production.
examples.analytical: Durability in engineering is not the same as permanence, because a durable structure must still yield to stress in ways that keep it intact.

nuance.analogy: Durability is like a good pair of work gloves: they keep their shape and protection after hundreds of uses.
nuance.etymology: From durable, from Latin durabilis, from durare, 'to last'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'DUR-a-bil-i-ty', which makes the word sound off.
Confusing 'durability' with 'durable' in a sentence where a noun is needed.

durability.etymology: From Middle English *durabilite*, from Old French *durabilité*, from Latin *dūrābilitās* (“durability”).

senses.definition: The extent to which a resource is used for the intended purpose.
senses.example: The efficiency of this loudspeaker is 40%.
