senses.definition: The extent to which time is well used for the intended task.
senses.example: The efficiency of the planning department is deplorable.

senses.definition: A one-room apartment.
senses.example: I have an efficiency available June through July.

senses.definition: The ratio of useful work to energy expended. Often given the symbol η.
senses.example: The efficiency of this loudspeaker is 40%.

senses.definition: (dated) The quality of producing an effect or effects.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: The ability to get a result with little wasted time, money, energy, or materials; how well a resource is used for its purpose.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, FISH, and the -ency ending is a reduced 'un-see', not 'en-SEE'. The 'ci' is pronounced like 'sh', so avoid saying 'ef-fi-SEN-see'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Efficiency is generally praised, though a very efficient person can sometimes sound cold if the word is used without warmth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use efficiency constantly at work, in engineering, and in everyday talk about appliances, cars, or routines. In statistics, a statistical efficiency describes how precisely an estimator uses data, with lower variance meaning higher efficiency. Saying 'That's a very efficient process' in a meeting is natural and approving.

distinctions.note: Efficiency is about doing something with less waste; effectiveness is about whether it achieves the desired result at all.
Productivity measures output produced, often per worker or per hour, while efficiency measures how well inputs are turned into that output.

examples.everyday: My new washing machine has great energy efficiency, so my electric bill dropped.
examples.professional: If we automate the reporting pipeline, we can improve efficiency and free up two analysts for modeling work.
examples.analytical: An estimator is judged not only by whether it is unbiased but by its efficiency, which compares how much variance it leaves against the best possible bound.

nuance.analogy: Efficiency is like a well-tuned car that goes far on a single tank of gas.
nuance.etymology: From Latin efficientia, from efficere, to accomplish, from ex- plus facere, to make.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as 'ef-fi-SHEN-cy'; the stress is on FISH.
Pronouncing the ending as 'en-see' with full vowels; it is reduced to 'un-see'.

senses.definition: (of a player) Receiving cards from the dealer first, before any other players.
senses.example: Under these rules, the player to the dealer's left is eldest and receives the first cards dealt.

senses.definition: (of a hand) Having higher, or superior cards.
senses.example: With three aces and a king, my hand was eldest, so I took the first trick.

senses.definition: The eldest child in a family, or individual in a group.
senses.example: My eldest is starting college in the fall, and I still can't believe it.

core.definition: Oldest, used especially for the first-born child among siblings or for the oldest member of a family or group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EL. The ending is -ist, not -est, and it is a short, quick sound, so do not add an extra vowel after the d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes age and birth order without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eldest mostly before a noun to describe siblings, such as 'my eldest son', and it is usually used for family members. For people in general, 'oldest' is more common, and eldest is rarely used for objects. In card games such as bridge, eldest is a technical term for the player to the dealer's left, but that sense is specialized.

distinctions.note: Oldest is the general superlative and can describe people, objects or places; eldest is mainly used for children and family members.
Elder is used for the older of two siblings and as a noun for a church office; eldest is used for three or more, though many speakers ignore this rule today.

examples.everyday: My eldest is starting college this fall, which still feels strange to me.
examples.professional: She's the eldest of the five partners, so she usually leads the strategy meetings.
examples.analytical: Primogeniture rules once made the eldest son the principal heir, shaping property and status across generations.

nuance.analogy: Like the first step on a staircase: the one who came first in the family line.
nuance.etymology: From Old English eldest, the superlative of eld or eald, 'old'; related to the word elder.
common_mistakes: Using eldest for objects or places, such as 'the eldest building'; use 'oldest' instead.
Saying 'eldest' for two siblings, where 'elder brother' or 'older brother' is more natural in American English.

senses.definition: To supply electricity to; to charge with electricity.
senses.example: to electrify a cable

senses.definition: To cause electricity to pass through; to affect by electricity; to give an electric shock to.
senses.example: to electrify a limb, or the body

senses.definition: To adapt (a home, farm, village, city, industry, vehicle, railroad) for electric power.
To strongly excite, especially by something delightful or inspiring; to thrill.
senses.example: Her performance in the play electrified the audience.

senses.definition: To make electric.

core.definition: To supply a place or machine with electric power, or to thrill or excite people strongly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LEK. The final -fy is a diphthong that sounds like 'eye', so it is not 'fih'. Keep the r clear in the middle of the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when used technically, positive when describing an exciting speech or performance.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, electrify most often describes making a railroad, car, or building use electricity, or describing an audience that is suddenly excited. Americans say 'electrified the crowd' with a positive sense. For a literal shock, say 'shock' or 'give a shock'.

distinctions.note: Energize means to give energy or motivation; electrify is stronger and suggests a sudden, visible excitement.
To shock is to surprise or to give an electric jolt; electrify more often means a thrilling effect or converting something to electric power.

examples.everyday: Her speech at the wedding electrified everyone, and people were still talking about it hours later.
examples.professional: The company plans to electrify its entire delivery fleet within five years.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that a bold idea can electrify a culture, changing its sense of what is possible.

nuance.analogy: To electrify a crowd is like plugging a crowd into a live socket: the energy spreads through everyone at once.
nuance.etymology: From electric plus the verb suffix -ify, 'to make into'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'electrify me' in casual speech to mean 'give me a shock'; it sounds odd.
Stressing the last syllable, as in ih-lek-TRY-fy; the stress is on LEK.

senses.definition: Of the sky or the heavens, and particularly relating to the highest celestial sphere in premodern cosmology; celestially refined.
senses.example: The empyrean light of the dawn sky made the mountains look otherworldly and pure.

senses.definition: (historical) The highest heaven, supposed by the ancients to be a region of pure light and fire or else composed of ether, and sometimes seen as the dwelling-place of God or other divine beings; the highest celestial sphere according to ancient and medieval astronomy.
senses.example: Dante's poem describes the empyrean as the final dwelling place of God and the blessed.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The highest heaven, in ancient and medieval cosmology a region of pure fire or light, often seen as God's dwelling.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on 'REE' and a light secondary stress on 'em'. The 'pi' sounds like the English word 'pie', and the 'ian' ending is reduced to 'un'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and elevated. It suggests the sublime, the divine, or the most exalted place.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in literature, history of science, and religious writing about the cosmos. It is rare in conversation. For the everyday idea of heaven, 'heaven' or 'the sky' is what most people say. Use 'empyrean' when you want to sound deliberately lofty or historical.

distinctions.note: Heaven is the everyday and theological word, while empyrean specifically names the highest sphere in ancient or medieval cosmology.
Firmament is the sky or vault of heaven in older Biblical language, while empyrean is the fiery outermost region in ancient cosmology.

examples.everyday: When my grandmother talked about her late husband, she sometimes said he had gone up to the empyrean, though she usually just said heaven.
examples.professional: In the museum guide I wrote, I described the ceiling fresco as showing the empyrean, the highest heaven of the old cosmos.
examples.analytical: Dante's Paradiso moves through the spheres toward the empyrean, where the divine light is no longer mediated by any celestial body.

nuance.analogy: Like the top floor of a tall building where the air is thinnest and the view is widest.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'empyrium', from Greek 'empyrios', fiery, from 'en' in and 'pyr' fire.
common_mistakes: Using it as a common word for sky in everyday speech, which sounds stiff.
Mispronouncing it with the stress on the first syllable.

empyrean.etymology: From Latin *empȳreus*, from Ancient Greek *ἐμπύριος*, from *ἐν* (“in”) + *πῦρ* (“fire”) (whence English *pyre*).

senses.definition: To make into an emulsion.

core.definition: To mix two liquids that normally separate, such as oil and water, into a smooth, stable blend called an emulsion.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'MUL', and the vowel is the American 'uh' sound, as in 'cut', not 'oo' as in 'pool'. The final syllable 'fy' rhymes with 'sky'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a process, with no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'emulsify' in cooking when they talk about making mayonnaise, vinaigrette, or hollandaise, and in food science or cosmetics. In a kitchen, a cook might say 'Whisk slowly so it emulsifies.' It is a more technical word than 'mix' or 'blend', so use it when the separation of the liquids is the point.

distinctions.note: 'Mix' is general and everyday, while 'emulsify' specifically means combining liquids that would normally separate into a stable blend.
'Blend' can mean any combining of ingredients, while 'emulsify' implies that the result stays uniform and does not separate.

examples.everyday: Whisk the egg yolk and oil slowly so they emulsify into a thick mayonnaise.
examples.professional: The formula is designed to emulsify the oil and water at room temperature so the product stays stable on the shelf.
examples.analytical: High-shear mixing allows the blender to emulsify two immiscible liquids into a dispersion that remains stable for weeks.

nuance.analogy: Emulsifying oil and water is like introducing two shy people at a party: with the right host and steady effort, they begin to mix and stay together.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'emulgere', to milk out, through the French 'émulsion' and the verb formed in English.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'emulsify' with 'emulate', which means to imitate or copy someone else.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as 'oo', as in 'ee-MOOL-sih-fy', rather than the American 'uh' sound.

senses.definition: Contained; held within a container.
senses.example: The gas is completely enclosed within the bottle.

senses.definition: Surrounded by a wall, fence or similar barrier.
senses.example: an enclosed garden

senses.definition: Having closed slats.
senses.example: The enclosed louvers on the attic vent kept birds out while letting air circulate.

core.definition: Surrounded by walls, fences or other barriers, or placed inside a container, envelope or area that is closed off.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KLOHZ, the second syllable. The first syllable is a reduced 'uhn', and the final -ed is a /d/ after the z sound, not a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes physical space or containment without emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say enclosed for a porch, garage, space or container with walls or a roof around it. In business writing, Please find enclosed sounds stiff and dated; in email, people usually write attached.

distinctions.note: Closed means not open, while enclosed means surrounded by walls or barriers on all sides.
Covered means having a top or roof, while enclosed means fully surrounded, though an enclosed space is often also covered.
Attached is the usual word for a file sent with an email, while enclosed is more common in paper letters or formal documents.

examples.everyday: We sat on the enclosed porch, out of the rain, and watched the storm roll across the yard.
examples.professional: The enclosed spreadsheet has the Q3 numbers, so please check the totals before our review on Thursday.
examples.analytical: An enclosed system exchanges no matter with its surroundings, which is what makes it a useful model in thermodynamics.

nuance.analogy: An enclosed room is like a box with a lid: nothing gets in or out except through a door.
nuance.etymology: From enclose, from Old French enclore, from Latin inclaudere, to shut in.
common_mistakes: Using enclosed for an email attachment; Americans normally say attached.
Adding an extra syllable, saying en-clo-zed instead of uhn-KLOHZD.

senses.definition: A person who delivers an encomium or eulogy.

core.definition: A person who delivers an encomium, which is a formal speech or piece of writing praising someone highly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KOH. The ending -ast rhymes with 'fast', with a short a, not 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, but it can suggest a flattering or overly devoted speaker.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word found in literary criticism, classical studies and formal writing. Americans would more often say 'a speaker who praised him' or 'a eulogist' at a funeral. It sounds elevated, so it is out of place in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: A eulogist usually speaks at a funeral, while an encomiast praises a person in any setting.
A panegyrist gives formal public praise, and the words are close, but panegyrist is more common in historical writing.

examples.everyday: My grandfather is our family encomiast, and he praises every meal Grandma cooks in full sentences.
examples.professional: The keynote speaker became the company's encomiast, praising the team's work in a long and polished tribute.
examples.analytical: Pindar appears in literary history as an encomiast whose victory odes celebrated athletes and the families who sponsored them.

nuance.analogy: An encomiast is like a press agent who writes only the glowing review.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'enkōmiastēs', from 'enkōmion' (a song of praise).
common_mistakes: Confusing encomiast (the person) with encomium (the praise itself).
Using encomiast for an ordinary fan; it implies a formal, deliberate speaker.

senses.definition: A papal letter, intended for general circulation in the Catholic Church.
senses.example: The pope's encyclical on climate and poverty was read aloud in parishes across the country this Sunday.

senses.definition: Intended for general circulation.
senses.example: The encyclical newsletter was sent to every member of the congregation, not just the board.

core.definition: A formal letter from the pope addressed to bishops and the faithful, usually on doctrine, morality, or social issues.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, SIK, and the final syllables are weak. The 'c' is a hard 'k' sound, so don't soften it to 's' in the middle of the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a formal, authoritative term in Catholic contexts and rarely used outside them.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use encyclical mainly in religious, academic, and news contexts, such as reports on a new papal letter. In everyday conversation people say 'papal letter' or 'the pope's letter.' As an adjective it is rare outside technical writing.

distinctions.note: A papal bull is a formal, solemn document with a seal, while an encyclical is a letter addressed broadly to the church.
An epistle is a letter in general or a New Testament letter; an encyclical is specifically a papal circular letter.

examples.everyday: The pope's new encyclical on care for creation got a lot of attention in the news this week.
examples.professional: Our policy team summarized the encyclical's main recommendations for the nonprofit's board.
examples.analytical: The encyclical grounds its social teaching in natural law and the dignity of the human person.

nuance.analogy: An encyclical is like a public letter from a leader that is meant to be read by everyone in a community, not just one person.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin encyclicus, from Greek enkyklios, meaning circular or general.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'c' as 's' in the middle of the word.
Confusing it with 'encyclopedia' because the two words share a root.

encyclical.etymology: From *encyclicus* + *-al*, from Ancient Greek *ἐγκύκλιος* (“circular, general”), from *ἐν-* + *κύκλος* (“circle”).

senses.definition: A person who is skilled at, or practices, endocrinology.
senses.example: My endocrinologist adjusted my thyroid medication after the latest blood test came back.

core.definition: A doctor who specializes in hormones, the endocrine glands that produce them, and related disorders such as diabetes and thyroid problems.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NAH, the third syllable. The -ist ending is a short ist, not est, and the -ol- in the middle is reduced to a light uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds professional and specialized, and patients often say it with respect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'my endocrinologist' in everyday talk, especially about diabetes or thyroid care. Insurance plans frequently require a referral from a primary care doctor first. In casual speech people may shorten it to endo.

distinctions.note: An internist is a general doctor for adults; an endocrinologist has additional training in hormone disorders.
A gastroenterologist treats the digestive system; an endocrinologist treats hormone-producing glands.

examples.everyday: My sister is seeing an endocrinologist because her thyroid levels keep swinging.
examples.professional: Please copy the endocrinologist on the discharge summary so the diabetes plan stays consistent across clinics.
examples.analytical: A good endocrinologist reads hormone panels as parts of feedback loops rather than as isolated numbers.

nuance.analogy: Like a mechanic who specializes in the car's internal messaging system rather than its brakes or tires.
nuance.etymology: From endocrinology plus the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Confusing endocrinologist, the doctor, with endocrinology, the field of study.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying en-duh-kri-NOL-uh-jist instead of stressing the third syllable.

senses.definition: One who enforces.
senses.example: The city's new housing inspector is a tough enforcer of the building codes.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of traffic enforcer.
A hired strongman, especially working for the underworld.
senses.example: The mobster hired a bruising enforcer to collect debts from the card players downtown.

senses.definition: The member of a group, especially of a gang, charged with keeping dissident members obedient.
senses.example: When Danny questioned the boss, the gang's enforcer pinned him against the alley wall.

core.definition: A person or thing that makes sure rules, laws, or orders are obeyed; also a hired thug for criminals.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on FAWR, the second syllable. The final -er is an American r-colored reduced vowel, so say sur, not say or ay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for rule enforcers, such as parking or code enforcers. Strongly negative for the criminal sense, a violent hired muscle man.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English an enforcer usually means someone who applies rules, such as a parking enforcer. In crime news and novels, it means a hired thug for a gang, which is strongly negative. In hockey and other sports, an enforcer is a player whose role is to intimidate opponents.

distinctions.note: Police officer is the general term for the job; enforcer is broader and can describe non-police roles, like parking enforcers.
Bully is a general word for a person who intimidates; enforcer describes a role of applying rules or intimidation.
A guardian protects people; an enforcer compels people to obey.

examples.everyday: The traffic enforcer on Main Street gave me a ticket for parking in the bus lane.
examples.professional: We need a clear enforcer for the data retention policy, someone who owns the deletion jobs.
examples.analytical: In Hobbes's account, the sovereign becomes the enforcer whose power keeps the war of all against all in check.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee: the rules belong to everyone, but the enforcer is the one who blows the whistle.
nuance.etymology: From enforce plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using enforcer for the rule itself; the rule is not an enforcer.
Saying in-FOR-cer with a long o; the vowel is the aw of law.

senses.definition: To give a soul or place in the soul.
senses.example: Many creation myths tell of a deity who is believed to ensoul humans.

core.definition: To give a soul to something, or to fill a person, place, or thing with spiritual life, meaning, or inner character.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, and make it a clear long o, as in 'soul.' Do not add an extra syllable or pronounce the 'l' as a vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, depending on context, often used in theology, philosophy, and poetry
nuance.usage_note: Americans seldom use 'ensoul' in everyday talk. It appears in religious writing, philosophy, and literature, especially when discussing what gives life or dignity to a being. In casual speech you would say 'give life to' or 'bring to life' instead.

distinctions.note: Animate means to give life or motion in a general way, while ensoul specifically means to give a soul or spiritual inner life.
Inspire means to motivate or fill with creative energy, while ensoul is a more philosophical word about giving a soul.

examples.professional: In the design review, someone argued that a conversational assistant cannot be ensouled by its training data alone.
examples.analytical: Some theologians argue that God ensouls human beings at creation, while others locate the soul in a process of growth.

nuance.analogy: To ensoul something is like lighting a lamp inside a clay pot, so the light shines through the whole form.
nuance.etymology: From en- (to make or put into) plus soul, from Old English 'sawol.'
common_mistakes: Using 'ensoul' as a synonym for 'enroll,' which is a different verb.
Putting a preposition after the verb, as in 'ensoul with,' when the object should follow directly.
nuance.biblical_note: The word 'ensoul' does not appear in Scripture, but Genesis 2:7 in the Revised Standard Version says that God formed man from the dust and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living being. The Hebrew word here is 'nephesh' (living being, soul), and the Greek Septuagint uses 'psyche' for the same idea.

senses.definition: Having a title.
senses.example: Her book is entitled 'My Autobiography'.

senses.definition: Having a legal or moral right or claim to something.
senses.example: As a natural-born citizen I am entitled to run for president.

senses.definition: Convinced of one's own righteousness (self-righteousness) or the justifiability of one's actions or status, especially wrongly so; demanding and pretentious.

core.definition: Having a legal or moral right to something; also, expecting special treatment without having earned it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -TY-, and the -tled ending is a single syllable where the l is syllabic, so the word is not 'in-TY-tul-ded'. The final d is short and quiet.

nuance.connotation: Mixed. Saying someone is entitled to something is neutral, but calling a person 'entitled' is a negative criticism of arrogance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'entitled to' neutrally for rights, as in 'You're entitled to a refund.' In casual speech, 'entitled' alone often criticizes someone who expects special treatment, as in 'He's so entitled.' Be careful with this second sense, which can sound rude; a natural reply is 'You have a point, but let's be fair.'

distinctions.note: Deserving means worthy because of merit or effort, while entitled in the critical sense means expecting a reward that is not earned.
Privileged describes an advantage from birth or status, and is more neutral; entitled focuses on the attitude of expecting it.
Arrogant is a broader word for overconfidence or pride, while entitled is specifically about demanding rights or special treatment.

examples.everyday: Some customers in the line were so entitled, yelling at the cashier as if it were her fault.
examples.professional: Employees are entitled to overtime pay under federal law if they work more than forty hours a week.
examples.analytical: A theory of justice must explain why some claims are truly entitled and others are merely demands.

nuance.analogy: Like a ticket that guarantees your seat; the right is real, but the attitude of expecting it everywhere is the problem.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of entitle; see entitle.
common_mistakes: Using 'entitled' as a neutral word in all contexts, when the criticizing sense is common and can sound rude.
Confusing 'entitled to' (a right) with 'entitled' as a criticism of attitude.
Pronouncing it with an extra syllable as 'in-TY-tuld-ed'.

senses.definition: The action of entering, or going in.
senses.example: make a grand entrance

senses.definition: The act of taking possession, as of property, or of office.
senses.example: the entrance of an heir upon his inheritance, or of a magistrate into office

senses.definition: The place of entering, as a gate or doorway.
senses.example: Place your bag by the entrance so that you can find it easily.

senses.definition: The right to go in.
senses.example: You'll need a ticket to gain entrance to the museum.

senses.definition: The entering upon; the beginning, or that with which the beginning is made; the commencement; initiation.
senses.example: a difficult entrance into business

senses.definition: The causing to be entered upon a register, as a ship or goods, at a customhouse; an entering.
senses.example: His entrance of the arrival was made the same day.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of entrance fee.
senses.example: I want to go to this place but the entrance is too expensive.

senses.definition: The angle which the bow of a vessel makes with the water at the water line.
senses.example: The naval architect measured the entrance angle at the waterline of the hull.

senses.definition: The bow, or entire wedgelike forepart of a vessel, below the water line.
senses.example: The entrance of the ship was damaged when it struck the submerged rock.

senses.definition: The beginning of a musician's playing or singing; entry.
senses.example: The violin's entrance came in a beat too early, ruining the quiet opening.

senses.definition: To delight and fill with wonder.
senses.example: The children were immediately entranced by all the balloons.

senses.definition: To put into a trance.
senses.example: The hypnotist's soothing voice entranced the whole audience within minutes.

core.definition: The place, such as a door, gate or opening, through which you go into a building or room.

pronunciation.tip: In the noun, stress falls on the first syllable, EN. The verb is stressed on the second syllable, en-TRANS, so the same spelling changes its stress with its part of speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to a physical place or to the act of coming in, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say the main entrance, the side entrance or the front entrance when giving directions. In very casual talk, people often say the door or the way in. The verb sense, to delight or fill with wonder, is literary and usually appears as entranced or entrancing.

distinctions.note: Entry can mean the act of coming in or permission to enter, and it is also used in phrases like entry-level. Entrance more often names the physical doorway.
Entryway is the small space just inside a door, often in a house. Entrance can refer to the doorway itself or the whole building entry.
Exit is the opposite: the way out. It is the most natural antonym in everyday American English.

examples.everyday: Meet me at the main entrance by the fountain, and we can go in together.
examples.professional: Please use the north entrance, since the lobby entrance is closed for renovation this week.
examples.analytical: The author's entrance into the debate in 1968 reshaped how economists framed inflation.

nuance.analogy: An entrance is like the threshold of a house: it is the point you cross to go from outside to inside.
nuance.etymology: From Old French entrer, 'to enter', from Latin intrare.
common_mistakes: Using the verb stress on the noun, saying en-TRANS for the doorway.
Using entrance when you mean the admission fee, which Americans usually call admission.

senses.definition: To catch in a trap or snare.
To lure (someone), either into a dangerous situation, or into performing an illegal act.
senses.example: Investigators worried the sting operation would entrap innocent teenagers into buying drugs.

core.definition: To trick someone into a harmful or illegal situation, or to catch someone in a trap.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, TRAP, and the first syllable is a weak 'in'. Do not say the prefix as 'ahn', and keep the r clear before the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies deception, manipulation or being caught against your will.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use entrap for trickery, such as a con artist, a scam or an illegal sting, and in literal contexts such as animals caught in traps. In everyday talk, people more often say trapped or caught. The legal sense is most important in news and courtroom discussions.

distinctions.note: Trap is the more general word for catching something. Entrap often implies deception or manipulation.
Ensnare is more literary and often means catching someone in a net or web. Entrap is more common in legal and everyday contexts.
Lure means attracting someone toward something. Entrap means catching them once they are there.

collocations: entrapped in a web of lies

examples.everyday: Don't let those hidden fees entrap you into signing a long contract.
examples.professional: The vendor's terms could entrap us in higher costs if we don't renegotiate soon.
examples.analytical: Marx argues that capitalist structures entrap workers in cycles of wage dependence.

nuance.analogy: To entrap someone is like setting a trap with bait, so the victim walks in willingly and then cannot get out.
nuance.etymology: From en- (in) plus trap.
common_mistakes: Using entrap as a noun, when the noun is entrapment.
Saying entrap to someone, when the usual pattern is entrap someone into doing something.

entrap.etymology: From Middle French *entrapper*, *entraper*, from Old French *entraper*, *antraper* (“catch in a trap”), equivalent to *en* + *trap*.

senses.definition: Of or relating to epithets.
senses.example: epithetic names for the gods

senses.definition: Of or relating to epithesis.
senses.example: an epithetic vowel

core.definition: Relating to an epithet, a descriptive word or phrase added to a name, such as Alexander the Great.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on THET, the third syllable, and the final -ic is a short 'ik'. Do not stress the first syllable as in the noun EP-ih-thet, which has its stress there.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a feature of language and can be mildly critical when applied to insulting language.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective mainly in literary criticism, linguistics and writing about style. In everyday talk they would more likely say a nickname or a label. When applied to people's insults it can sound pointed, so use it carefully in arguments.

distinctions.note: Epithet is the noun for the descriptive word or phrase itself, while epithetic is the adjective describing a style or language that uses epithets.
A nickname is usually a familiar name given by friends, while an epithet is a descriptive title, often more formal or lasting.

examples.everyday: His nickname for the coach was pretty epithetic, and everybody on the team used it.
examples.professional: The report uses epithetic language like reckless and bloated to describe vendors, which makes it sound biased.
examples.analytical: The poet's epithetic style, which attaches a stock descriptive phrase to each hero, follows the conventions of oral epic.

nuance.analogy: Epithetic language is like a name tag that tells you what someone is known for, such as the Wise or the Bold.
nuance.etymology: From Greek epitheton 'something added', from epitithenai 'to put on'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the adjective epithetic with the noun epithet, as in saying 'an epithetic' for a descriptive phrase.
Putting the stress on the first syllable instead of THET.

senses.definition: Synonym of epitomizer, a writer of epitomes.

core.definition: A person who writes an epitome, a short summary of a longer work, especially a book or history.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PIT, the second syllable. The middle -uh- is a reduced vowel, so the word is three quick syllables after the stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a scholarly or editorial craft.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word outside literary or classical scholarship. In everyday work you would say someone who writes summaries or a summarizer. It is a precise, somewhat old-fashioned term, so use it in writing about history or editing rather than in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Epitomizer is the more common modern synonym, while epitomist is rarer and more specialized in literary history.
A summarizer is a general term for anyone who condenses text, while epitomist is a literary term for a writer of formal epitomes.

examples.everyday: My teacher friend is a real epitomist, condensing whole textbooks into one-page handouts for her students.
examples.professional: The editor hired an epitomist to produce one-page summaries of each long report for the board.
examples.analytical: Medieval epitomists such as Justin preserved Pompeius Trogus's lost histories, so their work now stands in for the originals.

nuance.analogy: An epitomist is like a film trailer writer who has to show the whole plot in two minutes without spoiling the meaning.
nuance.etymology: Formed from epitome, from Greek epitomē 'a cutting short', with the suffix -ist for a person who does a practice.
common_mistakes: Using epitomist for a person who simply sums up a meeting; in ordinary work say summarizer.
Stressing the first syllable as in EP-ih-tomist; the stress belongs on PIT.

senses.definition: One who makes equal; a balancer.
senses.example: Death is the great equalizer.

senses.definition: A device that balances various quantities.
A device, such as a bar, for operating two brakes, especially a pair of hub brakes for an automobile, with equal force.
senses.example: The mechanic adjusted the equalizer so both rear hub brakes grabbed with equal force.

senses.definition: Any device for equalizing the pull of electromagnets.
senses.example: The engineer added an equalizer to keep the pull of both electromagnets balanced.

senses.definition: A conductor of low resistance joining the armature ends of the series field coils of dynamos connected in parallel.
senses.example: The low-resistance equalizer connects the armature ends of the parallel dynamos.

senses.definition: A sliding panel to preserve the lateral stability of an aeroplane.
senses.example: The pilot adjusted the equalizer panel to keep the airplane stable in crosswinds.

senses.definition: A set of arguments where two or more functions have equal values; the solution set of an equation.
senses.example: The equalizer of f and g consists of every x where the two functions agree.

senses.definition: A morphism whose codomain is the domain of a parallel pair of morphisms and which forms part of the limit of that parallel pair. Equivalently, a morphism which equalizes a parallel pair of morphisms in a limiting way, which is to say that any other morphism which equalizes that parallel pair factors through this limiting morphism; and moreover such factorization is unique.
senses.example: In category theory, an equalizer of two parallel morphisms is their universal limit.

senses.definition: A weapon, usually a blackjack or gun.
senses.example: He pulled an equalizer from his jacket and told the bartender to open the register.

senses.definition: A goal, run, point, etc. that equalizes the score.
An electronic audio device for altering the frequencies of sound recordings.
senses.example: I added an equalizer to the mix to boost the bass on the vocals.

core.definition: A goal or point that ties the score, or a device that adjusts the balance of sound frequencies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -er is a reduced American 'er' sound. Remember that the spelling uses z, which is American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive for a team; it is good for the trailing side and a neutral fact for others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use equalizer most often in sports, especially soccer and basketball, to mean a goal or score that ties the game. In audio, it refers to a graphic or parametric equalizer on a stereo or in a studio. Spell it with z, as Americans do; 'equaliser' is British.

distinctions.note: A tie is the state of equal score, while an equalizer is the goal or point that creates that tie.
Equalization is the process of making things equal, while an equalizer is the thing that does it.

examples.everyday: Our team got an equalizer in the last minute, so we're going to overtime.
examples.professional: Turn the equalizer down a little on the call, because the voices sound harsh.
examples.analytical: The equalizer in the second half changed the tactical balance, forcing the leading side to defend more deeply.

nuance.analogy: Like a fulcrum on a seesaw that lets both sides come back to level.
nuance.etymology: From equalize, from Latin aequalis 'equal', with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'equaliser', which is the British form.
Using equalizer to mean a tie in general, when it refers specifically to the goal that creates the tie.

senses.definition: The art or sport of horseriding; the skill required for it.

core.definition: The sport or skill of riding horses, including competitive disciplines such as dressage, show jumping, and eventing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KWES. The middle syllables are reduced, and the final '-ism' sounds like 'iz-um', with a short 'i' and a weak final schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests skill and athleticism, though it can also sound a bit elite.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'horseback riding' or 'riding' for everyday activity and use 'equestrianism' for formal or competitive riding sports. Using it for a casual trail ride may sound stiff or overly formal.

distinctions.note: Horseback riding is any activity of riding horses, while equestrianism refers to the organized sport or skill, usually competitive.
Dressage is one specific equestrian discipline, while equestrianism covers all of them.

examples.everyday: My niece started weekend lessons, but she says equestrianism costs far more than soccer ever did.
examples.professional: Our sponsorship team is considering equestrianism because its audience closely matches our target market.
examples.analytical: Equestrianism has long combined athletic discipline with aristocratic display, which complicates how we judge the rider's skill.

nuance.analogy: Like figure skating, where the athlete and a partner must perform as one unit.
nuance.etymology: From equestrian, from Latin equester, 'of horsemen', from equus, 'horse', with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'ih-kwes-TRAY-nism'.
Using 'equestrianism' for casual riding, which sounds overly formal to most Americans.

senses.definition: To speak using double meaning; to speak ambiguously, unclearly or doubtfully, with intent to deceive; to vacillate in one's answers, responding with equivoques.
senses.example: The senator continued to equivocate when reporters pressed him about the budget.

senses.definition: To render equivocal or ambiguous.
senses.example: Poorly chosen wording can equivocate survey results, making the trend hard to interpret.

core.definition: To speak vaguely or deliberately ambiguously, usually to avoid giving a clear answer or to mislead.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KWIV, with a lighter secondary stress on KAYT. Say the middle syllables quickly with a schwa, and do not pronounce the 'qu' as 'k' alone; it is a 'kw' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies evasion, dishonesty, or a reluctance to commit to a clear answer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'equivocate' in news, politics, and serious conversation when someone avoids a direct answer. It is a bit formal, so casual speakers often say 'dodge the question' or 'beat around the bush.' Saying 'Stop equivocating' to a friend sounds pointed but natural.

distinctions.note: 'Lie' means stating something false; 'equivocate' means avoiding a clear truth through careful wording.
'Hedge' is a softer, everyday word for qualifying a statement; 'equivocate' implies evasion or misleading intent.

examples.everyday: Stop equivocating and just tell me whether you want to go to dinner tonight.
examples.professional: The vendor kept equivocating about the delivery date, so I asked for a written commitment.
examples.analytical: A philosopher who equivocates on the term 'necessary' makes the argument appear valid when it is not.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who will not call a foul, pointing in different directions to avoid making a decision.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin aequivocare, 'to call by the same name,' from aequivocus.
common_mistakes: Using 'equivocate' with 'about' or 'on' inconsistently; both are acceptable, but 'on' is more common with questions.
Pronouncing the middle syllable too strongly.

equivocate.etymology: From Late Middle English *equivocaten*, from Medieval Latin *aequivocātus*, perfect passive participle of *aequivocō* (“to be called by the same name”), from Late Latin *aequivocus* (“ambiguous, equivocal”).

senses.definition: An irrational fear of or aversion to work.

core.definition: An irrational fear of or strong aversion to work or having to work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The last syllable is a reduced 'uh'. Do not pronounce the 'g' as a 'j' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or humorous; it can sound like a clinical label or a joke about laziness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this term in everyday speech. It appears in psychology writing or in humorous remarks about being lazy. Saying it casually at work may sound joking or condescending. A plain alternative is 'hates work' or 'avoids work'.

distinctions.note: 'Laziness' describes unwillingness to work, while 'ergophobia' suggests a strong fear or aversion, though it is not a standard clinical diagnosis.
'Procrastination' is delaying tasks, while 'ergophobia' refers to a deeper aversion to work itself.

examples.professional: Calling a colleague ergophobic in a meeting would sound unprofessional, so I just say they need more motivation.
examples.analytical: Labeling ergophobia as a pathology may obscure the structural conditions that make work feel hostile.

nuance.analogy: Ergophobia is a fear of the workbench, as if the job itself were a spider in the room.
nuance.etymology: From Greek ergon, 'work', and phobia, 'fear'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a serious clinical diagnosis; it is not standard in US medicine.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: The act of eschewing.
senses.example: Her eschewal of sugar surprised her friends at the holiday dinner.

core.definition: The deliberate avoidance or rejection of something considered harmful, unnecessary, or morally wrong, often as a matter of principle.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on CHOO, and the 'ch' sounds like 'church'. The ending is a reduced 'uhl', so do not say 'ess-CHEW-wall'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, since it describes a principled or careful choice to avoid something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use eschewal in everyday speech and prefer 'avoidance' or simply 'avoiding' something. You will mainly see it in formal writing, religious or moral discussions, or essays on lifestyle choices. The verb 'eschew' is more common than the noun, and it usually sounds slightly formal or literary.

distinctions.note: Avoidance is the everyday and neutral word for keeping away from something, while eschewal suggests a conscious, principled rejection.
Abstinence refers to refraining from pleasures or substances, often for health or religious reasons, while eschewal can apply to any practice, habit, or method.

examples.everyday: In her retirement toast, she praised his eschewal of shortcuts over forty years of teaching.
examples.professional: The committee's eschewal of unverified benchmarks kept the final report credible.
examples.analytical: Her eschewal of metaphysical speculation marks a deliberate break with earlier scholastic method.

nuance.analogy: Eschewal is like a careful cook who steps around a dangerous ingredient on purpose, not because they forgot it was there.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English eschewen, from Old French eschiver, of Germanic origin related to 'shy'.
common_mistakes: Using eschewal for an accidental or passive avoidance, when the word requires a deliberate choice.
Mispronouncing the stress as ess-CHEW-wall, with the second syllable stressed.
nuance.biblical_note: The English verb eschew comes from Hebrew and Greek ideas of turning away from evil. In Job 1:1 the RSV describes Job as one who turned away from evil, using the Hebrew sur, 'to turn aside.' Psalm 34:14 urges the reader to depart from evil and do good, and 1 Peter 3:11 says the one who loves life should turn from evil and do right. Scripture treats such turning away as an active moral choice, not merely a passive avoidance.

senses.definition: Unifying; having the power to shape disparate things into a unified whole.

core.definition: Able to shape many different elements into one unified whole; unifying disparate things into a coherent form.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, PLAS. Many learners stress the first syllable, but the ending -tic is a short, unstressed-sounding ik.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a mind or work that brings disparate things together.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use esemplastic outside literary criticism, philosophy, and essays about Coleridge. Speakers use it to praise a writer's or thinker's power to unify. In casual talk, say 'bringing everything together' or 'unifying.'

distinctions.note: Unifying is plain and common, while esemplastic is technical and tied to Coleridge's theory of imagination.
Coherent describes logical consistency, but esemplastic describes an active power that forms a whole out of separate parts.

examples.everyday: At the end of the toast, Dad somehow tied all our different stories together, which was almost esemplastic.
examples.professional: Her product strategy is esemplastic, bringing the separate teams' roadmaps into one coherent plan.
examples.analytical: Coleridge's esemplastic imagination, which he described in the Biographia Literaria, shapes fragments into an organic unity.

nuance.analogy: Like a skilled chef who blends many separate ingredients into a single sauce where no flavor stands out alone.
nuance.etymology: Coined by Samuel Taylor Coleridge from Greek roots meaning 'into one' and 'shaping' or 'molding'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the third.
Confusing it with 'simplistic', which means oversimplified.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of et cetera: and so on; used to note that the rest of a list or piece of information has been left out on the assumption that it is similar or already known.
senses.example: The grocery shop sells cucumbers, lettuce, radishes, etc.

core.definition: Short for et cetera, meaning 'and so on' or 'and other things,' used at the end of a list to show that more items exist.

pronunciation.tip: Say 'et' with a clear t, then stress 'SET' and reduce the last syllables to 'er-uh.' Do not say 'et-SET-ra' or 'ek-SET-ra.' In speech, Americans often say the full words 'et cetera.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound slightly dismissive if you use it to skip important items, but in ordinary lists it is perfectly polite.
nuance.usage_note: Americans write etc. at the end of lists in emails, notes and documents, and say 'et cetera' or 'and so on' aloud. In casual speech, people say 'and stuff' or 'and so on' more often. Do not write 'and etc.,' because etc. already means 'and.'

distinctions.note: Etc. refers to things or items; et al. refers to people, especially authors.
And so on is the natural spoken form; etc. is mainly for writing and notes.

examples.everyday: Can you grab milk, eggs, bread, etc., on your way home?
examples.professional: Please bring your laptop, badge, and onboarding forms, etc., to the Monday session.
examples.analytical: The model uses age, income, education, etc., but these are examples and not an exhaustive list of variables.

nuance.analogy: Like a trailing ellipsis: it points to the rest of the list without writing it out.
nuance.etymology: From Latin et cetera, 'and the rest.'
common_mistakes: Writing 'and etc.' (redundant, since etc. already means 'and').
Pronouncing etc. as 'ek-setter-uh' instead of 'et SET-er-uh.'

etc.etymology: From Middle English *et cetera*, *etc.*, from Latin *etc.*, an abbreviation of *et cetera* (“and the rest [of the things]; and the other things”).

senses.definition: The usual friendly reply when the server checks on you.
senses.example: When the server asked how things were, I smiled and said, 'Everything's great, thanks.'

core.definition: A friendly, polite answer meaning all is fine, used when someone asks how things are going.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EV and on GRAYT and THANKS, with the middle syllables light. Everything's often sounds like EV-ree-thingz, with the t softened and linked quickly.

nuance.connotation: Positive and polite. It is a friendly, low-stakes way to end a small-talk exchange.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this to a server, cashier, neighbor, or coworker who asks how things are going. It is usually a quick reply, and the other person often just says glad to hear it or have a great day. If something is actually wrong, people may say pretty good or can't complain instead.

distinctions.note: Good, thanks is shorter and more general, while everything's great is slightly more enthusiastic.
Not bad is a mild, understated reply that suggests things are okay but not wonderful.

examples.everyday: A server at a restaurant asks, How is everything tonight? and you reply, Everything's great, thanks.
examples.professional: A coworker asks in the hallway how the project is going, and you answer, Everything's great, thanks, and keep walking.
examples.analytical: In American small talk the reply Everything's great, thanks, performs politeness more than it reports the actual state of affairs.

nuance.analogy: It works like a polite handshake: a quick, warm exchange that keeps the conversation moving rather than a full report.
common_mistakes: Answering with a long explanation when the other person only wants a quick friendly reply.
Saying thank you alone without the rest of the phrase, which sounds abrupt in this context.

conversation.text: Everything's great, thanks. Could I get a refill?
Oh, everything's great, thanks. The pasta is amazing.
Everything's great, thanks; we're all set for now.

senses.definition: A growing mutation, usually abnormal.
senses.example: The biologist described the excrescent as a small, unusual growth on the stem.

senses.definition: (historical) A sound in a word without etymological reason.
senses.example: "B" in "nimble" is an excrescent.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Growing out in an abnormal or morbid manner or as a superfluity.
senses.example: The doctor removed the excrescent tissue growing along the patient's left wrist.

core.definition: Growing out abnormally or as an unnecessary extra, especially a malformed outgrowth on something that should be smooth or plain.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SKRES. The first syllable is reduced to 'ik,' not 'ex' with a long vowel, and the ending is a quick 'uhnt,' not 'ent.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word implies something abnormal, superfluous or unwelcome growing out of a thing where it does not belong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. You will see it in medical writing, literary criticism, or careful descriptions of design or language. In everyday speech, people say 'extra,' 'abnormal growth,' or 'bump.' The related noun 'excrescence' is more common than the adjective.

distinctions.note: Excessive means too much or beyond a reasonable amount. Excrescent means an outgrowth that is malformed or superfluous in its very nature, not just too large.
Superfluous is a common everyday word for something unnecessary. Excrescent is more formal and implies a growth that sprouts out of something, often in an abnormal way.

examples.professional: The editor cut the excrescent paragraphs that just repeated the introduction in different words.
examples.analytical: Critics argued that the baroque ornament was excrescent to the building's original design, adding nothing to its structure.

nuance.analogy: Like a wart sprouting on a smooth stone: something that grows out of place and adds nothing to what it grows on.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excrescere, 'to grow out,' from ex- ('out') and crescere ('to grow').
common_mistakes: Confusing excrescent with excessive; excrescent refers to a malformed or superfluous outgrowth, not just an amount.
Using it in casual speech, where 'extra' or 'bump' sounds more natural to Americans.

senses.definition: To make use of, to apply, especially of something nonmaterial; to bring to bear.
senses.example: He considered exerting his influence on John to gain an advantage for himself.

senses.definition: To put in vigorous action.
senses.example: I exerted myself in today's training.

core.definition: To use force, effort, influence or power to produce a result or to affect something or someone.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, and the vowel is the r-colored ur sound in bird. The x sounds like gz, so the first syllable is ig, not eg-zert with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive (exert effort, exert influence) or negative (exert pressure, exert control over someone). It implies deliberate, active force.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exert with effort, influence, pressure, control or force, as in 'She exerted her influence on the board.' Exert yourself is used for physical effort, often with a slightly formal or humorous tone, as in 'Don't exert yourself in this heat.' In casual speech people usually say put in effort or push, so exert sounds more at home in writing, business or politics.

distinctions.note: Exercise in the sense of use a right or power is close to exert, but exert emphasizes force or pressure, while exercise sounds more like putting a right into practice.
Apply is neutral and common, as in apply pressure; exert is stronger and implies more deliberate force or power.
Strain means pushing yourself so hard that you may be harmed; exert is neutral and does not imply harm.

examples.everyday: I don't want to exert myself too much in this heat, so let's walk slowly.
examples.professional: The manager tried to exert pressure on the vendor to meet the deadline.
examples.analytical: Institutions exert influence over individuals not only through law but through the norms that shape what people consider reasonable.

nuance.analogy: To exert is like leaning into a heavy door: you apply your weight deliberately to make it move.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exserere, 'to stretch out' or 'thrust forth', from ex 'out' and serere 'to join'.
common_mistakes: Using exercise instead of exert in phrases like exert influence; exercise influence is not natural.
Using exert with the wrong preposition: say exert pressure on someone or exert influence over something.
Pronouncing the stressed vowel as a long ee, as in eg-ZERT.

exert.etymology: From Latin *exsertus*, past participle of *exserō* (“to stretch or thrust forth or out”), from *ex-* + *serō*.

senses.definition: An instance of exhibiting, or something exhibited.
senses.example: The museum's new exhibition features paintings borrowed from private collections in Europe.

senses.definition: A large-scale public showing of objects or products.
senses.example: There was an art exhibition on in the town hall.

senses.definition: A public display, intentional or otherwise, generally characterized as negative.
senses.example: a shameful exhibition

senses.definition: A demonstration of personal skill or feelings.
senses.example: Her exhibition of calm under pressure impressed the entire selection committee.

senses.definition: A game which does not impact the standings for any major cup or competition.
senses.example: The Sunday match was merely an exhibition, so nobody cared about the final score.

senses.definition: To participate in sexual exhibitionism.

core.definition: A public show of art, objects, or products, often held in a museum, gallery, or trade fair.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'BISH,' with secondary stress on the first syllable. The vowels in the unstressed syllables reduce to a short 'ih' and 'un' sound, and the ending is 'shun.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a public showing, and can be negative only when used for a bad display.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'exhibition' for large public shows such as art exhibitions, trade shows, and museum displays. A smaller display is usually called an 'exhibit.' In sports, an 'exhibition game' is a preseason or non-scoring game. In a negative sense, as in 'a shameful exhibition,' the word sounds formal or literary.

distinctions.note: 'Exhibit' is one item or one displayed set, while 'exhibition' is the whole public event.
'Show' is broader and more casual, while 'exhibition' is formal and usually for art, objects, or products.
'Exhibitionism' means the habit of showing off or displaying oneself for attention, not an organized public show.

examples.everyday: We went to the car show, which was a huge exhibition of old cars.
examples.professional: The company is showing its new products at the trade exhibition in Chicago next month.
examples.analytical: The exhibition of the artist's late work challenges our assumptions about progress in modern painting.

nuance.analogy: Like a museum display, but scaled up to fill a whole building.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exhibitio, from exhibere 'to hold out, present'.
common_mistakes: Using 'exhibition' for a single object, where 'exhibit' is correct.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as 'ek-si-BISH-un' with weak vowels or 'EK-sih-bish-un'.
Confusing 'exhibition' (a public show) with 'exhibitionism' (showing off for attention).

senses.definition: To explain meticulously or in great detail.
senses.example: My homework is to explicate a poem.

core.definition: To explain something thoroughly and in careful detail, unfolding its layers of meaning or logic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EK. The -ate ending is a long ayt, and the middle syllables are short and reduced, so say EK-splih-kayt, not ex-PLAY-kate.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests careful, thoughtful analysis.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use explicate mainly in literary criticism, philosophy, theology, and academic writing. In everyday speech they would say explain or spell out. Using explicate in casual conversation can sound overly formal, though it is natural in a seminar or essay.

distinctions.note: Explain is the general everyday word, while explicate implies a detailed, layered analysis of a text or idea.
Elucidate means to make something obscure clear, while explicate means to unfold a complex idea step by step.
Expound is also formal and means to set out a theory at length, but explicate focuses more on interpreting a text or argument.

examples.everyday: Could you explicate the rules of that card game for me? I'm lost at the scoring part.
examples.professional: I'll explicate the model's assumptions in the appendix so reviewers can check each step.
examples.analytical: The essay explicates the idea that grace precedes human response, drawing out its implications for free will.

nuance.analogy: Like unfolding a folded map one panel at a time until the whole route is visible.
nuance.etymology: From Latin explicatus, past participle of explicare, to unfold or explain.
common_mistakes: Using explicate as a casual synonym for explain in everyday conversation, where it sounds stiff.
Stressing the last syllable, as in ex-plih-KATE, which is not the usual American pattern.

senses.definition: Able to be possessed or overcome.

core.definition: Able to be captured, conquered, or overcome by force or assault.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPUG, the second syllable. The 'gn' is pronounced as 'g' followed by 'n', and the ending is an unstressed 'uh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a rare, learned word from historical or literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Expugnable is very rare in American English and appears mainly in older literature or in discussions of fortifications and military history. Americans would normally say 'vulnerable to attack' or 'capable of being taken by force' in everyday or modern writing. Use it only when you want a precise, learned tone.

distinctions.note: Vulnerable is common and means open to harm or attack; expugnable is a rare, technical or literary word for something that can be conquered.
Inexpugnable is the opposite and means impossible to conquer; expugnable is its rare, positive counterpart.

examples.everyday: That old castle looks strong, but the historians say it was once quite expugnable.
examples.professional: The consultant described the legacy system as expugnable to any determined attacker, so we need stronger authentication.
examples.analytical: Classical strategists often asked whether a city was expugnable by siege or only by treachery.

nuance.analogy: An expugnable fortress is like a sandcastle at high tide: it looks solid but can be taken by a determined force.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expugnabilis, from expugnare, 'to take by storm', from ex- plus pugnare 'to fight'.
common_mistakes: Confusing expugnable with inexpugnable and using them as synonyms.
Using expugnable in everyday speech, where it sounds archaic.

senses.definition: Especially or extraordinarily fine or pleasing; exceptional.
senses.example: They sell good coffee and pastries, but their chocolate is exquisite.

senses.definition: Recherché; far-fetched; abstruse.
senses.example: The reviewer called his argument exquisite, though most readers found it far too precious to believe.

senses.definition: Of special beauty or rare excellence.
senses.example: The chef served an exquisite lemon tart with a delicate, almost translucent sugar glaze.

senses.definition: Exceeding; extreme; keen, in a bad or a good sense.
senses.example: exquisite pain or pleasure

senses.definition: Of delicate perception or close and accurate discrimination; not easy to satisfy; exact; fastidious.
senses.example: exquisite judgment, taste, or discernment

senses.definition: (rare) Fop, dandy.
senses.example: Every drawing room gossiped about the exquisite who wore silk waistcoats to breakfast.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Extremely beautiful, delicate, or refined; of the highest quality or skill.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EKS. The x is a /ks/ sound, and the final -ite is a weak, unstressed /ət/, not 'eet'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises fineness, beauty, or skill, and it can sound overblown when used for ordinary things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exquisite for fine craftsmanship, beautiful art, delicate food, or precise timing, usually in writing or formal speech. In casual talk people more often say 'really nice' or 'gorgeous.' Used sarcastically, it can mean 'terrible' (an exquisite mess), but that is informal. The sense 'fop' in dictionaries is archaic and not needed.

distinctions.note: Beautiful is general and common; exquisite implies a higher degree of refinement and delicacy.
Elegant stresses grace and good taste in style or form; exquisite stresses precision, delicacy, and intensity of quality.

examples.everyday: Wow, this cake is exquisite. Did you make the frosting yourself?
examples.professional: The designer's mockups have exquisite attention to detail, so the engineers should match the spacing exactly.
examples.analytical: Her essay offers an exquisite reading of the poem's imagery, attentive to every shift in tone.

nuance.analogy: An exquisite object is like a fine Swiss watch: every small part is precise and deliberately made.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exquisitus, 'sought out, carefully chosen,' from exquirere, 'to search out.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (ex-KWIZ-it); the stress is on the first syllable.
Using exquisite for ordinary good things in casual talk, which can sound overly formal.

exquisite.etymology: From Latin *exquīsītus* (“to be outsought”), perfect passive participle of *exquīrō* (“to outseek”).

senses.definition: To an extreme degree.

core.definition: To a very great degree; far more than usual or normal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -TREEM-, and the first syllable is a reduced 'ik'. The final -ly is a light 'lee' sound, not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral intensifier; it can attach to positive or negative adjectives.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extremely as a strong intensifier in everyday speech, as in 'extremely tired' or 'extremely helpful'. It is standard in both casual talk and formal writing. In casual speech, 'really' or 'super' is more frequent, but extremely is natural and slightly more emphatic. Avoid it with absolute adjectives like 'unique', which many Americans consider a mistake.

distinctions.note: Very is the everyday intensifier; extremely is stronger and suggests going beyond the normal range.
Really is casual and common in speech; extremely sounds more deliberate and is better suited to writing or careful speech.
Highly often pairs with positive or technical adjectives, like highly qualified; extremely works with any adjective, good or bad.

examples.everyday: The pad thai here is extremely spicy, so ask for it mild if you don't want to cry.
examples.professional: The model's accuracy on rare events is extremely sensitive to how we handle class imbalance.
examples.analytical: A theory that is extremely general may explain everything, which is exactly why it explains nothing in particular.

nuance.analogy: Like turning a dial past the highest mark on the scale.
nuance.etymology: From extreme plus the adverbial ending -ly, from Latin extremus, 'outermost'.
common_mistakes: Using extremely with absolute adjectives like 'unique' or 'perfect'; say 'really unusual' or simply 'unique'.
Using extreme where an adverb is needed, as in 'extreme tired' instead of 'extremely tired'.

senses.definition: A fluid that has exuded from somewhere; especially one that has exuded from a pore of an animal or plant.

core.definition: A fluid or substance that has seeped out of a plant or animal, especially through a wound, pore or damaged tissue, such as sap, resin or wound fluid.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EK. The final -ate rhymes with 'date', not 'it', and the x is pronounced as k plus s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical. It describes a substance without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exudate mainly in medicine, wound care, botany and forestry. A nurse might chart wound exudate as clear, serous or purulent, and a botanist might study tree resin. In everyday talk, people say 'fluid' or 'drainage' from a wound, or 'sap' or 'gum' from a tree.

distinctions.note: Discharge is a general word for any fluid leaving the body, while exudate specifically means fluid that has seeped out through inflamed or damaged tissue.
A secretion is made deliberately by a gland for a function, while an exudate leaks out through damaged or inflamed tissue.

examples.everyday: The bandage is soaked because the cut is still leaking exudate, so we should change it tonight.
examples.professional: Please note the color and odor of the exudate in the wound care log before the next dressing change.
examples.analytical: Amber forms when a conifer's resinous exudate hardens and traps insects, preserving them for millions of years.

nuance.analogy: Like a leaky window frame where moisture seeps out through the damaged seal, an exudate is fluid that escapes through damaged tissue.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exsudare 'to sweat out'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ate as 'uht' or 'it' instead of 'ayt'.
Confusing the noun exudate with the verb exude, which is the action of seeping out.

senses.definition: The hair that grows over the bone ridge above the eye socket.
A dormer, usually of small size, whose roof line over the upright face is typically an arched curve, turning into a reverse curve to meet the horizontal line at either end.
senses.example: The attic's eyebrow dormer lets in morning light and gives the old farmhouse roof a graceful curve.

senses.definition: A clump of waste fibres that builds up in a roller machine.
senses.example: The carding machine kept stopping because a large eyebrow of waste fibre had built up on the roller.

senses.definition: To build up waste fibres in a roller machine.
senses.example: If the rollers start to eyebrow, the operator must stop the machine and clear the fibres.

senses.definition: To signal with one's eyebrows.
senses.example: She eyebrowed me across the crowded room, silently asking whether I was ready to leave.

core.definition: The line of hair that grows on the bony ridge above each eye.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EYE. The second syllable rhymes with 'now' and 'how', not 'row'. Avoid pronouncing the word as 'eye-BROH', which is a common mistake.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; eyebrow shape and grooming can be discussed casually, and a raised eyebrow can signal doubt or interest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always say eyebrows in everyday talk, as in 'She has thick eyebrows.' The verb sense, to signal with the eyebrows, is more literary; in everyday speech, people say 'raise an eyebrow' to show surprise or skepticism. The word is also used of a small architectural dormer or a clump of fiber in a machine, but those are technical senses.

distinctions.note: Brow alone usually means the forehead in American speech, as in 'furrow your brow'; eyebrow is the hair itself.
An eyelash grows on the eyelid edge; an eyebrow grows on the bone ridge above the eye.

examples.everyday: My sister always plucks her eyebrows before a wedding, so her photos look sharp.
examples.professional: When the vendor said the audit would take one day, the whole team raised an eyebrow.
examples.analytical: In Renaissance portraiture, the raised eyebrow often signals a subject's skepticism toward the viewer's assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Like the shelf above a window that keeps rain from running down the glass; the eyebrow keeps sweat and water out of the eye.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ēagbrū, a compound of ēage (eye) and brū (brow).
common_mistakes: Using the singular for a pair, as in 'I have a thick eyebrow'; say 'thick eyebrows'.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'bro' with a long o; the vowel is the diphthong in 'now'.

eyebrow.etymology: From Middle English *eȝebreu*, alteration of Old English *ēaganbrū* (“eyebrow”), equivalent to *eye* + *brow*.

senses.definition: Positioned so as to face (in a particular direction)
senses.example: (Concluded on facing page)

senses.definition: Diverging in the direction of travel.
senses.example: The sign had two arrows facing outward, sending drivers in opposite directions from the exit.

senses.definition: The most external portion of exterior siding.
senses.example: The contractor replaced the cedar facing on the north wall after the storm.

senses.definition: Fabric applied to a garment edge on the underside.
senses.example: The tailor sewed a contrasting silk facing inside the collar to keep it stiff.

senses.definition: A powdered substance, such as charcoal or bituminous coal, applied to the face of a mold, or mixed with the sand that forms it, to give a fine smooth surface to the casting.
senses.example: The foundry dusted the mold with facing to give the bronze a smooth finish.

senses.definition: The collar and cuffs of a military coat, commonly of a different color from the rest of the coat.
senses.example: His dress uniform had dark blue facing on the collar and cuffs.

senses.definition: The movement of soldiers by turning on their heels to the right, left, or about.
senses.example: The sergeant barked an order for a facing movement to the left.

core.definition: Positioned so that its front or main side looks toward something, or located directly opposite something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FAY. The ending is a light sing with the ng sound, rhyming with placing, not a hard g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word describes direction or orientation and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use facing mostly to describe where something looks, as in an apartment facing the park or a house facing the street. Phrases like facing the music and facing a problem are common and natural, with facing the music being slightly informal. The noun facing, meaning a surface material on a wall or garment, is technical and used mainly by builders and sewers.

distinctions.note: Opposite describes the other side of a space or line, while facing describes the direction something points or looks.
Across suggests crossing a space, while facing emphasizes orientation toward something.

examples.everyday: Our apartment is on the fourth floor, facing the park, so we get good light in the mornings.
examples.professional: The team is facing a tight deadline, so we need to decide the scope by Friday.
examples.analytical: The orientation of many medieval churches, facing east toward Jerusalem, shaped the liturgy and the movement of the congregation.

nuance.analogy: Like a compass needle, which always points in a fixed direction.
nuance.etymology: Present participle of face, from Old French face, from Latin facies, face.
common_mistakes: Saying the ending as in singing with a hard g; say FAY-sing with the ng sound.
Saying I am facing to the door; the natural phrase is facing the door.

senses.definition: That has lost some of its former vividness and color.
senses.example: a faded tablecloth

senses.definition: That has lost some of its former strength or vigor.
senses.example: a faded rock star of the 1970s

senses.definition: High on drugs; stoned.
senses.example: He was faded on the couch, staring at the ceiling and laughing at nothing.

core.definition: Having lost some of its original color, brightness or strength over time, often from age, sun or use.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the ending a short 'id' sound after the d. Don't say 'fay-ded' with a long, separate 'ed' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. Faded jeans are often seen as stylish, while faded glory suggests loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly use faded for clothing, photographs, paint and walls, as in 'faded jeans.' It can also describe a glorious past, as in 'faded glory.' In slang, faded can mean high on drugs, but that sense is informal and can be confusing, so avoid it in most conversations.

distinctions.note: Washed out describes colors or people who look pale and tired; faded more often describes color that has been lost over time.
Faint means hard to see or hear; faded means it has lost color or strength over time.

examples.everyday: I love these faded jeans; they've gotten so soft after years of washing.
examples.professional: The slide was too faded to read on the projector, so I reprinted it in higher contrast.
examples.analytical: The poet describes a faded glory that still shapes the nation's sense of its own past.

nuance.analogy: A faded photo is like an old memory: the outline remains, but the colors have slowly drained away.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of fade, from Old French fade 'insipid, faded.'
common_mistakes: Using faded in a professional setting to mean drugged, which can cause confusion or embarrassment.
Pronouncing the ending as a separate syllable 'fay-ded.'

senses.definition: To be unsuccessful.
senses.example: Throughout my life, I have always failed.

senses.definition: Not to achieve a particular stated goal. (Usage note: The direct object of this word is usually an infinitive.)
senses.example: The truck failed to start.

senses.definition: To neglect.
senses.example: The report fails to take into account all the mitigating factors.

senses.definition: Of a machine, etc.: to cease to operate correctly.
senses.example: After running five minutes, the engine failed.

senses.definition: To be wanting to, to be insufficient for, to disappoint, to desert; to disappoint one's expectations.
senses.example: I've failed my parents many times growing up.

senses.definition: To receive one or more non-passing grades in academic pursuits.
senses.example: I failed English last year.

senses.definition: To give a student a non-passing grade in an academic endeavor.
senses.example: The professor failed me because I did not complete any of the course assignments.

senses.definition: To be wanting; to fall short; to be or become deficient in any measure or degree up to total absence.
senses.example: The crops failed last year.

senses.definition: To deteriorate in respect to vigor, activity, resources, etc. to become weaker.
senses.example: A sick man fails.

senses.definition: To become unable to meet one's engagements; especially, to be unable to pay one's debts or discharge one's business obligation; to become bankrupt or insolvent.
A failure, especially of a financial transaction (a termination of an action).
A failing grade in an academic examination.
A failure (something incapable of success).
Poor quality; substandard workmanship.
senses.example: The project was full of fail.

senses.definition: A piece of turf cut from grassland.
