pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'round,' which is pronounced with a reduced, r-colored first syllable 'uh.' Do not stress 'a' in 'around,' and keep 'head' short with an 'eh' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, often with a sense of struggle or eventual success.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for complicated ideas, rules, software, or instructions, often with 'can't' to express frustration. It is informal and fits meetings and casual talk alike. A natural reply is 'Take your time, it took me a while too.'

distinctions.note: 'Understand' is neutral and general, while 'get one's head around' emphasizes effort to grasp something hard or unfamiliar.
'Grasp' is more formal and can be literal, while 'get one's head around' is conversational and idiomatic.

collocations: can't get my head around it
get my head around the concept
get her head around the rules
take a while to get my head around
get our heads around the problem

examples.everyday: I still can't get my head around how the new phone settings work.
examples.professional: It took me a while to get my head around how the pipeline handles missing values.
examples.analytical: Students often cannot get their heads around the doctrine of the Trinity until they see how the early creeds were argued.

nuance.analogy: Like holding a large, awkward box and turning it until you can see all its sides, the mind works until the whole thing fits.
nuance.etymology: 'Head' comes from Old English 'heafod,' and 'around' combines 'a-' with 'round,' from Old French and Latin roots.
common_mistakes: Using 'get my head to understand' instead of 'get my head around.'
Pronouncing 'around' with a stressed first syllable, as in 'A-round.'

senses.definition: A function used to retrieve the value of some property of an object, contrasted with the setter.
senses.example: The class defines a getter for each private field so other code can read its value.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, gets.
senses.example: He was a real getter, always first to snag the best deals at auction.

senses.definition: A material which is included in a vacuum system or device for removing gas by sorption.
senses.example: Engineers added a titanium getter to the tube to absorb residual gases.

senses.definition: (historical) A miner who dug coal, contrasted with the putter, who took it to the surface.
senses.example: The getter swung his pick at the coal seam while the putter hauled the loads.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To remove gas by sorption, using a getter.
senses.example: Before sealing the tube, the technicians getter it to keep the vacuum pure.

core.definition: In programming, a method or function that returns the value of an object's property.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, GET. The final syllable is the reduced American 'er', not a full 'ur' or a rolled r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers use getter all the time in object-oriented code, often paired with a setter. In everyday speech the word means nothing special, so use 'accessor' or 'property' in general conversation. In vacuum technology, a getter is a material that absorbs gas.

distinctions.note: An accessor is the general term for both getters and setters; a getter is only the read-only part.
A property is a language feature that may use a getter behind the scenes; the getter is the function that reads it.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about it, the getter just returns the name field, nothing fancy.
examples.professional: I added a getter for the user's email so the view layer doesn't touch the raw field directly.
examples.analytical: A getter should be free of side effects, since callers assume that reading a property does not change the object's state.

nuance.analogy: Like a window in a locked room: you can look at what is inside, but the getter does not let you change it.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'get' with the agent suffix '-er'.
common_mistakes: Using 'getter' to mean a person who gets something; in English it is mainly a technical term.
Mispronouncing the final syllable as a full 'ur' sound; it is a reduced 'er'.

senses.definition: Gibberish, unintelligible speech.
senses.example: The old man's gibber from the back room made no sense to anyone at the table.

senses.definition: A stone or rock, of chalcedony or similar mineral, found strewn over arid regions of inland Australia; a gibber stone.
senses.example: Tourists photographed the gibber scattered across the red desert, glowing faintly in the afternoon sun.

senses.definition: Any small rock or stone, especially one used for throwing.
senses.example: The bored boys hurled a gibber at the tin can on the fence, cheering when it clanged.

senses.definition: A balky horse.
senses.example: The stubborn mare was a gibber, refusing every gate and planting her hooves whenever we neared the barn.

senses.definition: To jabber, talk rapidly and unintelligibly or incoherently.

core.definition: To talk rapidly and unintelligibly, in a jabbering or nonsensical way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the final syllable as a reduced 'er' with a rhotic r. Many learners add an extra vowel between the 'b' and 'r'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests meaningless or frantic talk that is hard to understand.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'gibber' in everyday speech; it sounds literary or old-fashioned. You are more likely to meet it in novels or older writing. In conversation, 'babble,' 'ramble,' or 'jabber' are more common choices.

distinctions.note: 'Jabber' is more common and often describes rapid, excited talk, while 'gibber' stresses that the speech is unintelligible.
'Babble' can describe the sound of running water or a baby's sounds; 'gibber' is more specifically about incoherent human speech.

examples.everyday: When he saw the spider, he started to gibber and jump around the kitchen.
examples.professional: During the outage call, the engineer began to gibber about logs, and nobody could follow him.
examples.analytical: The narrator's characters gibber in terror, and the author uses their broken speech to show a collapse of reason.

nuance.analogy: Gibbering is like a radio playing static over a station: the sound is there, but no message comes through.
nuance.etymology: Of imitative origin, probably related to the sound of unintelligible speech.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'gibber' with 'giggle' or 'gobble' because of similar sounds.
Using 'gibber' for ordinary talking; it implies incoherence, not just speed.

gibber.etymology: usually regarded as a (see *gibberish* for more).

core.definition: An ancient Hivite town in Benjamin, famous for its treaty with Joshua, its miracle of the sun standing still, and its role as a major sanctuary under Solomon.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -on is a reduced schwa-n sound, not a full 'own'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a place name from Scripture, used in Bible study and historical discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Gibeon in sermons, Bible study and historical writing about Israel. It is not used in everyday talk. People often mention it when discussing Joshua's battles or Solomon's worship at the high place.

distinctions.note: Gibeah was Saul's home town and the site of the crime in Judges 19; Gibeon was a Hivite city known for the treaty with Joshua.
Gibbethon was a town in Dan known for sieges; Gibeon was in Benjamin and was famous for the sun standing still.

examples.everyday: Our small group read about the sun standing still over Gibeon, and everybody had a different idea about it.
examples.professional: In the lesson on Joshua, I contrast the battle of Gibeon with the later treaty, so students see how the Israelites kept their promises.
examples.analytical: The Chronicler's notice that the tabernacle stood at the high place in Gibeon (1 Chronicles 16:39) raises questions about worship before the temple was built.

nuance.analogy: Like a city on a famous map, Gibeon is known more for a few dramatic moments than for its daily life.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Gibʿôn, a place name; its meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying the last syllable as 'own', which sounds like a different word.
Confusing Gibeon with Gibeah or Gibbethon.
nuance.biblical_note: Gibeon (Hebrew gibʿôn) is a town in Benjamin, inhabited by the Hivites (Joshua 9:3-7). The Gibeonites tricked Joshua into a treaty, and Joshua fought for them against an alliance of kings (Joshua 10:1-14), where the sun is said to stand still over Gibeon. Solomon offered sacrifice at the high place of Gibeon (1 Kings 3:4-5), and 2 Samuel 21 recounts the famine and the execution of Saul's descendants there.

core.definition: A native of Gath, one of the five Philistine cities; in 2 Samuel, men such as Ittai and Obed-edom are called Gittites.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GIT, and the final syllable rhymes with kite. Don't stress the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical and descriptive term with no modern negative or positive meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in Bible study, preaching and scholarship. It can be a noun or an adjective, as in 'a Gittite warrior'. In casual conversation, say 'a man from Gath' if you need to be understood.

distinctions.note: Philistine is the general name for the people; Gittite specifies a person from the city of Gath.
Hittites were a separate people of Anatolia; the similar spelling is a common confusion.

examples.everyday: Did you know the Bible mentions Obed-edom the Gittite in the story of the ark?
examples.professional: In my sermon on loyalty, I contrast Ittai the Gittite with the court advisers who abandoned David.
examples.analytical: The narrator's identification of Ittai as a Gittite signals a Philistine from Gath who swears loyalty to David, heightening the scene's irony.

nuance.analogy: Like a name that tells you someone's hometown, such as Bostonian or Dallasite, but for an ancient city.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Gittî, 'of Gath', and Gath means 'winepress'.
common_mistakes: Confusing Gittite with Hittite, which names a different people
Stressing the second syllable instead of GIT-ite
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Gittî, 'of Gath', from Gath, meaning 'winepress'. Gath was one of the five Philistine cities (Joshua 13:3). In 1 Samuel 17:4 Goliath is described as being of Gath, linking the name to the Philistine threat to Israel. In 2 Samuel 6:10 Obed-edom the Gittite receives the ark of the covenant into his house, and in 2 Samuel 15:18-22 Ittai the Gittite leads six hundred men from Gath who remain loyal to David in exile.

senses.definition: To collect (fruit, grain, or other produce) from a field, an orchard, etc. after the main gathering or harvest.
senses.example: After the combine passed, our neighbors gleaned wheat from the edges of the fields.

senses.definition: To gather (something, now chiefly something intangible such as experience or information) in small amounts over a period of time, often with some difficulty; to scrape together.
senses.example: She gleaned useful insights from years of customer interviews and scattered notes.

senses.definition: To take away (someone's) possessions; to strip (someone) bare.
senses.example: The highwaymen gleaned the travelers of their coins, their horses, and even their boots.

senses.definition: To collect fruit, grain, or other produce after the main gathering or harvest.
senses.example: After the combine passed, our neighbors gleaned wheat from the edges of the fields.

senses.definition: Of an animal, especially a bat or a bird: to feed by picking up or plucking (prey, mainly arthropods such as insects) from various places.
senses.example: Warblers gleaned caterpillars from the branches of the oak trees all morning long.

senses.definition: Of an animal, especially a bat or a bird: to feed by picking up or plucking prey, mainly arthropods such as insects, from various places.
senses.example: Warblers gleaned caterpillars from the branches of the oak trees all morning long.

core.definition: To gather information or facts bit by bit from various sources, often with effort.

pronunciation.tip: One long vowel, like 'ee', and a clear final 'n'. Do not add a second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests careful, patient work that produces something useful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glean in reports, interviews, and professional writing, such as 'we gleaned some insights from the survey'. In casual conversation, people usually say 'pick up' or 'figure out' instead.

distinctions.note: Gather is neutral and can refer to objects or information. Glean implies picking up small useful pieces from a larger, scattered source.
Learn is direct and general. Glean suggests indirect learning, collecting clues or details over time.

examples.everyday: I didn't get the full story from her, but I gleaned from her texts that the project got delayed.
examples.professional: We can glean useful signals from the customer feedback before the next sprint review.
examples.analytical: Historians must glean meaning from fragmentary sources, reading silences as carefully as explicit statements.

nuance.analogy: Like a farmer walking a field after the harvest, picking up what the big machines missed.
nuance.etymology: From Old French glener, of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Using glean for big, obvious facts. It implies collecting small pieces with effort.
Confusing the verb with the noun 'gleaning', which is a related but separate form.

glean.etymology: The verb is derived from Late Middle English *glenen* (“to gather, glean; to gather together, collect”), from Old French *glener*, *glainer*, from Late Latin *glenare*, the present active infinitive of *glenō* (“to make a collection”); further etymology…

senses.definition: To undergo, suffer, experience.
senses.example: I went through a lengthy immigration process before I was allowed across the border.

senses.definition: To examine or scrutinize (a number or series of things).
senses.example: Every morning, she went through her mail over a cup of coffee.

senses.definition: To travel from one end of something to the other.
senses.example: The train went through the tunnel.

senses.definition: To execute or carry out.
senses.example: They went through the process step by step and ended up with Beef Wellingtom.

senses.definition: To enact or recite the entire length of (something).
senses.example: The orchestra went through the entire symphony without a single mistake during the rehearsal.

senses.definition: To use up or wear out (clothing etc.).
senses.example: Her family drinks so much milk that they go through two gallons a week.

senses.definition: To progress to the next stage of something.
senses.example: If United don't lose by more than 2 goals, they should go through to the next round.

senses.definition: To reach an intended destination after passing through some process.
senses.example: My payment hasn't gone through yet.

senses.definition: To beat, fight or attack (someone).
senses.example: Three men went through him in the alley, leaving him bruised and bleeding.

senses.definition: To be present and intense.
senses.example: The cardamom goes through the cake.

senses.definition: (dated) To rob (someone), especially after searching through their clothes.
senses.example: The stagecoach passenger swore the highwayman had gone through his pockets and taken everything.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To experience something difficult, such as a hard time, a loss, or a process that takes effort.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on THROO, the second word. Make the th in through a voiceless th, with the tongue between the teeth, and do not pronounce it as t or f.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. It is often sympathetic when describing hardship, and it is practical when describing a process.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'go through' when talking about tough times, such as 'She's going through a divorce.' It is also common for checking procedures, as in 'We have to go through the checklist.' A common sympathetic reply is 'I'm sorry, that sounds really hard.' Do not confuse the hardship sense with the travel sense.

distinctions.note: Go over means to review something, while go through often means to examine each item in a list or to experience something.
Experience is a neutral, formal verb for undergoing something, while go through is more conversational and often suggests difficulty.

examples.everyday: My sister is going through a tough time right now, so please be patient with her.
examples.professional: Before the release, we need to go through every item on the checklist with the security team.
examples.analytical: Many people go through a crisis of faith before they can articulate what they actually believe.

nuance.analogy: Like walking through a tunnel: you are inside the hard stretch until you reach the other end.
common_mistakes: Using 'go through' for emotional hardship without an object, as in 'he is going through'; the hardship is usually named.
Confusing the review sense with 'go over', which is more about reviewing the whole thing.

conversation.text: She's going through a tough divorce.
I went through all my emails but couldn't find it.
We go through a gallon of milk every two days.
Did your loan for the new house go through?
My card didn't go through, so I paid with cash.

senses.definition: One who gobbles:
senses.example: My dog is such a gobbler: she can empty her food dish in less than a minute.

senses.definition: A turkey.
Especially, a male turkey.
One who eats food very quickly, without decorum.
senses.example: My dog is such a gobbler: she can empty her food dish in less than a minute.

core.definition: A male turkey, especially one heard gobbling during the spring hunting season.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GAHB, and the final syllable is a weak r-colored vowel, so say GAHB-ler, not GOH-bler.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a casual rural or hunting word.
nuance.usage_note: Gobbler is common in rural areas, on farms and among hunters, especially in spring turkey season. At Thanksgiving, families usually say turkey rather than gobbler. The sense of a person who eats greedily exists but is rare, and calling someone a gobbler would sound rude.

distinctions.note: Tom is the technical or hunting term for a male turkey, while gobbler is more casual.
Turkey is the general everyday word for the bird or its meat and covers both males and females.

examples.everyday: We saw a big gobbler strutting across the back pasture this morning.
examples.professional: Our poultry supplier said the gobblers will ship on Monday, along with the hens.
examples.analytical: The gobbler's display is a classic case of sexual selection, where ornament serves to attract mates.

nuance.analogy: A gobbler is the male turkey's loud advertisement for himself.
nuance.etymology: From gobble, from the male turkey's gobbling call, with the suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Thinking gobbler means any turkey; it usually means a male.
Using gobbler at a Thanksgiving table, where turkey is the expected word.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, goes.
Anything, especially a machine such as a motor car, that performs well, or operates successfully.
senses.example: I bought her secondhand, but she's a good little goer.

senses.definition: A foot (body part).
A fire incident in progress.
(dated) A horse, considered in reference to its gait.
senses.example: a safe goer
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A person who regularly goes to a particular kind of place or event, as in 'churchgoer' or 'moviegoer'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GOH. The final syllable is a reduced American 'r-colored' vowel, so the word ends like 'GOH-er' without a strong 'ur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes habit or attendance without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use goer almost always in compounds such as churchgoer, moviegoer, theatergoer, or regular goer. On its own, it is rare and can sound odd. For a single event, say attendee; for a place, say visitor or customer.

distinctions.note: An attendee is someone officially present at an event, often a formal meeting or conference; a goer is a habitual visitor to a kind of place or event.
A visitor is someone who comes to a place once or occasionally; goer implies regular attendance.

examples.everyday: Our church has a lot of regular goers who come every Sunday morning, even in the winter.
examples.professional: The conference drew about five hundred goers, well above last year's turnout, so we need a bigger room next time.
examples.analytical: Churchgoers and moviegoers differ in motives and loyalty in ways that a simple attendance count cannot capture.

nuance.analogy: A goer is like a regular at a coffee shop: the word describes the habit of showing up, not the quality of the visit.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gān (to go), with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using goer alone for a single event; say attendee or guest instead.
Confusing goer with go-er in a compound; in standard American spelling, use the closed compounds like churchgoer.

senses.definition: Sumptuously dressed.
Very beautiful.
senses.example: All the contest judges agreed that Brigitt was absolutely gorgeous.

senses.definition: (rare) Very enjoyable, pleasant, tasty, etc.
senses.example: Hummus is absolutely gorgeous.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Extremely beautiful, attractive, or impressive in appearance, such as a view, a dress, or a person.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the or sound is the vowel in door, not the long o of go. The last syllable is a reduced jus, with no separate ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Strongly positive. In casual speech it can be exaggerated, and calling a stranger gorgeous can sound flirtatious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gorgeous constantly in everyday talk about weather, food, views, clothes, and people, often with a strong tone. For a friend's partner or a stranger, it can sound flirtatious, so beautiful or nice is safer. A natural reply to a compliment is 'Thanks, it was a lot of fun.' In writing, gorgeous can sound informal, so use stunning or striking for a more formal tone.

distinctions.note: Beautiful is more general and neutral, while gorgeous is stronger and more emotional.
Stunning means striking at first sight, often used for something surprising, while gorgeous suggests richer, more lasting beauty.
Lovely is gentler and more pleasant, often used for kind or pleasant things, while gorgeous is more intense.

examples.everyday: Look at that sunset, it's absolutely gorgeous tonight!
examples.professional: The new dashboard design is gorgeous, and users finish their tasks faster than they did before.
examples.analytical: Milton's description of Eden is gorgeous in its sensory detail, but its theological purpose is to show innocence before the fall.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-made bakery window: dazzling enough to stop you on the sidewalk.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, as in gor-jee-us, when the word is two syllables.
Overusing gorgeous for everything, which can make speech sound exaggerated.

gorgeous.etymology: From Middle English *gorgeouse*, a borrowing from Middle French *gorgias* (“elegant, fashionable”), from Old French *gourgias*, *gorgias* (“gorgeous, gaudy, flaunting, gallant, fine”), of uncertain origin, but apparently connected with, from Old French…

senses.definition: The property or condition of being gracile.
senses.example: The dancer's gracility on stage made even experienced critics fall silent.

core.definition: The quality of being slender, slight, or delicately built, especially in form or physique.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the middle syllable, SIL. The first syllable is a weak schwa, and the final -ity is a light tee, so do not make it a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes slenderness or delicacy, often with admiration, but can be technical in anatomy or biology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans seldom use gracility in conversation. It appears in literary criticism, art, dance writing, and scientific description of slender bones or animal forms. For everyday speech, say slenderness or slimness instead.

distinctions.note: Slenderness is the everyday word for being thin, while gracility suggests a refined, delicate, elegant slimness.
Grace refers to smooth, pleasing movement or favor, while gracility refers specifically to a slender, delicate build or form.

examples.professional: The anatomy report describes the fossil's gracility as a sign of a lighter build.
examples.analytical: Critics of the sculpture read its gracility as a deliberate rejection of the heavy forms of earlier monuments.

nuance.analogy: Like a birch tree, slender and delicate, bending gently rather than standing heavy and firm.
nuance.etymology: From gracile (Latin gracilis, slender) plus the suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Confusing gracility with grace: gracility means slenderness of build, while grace means smooth movement or favor.
Stressing the first syllable, as in GRAY-sil-ity, instead of gruh-SIL-ih-tee.

senses.definition: Any of the statuettes awarded by the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences for outstanding achievements in the music industry.

core.definition: A gramophone-shaped award statuette given each year by the Recording Academy for outstanding achievement in the music industry.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GRAM, and the final syllable is a long ee sound like in happy. Do not pronounce it as grammy with a long a in the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Winning or being nominated for a Grammy is a prestigious achievement in music.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'won a Grammy' or 'a Grammy nomination,' and the plural is Grammys. The award is run by the Recording Academy, formerly the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences. Do not confuse it with grammie or granny, which are informal words for grandmother.

distinctions.note: An Emmy honors television, while a Grammy honors music recordings and related achievements.
An Oscar honors film, while a Grammy honors the music industry.

examples.everyday: She finally won a Grammy after twenty years of making records, and her mom cried on TV.
examples.professional: Her label is planning the campaign around the Grammy nomination, so the timing of the release matters.
examples.analytical: Grammy voting has long been criticized for favoring established artists, which shapes which genres get recognized.

nuance.analogy: A Grammy is to the music industry what an Oscar is to film: the most visible sign that peers have recognized excellence.
nuance.etymology: Named after the gramophone shape of the statuette; the award name is a proper noun.
common_mistakes: Spelling it grammie, which means grandmother in American English.
Saying the Grammy's as the plural possessive for several awards; use Grammys for plural and the Grammys for the ceremony.

senses.definition: A child of someone's child.

core.definition: The child of your son or daughter; a person whose parent is your child.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on GRAND, with a weaker secondary stress on child. Pronounce the final d clearly, and make the ch sound like the one in church.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It refers to family relationships and is usually said with warmth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say grandchild in neutral and formal contexts, while in everyday talk many people say grandkid or grandkids. The plural is grandchildren. In a family conversation you might say 'my grandkids are visiting' or 'our first grandchild is due in March.'

distinctions.note: Grandkid is a casual, friendly word used mainly in speech; grandchild is more neutral and appears in writing.
A great-grandchild is the child of a grandchild, two generations below you.

examples.everyday: Our first grandchild arrives in March, so we are finally getting a crib out of the basement.
examples.professional: I need Thursday morning off because my grandchild has a school play, so I will be out of the office.
examples.analytical: In demographic studies, the number of grandchildren a person has is an increasingly important measure of intergenerational support.

nuance.analogy: A grandchild is a branch growing from your child's branch on the family tree: one step further down, but still on the same trunk.
nuance.etymology: From grand- (generation removed) plus child.
common_mistakes: Using grandchildren as a singular for one child; the singular is grandchild.
Placing the stress on child, as in grand-CHILD, instead of GRAND-chyld.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture often speaks of 'children's children' rather than using one fixed word for grandchildren. Deuteronomy 4:9 tells parents to make God's deeds known to their children and their children's children, showing that faith is handed down across generations. Proverbs 17:6 says that grandchildren are a crown to the aged, presenting them as a sign of blessing.

senses.definition: To grip; to take hold, particularly with the hand.
senses.example: She reached down and grasped the rope tightly before the boat drifted away.

senses.definition: To understand.
senses.example: I have never been able to grasp the concept of infinity.

senses.definition: To take advantage of something, to seize, to jump at a chance.
senses.example: The startup grasped the chance to acquire a competitor when its founder suddenly offered to sell.

senses.definition: Grip.
senses.example: A vagrant gust of wind snatched the note from my grasp.

senses.definition: Understanding.
senses.example: Her grasp of statistics impressed the review board, which had expected a simpler proposal.

senses.definition: That which is accessible; that which is within one's reach or ability.
senses.example: The goal is within my grasp.

core.definition: To hold something firmly with your hand, or to understand an idea or situation fully enough to explain it.

pronunciation.tip: A single stressed syllable ending in a hard 'sp' cluster. Keep the r rhotic and do not add a vowel between the s and p.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests control or understanding.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, grasp is used more in written or formal speech than in casual talk. Americans more often say 'get it' or 'understand' in conversation. The noun 'grasp' describes understanding and is common in reviews, meetings and essays.

distinctions.note: Grip is physical and concrete, while grasp can be physical or mental.
Understand is the everyday word, while grasp suggests a firm, sometimes hard-won comprehension.

examples.everyday: I finally grasped how the new coffee maker works after reading the manual twice.
examples.professional: Before we present to leadership, we need to grasp the impact on the budget.
examples.analytical: A careful reader must grasp the author's premise before evaluating the argument.

nuance.analogy: A grasp is like your fingers closing around a rope: firm enough to hold, and you know exactly what you are holding.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'graspen', from Old English 'grăsp' related to grasping or clutching.
common_mistakes: Saying 'grasp about' instead of 'grasp' when meaning understand.
Adding a vowel between the s and p, pronouncing it as 'gras-ip'.

grasp.etymology: From Middle English *graspen*, *grapsen*, *craspen* (“to grope; feel around”), from Old English **grǣpsian*, from **graipisōn*, from Proto-Germanic **graipisōną*, from Proto-Indo-European **gʰrebʰ-* (“to take, seize, rake”), the same ultimate source as *grab*.

senses.definition: The state of being greedy; greed.

core.definition: The quality of being greedy; a strong, selfish desire for more than one needs or deserves.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GREE. The second syllable is a light ee sound, and the final -ness is a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative, an accusation of selfishness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often use the noun greed or the adjective greedy, so greediness sounds stiff or literary in everyday speech. It is occasionally used in essays or sermons about the character of a person or institution. People may find it an unusual choice in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Greed is the common noun for the vice; greediness emphasizes the character trait of being greedy.
Selfishness is a broad lack of concern for others; greediness is specifically a desire for more possessions or gain.

examples.everyday: I was annoyed by the greediness of the landlord who raised the rent again without warning.
examples.professional: The report criticized the greediness of short-term incentives, which encouraged managers to chase quarterly profits.
examples.analytical: The sermon links the greediness of the rich to the neglect of the poor, reading the parable as a condemnation of accumulated wealth.

nuance.analogy: Greediness is like a hungry bird that keeps taking seeds from the feeder until nothing is left for the rest of the flock.
nuance.etymology: From greedy, from Old English graedig, plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using greediness in casual talk where greed is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle vowel; it is a light ee sound, not a short i.

greediness.etymology: From Middle English *gredynesse*, from Old English *grǣdiġnes*; equivalent to *greedy* + *ness*.

senses.definition: Retail foodstuffs and other household supplies.
senses.example: Our grocery bill climbed past three hundred dollars once the kids came home from college.

senses.definition: A shop or store that sells groceries; a grocery store.
To go grocery shopping.
senses.example: We usually grocery on Sunday mornings before the stores get crowded.

senses.definition: To furnish with groceries.
senses.example: The church members groceried the struggling family for a month after the fire.

core.definition: Food and household supplies bought at a store; also a shop or store that sells groceries, like a grocery store.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the middle sound a reduced, quick uh, so the word is about three syllables. In fast speech, many Americans say GROH-shree, with the middle syllable almost gone.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and everyday. It refers to ordinary shopping and food, so it carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, groceries (plural) means the food and household items you buy, while grocery or grocery store means the shop. Saying I need to do the grocery is incomplete; say I need to go grocery shopping. Use grocery store, grocery shopping, and grocery bag as normal, everyday phrases.

distinctions.note: Groceries is the plural word for the items you buy, while grocery is the singular word used for the store or for the activity of shopping.
A supermarket is a large store with a wide range of departments, while grocery store is a general term that includes smaller shops.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the groceries from the trunk while I get the kids out of the car?
examples.professional: Our grocery delivery team needs a revised routing plan before the holiday weekend.
examples.analytical: Grocery prices have become a standard measure in inflation studies, because households buy them frequently and notice changes quickly.

nuance.analogy: Grocery is like a pantry on a bigger scale: the place where a household's everyday supplies come from.
nuance.etymology: From grocer, from Anglo-Norman and Old French grossier, a wholesaler, from gros, large.
common_mistakes: Saying I bought a grocery when you mean groceries; the plural is used for the food items.
Pronouncing it GROH-sər-ee, which mixes up the s and sh sounds; Americans say GROH-shuh-ree.

senses.definition: A writ ordering that a person be brought before a court or a judge, most frequently used to ensure that a person's imprisonment, detention, or commitment is legal.
To apply the legal principle of habeas corpus to an individual or situation.
senses.example: The attorneys moved to habeas corpus the detention, arguing that their client had been held without any charges.

core.definition: A court order requiring that a detained person be brought before a judge so the legality of the detention can be checked.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of each word, and keep 'corpus' with a clear r. The 'pus' ending is short, not 'poos'. Do not reduce 'habeas' too much; it has a clear 'bee' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this Latin legal term in courtrooms, news about detention or prisons, and law classes. Lawyers often say 'file a habeas petition' to mean asking a court to review detention. Most Americans would not use it in casual talk. Its full American legal meaning is about checking the legality of detention.

distinctions.note: Bail is money or a bond that lets a defendant wait for trial outside jail; habeas corpus challenges whether the detention itself is lawful.
A warrant authorizes an arrest or search; habeas corpus checks whether an existing detention is legal.

examples.everyday: I heard on the news that the lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition for the man held in that jail.
examples.professional: Our compliance team reviewed how detainees can file a habeas corpus petition if they believe their confinement is unlawful.
examples.analytical: The suspension of habeas corpus raises a basic constitutional question about whether state power can detain persons without judicial review.

nuance.analogy: It is like asking a guard to bring the prisoner in front of a judge and explain on what authority he is being held.
nuance.etymology: Latin, literally 'you should have the body', from the opening words of the writ.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'corpus' on the first syllable or saying 'KOR-pus' with a weak r.
Confusing it with the general word 'corpse' or with bail.

habeas-corpus.etymology: From Latin, referring to the body of the detainee (not the body of a victim, similar to *corpus delicti*).

senses.definition: The act of habituating, or accustoming; the state of being habituated.
senses.example: Her habituation to the late-night schedule made the jet lag easier to shrug off.

senses.definition: The process of becoming accustomed to an internal or external stimulus, such as a noxious smell or loud noise.
senses.example: Habituation to the constant hum of the refrigerator means you eventually stop noticing it.

core.definition: The gradual process of becoming used to something, so that you respond less to it over time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'AY', the syllable before '-shun'. In American speech the 'tu' is pronounced 'chu', as in 'Chuesday', so do not say 'hab-it-yoo'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a process in psychology or biology, not an emotional state.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use habituation in psychology, neuroscience, medicine and pharmacology. In everyday talk, people say 'getting used to it' or 'tuning it out'. In medicine, habituation can describe a milder early stage of dependence, so the word is sometimes used carefully to avoid implying addiction.

distinctions.note: Addiction is compulsive dependence with harmful effects, while habituation is a reduced response to a repeated stimulus that is not necessarily harmful.
Sensitization is an increased response to a repeated stimulus, while habituation is a decreased response.
Adaptation is a broader term for adjusting to conditions over time, while habituation specifically means responding less to a repeated stimulus.

examples.everyday: After a few weeks I stopped hearing the train at night, which is just habituation, my brain tuning it out.
examples.professional: The sensor readings may show habituation to repeated stimuli, so we should randomize the test order.
examples.analytical: Habituation, the simplest form of learning, shows that even organisms without complex brains can revise their responses to repeated stimuli.

nuance.analogy: Like a clock's tick that disappears from your awareness once you stop listening for it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin habituare 'to accustom', from habitus 'condition'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as 'tyoo' in the British style; Americans usually say 'choo'.
Confusing habituation with the everyday word habit, which is a behavior rather than a learning process.
Using habituation for conscious adjustment, when it refers to an automatic reduction in response.

habituation.etymology: From Middle English *habituacioun*, from Medieval Latin *habituātio*.

core.definition: In Genesis, the second son of Noah, who survived the flood on the ark and was the father of Canaan, Cush, Mizraim, and Put.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one short syllable with a short 'a' as in 'cat.' Do not add a final vowel; the 'm' is closed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when referring to the biblical figure. In everyday English, 'ham' also means pork or an overly dramatic actor, which is a different sense.
nuance.usage_note: In American church and Bible study conversations, Ham appears in Genesis 9 and is usually discussed with his brothers Shem and Japheth. Be careful, because 'ham' is also a common word for cured pork and for an exaggerated performer. Context makes the biblical sense clear.
word_family: Hamite (noun, historical term, now considered problematic)

distinctions.note: Shem was Noah's eldest son and, in Genesis, the ancestor of the Semitic peoples; Ham is a different son.
Japheth was Noah's third son, often associated with the peoples of Europe in traditional interpretation; Ham is a different son.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study group we talked about Noah and his sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and how their story is told.
examples.professional: In the Genesis sermon series, the pastor will explain why the curse in chapter nine falls on Canaan, not directly on Ham.
examples.analytical: Genesis 9:22 records that Ham saw his father's nakedness and told his brothers, and the subsequent curse is pronounced on Canaan, a point that exegetes have long debated.

nuance.analogy: Ham is like one son in a family story whose actions shape the rest of the narrative, even though the consequences fall on his own line.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ḥām, of uncertain meaning; some scholars connect it to a root meaning hot or warm, but this is not certain.
common_mistakes: Confusing the biblical Ham with the food 'ham' in religious discussions.
Assuming the curse falls directly on Ham; in Genesis 9 the curse is pronounced on Canaan.
Mispronouncing it with a long 'a' as in 'name'.
nuance.biblical_note: Ham is one of Noah's three sons, named with Shem and Japheth in Genesis 5:32 and 6:10. In Genesis 9:18 to 27, Ham sees his father's nakedness and tells his brothers, and Shem and Japheth cover Noah respectfully. Noah then curses Canaan, Ham's son, a passage that has been interpreted in many ways. Psalm 105:23 and Psalm 106:22 use 'the land of Ham' as a poetic name for Egypt, since Ham's descendants included Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt.

ham.etymology: Middle English *hamme*, from Old English *hamm* (“inner or hind part of the knee, ham”), from **hammu*, from Proto-Germanic **hamō*, **hammō*, **hanmō*, from Proto-Indo-European **kónh₂m* (“leg”).

senses.definition: Having a feeling arising from a consciousness of well-being or of enjoyment; enjoying good of any kind, such as comfort, peace, or tranquillity; blissful, contented, joyous.
senses.example: Music makes me feel happy.

senses.definition: Experiencing the effect of favorable fortune; favored by fortune or luck; fortunate, lucky.
senses.example: We were happy to find the last seat on the flight before the storm hit.

senses.definition: Content, willing, satisfied (with or to do something); having no objection (to something).
senses.example: Are you happy to pay me back by the end of the week?

senses.definition: Bringing or being an instance of favorable fortune; apt, felicitous, fortunate, propitious.
senses.example: happy coincidence

senses.definition: Favoring or inclined to use.
senses.example: slaphappy, trigger-happy

senses.definition: Dexterous, ready, skillful.
senses.example: The old carpenter had a happy hand with a plane and a chisel.

senses.definition: Implying “May you have a happy ⁓” or similar; used in phrases to wish someone happiness or good fortune at the time of a festival, celebration, or other event or activity.
senses.example: Happy birthday!

senses.definition: Often followed by up: to become happy; to brighten up, to cheer up.
senses.example: Once the sun came out, the whole town began to happy up.

senses.definition: Often followed by up: to make happy; to brighten, to cheer, to enliven.
senses.example: Her daughter's drawings always happy up the dull hallway at the clinic.

senses.definition: (rare) A happy event, thing, person, etc.
senses.example: The wedding was a happy in a year full of bad news.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Feeling pleasure, contentment or joy, or fortunate in circumstances. In everyday speech it describes a person who feels good or is pleased with something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with a short ee sound, not ay. The final y is a tense ee, which Americans often make very short and light.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it expresses good feelings and satisfaction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use happy constantly in everyday talk, as in I'm happy to help or happy with the result. It is often followed by with, about or to, depending on the sense. Saying I'm happy to do it is a warm, polite way to accept a request, while overusing it can sound flat.

distinctions.note: Glad is often used for a specific event or good news, while happy describes a general feeling or state of contentment.
Content suggests quiet satisfaction and acceptance, while happy suggests a more active, positive feeling.

examples.everyday: I'm happy to give you a ride to the airport on Friday.
examples.professional: I'm happy with the timeline, so let's send the proposal to the client today.
examples.analytical: Mill argued that a happy life is not simply one of pleasure, but of meaningful activity.

nuance.etymology: From the Middle English hap meaning chance or luck, so originally meaning fortunate.
common_mistakes: Using happy for an event, as in a happy day, where glad or pleased may sound more natural
Forgetting the preposition: say happy with or happy about, not happy of

happy.etymology: From Middle English *happy* (“fortunate, happy”), perhaps an alteration of Middle English *happyn*, *happen* (“fortunate, happy”), possibly related to or from Old Norse *heppinn* (“fortunate, happy”); and potentially assimilated to be equivalent to *hap* +…

conversation.text: I'm so happy for you guys. You deserve it!
The kids were so happy when it finally snowed.
Are you happy with your new apartment?

senses.definition: Made physically hard.
senses.example: hardened steel

senses.definition: Having been accustomed or desensitized to something unpleasant through exposure or experience; inured.
senses.example: hardened police officers

senses.definition: Unfeeling; pitiless; callous.
senses.example: The bloody scene could reduce even the most hardened soldier to tears.

senses.definition: Firmly established in a behavior seen as bad; unlikely to change one's ways; inveterate.
senses.example: hardened criminals

senses.definition: Having extra defences against attack; highly fortified.
senses.example: a hardened air base

core.definition: Made tougher or less sensitive by experience, repeated exposure or physical treatment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ened ending is usually a short unstressed syllable, so say HAR-dund and not HAR-den-ed with three full syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it can describe earned toughness (positive) or emotional callousness (negative).
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hardened for materials, such as hardened steel, and for people, especially in phrases like hardened criminal or hardened veteran. Describing a criminal as hardened is negative, while a hardened soldier sounds neutral. Hardened to something means accustomed to it, as in I'm hardened to bad news.

distinctions.note: Hard is the basic word, while hardened adds the idea of having become hard over time or through experience.
Callous is more clearly negative, meaning emotionally insensitive, while hardened can be neutral or admiring.
Inured is more formal and literary, meaning accustomed to something unpleasant, while hardened is the everyday equivalent.

examples.everyday: After ten winters on the farm, he's pretty hardened to cold weather.
examples.professional: Our senior engineers are hardened by years of outages, so they stay calm when production goes down.
examples.analytical: Simmel argued that the modern city hardens people against constant stimulation, producing a protective, blasé attitude.

nuance.analogy: A hardened person is like steel tempered by fire: stronger, but less flexible.
nuance.etymology: From harden, from Old English heardian, from hard plus the verb-forming suffix -en.
common_mistakes: Using hardened to mean stubborn, which is hardheaded
Assuming hardened by and hardened to are interchangeable; hardened to means accustomed to
Mixing it up with hard-boiled, which describes eggs or a tough detective style

senses.definition: Difficulty or trouble; hard times.
senses.example: He has survived periods of financial hardship before.

senses.definition: A burden, a source of difficulty that could impose a barrier.
senses.example: When you visit the museum, we invite you to make a donation of $10 if this will not be a hardship.

senses.definition: To treat (a person) badly; to subject to hardships.
senses.example: The drought hardshipped farmers across the county for three straight years.

core.definition: Difficulty, suffering, or trouble; a hard circumstance, such as poverty, illness, or scarcity, that makes life harder to bear.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HARD, and the r before the d is clear in General American. Say the two parts together without adding a vowel between d and sh, so it is not 'hard-ih-ship'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes suffering or deprivation, and it often suggests serious or prolonged difficulty rather than a passing annoyance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hardship for serious difficulties such as financial trouble, illness, or war, more than for minor inconveniences. The word also appears in official language, as in 'hardship exemption' or 'hardship withdrawal'. Calling a minor delay a hardship sounds exaggerated. A natural reply to someone describing one is 'I'm sorry to hear that. How are you holding up?'

distinctions.note: Difficulty is the general word for anything hard to do, while hardship implies suffering or deprivation, often over a longer period.
Suffering stresses pain, physical or emotional; hardship emphasizes external conditions such as poverty, scarcity, or danger.

examples.everyday: After the layoff, they went through real financial hardship, but their neighbors really helped them out.
examples.professional: The benefits team reviews each claim for hardship before approving a payment extension for the employee.
examples.analytical: Scripture presents hardship not as proof of God's absence but as a setting in which faith is tested and formed.

nuance.analogy: Hardship is the rough terrain a traveler must cross; the journey is harder, but it shapes the walker.
nuance.etymology: From hard plus the suffix -ship, from Old English -scipe, meaning 'state or condition'.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel, saying 'hard-ih-ship' instead of two clean syllables.
Using hardship for a minor inconvenience, such as 'the traffic was a hardship'; reserve it for serious difficulty.
nuance.biblical_note: Hardship translates several Greek words, often stenochoria (distress, a narrow place), which Romans 8:35 lists among things that cannot separate believers from Christ's love. In 2 Corinthians 6:4 Paul describes his ministry through endurance, afflictions, and hardships, presenting suffering as evidence of faithful service. In 2 Timothy 2:3 Paul urges Timothy to share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus, using the Greek verb kakopatheo, to suffer hardship.

senses.definition: In a harmless manner.

core.definition: In a way that does not cause injury, damage, or serious problems.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle syllables. The -less is a weak 'luhs,' and the final -ly is a clear 'lee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually reassures that something is safe or not dangerous, though it can sound dismissive if the harm is real.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use harmlessly to describe animals, pranks, games, and technical operations that do no damage, such as 'the raccoon wandered harmlessly through the yard.' In casual talk, 'harmless' as an adjective is far more common. Using harmlessly to downplay something serious can sound like an excuse, so be careful in serious discussions.

distinctions.note: Safely means without danger or accident, often emphasizing care or protection, while harmlessly emphasizes that the result causes no damage.
Innocently describes intent or appearance, implying no bad motive, while harmlessly describes the effect.

examples.everyday: The raccoon wandered harmlessly through the backyard while we were sitting on the porch.
examples.professional: The test script runs harmlessly in the sandbox, so it won't touch the production data.
examples.analytical: It is hard to say the lie was told harmlessly when its consequences damaged so many people's trust.

nuance.analogy: If a stone falls harmlessly into a soft pile of leaves, it lands without breaking anything.
nuance.etymology: Formed from harmless, from harm, with -less (lacking) and the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'harmlessly' to mean 'without harm to my feelings' when 'harmlessly' describes the effect on things or people, not the speaker's emotions.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable; the 'less' is weak and short.

senses.definition: A covering for the head, often in the approximate form of a cone, dome or cylinder closed at its top end, and sometimes having a brim and other decoration.
senses.example: She pulled a wool hat over her ears before walking into the cold wind.

senses.definition: A particular role or capacity that a person might fill.
senses.example: In her new role, she wears many hats, from budget analyst to mentor.

senses.definition: Any receptacle from which names or numbers are pulled out in a lottery.
senses.example: We're both in the hat: let's hope we come up against each other.

senses.definition: The lottery or draw itself.
senses.example: We're both in the hat: let's hope we come up against each other.

senses.definition: A hat switch.
senses.example: Press the hat switch on the joystick to change the flight camera view.

senses.definition: The circumflex symbol.
senses.example: In French spelling, the hat over the o in hôtel shows a vanished s.

senses.definition: The háček symbol.
senses.example: The Czech letter š carries a hat that softens the s into a sh sound.

senses.definition: The caret symbol ^.
senses.example: In many programming languages, the hat symbol means exclusive or, not exponentiation.

senses.definition: User rights on a website, such as the right to edit pages others cannot.
senses.example: Only trusted editors get the hat, so newcomers cannot edit the locked article.

senses.definition: To place a hat on.
senses.example: Grandma hatted the toddler in a knit cap before the snowy walk.

senses.definition: To appoint as cardinal.
senses.example: The pope will hat three archbishops as cardinals at next month's consistory.

senses.definition: To shop for hats.
senses.example: On Saturdays my aunt loves to go hatting, trying on every straw bonnet in town.

senses.definition: To collapse with a template a part of a discussion due to it being overly long, disruptive, or already addressed.
senses.example: Please hat the old thread now, since everyone already answered the question.

core.definition: A covering worn on the head, usually with a brim or crown, for warmth, sun protection, or style.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short, sharp vowel like the one in 'cat', and don't let it drift toward 'hot'. End with a crisp t and no extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain everyday object word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'put on' or 'wear' a hat and 'take off' a hat. People sometimes remove hats indoors as a courtesy, though many Americans no longer follow this strictly. The idiom 'wear many hats' means to have several jobs or roles at once.

distinctions.note: A cap usually has a brim only at the front and is often soft or sporty; a hat usually has a brim all the way around.
A helmet is a protective hard covering for safety; a hat is a general covering for warmth, sun, or style.
A beanie is a close-fitting knit cap without a brim; a hat can have a brim or a crown of many shapes.

examples.everyday: Don't forget your hat, because it's supposed to be windy at the game.
examples.professional: Everyone on the construction floor needs a hard hat before the safety inspection starts.
examples.analytical: Scholars of Renaissance portraiture often read a sitter's hat as a sign of social rank, not merely a matter of fashion.

nuance.analogy: A hat is like a roof for your head: it shields you from the weather and tells people something about who you are.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hæt, of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'put the hat' instead of 'put on a hat'; the verb needs 'on'.
Saying 'take the hat' when you mean removing one indoors; the natural phrase is 'take off your hat'.

hat.etymology: From Middle English *hat*, from Old English *hætt*, from Proto-Germanic **hattuz* (“hat”), perhaps from a late PIE root Proto-Indo-European **kedʰ-* (“to guard, cover, care for, protect”) or wanderwort.

senses.definition: One who hates.
One who expresses unfounded or inappropriate hatred or dislike, particularly if motivated by envy.
senses.example: Ignore the online haters; they post cruel comments about everyone who succeeds.

core.definition: A person who hates someone or something, or who constantly criticizes others out of dislike or envy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with a rhotic, unstressed 'er' (/ɚ/), with the r-coloring of the vowel. Do not say it as two separate words 'hate' and 'er'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It is often used to dismiss critics, so it can sound dismissive or mocking.
nuance.usage_note: 'Hater' is mostly slang from online culture. Americans use it to dismiss people who criticize them, as in 'ignore the haters.' Calling someone a hater can sound childish or defensive in a serious discussion, so in workplace conversation say 'critics' or 'people who disagree' instead. The phrase 'haters gonna hate' is a well-known internet expression.

distinctions.note: A critic offers a reasoned evaluation, while a hater dismisses others out of dislike or envy.
An enemy is an opponent in a real conflict, while a hater is a person with a personal, often irrational dislike.

examples.everyday: Don't read the comments, the haters will just bring your mood down.
examples.professional: We can't let a few haters drive the roadmap decisions for the whole team.
examples.analytical: Dismissing every critic as a hater makes it impossible to learn from legitimate objections.

nuance.analogy: A hater is like a loud heckler at a concert who has come only to shout, not to listen to the music.
nuance.etymology: From 'hate' plus the agent suffix '-er'.
common_mistakes: Using 'hater' for someone who simply disagrees with you, when the word implies personal animosity.
Using 'hater' in formal writing, where 'critic' or 'opponent' is more appropriate.

core.definition: A major Canaanite city in northern Israel, ruled by King Jabin and conquered by Israel under Joshua.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'or' is a rhotic 'r' sound, close to 'hay-zer' in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a biblical and archaeological place name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this name in Bible study, sermons, and archaeology discussions. It is rarely used in everyday speech. Archaeological sites at Tell el-Qedah are associated with the city.

distinctions.note: Hazor is a large Canaanite royal city in the north, while Hazeroth is a wilderness camp in the Exodus story.

examples.everyday: My friend is reading about Hazor because of a documentary on Israeli archaeology.
examples.professional: The lecture on Hazor covered the layers of Bronze Age fortifications and what they suggest about Canaanite urban life.
examples.analytical: The Joshua narrative presents the burning of Hazor as the climax of the northern campaign, which makes its theological and political significance central.

nuance.analogy: Hazor is like a capital city in a region's history book: the most important stronghold that the others were measured against.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Hazor, meaning enclosure or settlement.
common_mistakes: Confusing Hazor with Hazeroth.
Pronouncing the final 'r' as a separate 'er' sound instead of a light American 'r'.
nuance.biblical_note: Hazor was a large, fortified Canaanite city in the north of the land, the head of several kingdoms according to Joshua. Joshua 11:1-13 describes King Jabin of Hazor forming a coalition against Israel and Joshua defeating them, with Hazor burned. Judges 4:2 names Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor, and Sisera, his army commander, whom Deborah and Barak defeated. 1 Kings 9:15 says Solomon fortified Hazor among other cities.

senses.definition: To become aware of (a subject, person) through second-hand knowledge, or not through personal experience.
senses.example: I first heard of the Electra complex when I was studying psychology.

senses.definition: To permit or tolerate.
senses.example: I won't hear of you walking home alone after midnight, so I'm driving you.

core.definition: To have heard about someone or something from others, or to know that it exists, without personal experience of it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HEAR; 'of' is unstressed and reduces to 'uhv', so say 'HEER-uhv', not 'heer-OV'. The r is clearly American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the negative form 'I've never heard of that' can sound dismissive depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this constantly to say they know a name, place or product: 'Have you heard of that new taco place?' The phrase 'I wouldn't hear of it' means you refuse to allow something, often when turning down a kind offer such as paying the bill. A natural reply to 'Have you heard of him?' is 'Yeah, I know his work' or 'No, who is he?'

distinctions.note: Know about often implies knowledge from study or experience, while hear of means you have only encountered the name or idea.
Hear about is a close synonym and slightly more neutral; hear of more often introduces something you barely know.
Hear from means to receive a message or call directly from someone, not to learn about them from others.

examples.everyday: Have you heard of that new taco place on Main Street? My sister says it's great.
examples.professional: Have you heard of the new anomaly detection library the platform team is using for the dashboards?
examples.analytical: Many readers have never heard of the medieval controversy that the author treats as central to the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like knowing a town's name from a postcard before you have ever visited it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hīeran (to hear) and of (from, concerning).
common_mistakes: Using 'hear to' instead of 'hear of' in questions like 'Have you heard to it?'
Stressing 'of' as 'ov' with a strong vowel; in speech it is quick and reduced.

senses.definition: Belief in or worship of one deity without denying the existence of other deities.

core.definition: Belief in or worship of one god as supreme while not denying that other gods exist.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'THEE,' with a secondary stress on 'hen.' The ending '-ism' is a weak 'iz-um' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is used in religious studies, theology, and the history of religion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'henotheism' in religious studies, theology, and anthropology, not in everyday talk. It describes a religious stance that honors one god as the chief deity without denying other deities. In conversation, you might explain it to a friend as 'worshipping one god while accepting that other gods exist.'

distinctions.note: Monotheism holds that only one god exists, while henotheism accepts other gods while worshipping one.
Polytheism worships many gods equally, while henotheism focuses devotion on one chief god.

examples.everyday: My religion professor said some ancient cultures practiced henotheism, worshipping one main god while accepting others.
examples.professional: In the seminar paper, we distinguished henotheism from monotheism by focusing on how worship was directed.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether early Israelite faith was henotheistic, since texts like the Shema seem to assume the existence of other gods while demanding exclusive loyalty to the LORD.

nuance.analogy: Henotheism is like a family with one head of the household who is honored above others, though other relatives still exist.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'hen' (one) and 'theos' (god), with the suffix '-ism'.
common_mistakes: Using henotheism as a synonym for monotheism; they describe different beliefs about other gods.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the main stress is on 'THEE'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Shema in Deuteronomy 6:4 declares that the LORD is one, and Exodus 20:3 says 'You shall have no other gods before me.' Scholars debate whether these verses express strict monotheism or an earlier henotheistic commitment to one God above others. The Hebrew word Shema means 'hear', and the passage is central to Jewish and Christian worship.

senses.definition: One who practices henotheism.
senses.example: As a henotheist, she honored Krishna as supreme while respecting other gods as real.

core.definition: A person who worships one god as supreme while accepting that other gods exist.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on THEE, the syllable before -ist. Keep the 'oh' in the middle as a clear vowel, and start 'th' with a voiceless sound, as in 'think'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scholarly label, not an insult, but it can sound pedantic in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: The word is used mainly by scholars of religion, theologians and philosophers, especially when discussing ancient Israelite, Vedic or Greek religion. Americans outside academia rarely use it and may confuse it with monotheist or polytheist. In everyday conversation, it is clearer to say that someone worships one god above the others.

distinctions.note: A monotheist believes that only one God exists, while a henotheist worships one god as supreme but accepts that other gods exist.
A polytheist worships many gods, while a henotheist focuses worship on one god without denying the others.

examples.everyday: My sister studies religion, and at dinner she called some of the ancient peoples henotheists, which started a long debate.
examples.professional: In our comparative religion seminar, we used the term henotheist for the author's view that Yahweh was supreme among the gods.
examples.analytical: Some scholars argue that early Israelite faith was henotheistic, acknowledging other gods while insisting that Yahweh alone deserved worship.

nuance.analogy: A henotheist is like a loyal fan who believes one team is the best while admitting that other teams exist.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hen, 'one', and theos, 'god', with the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Don't confuse henotheist with monotheist; a henotheist accepts that other gods exist.
Don't stress the first syllable; it is hen-oh-THEE-ist.
nuance.biblical_note: Henotheism is a scholarly category used to describe how early Israelite religion may have treated Yahweh as supreme while recognizing other divine beings. The Hebrew word elohim can mean 'God' or 'gods', which is central to this debate. Deuteronomy 6:4 insists that the LORD is one, Exodus 15:11 asks who is like the LORD among the gods, and Psalm 82:1 pictures God presiding over a council of divine beings. Scholars read these passages differently, which is why the term is useful but debated.

senses.definition: Having six edges, or having a cross-section in the form of a hexagon.
senses.example: Nuts in engineering are generally hexagonal.

senses.definition: Having three equal axes which cross at 60° angles, and an unequal axis which crosses the others at 90° angle.

core.definition: Having six sides and six angles, like a hexagon; shaped like a honeycomb cell.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SAG, the second syllable. The g is hard, as in bag, and the last two syllables reduce to uh-nuhl.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise descriptive term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hexagonal in math, engineering, chemistry, and everyday descriptions of shapes such as bolts, tiles and honeycombs. In casual speech people often say six-sided for an object. Hexagonal is the adjective, and hexagon is the noun for the shape itself.

distinctions.note: Hexagon is the noun for the shape, while hexagonal is the adjective describing something as having that shape.
Hexahedral describes a solid with six faces, such as a cube, while hexagonal describes a flat six-sided shape or cross-section.

examples.everyday: The honeycomb in the box is made of tiny hexagonal cells.
examples.professional: Use a hexagonal socket wrench on this bolt, since the standard nut fits it best.
examples.analytical: The hexagonal lattice of graphene gives the material its unusual electrical properties.

nuance.analogy: Like a honeycomb cell: six walls that fit together with no gaps.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hexagōnos, 'six-angled', from hex ('six') and gōnia ('angle').
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; say hek-SAG-uh-nuhl, not HEK-suh-gon-al.
Using hexagonal as a noun; say hexagon for the shape itself.

senses.definition: Over here.
Only used in the phrase hither and thither.
senses.example: The lost hikers wandered hither and thither across the meadow until the fog finally lifted.

core.definition: To or toward this place; here. In modern American English it survives mainly in literary writing and fixed phrases.

pronunciation.tip: The 'th' is voiced, as in 'this', not unvoiced as in 'thin'. Stress the first syllable, and keep the final vowel weak and r-colored.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to old-fashioned. It sounds poetic or antique, and it can seem stiff in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'hither' alone in daily life; they say 'here'. You will mostly see it in the fixed phrase 'hither and thither', in poetry, or in old-style writing. In ordinary conversation, 'come here' is the natural choice, not 'come hither'.

distinctions.note: Here is the everyday word for the same place; hither is literary and old-fashioned.
Hitherto refers to time, meaning until now; hither refers to place, meaning to this place.
Thither means to or toward that place, the opposite direction; it is also literary and archaic.

examples.professional: The grant letter invited the research team to come hither for the opening symposium in the spring.
examples.analytical: The poem repeatedly sends its speaker hither and thither, mirroring a restless search for meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a signpost that says 'this way' in the language of an old storybook.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'hider', from the same root as 'here' and 'this'.
common_mistakes: Using 'come hither' in everyday speech, where 'come here' is the normal phrase.
Confusing 'hither' with 'hitherto', which means 'until now' and refers to time, not place.

hither.etymology: From Middle English *hider*, from Old English *hider*, from Proto-Germanic **hidrê*.

senses.definition: Behaving in a manner that shows honor; decent, having integrity.
senses.example: She was an honorable woman who always returned borrowed money on time.

senses.definition: Worthy of respect; respectable.
Complying with cultural rules regarding honor; not provoking shame or disgrace.
senses.example: That culture considered it no disgrace to be defeated in honorable combat.

senses.definition: A courtesy title, given in Britain and the Commonwealth to a cabinet minister, minister of state, or senator, and in the United States to the president, vice president, congresspeople, state governors and legislators, and mayors.
senses.example: The Honorable Maria Lopez, our state senator, spoke at the library opening.

senses.definition: A courtesy title, given in the United Kingdom to all sons and daughters of viscounts and barons and to the younger sons of earls.
senses.example: The Honorable Clara Hayes, daughter of a viscount, studied law at Oxford.

senses.definition: A politician or other person who bears the title of "honorable".
senses.example: The honorable from Ohio rose to speak, and the chamber fell silent.

core.definition: Deserving respect; acting with integrity, fairness and decency toward others.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. Americans spell it without a u, and the final -able is a quick syllabic l, so it has three syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive and formal; it praises character and conduct.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use honorable mainly for people of good character and for official titles, as in 'the Honorable Judge Smith.' In casual talk, 'That was an honorable thing to do' sounds respectful but a bit formal, and 'decent' or 'good' may be more natural. Judges, legislators and mayors are often addressed as 'the Honorable' in formal settings.

distinctions.note: Honest refers to telling the truth; honorable is broader and refers to moral conduct and reputation.
Respectable describes social standing or appearance; honorable emphasizes integrity and principle.

examples.everyday: He made an honorable offer to pay for the damage himself.
examples.professional: Thanks for raising this concern; it's an honorable way to handle a disagreement on the team.
examples.analytical: Kant's account of the honorable person rests on acting from duty rather than from the wish for reputation.

nuance.analogy: Like a fence that stands straight through every season, an honorable person's word holds steady when tested.
nuance.etymology: From Latin honorabilis, from honorare, to honor, from honor.
common_mistakes: Spelling it honourable, the British form, in American writing.
Using the title 'Honorable' in casual contexts; Americans use it for judges, legislators and mayors, not ordinary people.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, honor is owed to God and to parents, rulers and all people. The Hebrew kabod (weight, glory) and the Greek timē (honor, value) carry these meanings. Exodus 20:12 commands honoring father and mother. Romans 12:10 urges believers to outdo one another in showing honor. 1 Peter 2:17 tells Christians to honor everyone.

senses.definition: In an honorific manner.

core.definition: In a way that shows respect, usually by means of a title or form of address.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on RIF, so say ahn-uh-RIF-ih-klee. The -ically ending is pronounced ih-klee, not ik-al-ee.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes respect expressed through language, and it is used mainly in academic or technical writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use honorifically in conversation. It appears in linguistics, history, and discussions of titles such as Dr. or Your Honor, or of Japanese forms such as -san. Use it when you are describing how a title or word expresses respect, not for ordinary good conduct.

distinctions.note: Honorably describes conduct that is morally good, while honorifically describes the form of respect used in a title or word.
Formally refers to a proper or official manner, while honorifically specifically means as a sign of respect in titles or address.

examples.professional: The memo refers to the director honorifically as Dr. Patel in every formal communication.
examples.analytical: Titles are used honorifically when they signal respect for an office rather than a person's actual conduct.

nuance.analogy: Using an honorific is like taking off your hat when you enter a room: it is a small, formal gesture of respect.
nuance.etymology: From honorific, from Latin honorificus, meaning bringing honor.
common_mistakes: Using honorifically to mean honorably; honorably describes conduct, while honorifically describes a title or form of address.
Spelling it honorificly; the correct form is honorifically.

senses.definition: A real or fancied bristling of the hair of the head or body, resulting from disease, terror, chilliness, etc.
senses.example: Her skin broke into horripilation as the thunder crashed directly overhead.

core.definition: The raising of hairs on the skin, causing goosebumps, usually from cold, fear or strong emotion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the syllable -lay-. Many learners put the stress on the first syllable or fail to reduce the middle vowels; the three middle vowels are all short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a clinical or literary term for goosebumps.
nuance.usage_note: Americans would say goosebumps or get goosebumps in everyday speech. Horripilation appears in medical, scientific or literary writing, where it has a precise meaning. Using it in casual talk may sound overly technical or playful.

distinctions.note: Goosebumps is the everyday American term, while horripilation is a formal or medical word for the same reaction.

examples.everyday: The horror movie was so tense that I got goosebumps, and my friend laughed at my horripilation.
examples.professional: The clinical note records horripilation as a sign of the patient's chills during the fever episode.
examples.analytical: The writer uses the image of horripilation to convey the terror that makes the body respond before the mind understands the threat.

nuance.analogy: Horripilation is like the hair on the back of your neck standing up in a sudden chill, the body's old alarm system responding to fear.
nuance.etymology: From Latin horripilatio, from horrere, to bristle, and pilus, hair.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as 'hor-ri-PIL-a-tion'.
Using horripilation in casual speech where goosebumps is far more natural.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see hunt,‎ cat.
(rare) A cheetah.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Another name for a cheetah, the fast, spotted wild cat that is the fastest land animal.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on CAT, since it is a noun phrase; hunting is lighter. The final t in cat is unreleased, so stop the sound without a puff of air.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive, old-fashioned name with no emotional weight.
