examples.professional: Our church is sending a missionary team to Kenya, and they'll report back during the service next month.
examples.analytical: Paul's account of being sent to the Gentiles shows how the missionary task grew out of his understanding of the gospel.

nuance.analogy: A missionary is like a messenger carrying news into a place that has not heard it yet.
nuance.etymology: From Latin missio, 'a sending', from mittere, 'to send'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable or saying 'mish-uh-NAIR-ee'; the main stress is on the first syllable.
Using 'missionary' for anyone who promotes an opinion; the word usually implies a religious purpose.
nuance.biblical_note: The word itself is not in the RSV, but the idea rests on the Greek apostolos, 'one sent'. Matthew 28:19-20 describes Jesus sending his disciples to make disciples of all nations. Acts 1:8 describes the disciples as witnesses reaching to the ends of the earth. Romans 10:14-15 explains that preachers must be sent in order to proclaim the message.

senses.definition: Wrongly; erroneously.
senses.example: I mistakenly assumed that the shop was still there.

senses.definition: By accident; by mistake; in error (without intention to do so).
senses.example: Today I mistakenly took your packed lunch to work.

core.definition: Wrongly, or by accident, when you did not intend to; through an error.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, STAY. The middle syllable is reduced to 'kun', and the ending is 'lee', not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes an error without blame or intent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mistakenly' in news, email and formal writing to say that someone did something by error, as in 'mistakenly sent' or 'mistakenly believed'. In casual speech people more often say 'by mistake'. The word sounds slightly more formal than the everyday phrase.

distinctions.note: By mistake is the everyday spoken phrase, while mistakenly is more formal and often used in writing.
Accidentally stresses an unplanned event, while mistakenly stresses a wrong belief or action.
Wrongly can mean unjustly or incorrectly in judgment, while mistakenly focuses on error without intent.

examples.everyday: I mistakenly took your umbrella this morning, so here it is; sorry about that.
examples.professional: The system mistakenly sent the invoice to our old address, so we are reissuing it today.
examples.analytical: The defendant mistakenly believed the contract had expired, and that belief shaped his later actions.

nuance.analogy: Mistakenly doing something is like dropping a letter in the wrong mailbox: sent in good faith, but it lands in the wrong place.
nuance.etymology: From mistaken (see mistake) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'mistakenly' with 'mistakable', which means able to be mistaken for something else.
Pronouncing the second syllable with a full 'kay' sound; it reduces to 'kun'.

senses.definition: Outstanding in importance, of great consequence.

core.definition: Very important, with serious consequences for the future, such as a decision, event, or discovery.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, MEN. The final syllable is weak, so say 'tus' with a short, unstressed vowel, not 'toss'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or serious. It highlights historical or personal importance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use momentous in news, speeches, history, and formal writing, such as 'a momentous decision.' In everyday speech they usually say big, huge, or a really important day. It is not used casually for small events, and saying 'momentous lunch' would sound odd.

distinctions.note: Important is a general everyday word, while momentous is stronger and suggests a turning point with lasting effects.
Momentary means very brief, while momentous means of great importance; learners often confuse them because of their similar form.

examples.everyday: Graduating from college was a momentous day for our whole family.
examples.professional: Approving the merger is a momentous decision, so the board wants a full risk review first.
examples.analytical: The Reformation was a momentous rupture that reshaped Western theology, politics, and the church's understanding of authority.

nuance.analogy: A momentous event is like a bend in a river that changes the direction of everything downstream.
nuance.etymology: From Latin momentosus, from momentum 'importance, moving force'.
common_mistakes: Using momentous for small events in casual speech.
Confusing it with momentary, which means lasting only a short time.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'MOH-men-tus' instead of 'moh-MEN-tus'.

senses.definition: A black and white image, especially such a photograph.
A ceramic glaze of a single color; an object so glazed.
senses.example: The potter applied a celadon monochrome to the bowl, then fired it twice in the kiln.

senses.definition: (dated) A painting executed in shades of a single color.
senses.example: The gallery's dusty catalogue listed a sepia monochrome of a harbor, painted around 1890.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Having only one color.
senses.example: The old film poster had a monochrome design printed only in deep red ink.

senses.definition: Representing colors with shades of gray.
senses.example: The documentary used monochrome footage of the 1930s, with silver and charcoal tones throughout.

core.definition: A black-and-white image, especially a photograph, or an image made in shades of only one color.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAHN. The second syllable is a weak uh, and the final syllable is krohm, with a clear m at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise art, photography, or technical term rather than a casual one.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people usually say black and white for a photo or movie. Monochrome is used in photography, printmaking, and art, as in a monochrome print. It can also refer to glazes or screens in technical contexts. As an adjective it is common in design talk.

distinctions.note: Black and white is the everyday phrase; monochrome sounds more technical and can include shades of one color, not only black and gray.
Monochrome is usually a noun for an image, while monochromatic describes a quality or scheme and is usually an adjective.

examples.everyday: My grandmother keeps a monochrome photo of her wedding day on the living room wall.
examples.professional: The old device uses a monochrome display, which saves power but cannot show color graphics.
examples.analytical: Some photographers choose a monochrome image to remove distraction so that form and light become the subject.

nuance.analogy: A monochrome image is like a sketch in pencil: the drawing depends on lightness and darkness, not on color.
nuance.etymology: From Greek monochromos, meaning of one color.
common_mistakes: Using monochrome only as an adjective and forgetting it can be a noun for an image.
Spelling it monochrom, without the final e.

senses.definition: In a moving manner.

core.definition: In a way that strongly stirs your emotions, often with sympathy, sadness or admiration.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOO. The middle -ing is a short i, and the final -ly is a short ee sound, not lie.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises the emotional power of a speech, performance or piece of writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use movingly in book reviews, eulogies, speeches and news stories, as in 'She spoke movingly about her father.' It is rarely used in casual talk, where so touching or really moved me is more natural. It describes emotional impact, not physical motion.

distinctions.note: Touchingly is more specific to tenderness, while movingly can cover sadness, sorrow, inspiration or admiration.
Emotionally describes feeling in general and can be neutral, while movingly says the presentation strongly affected the listener.

examples.everyday: He told us about his immigration story so movingly that everyone at dinner went quiet.
examples.professional: The director spoke movingly about the team's first year, and then we went straight into the Q3 numbers.
examples.analytical: Augustine writes movingly of the restless heart, though his argument depends on the belief that rest is found only in God.

nuance.analogy: Movingly works like a well-tuned string: when the speaker plays the right note, the listener's feelings begin to resonate.
nuance.etymology: From moving, the adjective from move, plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Old English -lice.
common_mistakes: Using movingly for physical motion, as in the car moved movingly; use smoothly or slowly instead.
Confusing movingly, the adverb, with moving, the adjective: say a moving speech but she spoke movingly.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of a mugwump.
senses.example: His mugwumpish refusal to endorse either candidate annoyed both party leaders.

core.definition: Like a mugwump: independent in politics, refusing to follow one's party's lead.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the 'wump' vowel short. The final -ish is an ordinary 'ish' ending, so don't stress the second syllable as 'mug-WUMP'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly mocking; the speaker's tone decides.
nuance.usage_note: Mugwumpish is rare in American English and appears mainly in historical writing about 1880s Republicans or in commentary on political independence. In ordinary speech, Americans would say independent or maverick. Use it when the historical context or a playful tone is clear.

distinctions.note: Independent is the everyday, neutral word; mugwumpish is historical and more specific to refusing party lines.
Partisan describes strong loyalty to one party; mugwumpish describes the opposite stance.

examples.everyday: My uncle has a mugwumpish streak; he refuses to vote a straight party ticket.
examples.professional: The board chair's mugwumpish stance on the bill frustrated party leaders, who expected a unified vote.
examples.analytical: Her mugwumpish refusal to defer to party discipline shows a commitment to judgment over loyalty.

nuance.analogy: A mugwumpish voter is like a team captain who picks players by skill rather than by team colors.
nuance.etymology: From Massachusett mugquomp, meaning great chief or leader, via the 1884 political nickname mugwump.
common_mistakes: Spelling it mugwumpy; the standard adjective is mugwumpish.
Using it for everyday independence; it sounds literary or historical in most contexts.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to both muscles and the skeleton.

core.definition: Relating to both the muscles and the skeleton, as in pain or injuries affecting the body's support and movement systems.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SKEL, and the c in musc is silent, so the word starts with 'mus'. The final -al is usually pronounced as a reduced 'uhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical; it is used in medical and workplace contexts about health, injuries or safety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use musculoskeletal most often in medicine, workplace safety and insurance settings, such as 'musculoskeletal injuries' or 'musculoskeletal disorders'. In casual talk people usually say 'back pain' or 'sore joints'. It sounds technical, so use it when precision matters, for example when describing a diagnosis.

distinctions.note: Orthopedic refers to bones and joints and the doctors who treat them; musculoskeletal covers both muscles and bones together.
Muscular refers only to the muscles; musculoskeletal includes the skeleton as well.

examples.everyday: I've had musculoskeletal pain in my neck since I started working at a desk all day.
examples.professional: Our health plan covers physical therapy for musculoskeletal injuries, so check the network first.
examples.analytical: Musculoskeletal health cannot be reduced to muscle strength alone, since bone density and joint mechanics shape how the body moves.

nuance.analogy: The musculoskeletal system is like a building's frame and its cables working together: the beams carry the load and the cables pull the structure into motion.
nuance.etymology: From musculo- (from Latin musculus) plus skeletal (from Greek skeletos, 'dried up').
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in mus-kyuh-LOH-skeh-tuhl.
Pronouncing the silent c in musc.
Using it as a noun; it is only an adjective, so say 'musculoskeletal disorders' not 'a musculoskeletal'.

senses.definition: A comrade or fellow.
senses.example: My old college roommate was my musketeer, the friend who always had my back.

senses.definition: (historical) A foot soldier armed with a musket.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) In 17th- and 18th-century France, a member of the royal household bodyguard.
senses.example: The historical novel follows a young musketeer who protects the king in seventeenth-century Paris.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A soldier armed with a musket, especially in the 1500s to 1700s; also a bodyguard in France, made famous by Dumas' novel The Three Musketeers.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, which sounds like 'ear' with a strong American r. Do not say 'MUS-ker-tear' with a British vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to romantic. In everyday talk it often suggests adventure and swashbuckling, because of the famous novel and films.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans know this word from The Three Musketeers, so they usually mean the romantic figure rather than a real soldier. The phrase 'all for one and one for all' is the famous motto associated with them. In history classes, the word refers to infantry soldiers of an earlier era.

distinctions.note: Soldier is a general word for anyone in the army, while musketeer names a specific type of soldier with a specific weapon.
A rifleman carries a rifle with a grooved barrel, while a musketeer carries the older, less accurate musket.

examples.everyday: My daughter wants to be a musketeer for Halloween, so we're making a plastic sword and a big feathered hat.
examples.professional: The exhibit label describes the musketeer's uniform and equipment, so please check the historical sources before we print it.
examples.analytical: The musketeer was both a military figure and a symbol of courtly honor, and Dumas exploited that double meaning in his romance.

nuance.analogy: Think of a musketeer as an early version of a rifleman, with a heavier gun and much slower reloading.
nuance.etymology: From French mousquetaire, from mousquet, musket.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'MUS-kuh-teer'.
Spelling it 'musketier' or 'musketear'.

musketeer.etymology: From Middle French *mousquetaire* in the late 16th century.

senses.definition: One who or that which muzzles.
A pickpocket working individually, apart from their normal gang.
senses.example: The muzzler slipped his hand into the stranger's coat and vanished into the crowd.

senses.definition: A punch in the mouth.
A dram of spirits.
senses.example: After a long day at the docks, he downed a muzzler of gin at the tavern.

senses.definition: A wind from the intended direction of the vessel.
senses.example: The muzzler filled our sails and pushed the schooner straight toward the harbor.

core.definition: A person or thing that muzzles; especially a device that covers an animal's mouth, or something that silences people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'zl' cluster is pronounced with the z and then a quick, almost silent vowel; in American speech the final syllable is the r-colored 'er', not 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the device sense; negative when used figuratively for censorship or silencing people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use muzzler in everyday speech; they usually say 'muzzle' for the device or the act. The word appears mostly in literary writing, dictionaries and discussions of censorship. Its pickpocket sense is old slang and would sound odd or dated today.

distinctions.note: Muzzle is the common everyday word for the device or the act of covering a mouth; muzzler is rare and mostly literary.
A gag is a cloth or device placed in the mouth, or a rule that silences debate, while a muzzler is a more general agent of silencing.

examples.professional: The company's nondisclosure policy acted as a muzzler, silencing employees who raised safety concerns.
examples.analytical: Censorship works less as a single act than as a muzzler that prevents dissenting voices from ever entering public debate.

nuance.analogy: A muzzler is like a sock stuffed into a noisy alarm: it does not stop the sound at its source, it just keeps it from getting out.
nuance.etymology: From muzzle (verb) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using muzzler in everyday conversation where muzzle is the normal word.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'ler' with a strong 'l' rather than a light American 'er'.

senses.definition: In a natural manner.
senses.example: Although he was unused to the situation, he tried to act naturally.

senses.definition: Inherently or by nature.
senses.example: Boys are naturally aggressive.

senses.definition: Surely or without any doubt.
senses.example: I shall naturally protest at that decision.

core.definition: Of course, as one would expect; or in a relaxed, unforced way, without special effort or artificial help.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The middle syllable becomes a quick, reduced er, and the ending is lee. In fast speech, many Americans say nach-er-lee, not na-TU-ral-ly with four distinct syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. As a reply, it sounds friendly and enthusiastic; said flatly, it can sound curt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use naturally as a sentence adverb meaning of course. A friend might ask 'Are you coming to the party?' and you answer 'Naturally!' Used with a warm tone, this is friendly; with a flat tone, it can sound sarcastic. In careful writing, use it to describe how something happens: 'the lighting is natural'.

distinctions.note: Both mean 'as expected'; naturally sounds slightly warmer and suggests the answer follows from the situation.
Naturally can describe inborn talent, as in naturally gifted, and by nature is a more formal way to say the same thing.

examples.everyday: Are you coming to Sam's party on Friday? Naturally! I wouldn't miss the cake.
examples.professional: Naturally, the migration plan needs security sign-off before we schedule the cutover.
examples.analytical: Naturally occurring patterns in observational data should not be mistaken for causation without a controlled experiment.

nuance.analogy: Naturally is like water finding its way downhill: it happens without anyone pushing it.
nuance.etymology: From natural plus -ly, from Latin naturalis 'by nature'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with extra syllables, such as NAT-ter-al-ly, when Americans say NACH-er-lee.
Using naturally as an adjective; say natural lighting, not naturally lighting.

core.definition: A person from Nazareth; in the New Testament, a name for Jesus of Nazareth, and later a term for his followers.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on the last syllable, REEN, which is a long 'ee' vowel. The first syllable is 'naz' with a short a. Do not confuse it with Nazareth, which is stressed on NAZ.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in religious and historical contexts. It is respectful when used for Jesus, but it can sound old-fashioned in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Jesus of Nazareth more often than Jesus the Nazarene in everyday talk. The word appears in Bible studies, sermons, and the name of the Church of the Nazarene, a Protestant denomination in the Wesleyan-Holiness tradition. Outside religious contexts, the word is rarely used.

distinctions.note: Nazareth is the town in Galilee, while Nazarene is a person from there or a religious title.
A Nazirite is someone under a special vow of consecration to God, while a Nazarene is someone from Nazareth or a follower of Jesus.

examples.everyday: My neighbor goes to the Church of the Nazarene, so she's usually at the early service on Sundays.
examples.professional: In my sermon series, I explain why Matthew calls Jesus a Nazarene and what that title signals to the first readers.
examples.analytical: Matthew 2:23 says he shall be called a Nazarene, which has led scholars to debate which prophetic tradition is being cited.

nuance.analogy: A Nazarene is like someone who is known by their hometown, the way a person from Texas might be called a Texan; the name tells you where they come from and who they are connected to.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Nazōraios, from Nazareth; the origin of the town's name is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (NAZ-uh-reen); the stress belongs on REEN.
Confusing Nazarene with Nazareth; they refer to a person and a place respectively.
nuance.biblical_note: Greek Nazōraios, from Nazareth. In the Gospels and Acts, the term identifies Jesus as a man from Nazareth. Matthew 2:23 says that Jesus went to live in Nazareth so that the prophetic word would be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene; scholars debate which prophecy is meant. Acts 24:5 uses the word for the followers of Jesus, calling the Christians 'the sect of the Nazarenes' in the accusation brought against Paul. Mark 14:67 records a servant girl telling Peter that he was with the Nazarene, Jesus.

nazarene.etymology: In the sense "person from Nazareth", from Ancient Greek *Ναζαρηνός* (“of Nazareth”), an ethnonym of *Ναζαρέθ*.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being nebulous.
senses.example: The nebulousness of the project's goals frustrated the team during planning meetings.

senses.definition: Complex and opaque uncertainty.
senses.example: The nebulousness of the new regulations left small business owners unsure what to expect.

senses.definition: Cloudiness; the measured degree of cloudiness.
senses.example: Lab technicians recorded the nebulousness of each water sample using a turbidity meter.

core.definition: The quality of being vague, indistinct or hard to pin down; a lack of clear shape, form or meaning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, NEB. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick schwa, so say 'NEB-yuh-lus-nus' rather than giving each syllable equal weight.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It usually criticizes something as vague or unclear, as in a plan or argument, though it can describe a neutral lack of definition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nebulousness mostly in writing and in serious discussion, such as business reviews, academic critiques or op-eds. In casual speech, people say something is vague or 'up in the air' instead. Using it in a meeting can sound precise and a little formal, which is fine in most professional settings.

distinctions.note: Ambiguity means something can be understood in two or more specific ways, while nebulousness means it has no clear meaning at all.
Vagueness is a general term for imprecise language; nebulousness suggests something cloud-like with no firm outline.

examples.everyday: I'm tired of the nebulousness of his plans; just tell me what we're doing on Saturday.
examples.professional: The nebulousness of the project scope is why our timeline keeps slipping every sprint.
examples.analytical: The nebulousness of her central term makes it impossible to tell which claim she is actually defending.

nuance.analogy: Like a cloud with no edges: you can see that something is there, but you cannot tell where it starts or stops.
nuance.etymology: From nebulous, from Latin nebula, meaning mist or cloud.
common_mistakes: Confusing nebulousness with nebula, the astronomical term for a cloud of gas and dust, and using it in a literal space sense.
Stressing the last syllable (nebulousNESS) instead of the first syllable, NEB.

senses.definition: One who negotiates.
senses.example: The hostage negotiator spent six hours talking the gunman into releasing his captives.

senses.definition: A diplomat, moderator.
senses.example: The envoy served as a neutral negotiator between the two countries during the border dispute.

core.definition: A person who works to reach an agreement between two sides, such as in a deal, a dispute or a labor contract.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GOH, and the -tiate syllables sound like 'shee-ay-ter', with the t becoming an 'sh' sound. Keep the final -er rhotic and light, not a full 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes someone skilled and trusted, usually in a serious, respected role.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use negotiator for people in business, labor relations, diplomacy, and law enforcement hostage situations. It is respectful, and in a workplace you might say 'our lead negotiator' for the person handling a contract. In everyday talk people more often say 'the one who handled the deal'. Do not confuse the noun with the verb phrase 'negotiate with', which is common in both speech and writing.

distinctions.note: A mediator is a neutral third party who helps others reach agreement; a negotiator usually represents one side in the talks.
A diplomat represents a government abroad and may negotiate, but the word covers a wider professional role.

examples.everyday: My cousin is a really good negotiator, so she got the car dealer to drop the price by a thousand dollars.
examples.professional: Our lead negotiator will call the vendor tomorrow to push back on the renewal terms.
examples.analytical: A good negotiator must understand both the stated interests and the unspoken needs of the other party, not only the positions they take.

nuance.analogy: A negotiator is like a bridge builder between two shores: the bridge is not the destination, but it lets the parties reach agreement.
nuance.etymology: From negotiate, from Latin negotiari 'to carry on business', from negotium 'business', plus the agent suffix -or.
common_mistakes: Using negotiator as a verb, as in 'he negotiator the contract'; the verb is negotiate.
Stressing the middle syllable, as in nih-goh-shee-AY-ter, which sounds unnatural.

negotiator.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *negōtiātor* (“merchant, banker”), equivalent to *negotiate* + *or*.

senses.definition: A neoteric (newly coined) word or phrase.

core.definition: A newly coined word or phrase, or a new practice or innovation in language.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on OT, the second syllable, and the vowel in OT is the 'cot' vowel, an open 'ah' sound. The final -ism is weak, like 'um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly pejorative. It can suggest a newfangled coinage that some people find unnecessary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use neoterism. It appears in linguistic or literary writing, usually when someone wants to sound learned about new coinages. In normal talk, people say neologism, new word or slang. Using it in casual conversation may sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: Neologism is the standard term for a newly coined word or expression; neoterism is rarer and more literary.
Slang is informal and often social in origin; neoterism refers to any new coinage, formal or informal.

examples.everyday: My grandmother thinks 'selfie' is a silly neoterism, but everyone at her church uses it now.
examples.professional: The linguist's report lists several recent neoterisms in tech jargon, and our team uses half of them daily.
examples.analytical: Each neoterism reveals what a community finds worth naming, which makes new coinages a window into social change.

nuance.analogy: A neoterism is like a new tool added to a workshop: it may replace an old one, or it may just sit on the bench until someone finds a use for it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek neōterismos 'innovation,' from neōteros 'newer'.
common_mistakes: Confusing neoterism with neoteric, which is the adjective meaning modern or new.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress falls on OT.

senses.definition: Wakefulness and watchfulness; a state of sobriety following a period of catharsis.
senses.example: In the desert monastic tradition, nepsis was the watchful sobriety that guarded the mind against distracting thoughts.

core.definition: In Eastern Orthodox spirituality, watchfulness or sobriety of mind: an inner alertness that guards the heart against passing thoughts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, NEP, and the final s is a true s, not a z. Keep the middle vowel short, like the e in bed, rather than adding an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive within spiritual writing, describing a disciplined alertness; neutral when discussed as a historical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use nepsis outside Orthodox theology, monastic writing, or discussions of contemplative prayer. You might hear it in a seminar on the Desert Fathers or the Philokalia, where it is usually explained for listeners unfamiliar with the term. In ordinary conversation, say attentiveness or self-control instead.

distinctions.note: Vigilance is general alertness to danger, while nepsis is a spiritual watchfulness over one's thoughts and heart, rooted in prayer.
Sobriety in everyday American English usually means not being drunk, whereas nepsis means an inner sobriety of mind free from distraction.

examples.everyday: My coworker who goes to an Orthodox church says nepsis is the habit of keeping your mind calm and alert all day.
examples.professional: In our reading group on the Philokalia, the instructor explained nepsis as the foundation for guarding the heart against distraction.
examples.analytical: For Evagrius, nepsis is not merely bodily vigilance but a purification of thought that prepares the mind for prayer.

nuance.analogy: Like a night watchman who stays awake and calm, not because he fears one particular thief, but because he guards the gate of the heart.
nuance.etymology: From Greek nepsis, sobriety or watchfulness, from nephein, to be sober.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel and saying NEP-uh-sis instead of NEP-sis.
Assuming a link to nepotism or nephew, which have no connection to the word.
nuance.biblical_note: Nepsis is not a biblical word, but its concept draws on the New Testament call to sobriety and watchfulness. 1 Peter 5:8 calls believers to be sober and watchful against an adversary, and 1 Thessalonians 5:6 urges them to keep awake and be sober rather than sleep like the rest of the world.

senses.definition: Not remote in degree, kindred, circumstances, etc. closely allied; intimate.
senses.example: Ruth and Naomi were bound by a nigh kinship that no hardship could sever.

senses.definition: To draw nigh (to); to approach; to come near.
senses.example: As the wedding day drew nigh, the family grew more anxious about the weather.

senses.definition: Almost, nearly.
senses.example: We talked for nigh on to two hours.

senses.definition: Near; close to.
senses.example: The bakery sits nigh the train station, so the bread smell drifts across the platform.

core.definition: Almost or nearly; close to a time, point, or condition, as in well nigh impossible.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable that rhymes with sky and eye. Do not add a t sound from night, and do not pronounce the h.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it has an old-fashioned, solemn tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet nigh in older writing, poetry, religious texts, and the phrase well nigh meaning almost. In daily speech, say near, almost, or nearly instead. The phrase draw nigh appears in older Bible translations and sermons, but ordinary speech would say approach or get close.

distinctions.note: Near is the everyday word for physical or time closeness; nigh is literary and rare outside set phrases.
Almost is the everyday American word for nearly; nigh is mostly limited to fixed phrases like well nigh.

examples.everyday: It was well nigh impossible to find parking downtown on game day.
examples.professional: Maintaining that model in production was well nigh impossible with our current staffing.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the phrase the day draws nigh signals imminence rather than a fixed date, and the answer shapes how the passage is read.

nuance.analogy: Nigh is like an old road sign: still readable and meaningful, but no longer on most modern maps.
nuance.etymology: From Old English neah, meaning near.
common_mistakes: Using nigh alone in speech, where near or almost is natural.
Pronouncing it like night with a final t sound.

senses.definition: Excessive; extravagant; inordinate; vexatious.

core.definition: Excessive, extravagant or unreasonable; going beyond what is proper or necessary. This is an archaic word.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ious ending is two syllables here, 'ee-us', not the single 'shus' sound of 'precious'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests that something has gone too far beyond reasonable limits.
nuance.usage_note: This word is archaic and almost never used in modern American speech or writing. You may find it in older religious, moral or literary texts, or in dictionaries. Americans would say 'excessive', 'extravagant' or 'inordinate' instead.

distinctions.note: Numinous means filled with a sense of the sacred or spiritual, while nimious means excessive, so the two words are easily confused but unrelated in meaning.
Excessive is the common modern word for too much, while nimious is archaic and sounds old-fashioned.

examples.professional: The auditor flagged nimious travel spending in the department, so we need to review those expense reports.
examples.analytical: Older moralists condemned nimious pleasures as a departure from temperance, arguing that appetite must be kept within reasonable limits.

nuance.analogy: A nimious gift is like a bucket of water poured on a plant that needed only a cup: the intention is kind, but the amount has gone beyond what is useful.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'nimius', meaning excessive, from 'nimis', meaning too much.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'numinous', which describes a sense of the sacred.
Using it in modern conversation, where 'excessive' or 'too much' sounds more natural.
Stressing the second syllable or pronouncing it as a single 'nim-yus' sound.

senses.definition: A character in a role-playing game or computer game whose actions are not controlled by a player.
A person who does not think for themselves nor make their own decisions.
senses.example: Stop acting like a non-player character and just tell your boss what you actually think.

core.definition: A character in a video or role-playing game who is controlled by the game's software, not by a human player.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress falls on CHAR in character, with a secondary stress on play. The final -er is a reduced ter sound, and the r in character is clear in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in game design and conversation. Used informally online, it can describe a person who seems to act without independent thought, which is an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Gamers and game developers use the term constantly, and most Americans shorten it to NPC, said as the letters N-P-C. The term describes shopkeepers, guards and quest givers. Online, calling someone an NPC is a mocking insult implying they act without independent thought, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: A bot is software that acts automatically on a platform; an NPC is a scripted character inside a game world.
An avatar is the character the human player controls; an NPC is not controlled by any player.
AI agent is a broad technical term; NPC is a game-specific term for a character that the game controls.

examples.everyday: That shopkeeper is just an NPC, so he'll only ever say the same three lines.
examples.professional: Our team is designing NPC pathfinding so guards patrol without blocking the player's route.
examples.analytical: The NPC's behavior is governed by scripts and rules, so the player's sense of agency depends on how tightly those choices are limited.

nuance.analogy: Like extras in a film: they make the world feel alive, but they do not drive the story.
nuance.etymology: Formed from non- (not), player and character; the term comes from tabletop role-playing and video game design.
common_mistakes: Saying NPC as a word, like nip; Americans say the letters N-P-C.
Putting the strongest stress on non instead of CHAR in character.

senses.definition: Not directive.
A statement or utterance that is not a directive.
senses.example: Her nondirective comment about the schedule made it sound more like a suggestion than an order.

core.definition: Not giving instructions or advice; letting the person being helped set the direction, as in counseling or coaching.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on REK, and the first syllable is a reduced 'duh,' not 'dye.' The word sounds like 'directive' with a 'nahn' added to the front.

nuance.connotation: Positive in counseling and coaching, where it signals respect for the client's own judgment; it can sound vague or passive in management settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use this word for counseling, therapy, coaching, interviewing and some styles of leadership, where it means the helper deliberately avoids telling the other person what to do. Carl Rogers used the term for his early approach to counseling in the 1940s. As a noun, the word sometimes appears in linguistics for an utterance that is not a directive, but that use is rare in everyday English.

distinctions.note: A directive is an instruction from a manager or authority, while a nondirective style avoids giving instructions.
Client-centered is the name Rogers later used for the same approach, and nondirective emphasizes the helper's restraint from directing.
Laissez-faire is a general hands-off management style, while nondirective usually refers to a deliberate method of helping someone reflect.

examples.everyday: My sister is a counselor, and she's pretty nondirective; she just asks questions until you figure things out yourself.
examples.professional: For these interviews I will take a nondirective approach so candidates can describe their own process in their own words.
examples.analytical: Rogers's nondirective counseling assumed that the client possesses the resources for growth, so the therapist's role was to reflect feeling rather than to advise.

nuance.analogy: Like a good tour guide who asks where you want to go, rather than marching you down a fixed route.
nuance.etymology: non- + directive, from Latin directivus, from dirigere 'to direct.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'dye' or stressing the first syllable instead of the REK.
Using it for any relaxed or passive style of management, when it specifically means letting the other person set the direction.

senses.definition: Not open to the public; not available to or shared by the public; private.

core.definition: Not open to the public; not available to or shared with the public; private.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PUB, and the vowel in PUB is the short 'uh' sound as in 'cup'. The ending -lic is pronounced 'lik' with a short i, not 'leek'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes access or status rather than judging quality, though it often signals confidentiality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nonpublic in business, legal and education contexts, such as nonpublic information, nonpublic companies and nonpublic schools. A nonpublic school in the United States means a private school, often a religious one. In casual speech, people more often say 'private' or 'not public.'

distinctions.note: Private is the everyday word for something belonging to or concerning one person or a small group; nonpublic is the more formal label, often used in regulations and business.
Confidential implies a duty of secrecy; nonpublic describes only that the information has not been released to the general public.

examples.everyday: My kids go to a nonpublic school across town, so they don't follow the district's calendar.
examples.professional: Please don't share this forecast, because it's nonpublic information until the earnings call.
examples.analytical: The court distinguished between public and nonpublic records, arguing that disclosure rules should follow their purpose.

nuance.analogy: Like a family recipe book kept in a drawer: it exists and is used, but it is not on the shelf at the library.
nuance.etymology: Formed from non- and public, from Latin publicus 'of the people'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (non-pub-LIK) instead of PUB.
Pronouncing the ending -lic as 'leek'.
Using nonpublic for information that is secret in a legal sense without checking whether it is also confidential.

senses.definition: Unrandomized.
senses.example: a nonrandomized clinical trial

core.definition: Of a study or trial, not assigning participants or treatments by chance, so the groups were chosen by other means.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on RAN, the first syllable of 'random'. The ending -ized is one syllable, 'mizd', so the word has no extra beat at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In research it is a methodological label, though it can signal weaker evidence.
nuance.usage_note: Statisticians, medical researchers and social scientists use this word to describe designs in which the researcher or participants choose the groups. In American clinical research, a nonrandomized trial is considered weaker than a randomized controlled trial, because selection bias is more likely. Ordinary speakers would say 'not randomly assigned.'

distinctions.note: Unrandomized is nearly the same in meaning, but nonrandomized is more common in American research writing.
Observational means the researcher only watches and does not assign treatments; nonrandomized can include studies where the researcher assigns treatments but without chance.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the study I read was nonrandomized, so I wouldn't trust its results too much.
examples.professional: The nonrandomized pilot showed promise, but we'll need a randomized trial before rolling it out.
examples.analytical: Because the nonrandomized design let patients choose their own treatment, selection bias could explain the observed difference.

nuance.analogy: Like picking teams by hand instead of drawing names from a hat: you may be fair, but you can't be sure the groups are alike.
nuance.etymology: Formed from non- and randomized, from random, from Old French randon 'speed, force'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable (ran-DOM-ized) instead of RAN-duh-mizd.
Confusing nonrandomized with nonrandom, which describes data patterns rather than how groups were assigned.
Pronouncing -ized with a full 'eyes-d' ending, adding an extra syllable.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being nonviable; impracticality.
senses.example: The nonviability of the proposal was obvious to us all.

core.definition: The condition of being unable to survive or succeed, such as a fetus that cannot survive outside the womb, or a plan that cannot work.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress falls on BIL, with a weaker stress on NON. The 'vi' is pronounced 'vy', and the final syllable is 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to clinical in medicine or science; can be heavy in ethical debates about fetal life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nonviability mostly in medical, legal and policy discussions. In everyday conversation, people say 'not able to survive' or 'not workable'. It is a sensitive term in abortion debates, so choose your context carefully. The adjective nonviable is more common than the noun.

distinctions.note: Unviability is a rare, less standard word; nonviability is the usual form in medical and legal writing.
Impracticality means a plan is difficult to carry out; nonviability is stronger, meaning the thing cannot succeed or sustain itself at all.

examples.everyday: The doctor explained the nonviability of the plan, so we decided not to try that treatment.
examples.professional: The review board found that the proposed architecture showed nonviability under real traffic loads.
examples.analytical: Philosophers debating personhood often hinge their arguments on the criteria used to define nonviability.

nuance.analogy: Like a seed that never sprouts, it cannot grow into anything that lasts.
nuance.etymology: From non- ('not') plus viability, from French viable, from Latin vita ('life').
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable of 'viability'; the main stress is on BIL.
Using nonviability for a person's character; it applies to things, plans or organisms.

senses.definition: A small corner formed by two walls; an alcove.
senses.example: There was a small broom for sweeping ash kept in the nook between the fireplace bricks and the wall.

senses.definition: A hidden or secluded spot; a secluded retreat.
senses.example: The back of the used book shop was one of her favorite nooks; she could read for hours and no one would bother her or pester her to buy.

senses.definition: A recess, cove or hollow.
senses.example: We curled up in a sunny nook beside the bookshelf with a cup of tea.

senses.definition: The vagina-like genitalia of a troll, featured in Homestuck fanworks but not in canon.
(historical) An English unit of land area, originally ⁄4 of a yardland but later 12+⁄2 or 20 acres.
senses.example: The medieval charter granted the monks a nook of land near the river.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To withdraw into a nook.
senses.example: After the argument, he nooked himself away in the attic to cool off.

senses.definition: To situate in a nook.
senses.example: She nooked the reading lamp between two tall bookcases in the corner.

core.definition: A small, cozy corner or recess in a room or building, often with a sheltered or secluded feel.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the short oo of book, not the long oo of cook or nook sounding like nuke. Keep the k sound crisp at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. A nook suggests comfort, privacy, and a cozy retreat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use nook in home decor and real estate, as in breakfast nook, reading nook, or built-in nook. A plain corner is just a corner, while a nook feels tucked away. The verb sense, to withdraw into a nook, is rare and sounds literary.

distinctions.note: A corner is any place where two walls or lines meet, while a nook is a small recessed space that feels sheltered.
An alcove is an architectural recess that is often open to a room, while a nook can be any small cozy spot, including furniture arrangements.
A niche is a recess in a wall for a statue or object, and it can also mean a specialized market; a nook is an everyday, cozy space.

examples.everyday: She curled up in the reading nook by the window with a cup of tea.
examples.professional: The office has a quiet nook near the kitchen where people can take calls without disturbing others.
examples.analytical: Phenomenologists describe the nook as a small space that shelters imagination, giving a sense of being protected from the outside world.

nuance.analogy: A nook is like the spot on the couch where you tuck in with a blanket and a book.
nuance.etymology: Middle English nok, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long vowel, like nuke, instead of the short vowel of book.
Confusing nook with nock, the notch at the end of an arrow, which is pronounced the same way.

nook.etymology: From Middle English *noke*, *nok* (“nook, corner, angle”), of uncertain origin.

senses.definition: Not important; nothing to worry about.

core.definition: Not important or serious; nothing to worry about or make a fuss over.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on BIG and DEAL, with 'a' reduced to schwa. In fast speech, 'not a' links to sound like 'nah-duh,' and the stress on 'big' is stronger than on 'not.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or reassuring; it is used to comfort someone or downplay a problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this to reassure someone who apologizes, such as after a small mistake or late arrival. A natural reply to 'Sorry about that' is 'Oh, it's not a big deal.' It is casual and friendly, but avoid it in serious situations, where it can sound dismissive.

distinctions.note: 'No big deal' is nearly identical and equally common; both mean the matter is minor.
'It's nothing' is more polite and modest, especially for thanks, while 'not a big deal' explicitly downplays a problem.

collocations: not a big deal at all
it's really not a big deal
not a big deal to me

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, I got stuck in traffic. Oh, it's not a big deal, we just started ordering.
examples.professional: The client wants the report a day early, but that's not a big deal if we prioritize the dashboard tonight.
examples.analytical: Whether a minor error matters depends on context; calling it 'not a big deal' may mask consequences that only appear downstream.

nuance.analogy: Like a small pebble in your shoe, it may be annoying but not worth stopping for.
common_mistakes: Saying 'not a big deal' in formal writing where 'not significant' or 'minor' fits better.
Mispronouncing 'a' as the full vowel /eɪ/ instead of a reduced schwa.

conversation.text: Missing one class is not a big deal.
It's not a big deal, but please double-check the dates next time.
Don't worry about the spilled coffee. It's not a big deal.

senses.definition: An author of novels.

core.definition: A person who writes novels, which are long works of fiction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, NAH. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, and the ending -ist is 'ist', not 'eest'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting creative skill and literary work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'novelist' for anyone who writes novels, from bestselling authors to literary writers. In casual talk you might also say 'author' or 'writer', but 'novelist' is more precise. It is common in book reviews, interviews, and introductions.

distinctions.note: 'Author' is the broad term for anyone who writes books, while 'novelist' specifically means someone who writes novels.
'Writer' is the most general term and can include journalists and essayists, while 'novelist' is specific to long fiction.

examples.everyday: My cousin is a novelist, so she spends most of her mornings writing at the library.
examples.professional: Our marketing team hired a novelist to write the brand story, which we're now using in the company deck.
examples.analytical: The novelist's narrative choices reveal how memory shapes identity, since each chapter returns to earlier scenes with new details.

nuance.analogy: Like an architect of imagined worlds, building characters and plots that readers can walk through.
nuance.etymology: From novel plus the suffix -ist, 'one who writes or practices'.
common_mistakes: Using 'novelist' for writers of short stories or essays, which is too narrow.
Saying 'NO-vel-ist' with a long o; the American vowel is 'NAH'.

senses.definition: A beginner; one who is not very familiar or experienced in a particular subject.
senses.example: I'm only a novice at coding, so my programs frequently have bugs that more experienced programmers would avoid.

senses.definition: A new member of a religious order accepted on a conditional basis, prior to confirmation.
senses.example: The young woman entered the convent as a novice, preparing for her future vows.

senses.definition: Of a beginner; unfamiliar or unexperienced in a particular subject.
senses.example: As a novice programmer, he relied heavily on tutorials and asked many questions.

core.definition: A beginner who has little experience or skill in a particular activity, subject, or job.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NAH. The final syllable is 'is,' not 'ees,' so it rhymes with 'promise' without the final 'eez' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes inexperience without judgment, though it can imply being less skilled than others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use novice in workplace, sports, and skills contexts, as in 'a novice programmer' or 'a novice cook.' It is slightly more formal than 'beginner,' and in casual talk people might say 'newbie' or 'just starting out.' Saying 'I'm a novice' is a polite way to admit you are new without sounding helpless.

distinctions.note: Beginner is the everyday word for someone just starting; novice more often suggests someone who has some basics but lacks experience.
An amateur does something for enjoyment, not for money; a novice is simply new, whether paid or not.

examples.everyday: I'm a complete novice at gardening, so I'll probably kill these tomatoes.
examples.professional: We are pairing a novice analyst with a senior engineer so she can learn the pipeline quickly.
examples.analytical: A novice reasons from rules, while the expert perceives patterns, a difference that Dreyfus made central to skill acquisition.

nuance.analogy: A novice is like a new hiker on a trail: he knows the path exists, but he has not yet learned to read the terrain.
nuance.etymology: From Latin novicius, 'newly made,' from novus, 'new.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'no' with a long o, sounding like 'NO-vis'; American usage is 'NAH-vis.'
Using 'at' or 'in' incorrectly; say 'a novice at chess' or 'a novice in statistics,' not 'a novice of chess.'

novice.etymology: From Middle English *novice*, *novys*, from Anglo-Norman *novice*, Middle French *novice*, itself borrowed from Latin *novīcius*, later *novitius* (“new, newly arrived”) (in Late Latin as a noun, masculine *novicius*, feminine *novicia* (“one who has newly…

senses.definition: A minor distinction.
senses.example: hidden nuances

senses.definition: Subtlety or fine detail.
senses.example: Understanding the basics is easy, but appreciating the nuances takes years.

senses.definition: To apply a nuance to; to change or redefine in a subtle way.
senses.example: Before publishing, the editor nuanced the headline to avoid overstating the study's findings.

core.definition: A subtle difference in meaning, feeling, tone, or appearance that is often important but easy to miss.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the second as a light 'ahns' with a nasal n sound, not the 'nyoo' of British speech. In American English the word begins with a plain 'noo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests careful thinking and sensitivity to detail, though it can imply that something is complicated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nuance in meetings, reviews, academic discussions, and everyday conversation when someone wants to say that a situation is more complicated than it looks. Saying 'there's some nuance here' is a polite way to disagree without sounding harsh. The verb form is less common in everyday speech and mostly appears in writing.

distinctions.note: Difference is a general word for any contrast, while nuance is a subtle, often hard-to-see difference in meaning or tone.
Detail is a specific fact or item, while nuance is a subtle quality that changes how facts are understood.

examples.everyday: I know the movie got bad reviews, but there's a lot of nuance in how it handles grief.
examples.professional: The model's predictions look accurate overall, but we need to discuss the nuance in how it performs on smaller customer segments.
examples.analytical: A careful reading of the text reveals nuances in the author's use of irony that a simple moral reading would miss.

nuance.analogy: A nuance is like the slight shift in a color's shade: you may not notice it at first, but it changes the whole picture.
nuance.etymology: From French nuance, 'shade of color,' from nuer, 'to shade.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a 'nyoo' sound at the start, as British speakers often do.
Using nuance as a plural count noun without care, as in 'a nuance' for a large difference; it means a small, subtle one.

nuance.etymology: French *nuance*.

senses.definition: Trivial, trifling or of little importance.
senses.example: The committee dismissed his objection as nugatory, a complaint about the font color.

senses.definition: Ineffective, invalid or futile.
senses.example: Her efforts to fix the broken contract were nugatory, since the court had already ruled.

senses.definition: Having no force, inoperative, ineffectual.
Removable from a computer program with safety, but harmless if retained.
senses.example: The unused import statement is nugatory, so the compiler can safely remove it.

core.definition: Trivial or unimportant, or having no real effect, so that it is useless or ineffective.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllables are weak, and the final -ory is pronounced 'or-ee' with an American r, so it does not sound like 'tory'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something worthless or ineffective and usually appears in formal argument or legal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nugatory in formal writing, legal arguments, and academic discussion to say that something has no real effect. In everyday speech people say 'pointless,' 'useless,' or 'no big deal.' In a meeting, saying a point is nugatory can sound dismissive, so it is best used in written or precise argument.

distinctions.note: Trivial is common and general, while nugatory is more formal and emphasizes that something has no effect or validity.
Ineffective focuses on failing to work, while nugatory can also mean unimportant or lacking legal force.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the difference between the two plans is nugatory, so just pick whichever is cheaper.
examples.professional: Those last-minute changes to the slides are nugatory, so let's focus on the data validation issues.
examples.analytical: If the statute's exception is read broadly, the constitutional guarantee becomes nugatory, a result the drafters surely did not intend.

nuance.analogy: A nugatory argument is like a key that fits no lock: it looks official, but it does not open anything.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nugatorius, 'trifling,' from nugari, 'to trifle.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'tree' instead of 'or-ee'.
Using nugatory as a synonym for 'nutritious' or 'nugget'-like things, confusing it with unrelated words.

senses.definition: Physically unable to feel, not having the power of sensation.
senses.example: fingers numb with cold

senses.definition: Emotionally unable to feel or respond in a normal way.
senses.example: numb with shock; numb with boredom

senses.definition: Dumb or stupid.
senses.example: That was a numb thing to say in front of the investors.

senses.definition: To cause to become numb (physically or emotionally).
senses.example: The dentist gave me novocaine to numb my tooth before drilling, thank goodness.

senses.definition: To cause (a feeling) to be less intense.
senses.example: He turned to alcohol to numb his pain.

senses.definition: To cause (the mind, faculties, etc.) to be less acute.
senses.example: Too many double shifts numbed her mind and dulled her judgment.

senses.definition: To become numb (especially physically).
senses.example: My fingers numbed quickly in the December wind while we waited for the bus.

core.definition: Unable to feel anything in part of the body, such as from cold, injury or medicine; or emotionally unable to react normally.

pronunciation.tip: The word has one syllable, and the vowel is the short 'uh' sound as in 'come' and 'sum'. The b is silent, so do not add a 'b' sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical and physical use. In emotional use it suggests shock, grief or exhaustion and can sound sad or serious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'my foot is numb' or 'I feel numb' very often, both about cold weather and about shock after bad news. Calling a person 'numb' in the sense of stupid is informal and old-fashioned, so avoid it. The word is also used with numbing medicine, such as 'the gum is numb after the dentist'.

distinctions.note: Numb describes the state a person or body part is in, while numbing describes what causes that state.
Numb suggests you cannot feel anything, while tired means you have little energy; both can describe a long day but they are not interchangeable.

examples.everyday: My fingers went numb after we waited an hour in the snow.
examples.professional: After three back-to-back meetings, I was numb and couldn't follow the budget discussion.
examples.analytical: Repeated exposure to news of tragedy can leave people numb, so the same events matter less each time.

nuance.analogy: Numb is like a foot that has fallen asleep: the signal from the nerve is blocked, so you feel nothing until it comes back.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'nomen,' the past participle of Old English 'niman,' meaning 'to take' or 'seize,' so the original sense was 'seized' or 'deprived of feeling'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'NOOM' or 'NYOOM' with a long vowel; the vowel is short.
Using numb as an insult meaning stupid, which sounds dated and unkind in American speech.

numb.etymology: From the past participle of *nim* (“to take”).

senses.definition: In terms of coins or currency.

core.definition: In terms of coins, currency, or the collecting of money as objects.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -MAT-, the third syllable. The final -ly is a light 'lee' sound, and the middle vowels are short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise, specialized word.
nuance.usage_note: This adverb is specialized and appears mainly in collector, auction, and scholarly writing, describing something valued or examined as coins or money. Americans rarely say it in conversation; they would more likely say 'from a coin collector's point of view'. Speaking, 'numismatically speaking' is a natural phrase among collectors.

distinctions.note: Monetarily refers to money in general and economic terms; numismatically refers to coins and currency as collectible objects.
Economically concerns the financial or market value of something; numismatically concerns its value as a coin, such as its rarity or condition.

examples.professional: Numismatically, the coin is a rare die variety, so the auction house listed it as a separate lot.
examples.analytical: The hoard is numismatically significant because it dates the monetary reforms of the late empire.

nuance.analogy: Like judging a book by its binding and printing rather than by its story.
nuance.etymology: From numismatic, from Latin numisma 'coin'.
common_mistakes: Using it to mean 'numerically' because the two words look similar.
Using it outside contexts of coins or currency, where it sounds odd.

senses.definition: The act or process of objectifying something intangible.
senses.example: Her theology paper traced the objectification of sacred meaning into rituals, markets, and institutions.

senses.definition: The act or process of objectifying someone.
senses.example: Her theology paper traced the objectification of sacred meaning into rituals, markets, and institutions.

core.definition: Treating a person, or sometimes an abstract idea, as a mere object rather than a human being with feelings or value.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KAY, the fifth syllable, so the word ends in -shun with a reduced vowel. Non-native speakers often give the final syllable a full vowel like 'shawn' or stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use this word in discussions of gender, media, advertising, and respect at work, where it usually criticizes treating people as bodies or tools. In casual speech, people often say 'treating her like a thing' instead. In philosophy, it can also mean making an abstract idea seem concrete, which is a neutral use.

distinctions.note: Dehumanization is the broader stripping of human dignity from a person or group, while objectification focuses on treating someone as a thing to be used or looked at.
Reification is a philosophical term, used by Marx and Lukács, for treating social relations as if they were fixed things; objectification is more common in everyday ethical discussion.
Use is a neutral word for employing something, while objectification adds an ethical criticism that a person is being reduced to a function.

examples.everyday: My sister says that ad is pure objectification, and honestly, she's not wrong.
examples.professional: Our HR training covered how comments about coworkers' appearance can lead to objectification and create a hostile environment.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that objectification occurs when a person's agency is reduced to bodily appearance, making them usable rather than respected as subjects.

nuance.analogy: Like a store mannequin that looks like a person but exists only to display clothes, the objectified person is seen for what they can offer rather than who they are.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obiectum ('thing placed before'), plus the verb suffix -ify (from Latin facere, 'to make') and the noun suffix -ation.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'objectivity' (fairness and impartiality), which is a different idea.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'ob-JEK-tih-fih-kay-shun,' instead of placing the main stress on -KAY-.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being obnoxious.
senses.example: The obnoxiousness of his constant bragging made everyone at the office avoid him during lunch.

core.definition: The quality of being extremely annoying, rude or unpleasant to other people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NAH, the second syllable. The word has four syllables, and the final -ness is a short uh-nuhs, not a long ness sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names an unpleasant quality in a person's behavior or in something like an advertisement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use obnoxiousness to describe a general quality of annoying or attention-seeking behavior, as in 'his constant obnoxiousness.' It is more casual than formal and often appears in reviews, complaints or humorous comments. Speakers usually say it about a person's conduct rather than a single small mistake.

distinctions.note: Rudeness is a lack of courtesy, while obnoxiousness is a more attention-seeking kind of irritating behavior.
Arrogance is an attitude of superiority, while obnoxiousness is the annoying way that attitude or behavior shows up in public.

examples.everyday: I like the band, but the lead singer's obnoxiousness between songs ruins the show for me.
examples.professional: The obnoxiousness of the pop-up ads is hurting our conversion rate, so let's test a quieter design.
examples.analytical: The essay defines obnoxiousness not by any single rude act but by a pattern of behavior that forces attention onto oneself.

nuance.analogy: Like a smoke alarm that keeps chirping in the middle of dinner: the annoyance is the point.
nuance.etymology: From obnoxious, from Latin obnoxius 'exposed to harm', with the suffix -ness added in English.
common_mistakes: Confusing obnoxiousness with noxiousness, which refers to harmful or poisonous things.
Adding an extra syllable and saying ob-NOX-ee-us-ness.

senses.definition: The action of darkening or fact of being darkened, as with a cloud; obscuration.
Obscuration or clouding of the mind or faculties.
A veiling with or concealment in clouds.
senses.example: Hikers lost the trail in the obnubilation of mist that swallowed the valley each morning.

senses.definition: Something that obscures or causes confoundment; an obfuscation.
senses.example: The vague budget report was an obnubilation that made it impossible to tell where the money went.

core.definition: The act of darkening or clouding, literally as with a cloud, or figuratively in the mind; obscuration.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAY, the fourth syllable, and the -tion ending is shun. Say the nu as in 'new' without the y sound, and do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a clouding or dimming, with no judgment in itself.
nuance.usage_note: Obnubilation is rare, and most Americans will meet it only in literary, philosophical or older writing. In everyday speech, Americans say 'fog', 'cloud over' or 'dimming' instead. Recognize the word when you read it, but use plainer words in conversation.

distinctions.note: Obscuration is the more common synonym and can be used in both technical and general writing.
Obfuscation is deliberate confusion, often in politics or business, while obnubilation is simply a clouding or darkening.
Obscurity is the state of being unknown or hard to understand; obnubilation focuses on the act or process of clouding.

examples.everyday: After the long flight with no sleep, I had a kind of obnubilation in my head that I couldn't shake.
examples.professional: The fatigue caused a kind of obnubilation in the engineer's judgment during the outage, so we now limit on-call shifts.
examples.analytical: Plato's cave describes the mind's obnubilation by shadows, from which the philosopher must be turned toward the light.

nuance.analogy: Like a windshield fogging up on a cold morning until you can barely see the road.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obnubilare 'to cloud over', from ob- 'over' and nubilus 'cloudy', from nubes 'cloud'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable or the nu, as in OB-noo-bih-lay-shun.
Using obnubilation in casual conversation where fog or cloud would sound more natural.

senses.definition: Dark, faint or indistinct.
senses.example: The old lamp cast an obscure glow across the dim, cluttered study.

senses.definition: Hidden, out of sight or inconspicuous.
senses.example: The restaurant was tucked away in an obscure alley that few tourists ever found.

senses.definition: Difficult to understand; abstruse.
senses.example: an obscure passage or inscription; The speaker made obscure references to little-known literary works.

senses.definition: Not well-known.
Unknown or uncertain; unclear.
senses.example: The etymological roots of the word "blizzard" are obscure and open to debate.

senses.definition: To render obscure; to darken; to make dim; to keep in the dark; to hide; to make less visible, intelligible, legible, glorious, beautiful, or illustrious.
senses.example: Heavy fog began to obscure the highway, forcing drivers to slow to a crawl.

senses.definition: To hide, put out of sight etc.
senses.example: She tried to obscure the mistake in the report by burying it in footnotes.

core.definition: Not well known, or hard to see or understand because it is unclear or hidden.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SKYOOR, and the first syllable is a weak uh-b. The vowel in the second syllable is a long oo, and the final r is clear in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can describe something little known, or something deliberately unclear.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use obscure in everyday talk for things that few people know, like an obscure band or an obscure rule. It also describes something hard to understand, such as an obscure reference. As a verb, it is more formal and means to hide or make unclear, so you might say that headlines obscure the facts.

distinctions.note: Unknown means not known at all; obscure means known to few people or hard to see clearly.
Vague means not clearly defined; obscure suggests something hidden or difficult to understand.
Hidden means concealed; obscure may mean concealed or just little known and hard to find.

examples.everyday: I heard an obscure song on the radio last night that I hadn't thought about in years.
examples.professional: The dashboard's labels are so obscure that new analysts keep asking what the metrics mean.
examples.analytical: The author's obscure language in the epistle has led exegetes to propose very different readings of the passage.

nuance.analogy: Something obscure is like a path through a forest that few people walk and that is hard to see unless you know where to look.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obscurus, dark, covered, or hidden.
common_mistakes: Using obscure to mean unknown in every case; obscure can also mean hard to understand.
Confusing the adjective pronunciation with the verb, which is the same, so stress is important: ub-SKYOOR.

obscure.etymology: From Middle English *obscure*, from Old French *obscur*, from Latin *obscūrus* (“dark, dusky, indistinct”), from *ob-* + **scūrus*, from Proto-Italic **skoiros*, from Proto-Indo-European **ḱeh₃-*.

senses.definition: To take or use. To fill.
senses.example: The film occupied three hours of my time.

senses.definition: To fill.
senses.example: The film occupied three hours of my time.

senses.definition: To possess or use the time or capacity of; to engage the service of.
senses.example: The film occupied me for three hours.

senses.definition: To fill or hold (an official position or role).
senses.example: I occupy the post of deputy cat catcher.

senses.definition: To hold the attention of.
senses.example: I occupied her friend while he made his proposal.

senses.definition: To take or use space. To fill space.
senses.example: The historic mansion occupied two city blocks.

senses.definition: To fill space.
senses.example: The historic mansion occupied two city blocks.

senses.definition: To live or reside in.
To place the theodolite or total station at (a point).
senses.example: The surveyor occupied the benchmark and leveled the total station before measuring.

senses.definition: To have, or to have taken, possession or control of (a territory).
senses.example: Federal troops occupied the town for three years after the war ended.

core.definition: To take up or fill a space, place, or amount of time; also to live or stay in a place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AH. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, and the final -y sounds like 'eye.' Learners often stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is practical and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use occupy in everyday talk about space and time, such as occupying a seat or occupying yourself with a hobby. It also appears in political news, such as Occupy movements, which refers to protests. In casual speech people often say take up or keep busy. Occupy a space sounds natural, but it is less common for simple seating.

distinctions.note: Fill emphasizes making something full; occupy emphasizes using or holding a space or time.
Take up is more casual and common in speech; occupy is more formal and suitable for writing.

examples.everyday: The kids occupied themselves with puzzles while we waited for the food.
examples.professional: This role occupies most of my week, so I can only join the planning meetings on Thursdays.
examples.analytical: Descartes sought a foundation that would occupy the mind without any doubt remaining.

nuance.analogy: Like a guest who fills a chair at a dinner table, occupying a space means taking it for yourself.
nuance.etymology: From Latin occupare, 'to seize, take possession,' from ob- 'toward' plus capere 'to take.'
common_mistakes: Using occupy with a preposition, such as occupy in the room instead of simply occupy the room.
Confusing occupy with occupation, which is a noun.

occupy.etymology: From Middle English *occupien*, *occupyen*, borrowed from Old French *occuper*, from Latin *occupō* (“to take possession of, seize, occupy, take up, employ”), from *ob* (“to, on”) + *capiō* (“to take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **kap-* (“to…

senses.definition: Initialism of Original Design Manufacturer, a company that designs and manufactures a product that will be rebranded for sale by another company.
Initialism of OpenDocument Master, a computer file type.
senses.example: The archive stores each chapter as an ODM file for long-term preservation.

senses.definition: Initialism of OverDrive Media, a computer file type.
senses.example: I downloaded the audiobook as an ODM file from the library app.

core.definition: Original Design Manufacturer: a company that designs and builds a product that another company then sells under its own brand name.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters one by one: 'oh', 'dee', 'em', with the strongest stress on the final letter M. Do not say it as a single word like 'odum'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a business and manufacturing term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ODM in business, electronics, and supply-chain discussions. The term is often heard in talk about laptops, phones, and consumer devices that are designed in one place and sold under another brand. When explaining it, people often say the full phrase first and then use the abbreviation.

distinctions.note: An OEM, or Original Equipment Manufacturer, builds parts or products to a buyer's design, while an ODM also creates the design itself.
A contract manufacturer builds to specifications the client supplies, whereas an ODM brings its own design and sells it to brands.

examples.everyday: My friend's company is an ODM, so they design phones that other brands sell under their own name.
examples.professional: We are evaluating an ODM in Taiwan to build the next hardware line under our brand, which saves engineering time.
examples.analytical: The ODM model separates design and manufacturing from brand ownership, which shapes where bargaining power sits in the supply chain.

nuance.analogy: Like a restaurant kitchen that creates recipes and cooks the food, which another company then serves under its own name.
nuance.etymology: An initialism of 'original design manufacturer', from English words.
common_mistakes: Confusing ODM with OEM; an ODM designs the product, while an OEM builds to someone else's design.
Pronouncing the letters as a word, such as 'odum'; say each letter separately.

senses.definition: While flying.
senses.example: The hawks stayed on the wing for hours, riding thermals above the ridge.

senses.definition: During operation.
senses.example: Our backup generator stays on the wing during every storm, ready to take over instantly.

senses.definition: In motion.
Departing.
senses.example: The last bus was already on the wing when I reached the station.

core.definition: In flight, or in motion and not stopped; often describing someone who is always traveling or working between tasks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable wing, with a short ih vowel, not ee. The ng is one sound at the end, so do not split it into n and g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; evokes motion, freedom and busyness, with a poetic or literary tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use it in everyday speech; it appears mostly in literary or nature writing about birds in flight. The figurative sense, a person or project always in motion, shows up in business and journalism but sounds somewhat old-fashioned. In casual conversation, say on the move or in the air instead.

distinctions.note: In the air means flying or airborne, and in conversation it can also mean not yet decided; on the wing is more poetic.
On the move is common and casual for traveling or changing; on the wing is more literary and suggests flight.

collocations: shoot a bird on the wing

examples.everyday: We watched the hawks circling over the field, always on the wing.
examples.professional: Our account director is on the wing this month, so please send your questions in writing.
examples.analytical: Thoreau's journal entries capture a mind always on the wing, moving between close observation and reflection on what it saw.
