nuance.etymology: Tension comes from Latin tensio, 'stretching'; headache comes from Old English heafodece, from heafod 'head' and ece 'ache'.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two unconnected words such as 'tension head ache'.
Stressing the final syllable as 'head-AKE' rather than 'HED-ayk'.

senses.definition: Having left a legally valid last will and testament.
Having a test (external calciferous shell or endoskeleton)
senses.example: Foraminifera are single-celled protists, and many species are testate with calcium carbonate shells.

senses.definition: One who has left a valid will and testament.
senses.example: The lawyer read the will aloud because the testate had named her sole heir.

core.definition: Having made a legally valid will before dying, so that one's property is distributed as one directed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the ending is a clear long 'ay' sound, not 'it'. Learners often stress the second syllable or say 'TES-tit'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a legal and technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use testate almost only in legal, estate-planning or probate contexts, such as a lawyer asking whether a client is testate. In everyday speech people say 'she had a will' or 'he left a will'. The opposite, dying without a will, is intestate.

distinctions.note: Intestate means dying without a valid will, so state intestacy law decides who inherits; testate is the opposite condition.
Testamentary describes things connected with a will, such as a testamentary trust; testate describes the person who has made one.

examples.everyday: Grandpa was organized and died testate, so there was no fight over the house.
examples.professional: Before we open the file, please confirm whether the decedent was testate or left no will.
examples.analytical: Whether a person is testate or intestate determines whether the distribution of property reflects their own intention or the default rules of the statute.

nuance.analogy: Testate is like writing the instructions yourself, while intestate is leaving the court to guess what you wanted.
nuance.etymology: From Latin testatus, past participle of testari, 'to make a will' or 'bear witness', from testis 'witness'.
common_mistakes: Saying TES-tit instead of TES-tayt, which confuses it with other words.
Using testate to mean 'tested' or 'tested positive'.
Using testate in casual conversation, where 'had a will' sounds more natural.

testate.etymology: From Latin *testātus* (“testified”), perfect passive participle of *testor* (“to be witness, testify, attest; to make a will”), from *testis* (“witness”).

senses.definition: The conversion of language text into speech using voice synthesis.

core.definition: Software that converts written text into spoken audio using a synthetic voice.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SPEECH. In fast speech, to reduces to 'tuh', and the final t of text links smoothly into it.

nuance.connotation: Positive in accessibility contexts, where it helps people with visual impairments or reading difficulties. Otherwise neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use text-to-speech as a noun ('the text-to-speech feature on my phone') or as an adjective. It is common in discussions of accessibility, screen readers and AI voice products. Engineers often write TTS. The word is not usually used for spoken conversation.

distinctions.note: Speech recognition goes the other way, turning spoken audio into written text.
A screen reader is an assistive program that often uses text-to-speech to read a screen aloud.

examples.everyday: My phone's text-to-speech reads my messages out loud when I'm driving.
examples.professional: The new text-to-speech engine cut our audio generation costs in half.
examples.analytical: Modern text-to-speech systems model prosody as well as individual sounds, which is why synthetic voices now sound less mechanical.

nuance.analogy: It is like a reader who never gets tired and can read any document aloud on request.
nuance.etymology: A compound of the English words text, to and speech, formed in computing.
common_mistakes: Writing 'text to speech' without hyphens in technical documents.
Stressing to rather than SPEECH.

conversation.text: Text-to-speech converts written text into spoken audio.
Modern text-to-speech sounds natural, with realistic pauses and intonation.
Text-to-speech makes documents accessible to people who are blind or have low vision.

senses.definition: A field of scholarly enquiry dedicated to reconstructing the oldest form(s) of a text that is or are possible to retrieve and to explaining any attested variants.
senses.example: In her seminar on textual criticism, she compared dozens of medieval manuscripts of the Gospels.

core.definition: The scholarly discipline of recovering the earliest recoverable form of a text and explaining the variant readings found in its copies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of each word. The -ual ending is one unstressed syllable, uhl. Criticism ends in -izm, not -ism, and the critic is a neutral evaluator here, not a negative one.

nuance.connotation: Neutral scholarly term. Criticism here means careful evaluation, not hostility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in biblical studies, classics and literary scholarship, usually in seminaries, universities and journals. It is not everyday vocabulary. The person is called a textual critic. Lower criticism is an older name for the textual part of biblical criticism.

distinctions.note: Literary criticism interprets meaning and style, while textual criticism establishes what the original words were.
Higher criticism studies authorship, dates and sources, while textual criticism concerns the wording of surviving manuscripts.

examples.everyday: My seminary friend spends all day comparing old Greek manuscripts, which she calls textual criticism.
examples.professional: Our translation team relied on textual criticism to choose between two readings in the Greek.
examples.analytical: Textual criticism weighs the age, geographic spread and quality of manuscripts before deciding which reading most likely stood in the original.

nuance.analogy: It is like restoring a damaged painting by studying copies and fragments to recover what the artist first painted.
nuance.etymology: From Latin textus, 'text', and Greek kritikos, 'able to judge'.
common_mistakes: Assuming criticism means a negative judgment; here it means careful evaluation.
Stressing the last syllable of the first word; the stress is TEKST-choo-ul.
nuance.biblical_note: Not a biblical term, but central to Bible study: scholars compare Greek and Hebrew manuscripts to reconstruct the original wording. The longer ending of Mark, 16:9-20, is absent from the earliest manuscripts, and the story of the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53-8:11, is missing from them too, so textual critics treat both as later additions. The RSV marks such passages with notes rather than removing them.

senses.definition: Any of a group of inherited disorders in which the amount of hemoglobin in the blood is reduced.

core.definition: An inherited blood disorder in which the body makes less hemoglobin than normal, often causing anemia.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SEE, and the ending is 'mee-uh,' not 'mee-ah.' Start with a voiceless th as in 'think,' not a t or s sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and medical. It names a serious condition, so the tone is clinical rather than casual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thalassemia in medical settings, such as doctor visits, genetic counseling and patient support groups. Outside those contexts people usually say 'a blood disorder' or 'a genetic form of anemia.' Doctors often specify alpha or beta thalassemia, so listen for those terms.

distinctions.note: Both are inherited hemoglobin disorders, but thalassemia reduces how much hemoglobin is made, while sickle cell disease changes the shape of the hemoglobin molecule.
Anemia is a general condition of low red blood cells or hemoglobin, while thalassemia is one specific genetic cause of it.

examples.everyday: My cousin was diagnosed with thalassemia as a child, so she has always been careful about her iron levels.
examples.professional: Our health plan now covers genetic screening for thalassemia for members whose families have a Mediterranean background.
examples.analytical: Thalassemia illustrates how a single gene variant can reshape human biology while also providing partial protection against malaria.

nuance.analogy: Thalassemia is like a factory that makes fewer of the parts it needs, so the whole assembly line slows down.
nuance.etymology: From Greek thalassa, 'sea,' and haima, 'blood,' named because the condition was first described around the Mediterranean.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying thal-uh-SEM-ee-uh instead of thal-uh-SEE-mee-uh.
Confusing thalassemia with sickle cell disease or with anemia in general.

senses.definition: Said upon hearing good news that makes someone cease to be worried about something.
senses.example: The mechanic said the engine was fine, so that's a relief.

core.definition: Said when news ends a worry, meaning something you feared did not happen or has been resolved, so you feel calm again.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIEF, not REL. In fast speech 'that's a' links into 'thats-uh', and the 'a' is a weak uh.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It expresses relief that a worry has ended, and it is warm and sincere in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this right after hearing reassuring news, such as a clean test result or a late flight that finally lands. It is casual and friendly, often said with a sigh. Natural replies include 'Right? I was so worried' or 'Tell me about it.'

distinctions.note: That's great praises good news in general, while that's a relief specifically signals that a worry or fear has gone away.
Thank goodness is an emotional exclamation of gratitude; that's a relief is more conversational and comments on how the news affects you.

examples.everyday: Your flight landed early? Oh, that's a relief, I was getting nervous.
examples.professional: The security audit found no exposed customer data, so that's a relief for the whole team.
examples.analytical: If the model's error rates hold across subgroups, that's a relief, though it does not by itself prove the model is fair.

nuance.analogy: Like finally setting down a heavy bag you had forgotten you were carrying.
nuance.etymology: From Old French relef, from relever 'to raise up again', from Latin relevare.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on REL- instead of -LIEF (ri-LEEF).
Using it for any good news; it fits news that ends a specific worry.

senses.definition: To thaw completely.

core.definition: To become completely thawed, or to warm up a very cold person or body part until it is no longer numb.

pronunciation.tip: 'Thaw' is stressed lightly and 'out' gets the main stress. In speech, the t of 'out' is often a flap or a slight pause.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a practical or comfortable process of warming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'thaw out' about frozen food, pipes, or cold hands and feet after snow play or winter weather. It is common in everyday conversation. A typical comment is 'Come inside and thaw out by the fire.'

distinctions.note: 'Thaw out' emphasizes complete warming or returning to usable condition; 'thaw' can be a simple partial change.
'Warm up' is broader and suits people, rooms and food; 'thaw out' specifically implies something was frozen.

examples.everyday: We were freezing after the snowball fight, so we went inside to thaw out by the heater.
examples.professional: Leave the cooler at room temperature for an hour so the samples can thaw out before testing.
examples.analytical: The relationship took months to thaw out, and the change emerged only after both parties acknowledged the earlier harm.

nuance.analogy: Like a frozen windshield in the morning: you wait until it fully clears and becomes usable again.
common_mistakes: Saying 'thaw up' or 'thaw off' instead of 'thaw out'.
Using 'thaw out' as a noun phrase without a verb, such as 'the thaw out' in formal writing.

conversation.text: Let the steaks thaw out in the fridge.
I moved the chicken to the fridge last night to thaw out.
Frozen shrimp only take about ten minutes to thaw out in cold water.

core.definition: The last possible moment before a deadline or a critical event, when something must be done or decided to avoid failure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'lev' in 'eleventh' and 'ow' in 'hour'. The h in 'hour' is silent, and the final 'th' in 'eleventh' is a soft unvoiced sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or slightly tense, implying a last-minute rescue or a close call.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase for a last-minute deadline or a rescue at the final moment, often in news, business, politics, and everyday talk about plans. It is slightly formal, but common in casual speech too. A natural reply is 'Good thing you got it in at the eleventh hour,' or a thank-you for last-minute help.

distinctions.note: A deadline is the time limit itself, while the eleventh hour is the last moment just before that limit.
Last-minute is a common, casual adjective for plans or changes, while the eleventh hour adds a sense of drama or narrow escape.

collocations: save it at the eleventh hour

examples.everyday: My sister finally bought her plane ticket at the eleventh hour, right before the flight was going to sell out.
examples.professional: The vendor sent the revised contract at the eleventh hour, so legal had less than two hours to review it before signing.
examples.analytical: The eleventh hour is where a moral choice becomes real, because waiting too long can turn a decision into a missed opportunity.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner sprinting across the finish line just before the clock runs out.
nuance.etymology: From eleventh, the eleventh in order, and hour, a unit of time, used figuratively for the last moment.
common_mistakes: Writing 'eleventh hours' in the plural; the idiom is singular.
Saying 'the last hour' when the idiom is the eleventh hour, which is the standard expression.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase comes from Matthew 20:1-16 (RSV), the parable of the workers in the vineyard. Matthew 20:6 and 20:9 (RSV) describe workers hired about the eleventh hour, shortly before the end of the working day. The parable teaches that God's grace is generous and not earned by length of service. The Greek word is hora, meaning hour, and the phrase refers to the final period of the day.

core.definition: Exceptional patience and endurance under severe suffering, in reference to the biblical man Job.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'pay' in 'patience' and pronounce 'Job' to rhyme with 'robe'. Reduce 'of' to 'uv' in natural speech, and keep the 'shuns' ending soft.

nuance.connotation: Positive, admiring of endurance, though it can be used humorously for someone who tolerates annoyance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase to praise someone who remains calm through hardship or a long, frustrating process, and sometimes ironically for someone who lacks patience. It is common in church, literature, and everyday talk. A natural reply is 'You really have the patience of Job,' often said with admiration or humor.

distinctions.note: Patient is a general adjective for waiting calmly, while the patience of Job specifically refers to endurance through severe suffering.
Endurance is a general term for lasting through difficulty, while the patience of Job emphasizes calm trust during suffering.

collocations: a teacher with the patience of Job
you need the patience of Job

examples.everyday: My grandmother has the patience of Job when she teaches me how to make bread.
examples.professional: Our support lead has the patience of Job when handling angry customers on the phone.
examples.analytical: The phrase is drawn from James 5:11, where Job's endurance becomes an example of steadfast faith under suffering.

nuance.analogy: Like a deep well that never runs dry, its patience holds steady no matter how many buckets are drawn.
nuance.etymology: From the Book of Job and its famous figure of endurance under suffering, later turned into a common expression.
common_mistakes: Saying 'patient of Job' instead of 'patience of Job'.
Using it as a literal description of someone who is simply waiting in a line, where a more ordinary word works better.
nuance.biblical_note: Job is the central figure of the Book of Job, a righteous man who loses his family, wealth, and health. Job 1:1 (RSV) describes him as blameless and upright, and Job 1:21 (RSV) records his response of trust after losing his children and property. James 5:11 (RSV) refers to the steadfastness of Job as an example for believers in suffering. The Greek word for steadfastness in James is hypomone, meaning endurance or perseverance.

senses.definition: The act of theft, the act of stealing.
senses.example: This instance of thievery will not be overlooked.

core.definition: The act or practice of stealing; theft, especially when done repeatedly or on a small scale.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final -ry is a rhotic American 'ree' sound with a clearly pronounced r.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes wrongdoing and is often used in news, complaints, or casual talk about petty crime.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'thievery' for stealing as a general activity or a pattern, especially in news reports and everyday complaints. For a single act, they more often say 'theft' or 'stealing.' Legal writing typically uses 'theft' or 'larceny' rather than 'thievery.'

distinctions.note: 'Theft' is the legal and general term for taking property without permission; 'thievery' is more informal and emphasizes the activity.
'Burglary' is breaking into a building to steal; 'thievery' is any stealing and does not require a break-in.

examples.everyday: The neighborhood group says thievery has gone up since the store closed, so they installed cameras.
examples.professional: Our loss-prevention report shows that most of the thievery happens in the self-checkout lanes during evening shifts.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long asked whether thievery requires intent or whether taking without consent is enough to make the act wrong.

nuance.analogy: Thievery is like a leak in a roof: each drip seems small, but over time it causes serious damage.
nuance.etymology: From 'thieve' plus the noun suffix '-ery,' meaning the practice or activity of.
common_mistakes: Using 'thievery' for a single incident; use 'theft' or 'a theft' instead.
Confusing 'thievery' with 'thieving' as a noun; 'thieving' is usually an adjective or gerund, while 'thievery' is the standard noun.

senses.definition: A persistent difficulty or something very annoying that will not go away.

core.definition: A persistent source of irritation or trouble that will not go away; also Paul's unnamed affliction in 2 Corinthians 12.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on FLESH, with secondary stress on 'thorn'. Say 'th' in 'thorn' with the tongue between the teeth and pronounce the r clearly; link 'thorn in' as 'thor-nin'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: a lasting annoyance or burden. Often used with some humor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say 'a thorn in my side' (or 'in someone's side'), which is the usual idiom. 'Thorn in the flesh' is the form closest to Paul's phrase and sounds a bit more biblical or literary. It is used for people, rivals, or problems that keep causing trouble.

distinctions.note: This is the more common American idiom, with nearly the same meaning.
This is informal and about annoyance; a thorn suggests a lasting, sharper source of trouble.
A burden is something heavy you carry; a thorn is something that keeps irritating or hurting you.

collocations: a constant thorn in the flesh
remain a thorn in the flesh
a thorn in the flesh of the company

examples.everyday: That noisy neighbor has been a thorn in the flesh for our whole street since last spring.
examples.professional: That legacy billing system has been a thorn in the flesh of our engineering team for years.
examples.analytical: Scholars have long debated what Paul's thorn in the flesh was, proposing illness, opposition, or spiritual struggle.

nuance.analogy: Like a splinter you cannot reach: small, but you feel it with every move.
nuance.etymology: From 2 Corinthians 12:7, Paul's phrase for a painful affliction; the English idiom developed from Bible translation.
common_mistakes: Saying 'thorn on the flesh' instead of 'in the flesh'.
Using it for a one-time annoyance; it implies something persistent.
Pronouncing 'th' as /s/ or /t/.
nuance.biblical_note: In 2 Corinthians 12:7-10 Paul says a 'thorn was given me in the flesh,' a messenger of Satan to keep him from pride. The Greek 'skolops' means a stake or thorn, and 'sarx' means flesh. He prayed three times for its removal, and the Lord answered that his grace is sufficient and power is made perfect in weakness (12:9). Paul never names it, so interpretations vary: illness, persecution, or opponents. Numbers 33:55 uses a similar image, saying that those not driven out of the land will become thorns in the sides of Israel.

thorn-in-the-flesh.etymology: With reference to the Bible 2nd Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, chapter 12, verse 7.

senses.definition: Of cloth, clothing, furnishings, etc.: frayed and worn to an extent that the nap is damaged and the warp and weft threads show; shabby, worn-out.
senses.example: He wore a threadbare cardigan with frayed cuffs that he refused to throw away.

senses.definition: In poor condition; damaged, shabby; also, poorly equipped or provided for, inadequate, meagre, scanty.
Of an argument, excuse, etc.: used so often that it is no longer effective or interesting; banal, clichéd, trite.
senses.example: The senator's threadbare excuse about the budget didn't convince anyone at the hearing.

senses.definition: An argument or assertion with little in the way of substance or supporting evidence.

core.definition: Worn so thin that the fabric shows its threads, or, figuratively, used so often that it no longer seems fresh.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final 'bare' is a rhotic r, so say 'bair' clearly, and do not reduce it to 'buh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or sympathetic. It suggests poverty or wear, and it can criticize an idea as stale.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'threadbare' for old clothes, carpets, or furniture, and for stale arguments or excuses. It is a common word in descriptions and writing. In everyday speech, you might say 'worn out' or 'falling apart', but 'threadbare' is natural when describing shabby furnishings or a tired argument.

distinctions.note: 'Shabby' describes general poor condition and appearance. 'Threadbare' specifically describes fabric worn so thin that threads show.
'Worn out' is the everyday phrase for something no longer usable. 'Threadbare' suggests the item is still in use but very thin.

examples.everyday: I finally replaced my threadbare bathrobe because you could see through it.
examples.professional: The vendor's threadbare promise of a faster release did not convince anyone on the board.
examples.analytical: The author's threadbare metaphor of the journey has been used so often that it no longer shapes the argument.

nuance.analogy: A threadbare argument is like a sweater worn so long that the knit has worn through to the bare yarn.
nuance.etymology: From 'thread' and 'bare', so literally bare of thread, meaning worn down to the bare threads.
common_mistakes: Dropping the final 'r' sound in 'bare', saying 'bay' instead of 'bair'.
Spelling it as 'thread bare' with a space in formal writing.

senses.definition: To make clear; to elucidate; to provide an explanation for (something puzzling or mysterious).
senses.example: The new survey data should throw light on why turnout dropped in rural counties.

core.definition: To make something puzzling clearer or easier to understand by providing information or an explanation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on light, not on 'on,' which is weak and reduced to a quick 'un' or 'ahn' sound. In fluent speech it sounds like 'throh-LYTE-un.'

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes clarifying or explaining something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in news, academic and professional settings: 'The new data throws light on why customers leave.' In casual talk they more often say 'explain' or 'clear up.' A natural reply is 'That helps' or 'Got it.'

distinctions.note: Explain is general and direct; throw light on suggests partly clarifying something complex or obscure.
Clarify means making a statement clearer, often to fix confusion; throw light on can add new evidence or insight.

examples.everyday: Your story about the leaking roof throws light on why the ceiling is stained.
examples.professional: The new retention data throws light on why customers leave after the first month.
examples.analytical: Wittgenstein's remarks on rule-following throw light on the difficulty of fixing meaning in advance.

nuance.analogy: Like switching on a lamp in a dark room, so you can finally see the shape of the furniture.
nuance.etymology: From throw and light, using the image of casting light onto something.
common_mistakes: Saying 'throw light to' instead of 'throw light on.'
Stressing the 'on' in speech; the stress belongs on light.

senses.definition: Very small.
senses.example: The kitten was so tiny it fit in the palm of my hand.

senses.definition: A small child; an infant.
senses.example: The tiny sat in the high chair, banging a spoon against the tray.

senses.definition: Anything very small.
senses.example: The microscope revealed a tiny drifting through the sample, barely visible to the eye.

core.definition: Very small in size or amount.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final y sounds like a long ee, not a short i. Avoid stretching the first vowel into two syllables like 'tie-uh-nee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. It can be affectionate for children, pets, or small things, and dismissive when calling a problem 'tiny' to play it down.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tiny constantly in everyday speech, for things like 'a tiny bit,' 'a tiny apartment,' or 'a tiny baby.' Used for a person, it can sound affectionate, but calling an adult 'tiny' may sound patronizing unless you are describing their size. For a more emphatic or formal word, Americans may say minuscule or microscopic.

distinctions.note: Small is the general, neutral word; tiny is stronger and suggests something is especially little.
Minuscule is more formal and emphatic, often used for amounts or differences in writing or technical contexts.
Little is very common and can express affection or simply mean small; tiny is more emphatic about size.

examples.everyday: Can you pass me that tiny spoon? I need to taste the soup.
examples.professional: The model's error is tiny, so we can ship the update without rerunning the full pipeline.
examples.analytical: A tiny difference in the initial conditions can produce wildly different outcomes in a chaotic system.

nuance.analogy: Like a grain of sand on a beach: it exists and can be measured, but it barely changes the whole.
common_mistakes: Saying the vowel as a short i, as in 'tinny' (a different word meaning thin and metallic).
Using 'tiny' for a precise measurement; in technical writing, say 'a small' or give the exact number.

senses.definition: The state of being tired.

core.definition: The feeling of being tired; a lack of energy or a desire to rest or sleep.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The -ed ending is a quiet d, so say 'TYE-erd-nis' with no separate 'ed' syllable. The middle vowel is a light American r-sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an ordinary state and carries no judgment, though it can suggest a problem when it is strong or persistent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I'm so tired' or 'I'm exhausted' rather than using the noun. 'Tiredness' is used when describing a symptom or state, such as 'I've had tiredness all week.' In medical or workplace contexts, Americans often say 'fatigue' instead.

distinctions.note: Fatigue is more severe and often lasts longer, and it is common in medical and workplace language. Tiredness is the everyday word for feeling worn out.
Exhaustion means being completely drained of energy, which is stronger than ordinary tiredness.

examples.everyday: I can't shake this tiredness, so I'm going to bed early tonight.
examples.professional: The team reported tiredness after the long release weekend, so we moved the next standup to the afternoon.
examples.analytical: Tiredness is a state the body enters when energy reserves run low, and it is distinct from the deeper, chronic condition we call fatigue.

nuance.analogy: Tiredness is like a phone battery running low: it still works, but it needs a charge.
nuance.etymology: From tired, plus the suffix -ness; tired comes from the verb tire, from Old English tȳrian, to weary.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tiredness' when 'I'm tired' is more natural in casual speech.
Pronouncing it with three syllables, as 'TYE-ur-ed-ness'; it is two syllables plus a final -nis.

senses.definition: A container a restaurant gives you to take leftover food home.
senses.example: Can you put my leftover pasta in a to-go box, please?

core.definition: A container that a restaurant gives you to take leftover food home.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BOX. The 'o' in 'box' is the American vowel of cot and caught, so it sounds like 'bahks'. Say 'to-go' as one tight unit.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask 'Can I get a to-go box?' at restaurants when they want to take leftovers home. The usual term in casual speech is simply 'to-go box', and some call it a 'doggy bag', which is dated. A natural reply from staff is 'Sure, I'll bring one right out.'

distinctions.note: 'Doggy bag' is older and more playful; 'to-go box' is the everyday term in most restaurants today.
A takeout container is any packaging for food bought to eat elsewhere; a to-go box is mainly for leftovers from a meal eaten in the restaurant.

collocations: pack it in a to-go box

examples.everyday: Could you grab me a to-go box? I can't finish this steak.
examples.professional: Please pack the leftovers in a to-go box so the team can take them back to the office.
examples.analytical: The to-go box turns a private meal into a portable one, extending the restaurant's presence into the home.

nuance.analogy: Like the sealed bag of extra cookies a host sends home with guests.
nuance.etymology: Compound noun from 'to go' and 'box', dating to the 20th century.
common_mistakes: Saying 'take-out box' in a restaurant, which is understood but less natural than 'to-go box'.
Omitting the hyphen in speech-to-writing, which can cause confusion with 'to go box'.

conversation.text: Could we get a to-go box for the rest of this pasta?
The server brought us a to-go box without us even asking.
I always ask for a to-go box because the portions here are huge.

senses.definition: Transferred.
Metaphorical.
Passed down; transmitted from one to another.

core.definition: Passed on or transferred from one thing or person to another; metaphorical or figurative in sense, as an older term.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TISH, and the final -tious is pronounced 'shus'. The middle vowel is a quick, reduced 'uh', so avoid giving every syllable equal weight.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a bookish word used in older scholarship or literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word outside older scholarship, dictionaries, or literary writing. In modern English, say 'figurative' or 'metaphorical' for a non-literal sense, and 'traditional' or 'handed-down' for inherited customs. You will mainly meet it in older texts.

distinctions.note: Figurative is the common modern word for a non-literal sense; tralatitious is a rare, older synonym.
Traditional means handed down by custom; tralatitious has the older sense of a meaning carried over from one use to another.

examples.everyday: My grandmother uses some tralatitious phrases that sound strange to my kids.
examples.professional: In the grant report we avoid tralatitious terms and describe each finding in plain language.
examples.analytical: The poet's tralatitious use of 'bread' moves the word from its literal sense toward a sacramental meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a coin passed from hand to hand, the word carries its meaning into new contexts.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tralatitius, from translatio, 'transfer'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with traditional or tradition, which are much more common.
Stressing the first syllable instead of TISH.

senses.definition: Of or relating to tribes.
senses.example: social order through tribal law

senses.definition: Based on or organized according to tribes.
senses.example: a tribal society

senses.definition: Incorporating designs or styles typical of an indigenous people.
senses.example: tribal techno music

senses.definition: (historical) Phylogenic.
senses.example: tribal history
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: A design or image that has been influenced by indigenous peoples; especially such a tattoo.
senses.example: He showed off the tribal across his upper arm, inked years ago in Honolulu.

core.definition: Relating to a tribe or tribes, meaning a group bound by shared kinship, ancestry or traditions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress and the main vowel fall on TRY-, and the second syllable is a reduced 'buhl', not 'bell'. Avoid a short 'i' in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in anthropology and tribal government; negative when describing narrow group loyalty, as in 'tribal politics'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tribal for Native American nations in legal and government contexts, as in 'tribal council' or 'tribal lands'. Describing an individual person as 'tribal' can sound stereotyping, so say 'a tribal member' or name the specific nation, such as the Navajo Nation. In politics, 'tribal' is often a criticism of group loyalty. Tribal-style tattoos are very common in American culture.

distinctions.note: Ethnic refers to shared culture, language or origin across a population, while tribal refers more specifically to kin-based groups with their own leaders or councils.
Clannish is informal and often negative, describing groups that keep to themselves; tribal is broader and can be neutral.
Sectarian describes divisions within a religion or political movement, while tribal describes loyalty to a kin or community group.

examples.everyday: He got a small tribal design on his shoulder, inspired by his grandmother's heritage.
examples.professional: The tribal council approved the new housing project after months of consultation.
examples.analytical: Tribal loyalty can shape political behavior even when people share economic interests across groups.

nuance.analogy: Tribal loyalty works like a team jersey: it marks who belongs and can blind you to the score.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'tribalis', from 'tribus', one of the three traditional divisions of the early Roman people.
common_mistakes: Calling an individual 'tribal' as an insult or stereotype; say 'a member of a tribe' instead.
Using a short 'i' as in 'TRIB-ul'; the first vowel is the long 'eye' sound.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew 'shevet' (tribe, staff) and the Greek 'phylē' (tribe) name the groups within Israel. Genesis 49:28 describes Jacob blessing each of the twelve tribes of Israel. Romans 11:1 says Paul himself belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, showing that lineage still mattered. Revelation 7:4-8 lists the tribes of Israel who were sealed by God.

senses.definition: A period of three days (especially in Roman Catholic liturgy).

core.definition: In Roman Catholic worship, the three days of liturgy from Holy Thursday evening through Easter Sunday.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable; the 'dj' is pronounced like 'j' in 'jeep' in many American speakers, so say 'TRID-joo-um' or 'TRID-yoo-um', with a weak final 'um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to solemn; it signals religious seriousness and liturgical tradition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Triduum' mainly in Catholic and liturgical contexts, often as 'the Easter Triduum' or 'the Paschal Triduum'. Protestants usually say 'Holy Week', 'Good Friday' or 'Easter weekend'. In a parish conversation, a natural phrase is 'Are you coming to the Triduum services this year?'

distinctions.note: 'Holy Week' is the whole week before Easter; 'Triduum' refers only to the final three liturgical days.
A novena is a nine-day prayer devotion, not a liturgical celebration of three days.

examples.everyday: Our parish has services every evening during the Triduum, so I took Thursday to Sunday off work.
examples.professional: The parish office needs volunteers for the Triduum liturgies, so please check the schedule before booking meetings that week.
examples.analytical: The Triduum is theologically unified, since the Passion, burial and resurrection are read as one continuous mystery rather than three separate events.

nuance.analogy: Like a three-act play whose final act makes sense only because of what came before.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'triduum', a period of three days, from 'tres' (three) and 'dies' (day).
common_mistakes: Thinking 'Triduum' is a single day or a one-time event rather than a three-day liturgical period
Misspelling it as 'Trium' or confusing it with 'triumph'
nuance.biblical_note: The Triduum draws on the Gospel accounts of Jesus's death and resurrection over a few days. Matthew 12:40 (RSV) compares Jesus's time in the earth to Jonah's time in the great fish, a three-day-and-three-nights image that the Church later linked to the Triduum. Jonah 1:17 (RSV) describes Jonah in the fish for that period. 1 Corinthians 15:4 (RSV) says Christ was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.

traditions.view: The Triduum is the liturgical core of the Church year: Holy Thursday's Mass of the Lord's Supper, Good Friday's Passion, and the Easter Vigil form one unbroken celebration of the Paschal Mystery.

Orthodox Christians observe Holy Week with services such as Great and Holy Friday and the Paschal Vigil of Pascha; they do not use the Latin term 'Triduum', though the sequence of services is similar in spirit.

Practice varies: Anglican, Lutheran and some Reformed churches often observe Maundy Thursday, Good Friday and an Easter Vigil, while many Baptist and Pentecostal churches mark chiefly Good Friday and Easter Sunday.

senses.definition: Singular of trivia; anything of little importance.
senses.example: He dismissed the scandal as a trivium not worth discussing at the faculty meeting.

senses.definition: The three anterior ambulacra of echinoderms, collectively.
senses.example: Our zoology lab examined the trivium of a sea urchin, noting its three anterior ambulacra.

senses.definition: (historical) The lower division of the liberal arts in a medieval university; grammar, logic, and rhetoric.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: In medieval European universities, the lower three liberal arts: grammar, logic and rhetoric.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TRIV. The final syllable is a reduced um, not yum, and the word is not pronounced like the common trivia.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a historical academic term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trivium mainly when discussing medieval education, classical schooling or the seven liberal arts. It refers to grammar, logic and rhetoric, the lower arts, as opposed to the quadrivium. Some classical schools and homeschooling families use the term, but most Americans would not know it, so define it when you use it.

distinctions.note: The quadrivium is the upper four arts: arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy, studied after the trivium.
Trivia is the Latin plural of trivium, but in English it means trifles or a quiz game; the medieval term is a separate technical word.

examples.everyday: My kid's classical school teaches the trivium, so they study grammar, logic and rhetoric first.
examples.professional: Our curriculum committee wants to bring the trivium into the first-year writing sequence.
examples.analytical: Medieval scholars organized learning around the trivium, treating logic and rhetoric as tools for reading texts.

nuance.analogy: Like the three basic tools in a toolbox, which you need before building anything complex.
nuance.etymology: From Latin trivium, place where three roads meet, from tri- three and via road.
common_mistakes: Confusing trivium with trivial or trivia; trivium is a technical term for three arts, not the English word for trifles.
Stressing it as TRY-vee-um; the main stress falls on TRIV.

senses.definition: To test the look or fit of (a garment) by wearing it.
To attempt; to undertake.

core.definition: To put on a piece of clothing to see whether it fits or looks good before buying it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle ON, which is the stronger word here. In casual speech 'try it on' is often said as 'try-it-AHN', with the 'it' nearly disappearing and the t flapping in 'try' to a soft d sound. Note the American 'ah' in 'on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It describes an ordinary shopping action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'try on' constantly in stores, fitting rooms, and online shopping advice. Pronouns go between the verb and particle: 'try it on', not 'try on it'. A natural question is 'Can I try this on?' and a typical reply is 'Sure, the fitting rooms are in the back.'

distinctions.note: Try on is for clothes and fit, while try out is for testing equipment, products, or a person's ability.

collocations: try on in the fitting room

examples.everyday: This jacket looks nice, can I try it on before I buy it?
examples.professional: Our online store lets customers try on virtual outfits before they make a purchase.
examples.analytical: Shoppers often try on several sizes, which shows how fit remains a central problem in apparel retail.

nuance.analogy: Trying something on is like testing a key in a lock: you check whether it actually fits before you commit.
nuance.etymology: From 'try' and 'on', a phrasal verb in which 'on' indicates wearing.
common_mistakes: Placing the pronoun after the particle: say 'try it on', not 'try on it'.
Confusing it with 'try out', which is not used for clothing.

conversation.text: Can I try on these jeans?
Try it on before you buy it.
I had to try on three sizes before the medium fit right.
You should try it on first; their sizes run small.

senses.definition: A decisive point at which a significant change or historical event occurs, or at which a decision must be made.
senses.example: Losing the grant was the turning point that pushed the lab to change its strategy.

senses.definition: A maximum or minimum on a graph.
senses.example: On the graph, the stock price reached its turning point in March before falling.

senses.definition: A crossroads.
senses.example: The hikers reached a turning point where three trails split beneath the old pine.

senses.definition: A T-junction.
senses.example: Turn left at the turning point, then follow the gravel road for two miles.

senses.definition: A place at which one changes their direction of travel.
senses.example: The driver reached the turning point at the end of the cul-de-sac and reversed.

core.definition: A decisive moment when a situation changes direction, often for better or worse.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress falls on POINT, with a secondary stress on TURN. Keep the 'ing' short and the 'oi' as a clear diphthong, like 'coin'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, but the change can be good or bad depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for personal, business and political moments, for example 'The divorce was a turning point for her' or 'That win was the turning point of the season.' It is comfortable in everyday talk and in speeches. A natural reply is 'Yeah, looking back, it really was.'

distinctions.note: A milestone marks progress along the way and is usually positive; a turning point changes the direction of events, good or bad.
A crossroads is a moment that forces a choice, while a turning point emphasizes the change that follows the choice.

collocations: a turning point for the company
a turning point in the game

examples.everyday: Losing that job was a turning point for me, and it pushed me to start my own business.
examples.professional: The launch of the new analytics platform was a turning point for our team.
examples.analytical: The Reformation is often described as a turning point in Western theology, because it reopened questions about authority and grace.

nuance.analogy: Like a river bend that sends the whole current in a new direction.
nuance.etymology: Compound of turning (from turn) and point (from Latin punctum, a prick).
common_mistakes: Dropping the -ing and saying 'turn point', which is not the standard phrase.
Using turning point for any small change; it must be a decisive moment.

senses.definition: One of a pair of elongated pointed teeth (either cuspids or incisors) that extend outside the mouth of an animal such as walrus, elephant or wild boar, and which continue to grow throughout the animal's life.
senses.example: Until the CITES sales ban, elephant tusks were the 'backbone' of the legal ivory trade.

senses.definition: A small projection on a (tusk) tenon.
senses.example: The carpenter cut a small tusk on the end of the beam to lock the joint.

senses.definition: A tusk shell.
senses.example: Collectors on the beach found several tusk shells, slender and curved like tiny elephant tusks.

senses.definition: A projecting member like a tenon, and serving the same or a similar purpose, but composed of several steps, or offsets, called teeth.
senses.example: The joiner used a stepped tusk joint, its teeth offset to resist pulling apart.

senses.definition: A sharp point.
The share of a plow.
senses.example: The farmer replaced the worn tusk of the plow before spring planting.

senses.definition: An edible fish, Brosme brosme.
senses.example: Anglers off the coast of Maine often catch a tusk while fishing for cod.

senses.definition: To dig up using a tusk, as boars do.
senses.example: Wild boars tusked up the lawn overnight, leaving deep furrows across the garden.

senses.definition: To gore with the tusks.
senses.example: The enraged boar tusked the hunter's leg before the dogs drove it away.

core.definition: A long, pointed tooth that projects outside the mouth of animals such as elephants, walruses and wild boars.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single stressed syllable with a short u, like 'cup'. Clearly release the final k, and do not add a final e sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes an animal feature, though ivory and poaching carry serious associations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tusk for elephant, walrus, warthog and boar teeth, and news about ivory trafficking often uses the word. It is a plain, everyday word for animals and wildlife talk. Do not use it for horns or antlers, which are different structures.

distinctions.note: Horns are hollow, permanent growths on the head of animals such as cattle; tusks are elongated teeth.
Antlers are solid bone structures that deer shed and regrow each year; tusks are teeth that keep growing.
Fangs are sharp teeth used for venom or gripping prey, while tusks are long teeth that project outside the mouth.

examples.everyday: The walrus at the zoo has two long tusks that stick out of its mouth.
examples.professional: Our wildlife survey recorded tusk lengths across the elephant population in the reserve.
examples.analytical: The tusk keeps growing throughout life, so it becomes a record of the animal's diet and environment.

nuance.analogy: Like a canine tooth that has grown far beyond the lip.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tux, related to Germanic forms meaning tooth or pointed thing.
common_mistakes: Calling elephant tusks horns; tusks are teeth, while horns are hollow head growths.
Adding an extra vowel, as in 'TUS-kuh'; it is one syllable.

tusk.etymology: From Middle English *tusk*, from Old English *tūsc,tūx* (“canine tooth, tusk, molar”), from **tų̄sk,*tunsk*, from Proto-Germanic **tunþskaz* (“canine tooth”), extended form of **tanþs* (“tooth”), from Proto-Indo-European **h₃dónts* (“tooth”).

senses.definition: Not disconcerted or embarrassed.
Of actions, emotions, facts, etc.: that are not concealed or disguised, or not eliciting shame.
senses.example: His unabashed enthusiasm for statistics made him the loudest voice at every meeting.

core.definition: Not embarrassed or ashamed, especially when others might expect you to feel that way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BASH, the third syllable, and the ending is one quick sound, 'sht', not two syllables. The first syllable is weak, so keep the un-uh light.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral when praising confidence; it can sound negative when describing bold wrongdoing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unabashed for people who openly show their feelings or identity, such as an unabashed fan crying at a concert. It is slightly formal for casual chat and common in news and reviews. The negative equivalent is shameless.

distinctions.note: Shameless criticizes a lack of decency; unabashed is more neutral and simply describes someone who isn't embarrassed.
Brazen suggests bold, insolent behavior, often wrongdoing; unabashed is about not feeling embarrassed, not about boldness.

examples.everyday: My dad is an unabashed Cubs fan, and he wears the jersey to every game.
examples.professional: She gave an unabashed assessment of our project's weaknesses, and I appreciated the candor.
examples.analytical: Kant's essay is an unabashed defense of reason against sentiment, and it refuses to hedge its central claims.

nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus abashed, from Old French 'esbair', meaning to astonish or startle.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with abashed, which describes the person who feels embarrassed.
Stressing the first syllable, as in UN-uh-bashed.

senses.definition: Not answerable; impossible to answer.
Impossible to dispute or rebut; irrefutable; conclusive.
Something that cannot be answered.

core.definition: So conclusive that no one can dispute or refute it; or impossible to answer at all.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AN, the second syllable. The 'w' in 'answer' is silent, and the final '-able' reduces to 'uh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing an argument or evidence; negative or frustrated when describing a question that has no answer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in serious debate, legal or academic writing, and argument: 'His evidence was unanswerable.' Calling a question unanswerable often signals frustration: 'That's an unanswerable question.' In casual speech, 'there's no good answer to that' is more natural. A typical reply is 'Yeah, I don't think anyone really knows.'

distinctions.note: Unanswerable means no answer is possible or convincing; unanswered means no answer has been given yet, which may change.
Irrefutable applies specifically to an argument or proof that cannot be disproved; unanswerable can also describe a question with no possible reply.

examples.everyday: My kid asked why the sky is blue, and that's an unanswerable question for me before coffee.
examples.professional: Her point about data leakage was unanswerable, so the team agreed to rebuild the validation pipeline.
examples.analytical: Hume's problem of induction presents an argument that many philosophers have found hard to dispute, though not everyone considers it unanswerable.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess position where every possible move leads to the same loss.
nuance.etymology: From un- 'not' and answerable, from answer (Old English andswaru) plus -able.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'w' in 'answer'; it is silent, so say AN-ser.
Using it for a question that is simply unresolved but could be answered; 'unanswered' or 'open' fits better there.

senses.definition: Not beholden; not obliged or bound by duty or expectations.

core.definition: Not obligated or indebted to anyone; free from any duty or obligation to others.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on HOLD, and the middle syllable be- is weak, sounding like 'bih'. The final -en is a reduced syllable, so say 'uhn' and do not add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually signals independence, often in politics, business or personal integrity, and it is not a criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing or formal speech, for example when describing a politician who takes no money from special interests. In casual talk people say 'I don't owe anybody anything' or 'I'm free to do what I want'. A natural reply to a claim of independence is simply 'Good for you' or 'That's rare these days'.

distinctions.note: Independent is the everyday word for not relying on others; unbeholden stresses that you owe nothing to a specific person, group or donor.
Free is broad and common; unbeholden is narrower and focuses on the absence of a debt or obligation.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says he's unbeholden to anybody now that he's retired and paid off his house.
examples.professional: Our auditors are unbeholden to the department they review, which is why the board trusts their findings.
examples.analytical: A judge who is unbeholden to the electorate may decide cases on principle, yet that same freedom raises questions about democratic accountability.

nuance.analogy: Like a tenant who has paid the rent in full and owes the landlord nothing, the unbeholden person can walk away from any obligation.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the prefix un- and beholden, the past participle of an older sense of behold meaning to be held or bound.
common_mistakes: Using 'unbeholden' in casual conversation, where 'independent' sounds more natural.
Confusing 'beholden' (under obligation) with 'behold' (to see or look at).

senses.definition: Not converted.
senses.example: The sermon addressed the unconverted members of the congregation who had never truly repented.

core.definition: Not changed in belief, usually from one religion or faith to another, or not yet persuaded to adopt a new view.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VUR, with the r strongly pronounced in General American. The final -ed is pronounced 'id' because it follows the t sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, but can sound judgmental or condescending in religious contexts, where it implies a person who has not accepted a particular faith.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech this word appears mostly in religious settings, such as church, mission work, or discussions of faith. Outside religion, people usually say 'not yet persuaded' or 'still unchanged'. Using it about a friend can sound pointed, so it is safer to ask about their beliefs directly.

distinctions.note: Unchanged is a general word for something that stays the same, while unconverted specifically refers to not having adopted a new faith or belief.
Unbelieving means not having faith at all, while unconverted suggests a person who has not yet changed to a particular faith or position.

examples.everyday: My coworker is still unconverted, but she likes coming to the church picnic anyway.
examples.professional: The mission team reported that many of the unconverted villagers attended the workshops.
examples.analytical: Wesley's sermons addressed the unconverted as people who needed a living faith rather than mere religious habit.

nuance.analogy: Like a visitor who has seen the new house but has not yet moved in, the unconverted person stands near the change without yet making it their own.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus converted, from Latin convertere meaning 'to turn around'.
common_mistakes: Using it casually about people who simply disagree with you on politics.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable, as in un-kuhn-VURT.
Forgetting that the -ed is a full syllable, so 'unconverted' has four syllables.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb epistrephō means 'to turn' or 'to return', and it underlies the idea of conversion in the New Testament. Matthew 18:3 says that unless you turn and become like children you will not enter the kingdom of heaven, which describes conversion as a real turning. The idea of being unconverted is therefore a state of not yet having turned toward God.

senses.definition: Not covered or protected from the weather, etc.
Lacking insurance or security.
Bareheaded.

core.definition: Not covered, protected or insured; left open to the weather, damage, harm or financial loss.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, KUHV. The ending -ered is one syllable with a light r-colored vowel and a final d, with no separate e sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a description of a state, but it can imply vulnerability, especially in insurance or security contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use uncovered in plain descriptions such as an uncovered pool, uncovered food or a driver with no insurance coverage. In financial or insurance settings it means a risk is not included in a policy. Without context it can sound literal, so people often say unprotected or uninsured instead.

distinctions.note: Exposed suggests something is open to danger or view; uncovered focuses more on lacking a cover or protection.
Uninsured applies specifically to a lack of insurance; uncovered can refer to a physical or financial lack of protection in general.

examples.everyday: Can you put a lid on that bowl? The food has been sitting uncovered in the fridge all day.
examples.professional: Our policy leaves an uncovered gap for contractors, so we need to fix that risk before renewal.
examples.analytical: An argument left uncovered by evidence is not necessarily false, but it remains unsupported.

nuance.analogy: Like a bed left without a blanket on a cold night: the bed is still there, but nothing protects it from the cold.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus cover, from Old French covrir, from Latin cooperire, to cover completely.
common_mistakes: Saying uncovered for uninsured people in everyday talk; many Americans prefer uninsured for a person.
Using uncovered to describe a bare head in casual speech, which sounds odd; say bareheaded or without a hat.

senses.definition: Of an inappropriately or unusually low weight.
senses.example: He's so underweight he's had to buy smaller clothes.

senses.definition: Not too heavy for an intended purpose.
senses.example: The suitcase is just slightly underweight; I'll let it on the plane.

senses.definition: Being less invested in a particular area than market wisdom suggests.
senses.example: The fund is underweight in mining.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being underweight.
senses.example: Her doctor was concerned about her dangerous underweight after months of illness.

senses.definition: An underweight person.
senses.example: The clinic offers nutrition counseling for underweight adults and teenagers.

senses.definition: An underweight investment.
senses.example: Our fund holds several underweights in energy stocks this quarter.

senses.definition: To underestimate the weight of.
senses.example: The scale underweighted the crate, so the shipping charge was too low.

senses.definition: To give insufficient weight to (a consideration); to underestimate the importance of.
senses.example: Reviewers often underweight the importance of user feedback in product decisions.

senses.definition: To invest in less than conventional wisdom would dictate.
senses.example: The analyst underweighted bonds, betting that interest rates would stay low.

core.definition: Weighing less than is healthy or normal for one's height or age, or less than is needed for a particular purpose.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on UN, the first syllable. Say the middle syllable as a quick, reduced American der and don't add any sound for the gh that has disappeared from weight.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing a person's health, since it suggests a risk; neutral when describing a product, package, or statistic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use underweight about babies, animals, and adults in a medical sense, as in 'The baby was born underweight.' Saying an adult is underweight can sound blunt, so in casual talk people often say 'too thin' or 'not eating enough' instead. In finance, the word also describes holding less of an asset than a benchmark.

distinctions.note: Thin describes a slender body and can be a compliment, while underweight is a measured comparison to a healthy range and sounds clinical.
Skinny is informal and often judgmental, while underweight is neutral and used in medical or official contexts.
Light describes low weight in general, but underweight implies falling below what is considered normal or required.

examples.everyday: The pediatrician said our son is a little underweight for his age, so she wants him eating more.
examples.professional: Several sensor readings in the training set are underweight, so we should resample the data before fitting the model.
examples.analytical: Whether someone is classified as underweight depends on a threshold drawn from population norms rather than on individual health.

nuance.analogy: Like a suitcase packed so lightly that it can't hold what the trip actually requires.
nuance.etymology: From under plus weight; the weight element comes from Old English wiht.
common_mistakes: Using underweight as a casual noun for a thin person, which sounds clinical; say 'a person who is underweight' instead.
Saying 'I am underweight' in ordinary conversation, which can sound alarming unless a doctor is involved.

senses.definition: The state of being uneasy, nervous or restless.
An anxious state of mind; anxiety.
senses.example: A deep uneasiness settled over me when the test results came back late.

core.definition: A feeling of worry, nervousness, or discomfort that is hard to shake off.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EE, the second syllable. The final -iness is pronounced as a reduced ee-nuhs, and the middle -zi- is a light zee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative but mild; it names discomfort that is usually less intense than anxiety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use uneasiness to describe a vague sense that something is wrong, as in I have some uneasiness about the contract. In casual talk they often say I feel weird about it or I'm uneasy. It is softer than anxiety, which can suggest a clinical or ongoing condition.

distinctions.note: Anxiety is stronger and can be persistent or clinical, while uneasiness is a milder, situational discomfort.
Unease means the same thing but is more literary; uneasiness is more common in everyday English.
Apprehension is a more formal fear about something that might happen, often in advance.

examples.everyday: I felt some uneasiness when the car made that noise, so I pulled over to check it.
examples.professional: There is growing uneasiness on the team about releasing the model before the audit is finished.
examples.analytical: The essay traces the modern uneasiness about progress to a loss of inherited moral certainties.

nuance.analogy: Uneasiness is like a pebble in your shoe: small, but you keep noticing it.
nuance.etymology: From uneasy plus -ness; uneasy comes from un- (not) plus easy.
common_mistakes: Using uneasiness where the adjective uneasy is needed: say I am uneasy, not I am uneasiness.
Stressing the first syllable instead of EE.

senses.definition: Not ending; having no end; eternal.
senses.example: Her unending patience with the toddler amazed everyone at the daycare.

core.definition: Going on forever or seeming to; never stopping or coming to an end.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, END, not on un-. The final -ing is a light /ɪŋ/ with no hard g sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it can be wearying ('an unending stream of emails') or awed ('unending love'), depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for things that drag on, like meetings, bills or traffic, often with a sigh, and for grander things like love or praise. 'Endless' is the more everyday word in conversation; 'unending' sounds slightly more formal or emotional. It usually comes before a noun.

distinctions.note: Nearly identical in meaning; 'endless' is the everyday choice, while 'unending' sounds more formal or emotional.
Eternal means without beginning or end in time; unending only says there is no end, so it can describe a long but finite process.

examples.everyday: Between the kids and the dishes, it feels like an unending list of chores.
examples.professional: Our on-call rotation feels like an unending stream of alerts that nobody has time to triage.
examples.analytical: Some theologians argue that the soul's longing for God is unending, since it is directed toward a good that never runs out.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that never reaches the sea: the water keeps flowing, with no final point.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) and ending, from Old English ende; literally 'not ending'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'oo' (YOO-) instead of 'un' (uhn), and placing the stress on un- instead of END.
Using 'unending' for things that just last long; it implies no end at all, so a long meeting is not truly unending.

senses.definition: Consistently accurate; not missing a target.

core.definition: Always accurate or correct; never making a mistake or missing the target.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, AIR, which has an r sound in American English. The final -ing is a short ing, not eeng.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises precision, instinct, or judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unerring mostly in writing, speeches, and reviews to praise skill, such as an unerring eye for talent. In casual speech, people usually say never wrong or always right on. It is rarely used for physical objects except in phrases like unerring aim.

distinctions.note: Accurate is neutral and common for measurements or facts; unerring suggests a steady, almost instinctive reliability over time.
Precise emphasizes exact detail; unerring emphasizes that the result is never wrong.

examples.everyday: My dad has an unerring sense for which restaurant will have good tacos.
examples.professional: The senior engineer has an unerring instinct for which bugs will cause production failures.
examples.analytical: The poet treats the moral law as an unerring guide, one that never misleads the conscience that attends to it.

nuance.analogy: Like an arrow that always lands in the center of the target, even when the archer is far away.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus erring, from Old English and Middle English err, from Latin errare, meaning to wander or go astray.
common_mistakes: Using unerring for a single lucky result; it describes consistent reliability, not one success.
Pronouncing the ER as UR-ing without the American r sound.

senses.definition: Not finished.
senses.example: unfinished business

senses.definition: Not completed; unresolved.
senses.example: unfinished business

senses.definition: Not having had any finish or finishing (such as coating or polishing) applied.
senses.example: unfinished furniture

senses.definition: Not having had any finish carpentry and other finishing (such as painting) applied.
senses.example: unfinished basement

core.definition: Not completed or finished; still in progress, unresolved, or lacking a final coat of finish.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FIN, and reduce the second syllable to a quick 'ih'. The final -ed is silent and sounds like a t, so say 'finisht', not 'finished' with a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a state of incompleteness and can sound slightly negative when a project seems stalled.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unfinished for projects, tasks, business, and conversations: 'unfinished business' or 'an unfinished draft'. In casual speech, 'unfinished business' often means a problem or argument that is still unresolved between people. For furniture or wood, it can describe a surface that has not been stained or sealed.

distinctions.note: Incomplete is more neutral and factual, often used for forms or data; unfinished suggests work that someone meant to finish but has not yet.
Half-done is informal and casual, suggesting something partly done in a rough way; unfinished is standard and can describe a finished-looking work that was never completed.

examples.everyday: We still have some unfinished business from last weekend, so let's talk tonight.
examples.professional: The migration is still unfinished, so the legacy database needs to stay online until the last tables move.
examples.analytical: Her theory is powerful but unfinished, leaving unresolved the problem of how concepts acquire meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a sentence that trails off without its last word, an unfinished task hangs in the air until someone completes it.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus finished, from finish, from Latin finire 'to end', from finis 'end'.
common_mistakes: Confusing unfinished with unfinishable or unfinishing; unfinished simply means not yet complete.
Saying 'unfinished yet' in casual talk; 'not finished yet' or 'still unfinished' is more natural.

senses.definition: Not able to be impeached or reproached.
senses.example: a gentleman of unimpeachable integrity

senses.definition: Blameless.
senses.example: The judge's record is unimpeachable, with no hint of bias or misconduct.

senses.definition: Beyond doubt.
senses.example: an unimpeachable alibi

core.definition: So honest, reliable or well-founded that nothing can reasonably be doubted or criticized.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PEE, the third syllable. The -tch- is a single sound, and the final syllables are reduced to a soft 'buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it strongly praises someone's honesty, judgment or evidence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unimpeachable in serious writing and speech, such as about a source, a reputation or evidence. It is not used for everyday objects. In casual talk, 'totally reliable' or 'rock solid' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Reliable describes something that works consistently, while unimpeachable describes something so trustworthy that no challenge is possible.
Impeccable means flawless in form or manners, while unimpeachable concerns trustworthiness and credibility.

examples.everyday: My uncle is an unimpeachable mechanic, so I trust his advice on the car.
examples.professional: We need an unimpeachable source for the data before we report it to the board.
examples.analytical: The historian relied on unimpeachable documents, though he acknowledged the gaps in the archive.

nuance.analogy: Unimpeachable evidence is like a clear window: there is nothing to question about what you see through it.
nuance.etymology: From 'impeach' (from Old French 'empecher', to hinder) with 'un-' and '-able'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'impeachable', which means something can be charged with wrongdoing.
Using it for physical objects, where 'flawless' or 'perfect' is more natural.

senses.definition: Not inspiring.
senses.example: The conference keynote was uninspiring, reciting the same metrics we had seen all year.

core.definition: Failing to stimulate or excite enthusiasm; not motivating, exciting or interesting.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SPY, the middle syllable, and the un and in are light. Pronounce the r clearly, and end with /ɪŋ/, not /iŋ/ as in 'sing' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative: it says something fails to motivate, but it is softer than calling it boring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use uninspiring to describe meetings, speeches, places or plans that leave people unmotivated. It is less harsh than 'boring' and common in workplace feedback. To soften it further, say 'not especially inspiring'.

distinctions.note: Uninspiring describes something that fails to motivate people; uninspired describes work or ideas that lack originality.
Dull is plainer and more general, meaning not bright or interesting; uninspiring specifically refers to a lack of motivation or emotion.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the hotel room was clean, but the view of the parking lot was pretty uninspiring.
examples.professional: The quarterly review was accurate, but the slides were so uninspiring that nobody asked follow-up questions.
examples.analytical: A theology that treats doctrine as a set of rules can be uninspiring, even when its arguments are carefully built.

nuance.analogy: An uninspiring talk is like a flashlight with a weak bulb: it is on, but it does not light anything up.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus inspiring; inspire comes from Latin inspirare, 'to breathe into', from in- 'into' plus spirare 'to breathe'.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on the first syllable, 'UN-inspiring', instead of on SPY.
Using uninspiring to describe a person's creativity; for people or their ideas, use uninspired.

senses.definition: Maintenance; the act or effort of keeping something in good and working condition.
senses.example: I would enjoy having a swimming pool, but I don't want to deal with the upkeep.

core.definition: The effort or cost of maintaining something, such as a house, car or yard, in good and working condition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, as in the noun. The second syllable has a long e as in 'keep', and the vowel of 'up' is short and relaxed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but often implies a cost or ongoing burden, so it can sound negative when expensive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use upkeep for homes, yards, cars, equipment and public places, especially when talking about cost. As in 'The upkeep on this old house is steep.' For the verb, people say keep up or maintain, not upkeep.

distinctions.note: Maintenance is more technical and used in professional or engineering contexts, while upkeep is everyday and personal, often about homes or property.
Repair fixes something that is broken, while upkeep is regular care that prevents problems.

examples.everyday: The upkeep on this old house is killing my budget.
examples.professional: Upkeep for the data center cooling systems is budgeted every quarter.
examples.analytical: Cultural institutions depend on sustained upkeep as much as on their original design.

nuance.analogy: Like brushing your teeth every day: the routine work that keeps the original good condition from decaying.
nuance.etymology: From up and keep, from the phrase keep up, meaning to maintain.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, as in 'up keep', when used as a noun.
Using upkeep as a verb, as in 'I upkeep the car'; say 'I keep up the car' or 'I maintain the car'.

core.definition: Jesus' words in Matthew 16:18, 'on this rock I will build my church,' variously understood as referring to Peter, his confession, or Christ.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on ROCK, the last word. 'Upon' has a clear ah vowel in American English, and the final k should be crisp.

nuance.connotation: Solemn and foundational; it suggests a lasting base.
nuance.usage_note: 'Upon' sounds formal and is more common in scripture and sermons than in speech. Americans normally say 'on' in daily talk. The phrase may be quoted as an allusion to a solid foundation.

distinctions.note: 'On' is ordinary American usage; 'upon' is formal or elevated.
Greek Petros is a name for Peter, while petra means a mass of rock, and interpreters debate the link.
A cornerstone is a specific foundational stone; 'rock' here speaks of the whole foundation.

examples.everyday: The preacher read 'upon this rock I will build my church' and then stopped to ask what the rock was.
examples.professional: In tonight's lesson we will examine the three main readings of 'upon this rock'.
examples.analytical: The wordplay between Petros and petra has sustained centuries of debate over whether the rock is Peter, his confession, or Christ.

nuance.analogy: Like a building's foundation that the whole structure depends on.
nuance.etymology: From Matthew 16:18, in which Jesus says Peter is a rock and on this rock he will build his church.
common_mistakes: Using 'upon' in casual speech where 'on' sounds more natural.
Pronouncing 'rock' with a long 'o' instead of 'ah'.
Assuming there is only one accepted interpretation.
nuance.biblical_note: Matthew 16:18 says Jesus calls Simon 'Peter' (Greek Petros) and builds his church on this rock (petra), promising that the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. 1 Corinthians 10:4 calls Christ the spiritual rock. Matthew 7:24-25 contrasts the wise builder on rock with the foolish builder on sand.

traditions.view: Many Fathers take the rock to be Peter's confession of faith, with Peter as its representative, and reject any unique primacy for him and his successors.
The rock is Peter himself as the first pope, a basis for the Petrine office and the primacy of the bishop of Rome.
Most Protestants read the rock as Peter's confession or Christ himself, though some accept that Peter has a foundational role among the apostles. They reject papal primacy.

senses.definition: Maintained, owned, or associated with the original developers of the given software; in contrast to a modified version downstream.
senses.example: The outage was caused by an upstream error in a payments library.

senses.definition: In a direction against the flow of a current or stream of fluid (typically water); upriver.
Occurring earlier than something else; being an influence on something else; causing a consequence for something else.
senses.example: Input entry is upstream of input validation in the runtime process.

senses.definition: Involving exploration and pre-production rather than refining and selling.
In the direction from the client to the server.
Towards the leading end (5′ end) of a DNA molecule.
To have (a software library, patch, etc.) accepted by the original developers of the related software, so that they maintain and distribute it.
senses.example: I'd be more than happy to upstream your patch.

senses.definition: To stream upward.
The original developers or maintainers of software.
Part of the river towards the upstream direction.
Against the current.

core.definition: Toward the source of a river, or at an earlier stage of a process; in software, describing code or a project maintained by the original developers, as opposed to a modified copy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. The 'r' is American, so pronounce it clearly, and the final vowel is a long 'ee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: In American software teams, 'upstream' is used constantly to describe the original project from which your code comes, as in 'send this fix upstream.' In everyday speech it means moving against a river's current. Developers usually say 'upstream' with 'downstream' in the same discussion.
