distinctions.note: 'Downstream' refers to modified copies or later stages, while 'upstream' refers to the origin or earlier stage.
A 'fork' is a copy of a project that is changed separately; 'upstream' is the project the fork came from.

examples.everyday: The river is high, so the fishing boat has to go upstream slowly.
examples.professional: Please send your bug fix upstream so the library maintainers can include it in the next release.
examples.analytical: In open source ethics, contributing changes upstream is often seen as a duty that prevents fragmentation of the codebase.

nuance.analogy: Like a salmon swimming back to the place where it began.
nuance.etymology: From 'up' plus 'stream,' originally describing movement against a current and later used figuratively in software and business.
common_mistakes: Using 'upstream' to mean 'upward' in general, as in climbing a building.
Forgetting that in software it usually refers to the original project rather than a direction.

senses.definition: A walk-in medical facility that provides treatment on a customer basis, typically focusing less serious complaints than would be treated at a hospital.
senses.example: I went to urgent care after spraining my ankle, and I was seen within an hour.

senses.definition: The type of treatment offered at such facilities.
senses.example: Urgent care for my son's ear infection was quick and affordable.

core.definition: A walk-in medical clinic, usually without an appointment, that treats non-life-threatening illnesses and injuries that need prompt attention.

pronunciation.tip: Both words have primary stress, with UR and KAIR carrying the strongest beats. The middle vowel of urgent is a reduced uh sound. The final r in care is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It suggests a convenient, faster alternative to an emergency room for minor problems.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly say 'I went to urgent care' when they have a cold, sprain, minor cut or infection and cannot get a same-day doctor appointment. It is cheaper and faster than an emergency room, but it does not handle life-threatening emergencies, where people should call 911. A natural reply is 'Did they help you?' or 'Did they give you anything?'

distinctions.note: An emergency room treats life-threatening conditions and is open all the time; urgent care handles less serious problems and usually costs less.
Primary care is ongoing care from a regular doctor; urgent care is a one-time walk-in visit for an immediate problem.

examples.everyday: I hurt my ankle on the stairs, so I went to urgent care instead of waiting for my doctor.
examples.professional: Our health plan covers urgent care visits, but employees need to check whether the clinic is in network first.
examples.analytical: The growth of urgent care has changed how Americans think about the boundary between routine illness and hospital-level emergency.

nuance.analogy: Urgent care is like a fire station for minor emergencies: quick, local and walk-in, but not built for the biggest fires.
nuance.etymology: Urgent comes from Latin urgens, 'pressing'; care comes from Old English caru, 'worry' or 'concern.'
common_mistakes: Taking a life-threatening emergency to urgent care instead of calling 911 or going to the emergency room.
Saying 'urgent clinic' or 'urgency care'; the normal American term is urgent care.

conversation.text: I twisted my ankle, so I went to urgent care.
Urgent care is cheaper than the emergency room for small things.
The urgent care down the street is open until nine.

senses.definition: One who uses or makes use of something, a consumer or client or an express or implied licensee (free user) or a trespasser.
senses.example: As a free user, you may access the library's reading room without a card.

senses.definition: A person who uses drugs, especially illegal drugs.
senses.example: Police say the man was a regular user who had overdosed twice.

senses.definition: A person who uses a computer or a computing network, especially a person who has received a user account.
senses.example: The new user account requires a password reset before the first login.

senses.definition: Clipping of username.
senses.example: The forum said my user was taken, so I added numbers to the end.

senses.definition: An exploiter, an abuser (a person who exploits others, that is treats and regards people unfairly, selfishly or unethically).
senses.example: That landlord is a user who preys on tenants who cannot afford lawyers.

senses.definition: (dated) In land law, meaning either 1. or 2. above or use. Usually in singular form to mean use wherever there is assiduous re-use of precedents and aloof textbooks verbatim. (clarification of this definition is needed)
senses.example: Under the old law, his user of the land gave him rights without any title.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A person who uses a product, service, or computer system, especially someone who regularly operates it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the final '-er' is the American rhotic schwa, so the r is pronounced. Do not say 'YOO-zuh' or 'yoo-ZAY.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technology and business. In conversations about drugs, the word refers to illegal drug use and can sound judgmental.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, 'user' is common in tech settings and product talk: 'the app has millions of users.' In casual talk about products, people more often say 'people who use it' or 'customers.' Be careful with the drug sense: 'a user' can imply addiction in news or medical contexts, so use it with care when talking about people.

distinctions.note: A customer buys something, while a user actually operates or uses it, and the two may be different people, such as a company that buys software for its staff.
Consumer emphasizes buying and spending goods, while user emphasizes the act of operating or using a thing.
A client receives a professional service from a lawyer, consultant, or agency, and the term is more formal and relational.

examples.everyday: My phone company says I'm one of their most active users, but I mostly just use it for maps.
examples.professional: Our support team tracks how many new users sign up each week and where they get stuck.
examples.analytical: A theory of technology should ask not only who designed a tool but how real users adapt it to purposes the designers never imagined.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver of a rental car: the company owns the car, but the person behind the wheel is the one who actually uses it.
nuance.etymology: From 'use' (verb) plus the agent suffix '-er'; ultimately from Latin uti, 'to use.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'an user' instead of 'a user.' The word begins with a /j/ consonant sound, so 'a' is correct.
Using 'user' for someone who simply buys something, when 'customer' or 'buyer' is more accurate.

senses.definition: A day when one is permitted to not attend work in order to go on a vacation or attend to other matters.
senses.example: I used a vacation day to attend my daughter's school play on Thursday.

core.definition: A day off from work that you take as paid leave for a trip, rest, or personal errands.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress is on DAY, with a lighter stress on -KAY- in vacation. Say 'shun' for the -tion ending, not 'tee-ohn'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It refers to time off that a worker is entitled to, and people often treat it as a valued benefit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'vacation day' or 'PTO' (paid time off) at work, and many employers combine vacation, sick, and personal days into one PTO bank. To request one, people usually say 'I'd like to take Friday as a vacation day' or ask a manager to approve the time. In casual talk, 'a day off' is more common than 'vacation day'.

distinctions.note: A sick day is time off for illness, and some employers track it separately. A vacation day is planned leisure or personal time.
PTO stands for paid time off and combines vacation, sick, and personal leave in one balance. A vacation day is one specific use of that leave.
A holiday is a public or religious day when many people are off work, such as Christmas. A vacation day is one that an individual chooses or requests.

examples.everyday: I'm taking a vacation day on Friday to get my car serviced.
examples.professional: Can you approve my vacation day request for the fourteenth? I'll be out of the office that afternoon.
examples.analytical: Vacation days are a form of compensation, and their unequal distribution across jobs reveals how leisure is valued in the labor market.

nuance.analogy: A vacation day is like a coin from a savings account of paid time off: you spend it when you need a break.
nuance.etymology: Vacation comes from Latin vacatio, 'freedom from duty,' from vacare, 'to be empty'; day is an Old English word.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am on vacation day' when you mean you are taking one day off. Say 'I'm taking a vacation day' or 'I'm taking Friday off'.
Pronouncing vacation with a broad /ɑ/ like 'vah-KAY-shun'. American speakers use /eɪ/ in the first syllable.

senses.definition: To farewell; to make a valediction or parting gesture.
Valedictorian.

core.definition: To say farewell formally, especially at a graduation or ceremony, by giving a speech or gesture of parting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, VAL. The middle syllable is a reduced 'uh,' and the final -ict is a short 'ikt' sound, not 'eekt.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to formal. It belongs to ceremonial or academic language rather than casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'valedict' as a verb in daily life; they more often use 'valedictory' for the speech and 'valedictorian' for the student who gives it. In conversation, people say 'say goodbye' or 'give a farewell speech.' The word is most natural in writing about graduations or formal occasions.

distinctions.note: Say goodbye is the everyday phrase, while valedict is formal and suggests a planned, ceremonial parting.
Valedictory is an adjective or noun for the speech itself, whereas valedict is the verb for the act of bidding farewell.

examples.everyday: At the dinner, my uncle stood up to valedict his old coworkers before they moved away.
examples.professional: The department chair will valedict the graduating cohort at the Friday ceremony, so please confirm your attendance.
examples.analytical: The poem valedicts the departing lover with a formal dignity that masks a deeper grief.

nuance.analogy: To valedict is like closing a book properly, with a final page that tells the reader how the story ends.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'valedicere,' to say farewell, from 'vale,' be well, and 'dicere,' to say.
common_mistakes: Using 'valedict' in casual conversation, where 'say goodbye' sounds more natural.
Confusing the verb 'valedict' with the noun 'valediction,' which names the farewell itself.

valedict.etymology: From Latin *valedictus*, past participle of *valedīcō*, from Latin *valē* (“farewell”) + Latin *dīcō* (“to speak”).

senses.definition: Having no value; worthless.

core.definition: Having no worth in money, usefulness, or importance; worthless.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VAL, and the ending -less is a short 'liss' with no extra vowel. The middle syllable is a quick 'yoo', not 'lyoo'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it says something has no worth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use valueless more in writing or serious discussion than in casual talk. In speech, worthless is more common and blunter. Valueless can also describe moral emptiness, as in valueless entertainment.

distinctions.note: Worthless is everyday and blunt, used for bad objects or ideas; valueless is more formal and can describe something with no intrinsic or market value.
Valueless means having no worth, while value-free means free of moral judgments; the two are not interchangeable.

examples.everyday: That old phone is basically valueless now, so just recycle it.
examples.professional: Our legacy dashboard is nearly valueless to the new analytics team, so we will retire it next quarter.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that a life devoted only to pleasure is valueless, while hedonists would reject that claim.

nuance.analogy: A valueless coupon is like a ticket to a canceled concert: the paper is still there, but it no longer gets you anything.
nuance.etymology: From value plus the suffix -less, meaning without, from Old English leas.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as valuless; the correct spelling keeps the e: valueless
Using valueless for things that are merely cheap; it means worthless, not inexpensive

senses.definition: A covered motor vehicle used to carry goods or (normally less than ten) persons, usually roughly cuboid in shape, Depending on the type of van, it can be bigger or smaller than a pickup truck and SUV, and longer and higher than a car but relatively smaller than a truck/lorry or a bus.
senses.example: We rented a white van to haul the furniture across town on Saturday.

senses.definition: A large towable vehicle equipped for the repair of structures that cannot easily be moved.
senses.example: The crew hitched a repair van to the collapsed bridge to start the work.

senses.definition: Clipping of vanguard.
senses.example: The van of the army crossed the river before the main force arrived.

senses.definition: A shovel used in cleansing ore.
senses.example: The miner lifted the wet ore with a van and tossed away the waste.

senses.definition: A fan or other contrivance, such as a sieve, for winnowing grain.
senses.example: The farmer tossed the wheat in the van to separate the chaff.

senses.definition: A wing with which the air is beaten.
senses.example: The bird beat its van rapidly as it lifted off the frozen lake.

senses.definition: (dated) A light wagon, either covered or open, used by tradesmen and others for the transportation of goods.
senses.example: The grocer's van rattled down the cobbled lane with fresh bread and eggs.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To transport in a van or similar vehicle (especially of horses).
senses.example: The stable hands vanned the racehorses to the track before dawn.

senses.definition: Of law enforcement: to arrest (not necessarily in a van; derived from party van).
senses.example: The cops vanned him downtown after the bar fight got out of hand.

senses.definition: To wash or cleanse, as a small portion of ore, on a shovel.
senses.example: He vanned the crushed ore on the shovel, rinsing away the lighter dirt.

core.definition: A large enclosed motor vehicle used to carry goods or a group of passengers, such as a cargo van or a minivan.

pronunciation.tip: It is a short, clear vowel like the one in 'man', with the n at the end. Do not add a vowel or make it sound like 'vahn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is purely descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use van for cargo vans, delivery vehicles, moving vans, and family minivans. For a family vehicle with sliding doors, Americans often say minivan. Americans say truck, not lorry, for large freight vehicles. A van can be a good, practical vehicle for moving, camping, or carrying a band's equipment.

distinctions.note: A smaller passenger van with a car-like body, used for families, while van can also mean a large cargo vehicle.
A truck usually has a separate cargo bed or a large open or enclosed trailer, while a van has a fully enclosed body.

examples.everyday: We rented a van to move the couch and the boxes to our new apartment on Saturday.
examples.professional: Our field team takes the cargo van to job sites, so it needs a new set of tires before winter.
examples.analytical: A van blurs the line between the private car and the commercial truck, which is why regulations treat it differently in different countries.

nuance.analogy: A van is a box on wheels, built to hold more people or goods than a car while staying easy to drive.
nuance.etymology: Short for caravan, a term for a covered vehicle.
common_mistakes: Using lorry, which is British, instead of truck.
Saying vahn with a broad vowel instead of the short American vowel in man.

senses.definition: A person who does not eat animal flesh, or, in some cases, use any animal products.
An animal that eats only plants; a herbivore.
senses.example: Elephants are vegetarians, feeding on grasses, leaves, and bark all day long.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the type of diet eaten by vegetarians (in all senses).
senses.example: Her vegetarian diet has helped her manage her cholesterol without giving up cheese.

senses.definition: Without meat.
senses.example: The restaurant's vegetarian chili uses black beans, corn, and peppers instead of beef.

senses.definition: Of a product normally made with meat, having non-meat substitutes in place of meat.
senses.example: Those sausages are vegetarian, made with soy protein instead of pork.

senses.definition: That does not eat meat.
senses.example: I have a vegetarian brother

core.definition: A person who does not eat meat, fish, or poultry, and in some cases avoids all animal products, such as eggs or dairy.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, 'TAIR'. Americans say the 'r' clearly, and the final 'ian' is weak, so avoid saying 'veh-jih-TAIR-ee-AN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a diet choice. Some people find it a label they identify with strongly, so it is best to ask before assuming someone's diet.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I'm vegetarian' or 'Are you vegetarian?' in restaurants and at parties. If someone eats fish but no other meat, Americans may say 'pescatarian' instead. Strict vegans avoid all animal products, so do not call them vegetarians.

distinctions.note: A vegan avoids all animal products, including dairy and eggs, while a vegetarian may still eat them.
A pescatarian eats fish and seafood but no other meat, which a vegetarian does not.

examples.everyday: I'm vegetarian, so could I get the black bean burger instead of the beef one?
examples.professional: Please make sure the catering includes a vegetarian option for the team lunch on Thursday.
examples.analytical: Ethical arguments for vegetarianism often rest on the claim that animals have interests that weigh against killing them for food.

nuance.analogy: A vegetarian's plate is like a team roster that leaves out one position: the rest of the squad still plays, but the menu is filtered by one rule.
nuance.etymology: From vegetarian, coined in English in the 1840s from vegetable, with the suffix -arian meaning a follower of a practice.
common_mistakes: Saying 'vegetarian' for someone who eats fish; the American term is 'pescatarian'.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as 'VEJ-uh-TAIR-ee-un'.

vegetarian.etymology: From *vegetable* + *-arian*; popularized following the foundation of the British Vegetarian Society in 1847.

conversation.text: I'm vegetarian. Is the soup made with chicken broth?
The menu has a whole vegetarian section.
Priya has been vegetarian her whole life.

senses.definition: The moment at which the Sun crosses the celestial equator, appearing to tilt toward the observer, occurring in March in the Northern Hemisphere and in September in the Southern Hemisphere.
senses.example: We planted the garden on the vernal equinox, when days and nights are nearly equal.

core.definition: The moment in March when the sun crosses the celestial equator heading north, marking the start of spring in the Northern Hemisphere.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word lightly and the second word more strongly, with EQUINOX getting the main stress. Say 'equinox' as 'EE-kwih-nahks,' with the final vowel in 'nahks' like the 'o' in 'hot.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a scientific or calendar term, also used in everyday talk about spring starting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in astronomy, weather, and casual talk about the start of spring. Most people say 'the first day of spring' in everyday conversation and reserve 'vernal equinox' for precise or scientific discussion. In the Southern Hemisphere, the same date in September is called the 'spring equinox.'

distinctions.note: The vernal equinox is in March in the Northern Hemisphere and starts spring, while the autumnal equinox is in September and starts fall.
A solstice is when the sun reaches its farthest point north or south, giving the longest or shortest day, while an equinox is when day and night are roughly equal in length.

collocations: celestial equator at the vernal equinox

examples.everyday: We plant the garden on the first warm weekend after the vernal equinox.
examples.professional: The team scheduled the seasonal data refresh for the vernal equinox, since the forecast model depends on solar position.
examples.analytical: Many ancient calendars anchored their year on the vernal equinox, because the sun's position there marked a reliable astronomical event.

nuance.analogy: Like a seesaw balanced perfectly level: day and night sit at equal height for a moment.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vernalis, 'of spring,' from ver, 'spring,' and Latin aequinoctium, from aequus, 'equal,' and nox, 'night.'
common_mistakes: Stressing 'vernal' as 'ver-NAL,' when the stress falls on the first syllable 'VUR.'
Saying 'spring equinox' in a Northern Hemisphere context without realizing that it is the same event as the vernal equinox, but in the Southern Hemisphere it falls in September.

senses.definition: The integrating of successive stages in the production and marketing process under the ownership or control of a single management organization.
senses.example: The oil company's vertical integration let it drill, refine, and sell gasoline under one corporate roof.

core.definition: The control of several successive stages of production or distribution by a single company, such as owning both suppliers and sales outlets.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -GRAY- in integration, and the first word reduces to a light 'vur-tih-kul' with no hard 't' sound between the vowels. Non-native speakers often give every syllable equal weight or stress the -ti- of vertical.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in business settings, but it can sound negative in antitrust debates, where critics warn that a dominant firm controlling several stages may shut out competitors.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in business, economics and law, especially when discussing mergers and antitrust review. It describes a company that owns its suppliers (backward integration) or its distributors (forward integration). In everyday talk, people say 'they own their own farms' or 'they make their own parts' instead.

distinctions.note: Horizontal integration combines competitors at the same stage of production, while vertical integration combines different stages of one supply chain.
A conglomerate combines businesses in unrelated industries, whereas vertical integration links stages that depend on each other.

collocations: vertical integration of the supply chain

examples.everyday: My uncle says that grocery chain owns its own dairy farms, which is a kind of vertical integration.
examples.professional: Our leadership team is evaluating vertical integration as a way to reduce our dependence on outside cloud vendors.
examples.analytical: Vertical integration can lower transaction costs, but it can also raise barriers to entry for rivals that depend on the same supplier.

nuance.analogy: A pizza chain that grows its own wheat, mills its own flour, and runs its own delivery trucks is like a single hand doing every step of the job.
nuance.etymology: Vertical comes from Medieval Latin verticalis, from vertex 'top'; integration comes from Latin integrare 'to make whole'.
common_mistakes: Using vertical integration for any merger; it specifically means combining stages of one supply chain.
Confusing it with horizontal integration, which joins competitors at the same stage.

senses.definition: In a vertical direction or position.
senses.example: This story needs to be read vertically to be understood correctly.

core.definition: In a vertical direction or position; straight up and down, or at a right angle to the horizon.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the -cally ending reduces to 'kuh-lee'. Non-native speakers often pronounce the full 'ka-lee' or drop the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain, descriptive term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'vertically' with verbs like move, stack, align, scroll and split, both in everyday talk and in technical writing. In casual speech, people often say 'straight up' or 'up and down' instead. The informal use of 'vertical' as an adverb ('it went vertical') is common in sports and news, but 'vertically' is safer in writing.

distinctions.note: Upright describes the position of a thing standing straight, while vertically describes the direction of movement or arrangement.
Straight up is informal and conversational, while vertically is more precise and common in writing.

examples.everyday: Can you stack those boxes vertically so they fit in the closet?
examples.professional: Please set the chart to scroll vertically so the whole report fits on one screen.
examples.analytical: In this setup, the light waves oscillate vertically, which is why the filter blocks them.

nuance.analogy: Stacking pancakes on a plate arranges them vertically, one on top of the other.
nuance.etymology: Vertically is formed from vertical, from Medieval Latin verticalis, from vertex 'top', with the suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Dropping the -al- in the spelling and writing 'verticly'.
Pronouncing the full 'ka-lee' ending instead of the reduced 'kuh-lee'.

senses.definition: The act of vibrating or the condition of being vibrated.
senses.example: I could feel the vibration of the subway train through the soles of my shoes.

senses.definition: A single complete vibrating motion.
senses.example: The engineer counted each vibration on the oscilloscope to measure the frequency.

senses.definition: A vibrational energy of spiritual nature through which mediumistic and other paranormal phenomena are conveyed or affected.
senses.example: The medium claimed the séance room held a lingering vibration of grief from the house's former owner.

senses.definition: An instinctively sensed emotional aura or atmosphere.
senses.example: Something about the quiet office gave me a tense vibration that I couldn't shake.

senses.definition: Any periodic process, especially a rapid linear motion of a body about an equilibrium position.
senses.example: A pendulum's vibration slows over time as friction and air resistance drain its energy.

core.definition: A rapid back-and-forth shaking movement, or a quiver felt in an object or body.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'BRAY', and make the 'shun' ending soft and reduced. Don't stress the first syllable, which is the most common mistake.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical and everyday use. In casual speech, 'good vibrations' or 'good vibes' can be positive, but the spiritual sense is esoteric.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'vibration' in everyday talk about a phone buzzing, a car engine shaking, or the bass from a speaker, and in engineering or physics. In ordinary conversation, 'buzz' or 'shake' might be more natural. The spiritual sense, a subtle energy, is found in New Age circles and is not a standard meaning in science or theology.

distinctions.note: 'Oscillation' is repeated motion back and forth around a center point, often used technically, while 'vibration' is the rapid shaking of a body or structure.
'Tremor' usually refers to an involuntary shaking of a person or the ground, while 'vibration' is more general and often mechanical.

examples.everyday: I can feel the vibration of the bass from the car next door.
examples.professional: The team flagged excessive vibration in the server rack fans during the load test.
examples.analytical: The poem's language moves through sound and sense together, so its meaning resists a single fixed vibration.

nuance.analogy: A vibration is like a guitar string after it is plucked: it shakes quickly back and forth until the energy fades.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'vibrationem', from 'vibrare', to shake or quiver.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable: 'VY-bray-shun' is wrong.
Using 'vibration' where 'buzz' or 'shake' is more natural in casual conversation.

vibration.etymology: From French *vibration*, from Latin *vibrātiō* (“a shaking or brandishing”), from *vibrō* (“shake, vibrate”); see *vibrate*.

senses.definition: To fight for superiority; to contend; to compete eagerly so as to gain something.
senses.example: Her suitors were all vying for her attention.

senses.definition: To do or produce in emulation, competition, or rivalry; to put in competition; to bandy.
senses.example: The two brothers vied for their father's attention by trying to outdo each other in everything.

senses.definition: To stake; to wager.
senses.example: Old Tom would vie his last dollar on any hand of cards at the county fair.

senses.definition: To stake a sum of money upon a hand of cards, as in the old game of gleek. See revie.
senses.example: In the old tavern, the players would vie a shilling on every hand of gleek.

core.definition: To compete eagerly with others to win or gain something, such as attention, power or a position.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long 'i' like 'eye'. Do not pronounce it like 'vee' or 'vy-eh'. Say it crisply, and do not add a final sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests strong, eager competition, sometimes unfair.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use vie most often in the phrase 'vie for', as in 'vie for a promotion' or 'vie for attention'. It appears in news, business and sports writing. In everyday talk people more often say 'compete' or 'fight for', so 'vie' sounds slightly formal.

distinctions.note: Compete is the everyday word and can describe organized contests; vie stresses eager rivalry for something prized.
Contend is more formal and often suggests argument or struggle; vie is closer to competing for a prize.

examples.everyday: Our two kids always vie for Grandma's attention when we visit.
examples.professional: Three vendors are vying for the contract, so the decision will come next week.
examples.analytical: Political parties vie for legitimacy in the public mind, and their claims often rest on competing visions of justice.

nuance.analogy: To vie is like runners crowding for the same finish line, each pushing to be first.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English vien, from Old French envier, 'to challenge', from Latin invitare, 'to invite'.
common_mistakes: Using 'vie' without a preposition; say 'vie for', not just 'vie the prize'.
Pronouncing it 'vee' or 'vye-ay' instead of a single syllable 'vye'.

vie.etymology: from Middle English *envien*, from Old French *envier*, from Latin *invītō*.

senses.definition: Physically strong and active.
senses.example: a vigorous scrub

senses.definition: Mentally strong and active.
Rapid of growth.
senses.example: a vigorous shrub

core.definition: Full of physical or mental energy; strong, active, and forceful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, and the r is pronounced in American speech. Avoid saying 'vi-GOR-us,' which stresses the wrong syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests strength, health, and enthusiasm, though it can sometimes suggest excessive forcefulness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use vigorous for exercise, debate, growth, or discussion, such as 'a vigorous debate.' In casual speech, 'intense' or 'strong' might be used instead. It sounds natural in both spoken and written American English.

distinctions.note: Energetic describes a person's natural liveliness; vigorous often describes a particular action or effort that is forceful.
Intense stresses strong feeling or concentration; vigorous stresses physical or mental activity and force.

examples.everyday: We went for a vigorous walk up the hill before dinner.
examples.professional: The board had a vigorous discussion about the budget before approving the plan.
examples.analytical: A vigorous defense of free speech requires that we tolerate arguments we find deeply mistaken.

nuance.analogy: A vigorous plant pushes out new leaves quickly, showing health and force.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin vigorosus, 'full of vigor,' from Latin vigor.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (vi-GOR-us) instead of the first.
Dropping the middle syllable so it sounds like 'VIG-russ.'

vigorous.etymology: From Anglo-Norman *vigrus*, from Old French *vigoros* (whence French *vigoureux*), from Medieval Latin *vigōrōsus*, from Latin *vigor*.

senses.definition: By means of sight.
senses.example: The radar's detection was confirmed visually, because seeing is believing.

core.definition: In a way that relates to sight or how something looks; in terms of what can be seen.

pronunciation.tip: The correct General American pronunciation has a zh sound and a weak middle syllable, so say VIZH-oo-uh-lee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive word and rarely carries emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use visually in everyday speech and at work, often in phrases such as visually appealing or visually impaired. In casual talk, people often say it looks or in terms of how it looks. It is common when describing design, art or products.

distinctions.note: Visibly means noticeably, in a way others can clearly see; visually refers to the sense of sight or to how something appears.
Aesthetically concerns beauty and design in general, while visually is more literal about what the eye takes in.

examples.everyday: Visually, the new couch matches the rug, so it looks great in the room.
examples.professional: Visually, the new dashboard is cleaner, but the numbers still need the same careful checks.
examples.analytical: The painting works visually before it works intellectually, so its first impact is perceptual.

nuance.analogy: Visually is like the first glance at a menu: before you read a word, the layout has already shaped your choice.
nuance.etymology: From visual, plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using visually to mean obviously or clearly in a general sense, as in It is visually a problem; say it is clearly a problem.
Pronouncing the middle syllables as separate strong sounds, such as VIZ-yoo-al-ly.

senses.definition: To spoil, make faulty; to reduce the value, quality, or effectiveness of something.
senses.example: Careless sampling procedures can vitiate the results of even the most carefully designed experiment.

senses.definition: To debase or morally corrupt.
senses.example: Years of unchecked power had vitiated the young king, turning his generosity into cruelty.

senses.definition: To make something ineffective, to invalidate.
senses.example: A single forged signature can vitiate the entire contract, making it unenforceable in court.

core.definition: To weaken or spoil something so that it loses its value, effectiveness or validity.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ti' is pronounced 'sh', as in 'vish'. The final syllable rhymes with 'eight', so say 'ayt' clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes something being damaged or undermined.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use vitiate in formal writing, legal arguments and literary criticism. It is more common in print than in speech. In everyday conversation people say ruin, spoil or undermine. Use it precisely, since it often refers to abstract things like arguments or agreements.

distinctions.note: Ruin is blunt and everyday, while vitiate is formal and often implies weakening something from within.
Undermine means gradually weakening support, while vitiate often means making something faulty or invalid.

examples.everyday: That one rude comment really vitiated the fun of the whole dinner.
examples.professional: The biased sample could vitiate our conclusions, so we need to rerun the survey with random selection.
examples.analytical: A premise based on equivocation vitiates the whole argument, however elegant its structure.

nuance.analogy: To vitiate something is like pouring a drop of ink into clean water, slowly clouding and spoiling it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vitiatus, past participle of vitiare, 'to spoil,' from vitium, 'fault.'
common_mistakes: Confusing vitiate with vitalize, which means to give life or energy.
Using vitiate for a physical object without a sense of damaged quality.

vitiate.etymology: From Latin *vitiātus*, the perfect passive participle of *vitiō* (“damage, spoil”), from *vitium* (“vice”).

senses.definition: The art, occupation, or performance of a voice actor.
senses.example: She built a career in voice acting, mostly narrating audiobooks and cartoon characters.

core.definition: The work of performing a character's lines with your voice only, in animation, video games, audiobooks, or commercials.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on ACT, with a lighter stress on VOICE. The t in acting is a clear stop before ing, not a flap, so do not say 'AK-ting' with a soft d sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a skilled, creative profession, though many people undervalue how demanding it is.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say voice acting for the job or art of voicing characters, and say voice actor for the person. It is common in conversations about TV, movies, games and anime. People often ask 'Do you do any voice acting?' when they meet someone in the entertainment industry.

distinctions.note: Voice-over is narration or off-screen speech, often without a visible character. Voice acting usually means playing a character.
Dubbing replaces the dialogue of a film or show with another language. Voice acting can be done in any language, including original-language productions.
Acting in general includes on-screen performance with body and face. Voice acting uses only the voice.

examples.everyday: My brother got a voice acting gig for a cartoon, so now we hear him on TV every Saturday.
examples.professional: Our studio hires experienced voice acting talent for the game, then records the lines in several takes.
examples.analytical: Voice acting raises questions about authorship, since a single performance can give a character its whole emotional identity.

nuance.analogy: Voice acting is like a stage actor whose only prop is the sound of their voice, so every breath and pause carries the character.
nuance.etymology: Voice from Latin vox 'sound'; acting from Latin agere 'to do', through English act 'to perform'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'voice actor work' for the art itself; the usual phrase is voice acting or 'I do voice work'.
Stressing voice and acting equally, which makes the phrase sound flat; ACT should be the strongest beat.

senses.definition: An easy victory; a walkaway.
A horse race with only one entrant.
senses.example: Her horse won the Saturday stakes as a walkover after every rival scratched that morning.

senses.definition: Someone who does not stand up for themselves when mistreated; a doormat.
senses.example: Everyone at the office knew he was a walkover, so the manager kept piling on extra work.

senses.definition: A backbend combined with a handstand.
senses.example: In the warm-up, she practiced a walkover backbend into a handstand before her floor routine.

senses.definition: A match whose winner is declared because the other boxer does not appear in the ring within one minute of the official time.
senses.example: The referee awarded the walkover after the challenger failed to appear in the ring within a minute.

senses.definition: A type of railroad passenger car seat, having reversible seat backs that can be moved across the seat to face either direction of travel.
senses.example: The train's walkover seats are turned by the crew.

senses.definition: An ecological survey carried out by walking across and examining a piece of land.
senses.example: Before building the trail, the ecologists conducted a walkover survey of the meadow, noting every plant and animal sign.

senses.definition: A bye or victory awarded to a competitor when a scheduled opponent fails to play a game.
senses.example: Our team advanced to the semifinals by walkover when the other school could not field a team.

senses.definition: Someone easy to defeat.

core.definition: An easy victory in which the opponent offers little or no real competition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, WALK. The l in the spelling is silent, so do not insert it, and the final -er is a reduced r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive for the winner, negative for the loser. It suggests the winner dominated without effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use walkover for an easy win in sports, politics, business or school competitions. Saying it of a game implies the other side barely competed, which can sound unkind toward them. In everyday speech Americans sometimes say it is a cakewalk or a blowout instead.

distinctions.note: A landslide is a decisive victory in an election, usually by a large margin of votes, while a walkover suggests the opponent barely resisted.
A blowout is a game or match won by a large score, while a walkover implies the loser did not really compete.
A pushover is a person who is easily persuaded or taken advantage of, a sense of walkover that is more common in American speech.

collocations: a walkover in the first round

examples.everyday: Last night's game was a walkover, since we won ten to zero and the other team barely showed up.
examples.professional: The sales team won the pitch so easily that it felt like a walkover, and leadership wants to know why the competitor did not put up a fight.
examples.analytical: In political or moral contests, a walkover tends to reveal the weakness of the defeated party more than the strength of the winner.

nuance.analogy: Like a path with no obstacles, where you simply walk to the finish line.
nuance.etymology: From the phrase walk over, meaning to cross a course without opposition, formed from walk and over.
common_mistakes: Writing walk over as one word in the noun sense; the noun is walkover, but the verb is two words.
Using walkover when the opponent really competed well; it means the win was easy.

senses.definition: A large retail store holding a wide selection of goods for sale at discounted prices to members of the club.
The club itself.
senses.example: We joined the warehouse club so we could buy paper towels in bulk every month.

core.definition: A large discount store where members pay a fee to buy goods in bulk at low prices.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'WARE' in the first word, with a lighter stress on 'club.' Keep the final s in 'warehouse' as a clear s, not a z, and keep 'club' short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Shoppers often see it as a way to save money, though some find the membership fee or bulk quantities inconvenient.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say warehouse club for large membership stores such as Costco, Sam's Club, and BJ's Wholesale Club. You usually need a membership card to shop there. The phrase can also refer to the company or the club itself. People often shorten it to 'the club' in casual speech, for example 'Let's pick up paper towels at the club.'

distinctions.note: A discount store generally sells at low prices without requiring membership, while a warehouse club requires a paid membership and sells in bulk.
A supermarket sells mainly groceries in regular package sizes, while a warehouse club sells groceries and many other goods in large quantities.

collocations: buy in bulk at a warehouse club

examples.everyday: Let's stop at the warehouse club on the way home, since we are almost out of paper towels.
examples.professional: Our purchasing team compared prices at two warehouse clubs before approving the bulk order.
examples.analytical: The warehouse club model depends on membership fees that subsidize thin retail margins, which changes how retailers compete on price.

nuance.analogy: A warehouse club is like a members-only bulk pantry: you pay a small fee for the right to buy in big quantities.
nuance.etymology: Warehouse comes from ware plus house; club comes from Old Norse klubba, meaning a heavy stick or cudgel, later a group of people.
common_mistakes: Using warehouse club for any discount store, when the term specifically means a membership-based bulk retailer.
Using the wrong preposition, saying 'in the warehouse club' when Americans often say 'at the warehouse club.'

senses.definition: Be careful about what and how much you eat, usually for health.

core.definition: To be careful about what and how much you eat, usually to stay healthy or control your weight.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EAT, and 'watch' has secondary stress. Reduce 'what you' to 'wuht yuh' or 'wuht yoo' in fast speech. Link 'watch what' so it sounds like 'wah-CHUH-wuht'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly cautionary. It can be a helpful health tip or a mild criticism of someone's diet.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when they mean to limit sugar, fat or calories, often because of a doctor's advice or a health goal. It can sound judgmental if said to someone who has not asked for advice. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I'm trying to' or 'I know, I'm working on it'.

distinctions.note: A diet is a planned eating pattern, often with a goal. 'Watch what you eat' is a general caution rather than a formal plan.
'Eat healthy' describes a positive choice of foods. 'Watch what you eat' suggests limiting or avoiding some foods.

collocations: have to watch what you eat
watch what you eat for your heart

examples.everyday: My doctor said I have to watch what I eat, so no more fried food for me.
examples.professional: At the offsite lunch, I'm going to watch what I eat because I'm trying to lose some weight.
examples.analytical: Public health campaigns often urge people to watch what they eat, although this advice can overlook food access and cost.

nuance.analogy: Watching what you eat is like checking your bank balance before shopping: you keep track so you do not overspend your health.
nuance.etymology: From 'watch' (Old English wæccan) and 'eat' (Old English etan), used idiomatically in American English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'watch your eat' instead of 'watch what you eat'.
Using it as a question about food safety; it is usually about health or weight.

conversation.text: My doctor said, "At your age, you really have to watch what you eat."
If you want to lose weight, you have to watch what you eat.
Are you still watching what you eat, or should I order dessert for two?

senses.definition: A group activity in a crowd imitating a wave going through water, where people in successive parts of the crowd stand and stretch upward, then sit.
senses.example: At the rock concert, the crowd started a wave that circled the stadium twice.

senses.definition: A moving disturbance in the level of a body of liquid; an undulation.
senses.example: The wave traveled from the center of the lake before breaking on the shore.

senses.definition: A shape that alternatingly curves in opposite directions.
senses.example: Her hair had a nice wave to it.

senses.definition: Any of a number of species of moths in the geometrid subfamily Sterrhinae, which have wavy markings on the wings.
senses.example: The entomology class caught a wave on the porch light and pinned its wings for study.

senses.definition: A loose back-and-forth movement, as of the hands.
senses.example: He dismissed her with a wave of the hand.

senses.definition: A sudden, but temporary, uptick in something.
senses.example: A wave of shoppers stampeded through the door when the store opened for its Christmas discount special.

senses.definition: Any of a series of orders to be fulfilled in one short interval of time, planned as part of wave picking.
senses.example: The warehouse split the afternoon orders into three waves to speed up picking.

senses.definition: A movement or trend in popular culture.
senses.example: New Wave

senses.definition: One of the successive swarms of enemies sent to attack the player in certain games.
senses.example: On the hardest level, the third wave of alien ships nearly overwhelmed my defenses.

senses.definition: A moving disturbance in the energy level of a field.
senses.example: Gravity waves, while predicted by theory for decades, have been notoriously difficult to detect.

senses.definition: (poetic) The ocean.
senses.example: The old hymn spoke of the wave that carries our sorrows out to sea.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: To move one's hand back and forth (generally above the shoulders) in greeting or departure.
To call attention to, or give a direction or command to, by a waving motion, as of the hand; to signify by waving; to beckon; to signal; to indicate.
senses.example: I waved goodbye from across the room.

senses.definition: To move back and forth repeatedly and somewhat loosely.
senses.example: The flag waved in the gentle breeze.

senses.definition: To have an undulating or wavy form.
senses.example: The wheat in the field waves gently when the summer breeze blows across it.

senses.definition: To raise into inequalities of surface; to give an undulating form or surface to.
senses.example: Frost and heat over the decades had waved the old tin roof into uneven ridges.

senses.definition: To style (the hair) so as to produce a wavy texture.
senses.example: She waves her hair every morning so the curls look soft and natural.

senses.definition: To cause to move back and forth repeatedly.
senses.example: The starter waved the flag to begin the race.

senses.definition: To signal (someone or something) with a waving movement.
senses.example: The usher waved the late guests toward the empty seats near the back.

senses.definition: To move like a wave, or by floating; to waft.
senses.example: Silk scarves waved in the breeze above the market stalls all afternoon.

senses.definition: To generate a wave.
senses.example: The plucked string waves outward, carrying energy that reaches the listener's ear.

senses.definition: To swing and miss at a pitch.
senses.example: Jones waves at strike one.

core.definition: To move your hand back and forth, usually above the shoulder, to greet someone or say goodbye.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a diphthong that glides from /eɪ/ to /v/, so do not add a vowel after the a sound. Many learners say 'wave' with a short e, so keep the long A clearly.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Waving is a friendly, warm gesture, though a wave can also be a dismissive brush-off, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans wave to people they know across a street, from a car, or at the start of a visit or goodbye. You can say 'wave at someone' or 'wave to someone,' and 'wave hi' or 'wave bye' is casual and common with children. A natural reply is simply to wave back or say 'hey!'

distinctions.note: Waive means to voluntarily give up a right or claim, as in 'waive the fee,' and it is a different word despite the same sound.
To flag someone down means to signal a driver or taxi to stop, which is more deliberate than a casual wave.

examples.everyday: When my neighbor drove by, she waved at me from her car.
examples.professional: Could you wave at the camera when you join the video call so the team knows you're here?
examples.analytical: In the ethnography, the researcher notes that a simple wave signals acknowledgment and belonging among residents.

nuance.analogy: A wave of the hand is like a short hello sent through the air.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wafian, to wave or move to and fro.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'wave' with 'waive,' which means to give up a right.
Saying 'wave to me' without understanding that 'wave at me' is equally natural in American English.

conversation.text: That wave totally knocked me over!
The waves are huge today, so the surfers are all out.
She gave us a wave from the lifeguard stand.

senses.definition: The condition of being weak.
senses.example: In a small number of horses, muscle weakness may progress to paralysis.

senses.definition: An inadequate quality; fault.
senses.example: His inability to speak in front of an audience was his weakness.

senses.definition: A special fondness or obsessing desire.
senses.example: She is an athlete who has a weakness for chocolate.

core.definition: The condition of being weak; also a flaw, or a strong, hard-to-resist fondness for something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and use a short i in the final syllable, as in 'bit'. Do not add an extra vowel between the k and the n.

nuance.connotation: Negative in general, but the 'weakness for' sense is light and often affectionate, as when admitting a love of sweets.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, 'a weakness for' something is a playful admission, as in 'I have a weakness for cheesecake.' Calling something a weakness in a performance review or politics is more pointed. Admitting a weakness in a job interview is common when you also explain how you are improving.

distinctions.note: A weak point names a specific area; weakness can be a general state, a flaw, or a fondness.
A flaw is a defect or imperfection; weakness can also mean a fondness, and it sounds less harsh than flaw.

examples.everyday: I have a weakness for cheesecake, so don't ask me to order dessert.
examples.professional: In the interview I named my weakness as delegation and explained what I am doing about it.
examples.analytical: Paul turns the apparent weakness of the cross into the place where divine power becomes visible to believers.

nuance.analogy: Like a crack in a dam: most of the wall holds, but the water finds that one spot.
nuance.etymology: From 'weak' plus the suffix '-ness', from Old English wāc and the noun-forming suffix -nes.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a weakness of chocolate' or 'weakness to chocolate'; the natural phrase is 'a weakness for chocolate'.
Pronouncing it with a long e in the last syllable; the ending is a short 'nis'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is astheneia (ἀσθένεια), meaning lack of strength, infirmity, or frailty. Paul often treats weakness as the place where God's power becomes visible. 1 Corinthians 1:25 says the weakness of God is stronger than human strength. 2 Corinthians 12:9 records God's answer to Paul that his power is made perfect in weakness. Romans 8:26 says the Spirit helps us in our weakness, even when we do not know how to pray.

senses.definition: A person's or a group's conception, philosophy or view of the world; a worldview.
senses.example: Your background and experiences must give you a unique weltanschauung.

core.definition: A person's or group's overall philosophy or view of the world, including its basic assumptions about life and meaning.

pronunciation.tip: The initial W is pronounced as a V, as in German, and the stress falls on the first syllable with a lighter secondary stress on the second. Americans often say the final -ung as a plain 'ng', so don't add an extra g sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a worldview without judging it, though it signals an intellectual or academic register.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in philosophy, religion, literature and social science, not in casual talk. You might hear it in a seminar or when discussing a writer's outlook. In everyday speech, 'worldview' or 'outlook on life' is the natural choice. A common reply is simply to ask what the person means by it.

distinctions.note: Worldview is the everyday American equivalent and is far more common. Weltanschauung sounds academic and often refers to a systematic philosophical outlook.
Ideology implies a political or social program and often a set of beliefs one defends. Weltanschauung is broader and covers a general way of seeing reality.

examples.everyday: My brother's whole weltanschauung changed after he moved to Japan.
examples.professional: Our product team has a very different weltanschauung from the marketing team, so we keep talking past each other in meetings.
examples.analytical: Kant's critical philosophy challenges any single weltanschauung that claims to grasp reality without first examining the limits of human reason.

nuance.analogy: A weltanschauung is like a pair of tinted glasses that colors everything you see, so that you rarely notice the lenses themselves.
nuance.etymology: From German Welt (world) and Anschauung (view, perception).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the initial W as a W instead of a V.
Using it in casual conversation where 'worldview' sounds more natural.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'weltan-SHOWNG'.

senses.definition: The breast portion of poultry.
Meats whose color, either before or after cooking, is considered white as opposed to red, including poultry, seafood, and pork in some uses.
senses.example: Turkey breast is white meat, while the dark thigh meat has more fat.

senses.definition: (historical) Dairy produce (occasionally including eggs).
senses.example: In the old cookbook, white meat referred to milk, cream, butter, and cheese.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Pale meat from poultry, especially the breast of chicken or turkey, as opposed to darker meat from the legs and thighs.

pronunciation.tip: 'Meat' has a long e, so it rhymes with 'street' and 'sweet,' not 'met.' Keep the t sound crisp at the end, and don't let the two words run together into 'wite-meet.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Americans often see white meat as leaner and healthier, though this is a dietary claim, not a precise category.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'white meat' almost always meaning chicken or turkey breast, and dark meat means the thighs and legs. The phrase 'the other white meat' was a famous pork marketing slogan, so pork can be called white meat in US marketing. At restaurants and grocery counters, people ask for 'white meat' or 'breast meat' when they want leaner chicken.

distinctions.note: Dark meat comes from the legs and thighs, has more fat and iron, and is richer in flavor.
Red meat usually means beef, lamb or pork; in US nutrition talk, it is contrasted with poultry and fish.
Lean meat describes low fat content, not color, so a lean cut of beef is still red meat.

collocations: the white meat of a chicken

examples.everyday: Could you cut me a piece of the white meat? I'm trying to eat less fat tonight.
examples.professional: The catering order specifies white meat for the lunch line, so we need enough chicken breasts for about two hundred guests.
examples.analytical: Nutrition studies often describe white meat as leaner than dark meat, although the difference depends on the cut and how it is cooked.

nuance.analogy: Like the difference between a lighter and darker wood grain: the color comes from the muscle's use and its fat and iron content.
nuance.etymology: White from Old English hwīt; meat from Old English mete, meaning food in general.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'meat' like 'met,' which changes the word.
Using 'white meat' for fish; Americans normally say 'fish' or 'seafood' for seafood.

white-meat.etymology: From Middle English *whyte mete*, *wyttemet*, equivalent to *white* + *meat*.

senses.definition: Out of breath.
senses.example: She felt winded from her long run.

core.definition: Out of breath after exertion, unable to breathe easily for a moment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel is short, as in 'win'. It rhymes with 'minded', not with the long i of the verb 'wind'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a lighthearted way to describe temporary tiredness, not a serious condition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say winded after running, climbing stairs or a hard game, and often use 'get winded' or 'a little winded'. It is casual and very common in everyday talk, and you can say it about yourself with a laugh. For real trouble breathing, say 'short of breath' instead.

distinctions.note: Out of breath is a neutral phrase you can use anywhere, while winded is a more casual single-word description of the same state.
Short of breath is a more serious term for trouble breathing, while winded is usually temporary and lighthearted.

examples.everyday: I jogged to the bus stop and got winded before I even reached the corner.
examples.professional: After the stand-up I was winded from running up to the fourth floor for the demo.
examples.analytical: The word winded keeps the older idea of breath as wind, a link that makes physical exhaustion sound like a momentary loss of spirit.

nuance.analogy: Like a sail that suddenly goes slack, a winded person loses the breath that was driving them forward.
nuance.etymology: From the noun wind in its older sense of breath, which goes back to Old English wind, moving air.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with the long i of the verb wind, which is a different word.
Using winded for serious breathing problems, where short of breath is more appropriate.

senses.definition: A desire, hope, or longing for something or for something to happen.
senses.example: make someone's wish come true

senses.definition: An expression of such a desire, often connected with ideas of magic and supernatural power.
senses.example: make a wish

senses.definition: The thing desired or longed for.
senses.example: My dearest wish is to see them happily married.

senses.definition: A water meadow.
senses.example: The cows grazed quietly in the wish beside the river all afternoon.

senses.definition: To desire; to want.
senses.example: I'll come tomorrow, if you wish (it).

senses.definition: To hope (+ object clause with may or in present subjunctive).
senses.example: I wish the rain may hold off until the parade ends.

senses.definition: To hope (for a particular outcome), even if that outcome is unlikely to occur or cannot occur.
senses.example: I wish I could go back in time and teach myself what I know now.

senses.definition: To bestow (a thought or gesture) towards (someone or something).
senses.example: We wish you a merry Christmas.

senses.definition: To request or desire to do an activity.
senses.example: Anyone who wishes to may leave now.

senses.definition: To recommend; to seek confidence or favor on behalf of.
senses.example: She wished the young analyst to the hiring committee, praising his statistical skills.

core.definition: To want something that is not true or not possible now, or to hope that something will happen.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short i as in 'sit' and end with a clear sh sound. Do not stretch the vowel into 'weesh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it expresses longing, often with regret when it concerns something impossible.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, 'I wish' often expresses regret about something you cannot change, as in 'I wish I had called you.' Americans use 'I hope' for realistic future hopes and 'I wish' for unlikely or unreal ones. For polite requests, 'I'd like' is more natural than 'I wish'.

distinctions.note: Hope usually concerns a realistic possibility; wish often concerns something unlikely or impossible.
Want is a plain desire; wish is softer and often takes the past or subjunctive, as in 'I wish I were'.
Would like is the polite request form; wish sounds more formal or emotional in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: I wish I could come to your party, but I'm working late that night.
examples.professional: I wish we had more time to test the model before the release, but the deadline is fixed.
examples.analytical: Philosophers distinguish wishing for an outcome from believing it will occur, since we can wish for things we know are impossible.

nuance.analogy: A wish is like a ticket to a destination you may never reach: you can hold it, but the trip is not guaranteed.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wȳscan, meaning to desire; related to German wünschen.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I wish I would have' for past regret; the standard form is 'I wish I had'
Using 'I wish' for a polite request in speech; 'I'd like' is more natural

wish.etymology: From Middle English *wisshen*, *wischen*, *wuschen*, from Old English *wȳsċan* (“to wish”), from **wunskijan*, from Proto-Germanic **wunskijaną* (“to wish”), from Proto-Indo-European **wenh₁-* (“to wish, love”).

senses.definition: A person (now usually particularly a woman) who uses magical or supernatural powers to influence or predict events, particularly one with malicious motives.
senses.example: The villagers whispered that the old woman was a witch who had cursed their cattle.

senses.definition: A person of any gender who harmfully employs magical power (especially innate rather than ritual)
senses.example: In the novel, the quiet girl turns out to be a witch with dangerous, innate powers.

senses.definition: A person who follows Wicca or similar New Age pagan beliefs.
senses.example: She joined a local circle and openly calls herself a witch after years of practicing Wicca.

senses.definition: An ugly or unpleasant woman.
senses.example: I hate that old witch.

senses.definition: One who exercises more-than-common power of attraction; a charming or bewitching person.
senses.example: Everyone at the party adored her; she was a real witch on the dance floor.

senses.definition: One given to mischief, especially a woman or child.
senses.example: Get back here, you little witch, and give me my phone right now!

senses.definition: A witch of Agnesi (cubic plane curve)
senses.example: In calculus class, we graphed the witch of Agnesi to study its bell-shaped curve.

senses.definition: A storm petrel.
Any of a number of flatfish of species:
Glyptocephalus cynoglossus (witch flounder or Torbay sole), found in the North Atlantic.
senses.example: Fishermen in the North Atlantic often catch the witch flounder in deep, cold water.

senses.definition: Lepidorhombus whiffiagonis (megrim), found in the North Atlantic.
Caulopsetta scapha (syn. Arnoglossus scapha), found near New Zealand.
senses.example: Researchers recorded a specimen of the witch sole in coastal waters near New Zealand.

senses.definition: Any member of the species Araotes lapithis of Indomalayan butterflies, of the family Lycaenidae.
senses.example: Collectors prized the rare witch butterfly, which lives in the forests of Southeast Asia.

senses.definition: A cone of paper which is placed in a vessel of lard or other fat and used as a taper.
senses.example: She lit the paper witch in the lard jar and used it as a taper to light the lamp.

senses.definition: A bitch.
senses.example: Ignore him; he's just a jealous witch who hates everyone else's success.

senses.definition: To dowse for water.
senses.example: My grandfather used a forked hazel branch to witch for water on our farm.

senses.definition: To practice witchcraft.
senses.example: In the old stories, the midwife would witch by moonlight to heal the sick children.

senses.definition: To bewitch.

core.definition: A person, usually a woman, believed to use magic or supernatural power, especially to harm or control others.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short i as in sit, not a long ee. The ch is the same sound as in church, not a k sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative in its traditional sense of a malicious magic user. In modern Wicca and pagan contexts it is neutral or positive, so the context matters a great deal.
nuance.usage_note: Calling a real person a witch is usually an insult in American speech, implying malice or manipulation. In Halloween, fantasy, and pagan contexts it is neutral, as in a costume or a Wiccan practitioner. Many modern practitioners prefer terms like Wiccan or pagan, and warlock is the traditional masculine counterpart, though it is also negative.

distinctions.note: Wizard is usually male and, in fantasy stories, often a benevolent or learned figure, while witch is more often associated with folk magic and sometimes malice.
Sorcerer is more formal and often suggests learned or ancient magic, whereas witch is the common everyday word.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor dressed up as a witch for Halloween, complete with a pointed hat and a green face.
examples.professional: Our senior engineer is a witch with regular expressions, and she can fix the parser in ten minutes.
examples.analytical: Early modern courts often defined a witch by a supposed pact with the devil, a category that made accusation possible without firm evidence.

nuance.analogy: A label that sticks to a person like a spell, and is hard to remove once it is cast.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wicce (feminine) and wicca (masculine), of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using a long i sound as in white, /waɪt/, instead of the short i in /wɪtʃ/.
Using witch for male practitioners; American speakers usually say warlock, wizard, or male witch, depending on the setting.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, the idea of a witch is expressed mainly through the verb kashaph, meaning to practice sorcery or magic, and the word ov, meaning a medium who consults the dead. Exodus 22:18 forbids allowing a sorceress to live, which the RSV renders with its own terms for magical practitioners. Deuteronomy 18:10-12 lists forbidden practices such as divination, sorcery, and consulting the dead, which the Lord sees as abominable. In 1 Samuel 28:7-20, King Saul asks a medium at En-dor to call up the prophet Samuel, a story often popularly called the witch of Endor.

senses.definition: Someone who or something which is harmful or threatening but disguised as something peaceful or pleasant.
senses.example: That friendly new coworker turned out to be a wolf in sheep's clothing, stealing clients for his own firm.

core.definition: A person or thing that seems harmless or friendly but is actually dangerous or hostile.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'WOOLF,' 'SHEEPS,' and 'KLOH' in this phrase. The 'in' is weak, sounding like 'un,' and 'clothing' is 'KLOH-thing' with the 'th' sound as in 'thin.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It warns about hidden danger or deception, often in news, business, or politics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in everyday talk, news, and business settings to warn that someone seems nice but may have bad motives. It works well for a salesperson, a politician, or a company. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I'd be careful with that offer.'

distinctions.note: A hypocrite pretends to have good values they don't live by; a wolf in sheep's clothing deliberately hides dangerous intentions.
A con artist is a criminal who tricks people for money; the idiom is broader and can describe any harmful disguised person or thing.

collocations: a wolf in sheep's clothing scam
disguised as a wolf in sheep's clothing
warn of a wolf in sheep's clothing

examples.everyday: That new neighbor seems friendly, but I'm starting to think he's a wolf in sheep's clothing.
examples.professional: The vendor's proposal looked reasonable, but a closer review showed it was a wolf in sheep's clothing with hidden fees.
examples.analytical: Jesus warns that false prophets come as a wolf in sheep's clothing, so their outward gentleness cannot be trusted.

nuance.analogy: A wolf in sheep's clothing is like a fake friendly sign on a door that hides a trap behind it.
nuance.etymology: From an image in Matthew 7:15 and in fables, where a predator disguises itself among sheep.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'in' or 'sheep's' in casual speech, which makes the idiom less clear.
Using the idiom for an honest person who is just quiet or shy.
nuance.biblical_note: Matthew 7:15 in the Revised Standard Version warns: 'Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.' The Greek words are 'lykoi,' meaning wolves, and 'probaton,' meaning sheep. The passage teaches that religious teachers should be judged by their fruits, not by their outward appearance. The image shows that harmful teaching can look gentle and pious.

wolf-in-sheep's-clothing.etymology: From Matthew 7:15 in the Bible: “Beware of false prophets which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”

senses.definition: A panacea.
senses.example: Her critics called the startup's software a wonder drug that would fix every broken process.

senses.definition: A medication that gives remarkable benefits.
senses.example: The new antibiotic proved to be a wonder drug for patients with resistant infections.

core.definition: A medicine that works remarkably well and seems almost miraculous for a serious condition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DRUG, the strongest word, while wonder keeps a secondary stress and a reduced -er ending. Pronounce the r in drug clearly, and link the words smoothly as 'wun-der-DRUHG.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a treatment or product, but it can be used ironically or as hype when a product is oversold.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wonder drug in everyday talk about medicine and in news about new treatments. It is informal enough for conversation but also appears in health writing. Doctors may be skeptical of the phrase, since few drugs are miracles, so it often signals enthusiasm. A natural reply is to ask what it treats or how well it worked.

distinctions.note: Miracle drug is nearly synonymous and very common; wonder drug is a little less dramatic and sounds slightly more ordinary.
Panacea is a formal word for a cure for everything, while wonder drug refers to a medicine that works remarkably well for a particular problem.

examples.everyday: Honey and lemon tea isn't a wonder drug, but it really helps my sore throat.
examples.professional: The company hopes the new therapy will become a wonder drug for patients with chronic pain.
examples.analytical: Economists warn that treating the internet as a wonder drug for productivity ignores its real costs.

nuance.analogy: A wonder drug is like a master key that opens many locks at once, though in reality few keys are that powerful.
nuance.etymology: Wonder from Old English wundor; drug from Old French drogue, possibly from Dutch droge.
common_mistakes: Using wonder drug for any ordinary medicine; it describes a remarkable or almost miraculous effect.
Saying wonder medicine in American English, where wonder drug or miracle drug is more natural.

core.definition: The personal name of the God of Israel in the Hebrew Bible, the four Hebrew letters rendered LORD in small capitals in the RSV.

pronunciation.tip: Scholars reconstruct the name as Yahweh, with stress on the second syllable. Jews traditionally did not pronounce the name and read Adonai instead.

nuance.connotation: Reverent and sacred. Many Jews regard the name as too holy to pronounce, so speak it with care.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches and seminaries, people say LORD when reading Scripture aloud and Yahweh in scholarly discussion. Do not use the name casually or as an exclamation. In a Bible study, saying YHWH is acceptable when discussing the text.

distinctions.note: A general Hebrew word for God or gods, while YHWH is the personal covenant name of the God of Israel.
Hebrew for my Lord, which readers say in place of YHWH when reading Scripture aloud.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study, the leader explained why the name YHWH is usually translated as LORD.
examples.professional: In the seminar we debated whether Yahweh is the best scholarly reconstruction of YHWH.
examples.analytical: The name YHWH in Exodus 3:14 is commonly connected with the Hebrew verb meaning to be.

nuance.analogy: Like a person's personal name compared with a title such as Doctor, which says what they do rather than who they are.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew root hayah, to be; the four consonants are called the Tetragrammaton, meaning four letters.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the four letters separately as an initialism; it is a name, not an acronym.
Writing LORD in ordinary capitals; the RSV uses small capitals to show it translates the divine name.
nuance.biblical_note: YHWH, Hebrew יהוה, is the personal name God reveals to Moses, connected with the verb hayah, to be. Exodus 3:14-15 has God declare I AM WHO I AM and link that name to his identity as the God of the fathers. Exodus 6:2-3 says God was not known to the patriarchs by this name. Deuteronomy 6:4 is the Shema, which affirms that the LORD is our God and that the LORD is one.

senses.definition: That goes zoom!
Sleek, speedy, streamlined.
senses.example: zoomy but faded paint jobs

senses.definition: Stylish, as a zoomy car, or as someone who looks like they would drive a zoomy car.
Obviously characteristic of a zoom lens.
senses.example: relies upon zoomy close-ups

senses.definition: Evocative of Generation Z, or zoomers.
senses.example: His love of avocado toast is so zoomy.

core.definition: Sleek, fast-looking, and streamlined, usually describing a car, bike, or design that looks speedy.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, 'ZOO.' The final 'y' is pronounced as a long 'ee,' so do not say 'zoo-MY.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and playful. It praises a look of speed and style, though it can sound a little slangy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'zoomy' casually, usually about cars, bikes, or gadgets that look fast and modern. It is informal, so avoid it in formal reports or academic writing. A natural reply is 'Yeah, it looks fast' or 'It really does look zoomy.' It is most common among enthusiasts and in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Sleek is a standard word for smooth and elegant, while zoomy adds the sense of looking fast and energetic and is more playful.
Sporty describes a style or the feel of a sports vehicle, while zoomy focuses on the impression of speed in shape or design.

examples.everyday: That little red Mazda looks so zoomy that I bet it's fast.
examples.professional: The design team wants a zoomy, streamlined look for the new app icon.
examples.analytical: The critic's praise for the film's zoomy editing describes speed more than meaning, which is a revealing choice of words.

nuance.analogy: A zoomy car looks like it is already moving even when parked, like a greyhound standing still.
nuance.etymology: From 'zoom' (imitative of a fast whirring sound) with the adjective suffix '-y.'
common_mistakes: Using 'zoomy' in formal writing where 'streamlined' or 'sleek' would be more appropriate.
Pronouncing it 'zoo-MEE' with stress on the second syllable.
